The Christians, when they wanted to make their children Christians, placed them in water they claimed was a sanctification — like the major ablution among the Muslims — and a dye for them in Christianity. So God said, when they invited His Prophet and the believers, "Be Jews or Christians and be guided": tell them, O Muḥammad, rather follow the creed of Ibrāhīm — the dye of God, which is the best of dyes, for it is the ḥanīf submission — and leave behind the association of others with God and straying from the road of His guidance. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammatical analyses: al-Akhfash and others read *ṣibghat Allāh* as God's religion, standing as a substitute for "creed"; al-Kisāʾī took the accusative with an implied "follow," or as an incitement — "cling to" — while the nominative would also be correct, "it is the dye of God." **[Ṭabarī]** notes the same options: the accusative as a substitute for "creed," the nominative as a fresh sentence, or the accusative connected to the long creed of 2:136 — "say: we believe in God..." — so that the faith itself is the dye of God. And Qatāda's version states the contrast the metaphor draws: the Jews dye their children Jews, the Christians dye theirs Christians, and God's dye is Islam — there is no dye better or purer, for it is the religion of God with which He sent Nūḥ and the prophets after him. **[Jalālayn]** makes the point of the metaphor explicit: the dye leaves its mark on the person as a dye leaves its mark on a garment; and the phrase closes with its fitting seal — "and Him we worship."

**Baptism and the fiṭrah.** **[Maʿārif]** reads the verse as disposing of a Christian ceremony: on the seventh day of an infant's life the Christians bathed it in coloured water, which was supposed to substitute for circumcision and guarantee the child's outward and inward purification — the fast and indelible "colouring" of Christian faith, so to speak. The verse suggests that this colour washes away with the water, leaving no trace within or without, and does not do the work of circumcision or cleanse a person of physical impurity; the only colouring worth the name is that of a genuine and unabrogated religion, that is, Islam — the only colouring that guarantees outward and inward purification and the only one that remains. Then he opens the deeper sense: as a colour is openly and clearly visible to the beholder, so the signs of genuine and pure faith are visible in the one who bears them; and, setting 2:135 beside 2:138, he derives a conclusion about the whole history: Islam — or any authentic religion — is essentially the religion of God, and the association of a religion with the name of a particular prophet can only be symbolic. **[Qurṭubī]** records Mujāhid's reading of *ṣibghah* as the *fiṭrah*, the natural disposition with which God created people, and al-Zajjāj's observation that Mujāhid's view returns to Islam, since the *fiṭrah* is the beginning of creation and the beginning of what human beings were created upon is Islam — which is why he and others also reported from Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Abū al-ʿĀliyyah and Qatāda simply: the dye is the religion. **[Study Quran]** collects the range — the dye of God referring back to the creed of Ibrāhīm in 2:135, or connected to "we believe in God" in 2:136; the *ṣibghah* as the primordial nature human beings bear as cloth bears its original colour, which is the upright religion of 30:30; the Christian baptism, with the verse asserting Islam as the true dyeing of God; purification; God's unchanging wont (17:77; 33:38; 48:23); and God's religion — and observes that these interpretations can be seen as complementary, since God's wont, religion, creed and purification overlap in significance, all brought out by the term's root sense of an original coloration given by God to the fabric of existence.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the practical sense of the metaphor: cling to the dye of God, which is His religion, and stand by it completely — in all its works, outward and inward, and all its doctrines, at every time — until it becomes a dye and a trait among your own traits. And when it becomes a trait of yours, that necessarily brings you to obey His commands willingly, by choice and out of love; the religion becomes a second nature to you, like a complete dye on a cloth, of which it has become a quality. Then the felicity of this world and the next follows, because the religion urges noble character, beautiful deeds and lofty aims. Hence the verse's exclamation, addressed to sound minds as a settled wonder: who is better than God at dyeing? And if you want to see the difference between God's dye and any other, he says, compare a thing with its opposite: look at a servant who believes in his Lord with a sound faith that has left its trace on him — the heart humbled, the limbs submitted — adorning himself with every good quality, beautiful deed, complete character and noble trait, and stripping himself of every ugly quality, vice and defect.

**Reflection.** The verse gives the new community the word it will carry: not a tribe's name, not a founder's label, but a colour. The metaphor does several things at once — it explains why the invitation to "become" something else was refused (one cannot be re-dyed after the dye has taken), it exposes the older rites as washes that leave no trace, and it relocates identity in the substance of a life rather than in a genealogy. **[Maʿārif]**'s observation is the verse's widest reach: if the religion is God's dye, then it was never the property of one prophet's people, and the men who named it after themselves named it after the brush rather than the hand.


## 2:139

*"Say: 'Will you dispute with us concerning God, when He is our Lord and your Lord? And ours are our deeds and yours are your deeds; and we are sincere toward Him.'"*

**Meaning.** The section closes with a question addressed to the claim of advantage [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn]. **[Qurṭubī]** reports what the disputation was: al-Ḥasan said it was their saying, "We are closer to God than you, because we are the sons of God and His beloved"; others, because of the precedence of their fathers and their Books, and because they never worshipped idols. So the sense of the verse is: say to these Jews and Christians who claimed to be God's sons and beloved and to be closer to Him for the antiquity of their ancestors and scriptures — will you argue with us over your claim, when the Lord is one and each is requited for his deed? What weight does the antiquity of a religion carry then? "Concerning God" means concerning His religion, nearness to Him and standing with Him. **[Jalālayn]** notes the interrogative as one of rejection, and reads the clauses that follow as circumstantial qualifiers of the question — the Lord who is ours and yours, the deeds that belong to each, and the sincerity that belongs to us — adding that the last clause, "we are sincere toward Him," means sincere in religion and in deed, unlike you; which is why we are the more worthy to be chosen. **[Ibn Kathīr]** renders the deed-clause as a mutual disavowal: we disown you and what you worship, just as you disown us — with 10:41 in parallel, "for me are my deeds and for you are your deeds; you are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do," and 3:20, "so if they dispute with you, say: I submit my face to God, and so do those who follow me."

**Rulings — the ethics of disputation.** **[Saʿdī]** pauses over the word *muḥājjah*, since the verse opens with a dispute and ought to teach how to conduct one. It is the argumentation between two or more parties over contested questions, each seeking to support his own position and nullify his opponent's, and each striving to establish his proof; what is required of it is that it be conducted in the best manner and by the shortest route that returns the erring to the truth, establishes the proof against the obstinate, clarifies what is right and shows what is false. If it leaves these purposes, it becomes wrangling and quarrelsomeness, in which there is no good and out of which comes whatever evil comes. Then he applies it: the People of the Book claimed to be closer to God than the Muslims, and this is a mere claim needing proof and evidence. Since the Lord of all is one, and He is not Lord to you rather than to us, and each of us has his own deeds — by that reckoning we and you are equals, and equality in a matter cannot make one of the two parties more deserving than the other; to differentiate between two equals without a differentiating cause is an invalid claim and an evident stubbornness. Preference is attained only by sincerity of good deeds to God alone — and that is the description of the believers alone; so it is settled that they are the closer to God, because sincerity is the road to nearness.

**Context.** **[Maʿārif]** reads the verse as closing the section in which the claims of the Jews and Christians have been refuted — their assertion that Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the prophets of his line were Jews or Christians, and their claim to be the chosen people with the exclusive privilege of entering Paradise. The earlier verses established that the religion of all these prophets was Islam in the general sense, that the earlier Sharīʿahs have now been abrogated, and that the title of Islam is now given to the religion of Muḥammad ﷺ. Should the two communities still persist in denial out of stubbornness, God asks His Prophet and the Muslims to declare plainly that God, being the Lord of all, cannot show special favour to any particular group of His creatures, and that on the Day of Judgement He will assess Jews, Christians and Muslims alike by what each believed and how each behaved — a principle the People of the Book themselves accepted. And the Muslims are asked to announce that they recognize no other god but Allah and have purified their religion of every trace of association. **[Study Quran]** adds the possible referents of the dispute: the Jews objected to a prophet coming from outside the Children of Israel, while the idolatrous Arabs thought that if a prophet came he should be a man of higher social status than Muḥammad ﷺ (see 3:26 and 43:31); and it lists the parallel passages on disputation, 10:41, 2:258, 3:20 and 6:80.

**Reflection.** The verse is a compact theory of controversy. It removes the two currencies in which religious quarrels are usually conducted — priority of descent and priority of documents — and leaves one: deeds performed sincerely for God. What is striking is that the verse does not claim the argument away on the Muslims' behalf; it puts both communities on the same footing before the same Lord, and then locates the difference in the last clause, where the claim is not to privilege but to sincerity. **[Saʿdī]**'s remarks on disputation belong beside it: the same verse that opens a dispute also sets the terms on which a dispute is worth having — toward the truth, by the shortest road, and never for the pleasure of winning.

## 2:140

*"Or do you say that Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and the Tribes were Jews or Christians? Say: 'Are you more knowing, or God?' And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God? And God is not heedless of what you do."*

**Meaning.** The claim to the patriarchs is repeated and then demolished by a question [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** reports the two readings — *am taqūlūn*, the address continuing, and *am yaqūlūn*, a fresh question about them — and prefers the reading with the *tāʾ*, so that the sentence is joined to "will you dispute with us concerning God," the sense being: which of these two things do you do — argue with us, or assert that Ibrāhīm and his sons were Jews or Christians? The answer then takes the form of a comparison the opponents cannot win: "are you more knowing, or God?" — for God has told us what they were, and it was neither. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that the verse's force is the same as in 2:135 and 2:139: the claim is asserted without evidence, while revelation has settled the matter. **[Jalālayn]** gives the reply as the verse does: say to them, are you more knowing, or God? — knowing that God has informed us they were ḥanīf Muslims.

**The concealed testimony.** "And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from God?" [Ṭabarī] [Ibn Kathīr]. The testimony is what their Books contain — the description of the Prophet ﷺ, the religion of Ibrāhīm, the truth about the patriarchs — which they knew and suppressed; so that the verse's charge is not error but concealment. **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets it beside the passages in which the People of the Book are said to hide the truth they were given, and notes the closing clause: God is not heedless of what you do — no concealment goes unrecorded. **[Qurṭubī]** reports the grammatical point that in the analogous passages the concealment of a testimony God has given is among the gravest of offences, since it deprives others of what they have a right to know; and the verse's final words answer the assumption that hidden things are safe.

**Reflection.** The verse is a courtroom scene with an unusual witness: not the Muslims, but God — whose testimony has been given, and whose testimony cannot be rebutted. Once the question "are you more knowing, or God?" has been asked, the argument is over; what remains is the second charge, and it is the sharper one: the problem is not that they do not know, but that they have covered up what they know. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s parallel makes the offence concrete — this is the same concealment the Sūrah has already named in 2:146, where they recognize the Prophet as they recognize their own sons — and the closing clause makes it futile: the concealment is invisible to the world, and God is not heedless of it.

## 2:141

*"That is a community that has passed away. Theirs is what they earned, and yours is what you earn; and you will not be asked about what they used to do."*

**Meaning.** The words of 2:134 return to close the section, with the same force [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Ṭabarī]**'s reading of the earlier verse applies here word for word: Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb and their sons are a generation that has gone its way, having emptied itself of the world and become solitary in it; to them belongs what they earned and to you what you earn; and you — the Jews and Christians who have fastened your religions on them — will not be asked about what they used to do, any more than they will be asked about you. **[Jalālayn]** notes the symmetry: they will not be asked about what you did, just as you will not be asked about what they did, the second clause affirming the first. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the Prophet's ﷺ sentence that states the principle's application: "Whoever was slowed by his deeds will not be sped up by his lineage" — and notes that the verse's repetition at both ends of the passage on Ibrāhīm is a frame: the lesson of the section is stated at its opening and again at its close, so that what comes between is read as illustration rather than as story.

**Reflection.** The repetition is the point. The Sūrah has, between these two sentences, told the story of the brothers they claim — the trial of Ibrāhīm, the building of the House, the prayers, the bequest to the children of Yaʿqūb — and now it names the moral again, so that the reader cannot close the passage with the comfort of descent: the men in the story have finished, their account is closed, and what remains open is the ledger of whoever is reading. It is the same frame the Sūrah will use elsewhere, and it is the reason the passage about the friend of God leaves its readers, not with an ancestry, but with a question about their own deeds.


## 2:142

*"The fools among the people will say, 'What has turned them away from the qiblah they used to face?' Say: 'To God belong the East and the West; He guides whom He wills to a straight path.'"*

**Meaning.** The verse announces the coming objection before it is made, so that the believers need not be shaken by it [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies the fools as the ignorant among the people — the Jews and the hypocrites — and explains the naming: they *safihū* the truth, that is, they were ignorant of it; so the rabbis feigned ignorance and the leading ignorant among them swelled with pride against following Muḥammad ﷺ because he was from the Arabs and not from the Children of Israel, while the hypocrites were left bewildered and stupefied. **[Qurṭubī]** gives further definitions and the range of identifications: the *sufahāʾ* are the light-witted — from a garment that is *safīh* when it is loosely woven; al-Muʾarrij said the *safīh* is the liar who deliberately asserts the opposite of what he knows; Quṭrub, the unjust and ignorant; and while Mujāhid said they are the Jews of Madīnah and al-Suddī the hypocrites, al-Zajjāj said they were the disbelievers of Quraysh, who when they heard of the change of qiblah said that Muḥammad had grown homesick for his birthplace and would soon return to their religion, while the Jews said his affair had become confused on him and he was bewildered, and the hypocrites asked, "What has turned them from their qiblah?" and mocked the Muslims. The verb *sayaqūl* is future in form, though the sense is present and continuing — the future used for what is settled, to indicate that they will persist in that talk [Qurṭubī].

**What the objection was, and how it was answered.** **[Saʿdī]** sets out the verse's construction with precision. It contains a sign of prophecy, a consolation, a reassurance of the believers' hearts, an objection and its answer, and — in the two descriptions — the portrait both of the objector and of the one who submits to God's ruling and religion. The Muslims had been commanded to face Bayt al-Maqdis during their stay in Makkah and then for about a year and a half after the migration, and then God's wisdom required that they be commanded to face the Kaʿbah. So God told His Prophet in advance that the fools would certainly say, "What has turned them away from the qiblah they used to face?" — an objection to God's ruling, His law, His grace and His kindness — and consoled him by informing him that it would happen, that it would come only from a person marked by folly, shallow intellect, little forbearance and weak religion, and that they were therefore not to be heeded, since the source of the talk was known: the wise man pays no attention to the objection of a fool and does not occupy his mind with it. And the verse thereby establishes a principle: no one objects to God's rulings but a foolish, ignorant, obdurate person; the rightly guided believer of sound mind receives his Lord's rulings with acceptance, submission and surrender — as 33:36 has it, "when God and His Messenger decide a matter, no believing man or woman has a choice in it," and 4:65, "no, by your Lord, they shall not believe until they make you judge over what they dispute," and 24:51, "the saying of the believers when they are called to God and His Messenger to judge between them is: we hear and we obey." Then God answers the objection from three sides. First, the East and the West belong to God: if every direction is His property and no direction lies outside His dominion, and He has commanded this one, what grounds can there be for objection, since they did not face a direction that was not His? Second, God guides whom He wills to a straight path — and the guidance to this qiblah of theirs is guidance to the religion of their father Ibrāhīm, so the objector is objecting to God's favour out of envy and aggression. And third, since the guidance of whom He wills is stated absolutely while the absolute is read in light of the qualified — for guidance and straying have causes that God's wisdom and justice have set — the Sūrah at once names the cause that brought this community its guidance, in the verse that follows.

**The qiblah as a subject and a symbol.** **[Study Quran]** notes the use of the future "will say" and observes that it does not exclude reference to the past, as a settled trait rather than only a prediction — and that the verse serves to remind the reader that it is not the place itself, Jerusalem or Makkah, that merits being the direction of prayer, but the fact that God has commanded it to be so. It records the reports of the number of months the Prophet ﷺ faced Jerusalem after the migration — thirteen to twenty in the various narrations, with most saying sixteen or seventeen — and the accounts that while still in Makkah he prayed toward the Kaʿbah and then faced Jerusalem briefly after migrating and then faced the Kaʿbah again, while others say that even in Makkah he faced Jerusalem. Some commentators, it notes, held that the question about the change came from the hypocrites and was therefore not sincere but cynical — and it records that the change of qiblah is significant for the doctrine of abrogation, being the first instance of it in the chronological order of revelation and often cited as its paradigm, though it is an instance of the Qurʾān abrogating the Sunnah (for which see 2:106). It also mentions the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs near Madīnah, which received its name because a caller is said to have come to a congregation mid-prayer with the news of the change, and the congregation turned where they stood. And it records the long debate over determining the qiblah in locales far from Makkah, with the several methods used over the centuries — including the early system that divided the Islamic world into geographic sectors, each praying toward one wall of the Kaʿbah, extended horizontally over the earth.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes that the verse specifies "among the people" because *safah* — folly — can be attributed to inanimate things and animals too, and that the plural *sufahāʾ* has the singular *safīh*. **[Jalālayn]** reads the answer as the removal of the difficulty: to God belong the East and the West — that is, all directions — so He commands them to face whichever one He wills, and there can be no objection; He guides whom He wills, His guidance being the religion of Islam, and you are among those guided. **[Maʿārif]** supplies the underlying question the whole passage addresses: since God is not limited to any direction but transcends all dimensions, the logic of the fact would allow each worshipper to choose whatever orientation he likes and to change it at will — but divine wisdom found it more fitting that worshippers turn to one direction, because worship includes forms that are collective as well as private, and the collective forms — prayer and pilgrimage — carry a social function beside their devotional one. The uniting principle Islam chose is not race, colour, homeland or language, all of them arbitrary and divisive, but the unity of mind arising out of doctrinal unity: the worship of the one God, which alone can draw together people of every place and every age into a single body — and the qiblah gives that inner unity a visible form.

**Reflection.** The verse names its opponents before they speak, and the naming is the answer: to object to a change of direction is the mark of a fool, because the objection rests on a premise — that some piece of ground could hold God — that no thoughtful person holds. Once the premise is gone, the only question left is obedience, and the Sūrah's insistence is that the objection was never really about geography; it was about whose command one is willing to follow. **[Saʿdī]**'s two portraits are the verse's real subject: the fool, who weighs God's ruling against his own convenience and calls the verdict arbitrary; and the believer, whose whole part in the matter is a single sentence — we hear and we obey.


## 2:143

*"And thus We made you a middle community, that you might be witnesses over the people, and that the Messenger might be a witness over you. And We did not appoint the qiblah you were facing except that We might know who follows the Messenger from the one who turns on his heels. And it was a grave matter, save for those whom God guided. And God would never let your faith be in vain; surely God is Kind, Merciful to people."*

**Meaning.** The verse names what the community was made into, and what the change of direction was for [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads the opening as a parallel: just as God guided the believers through Muḥammad ﷺ and singled them out for the qiblah of Ibrāhīm and his religion, preferring them thereby over the followers of other creeds, so He singled them out and preferred them by making them a middle community. And *wasaṭ*, he says, is in the Arabs' speech the choice: one says a man is *wasaṭ* in his lineage among his people when one intends his elevation in it — with Zuḥayr's line, "they are a middle folk, with whose judgement mankind is content when one of the nights brings a great matter." He records the exegetes' preference for the sense of justice and then states his own view: the *wasaṭ* intended here is the middle part between two extremes — like the middle of a house — and God made them that, he argues, because He describes them elsewhere as a community that does not exceed the bounds nor fall short. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the fuller development: as the Kaʿbah is the middle of the earth, so you are a middle community — below the prophets and above the nations; the middle is justice, and the truest things are the middlemost; al-Tirmidhī reports from Abū Saʿīd, from the Prophet ﷺ on this verse, "just," graded sound; in the Qurʾān, "the middermost of them said" (68:28) means the most just and the best of them; and the middle of a valley is its best spot, with the most pasture and water. Since the middle avoids both excess and deficiency, it is praiseworthy, and the community described here did not exceed as the Christians exceeded concerning their prophets, nor fall short as the Jews fell short concerning theirs. He records the ḥadīth, "the best of affairs are their middlemost," and ʿAlī's instruction, "keep to the middle course; the one who lags will catch up to them, and the one who goes beyond will return to them."

**The two witnesses.** "That you might be witnesses over the people, and that the Messenger might be a witness over you" [Jalālayn] [Study Quran]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the setting: on the Day of Resurrection you will testify that their messengers delivered the message, and the Messenger will testify that he delivered it to you. **[Study Quran]** explains that to be a witness is to have a consequential role in the judging of a thing through one's knowledge of it — as 36:65 has it, "their hands will speak to Us, and their feet will bear witness to what they used to earn" — and reports the ḥadīth in which the Prophet ﷺ said that God will cause to enter the Garden any Muslim for whom four people bear witness, then three, then two — while ʿUmar said he did not ask about one — and the Prophet's saying, "you are God's witnesses over mankind." It mentions the reports in which, on the Day of Judgement, this community will testify to the faithfulness of other prophets to their missions even when their own peoples do not, with the discussion belonging to 4:41.

**The middle as equilibrium.** **[Maʿārif]** gives the middle its larger frame. The word covers more than geography or morals: in the human body, health depends on the four humours being properly balanced against one another, and disease comes when one increases or decreases immoderately, so that, if the balance is not restored, the body may die; so too in the ethical and spiritual sphere, health depends on temperateness and inner equilibrium, and illness arises from intemperance and disequilibrium, which, if it grows, becomes spiritual death. And since what places a human being at the head of creation is not the physical states he shares with the animals but something higher — spiritual perfection, in Rūmī's phrase, that manhood does not lie in flesh or fat or skin but in seeking to please the Friend — the one who deserves the title of the Universal Man is he who has attained ethical and spiritual equilibrium along with physical equilibrium; this has been granted in special measure to the prophets, and in its most perfect form to the Prophet ﷺ. Just as God created a whole system of medicines, instruments and physicians for the body's well-being, He sent the prophets with guidance for the soul's, so that they might promulgate the law of moderation and equilibrium in the world.

**The test, and the reassurance.** "And We did not appoint the qiblah you were facing except that We might know who follows the Messenger from the one who turns on his heels" [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Jalālayn]** fills in the story: the qiblah appointed was the Kaʿbah, which the Prophet ﷺ used to face in prayer, until after the migration he was commanded to face Bayt al-Maqdis — to win the hearts of the Jews — and he prayed that way for sixteen or seventeen months; and the *knowing* here is manifest knowledge, so that it be seen who follows the Messenger and believes in him, and who turns back on his heels to unbelief, doubting the religion and thinking the Prophet ﷺ confused about the matter — and a number of them apostatised because of it. **[Saʿdī]** adds the point of the test and its comfort: the one whose aim is the truth has his faith increased by such a change, since it is obedience to a command and since the earlier Books had foretold that he would face the Kaʿbah; while the one who turns on his heels away from the truth, following his desire, only adds disbelief to his disbelief and confusion to his confusion. "And it was a grave matter, save for those whom God guided" — grave and burdensome, save for those whom God guided, who recognized God's blessing in it and gave thanks and acknowledged His kindness in turning them toward this great House, which He preferred over the rest of the earth's regions and made a pillar of Islam and a remover of sins; so it was light for them and heavy for everyone else. Then the reassurance: "God would never let your faith be in vain" — it is impossible and unworthy of Him; and **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives its occasion from al-Bukhārī's report of al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib: some Muslims who had prayed toward the former qiblah had died or been martyred, and the people did not know what to say about them, until God revealed, "and God would never let your faith be in vain." **[Saʿdī]** draws out the two senses in which God preserves faith: preservation from loss — by His protection from everything that would corrupt, remove or diminish it; and preservation by growth — His enabling them to increase in faith and to complete their certainty; and he notes what the verse contains for the doctrine of the people of the Sunnah: that faith includes the deeds of the limbs, since God calls the prayers offered toward the former qiblah "your faith," and promises not to waste them. And the closing pair of names: *raʾūf raḥīm* — intense and abundant mercy — shown in that He completes the blessing He began, distinguishes the one who entered faith with his tongue only from the one who entered with his heart, tests them with a test that increases their faith and raises their rank, and turns them toward the noblest of houses [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** describes the *wasaṭ* the same way the tradition does — the Prophet's gloss "just," the proverb that the best of things is their middle, the sense of a people's middlemost as among its best and most esteemed, the middle as the choicest part — and adds the applications the exegetes have made: with regard to faith and practice, avoiding extremes, so that courage lies between recklessness and cowardice and generosity between prodigality and miserliness; in relation to other communities, Islam balancing law and love, the exoteric and the esoteric, this world and the next; and, at one level, the geographical middle belt of the world. It also reads the first word of the verse as connecting it to what precedes: "just as the Kaʿbah is the centre of the earth, so are you the middle people," or "just as We guided you, so We made you a middle community."

**Reflection.** The verse gives the community its standing and its job in the same sentence: it is placed in the middle not for privilege but for testimony — the position from which one can be heard on both sides. And the change of qiblah, which the fools treated as a scandal, is revealed as the opposite: a test deliberately designed, as **[Saʿdī]** says, to distinguish the one who follows the Messenger from the one who was following his own confidence that the Messenger would never do anything surprising. The last clause is the mercy added to the test: those who had obeyed before the command changed had not lost their obedience, for God does not waste faith — which is both a reassurance about the dead and a definition of what faith is, since the verse calls their prayers by that name.


## 2:144

*"We have indeed seen the turning of your face to the heaven; so We shall surely turn you to a qiblah that will please you. Turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. And those who were given the Book know that it is the truth from their Lord; and God is not heedless of what they do."*

**Meaning.** The command arrives as an answer to a longing the Prophet ﷺ had not spoken [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains the opening: We see, O Muḥammad, your turning of your face — its movement and shifting — toward the heaven, that is, in the direction of the heaven; and he reports Qatāda's account that the Prophet ﷺ used to turn his face to the sky before the change of his qiblah, waiting for God's command to shift toward the Kaʿbah, loving that God should turn him to it — until God turned him. **[Qurṭubī]** gives al-Zajjāj's alternative: the turning of your eyes in looking to the heaven, which comes to the same; and he notes why the heaven is specified — because it is the locus of what is attributed to it and descends from it: rain, mercy and revelation. He records al-Suddī's report that when the Prophet ﷺ prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis he would raise his head to the sky, watching for what he was commanded, and loved to pray toward the Kaʿbah — and al-Barāʾ's report that he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, loving to be turned toward the Kaʿbah. **[Saʿdī]** notes the delicacy of the wording: God said "your face," not "your sight," because of the intensity of his concern, and because turning the face entails turning the sight. And "a qiblah that will please you" is the Kaʿbah — and in that is a declaration of his rank, that God hastens to satisfy him. Then the command is made explicit: turn your face *shaṭra* the Sacred Mosque, that is, in its direction; and "wherever you are" — on land or sea, east or west, south or north — "turn your faces toward it."

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** draws from the command three legal conclusions: that facing the Kaʿbah is required for all prayers, obligatory and supererogatory alike; that if one can face the House itself, that is required, and otherwise its direction suffices — since the command is to turn the face "toward" it, and the obligated person does what he is able; and that turning the body away from the qiblah during prayer invalidates it, because the command to do a thing is a prohibition of its opposite. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes the same with the reports of the first abrogation in the Qurʾān being the qiblah, and the congregational scenes: the news coming to a group of the Anṣār while they were praying the afternoon prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis, so that they turned where they stood; and the report of Ibn ʿUmar that while the people were at Qubāʾ in the dawn prayer, a man came and said that a portion of the Qurʾān had been revealed that night, commanding the Prophet ﷺ to face the Kaʿbah — and they turned toward it, having been facing Syria.

**Context.** **[Maʿārif]** lays out the explanations of the Prophet's longing, holding that they do not contradict one another. Before prophethood he followed, by the impulse of his own nature, the way of Ibrāhīm; when revelation came, the Qurʾān itself designated his Sharīʿah as in total accord with the Abrahamic way; and the qiblah of Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl had been the Kaʿbah — so it was natural for him to wish that the Kaʿbah be appointed. An additional factor was that the Arab tribes, though associators, claimed to be followers of the Abrahamic way and acknowledged the Kaʿbah as their qiblah in contrast to the Jews; once the Kaʿbah became the Muslims' qiblah, the Arabs could be expected to find Islam more acceptable. And the hope that facing Bayt al-Maqdis would draw the Jews closer had been dashed by the events of sixteen or seventeen months, in which their hostility, fed by vanity, had only intensified. **[Study Quran]** records the same motives — the Jews' taunt that he followed their religion and used their qiblah, which displeased him, and the alternative accounts of his love for the House of Ibrāhīm and his hope for the Arabs' receptiveness — and notes that while a few commentators held that the Prophet chose Jerusalem of his own accord to build a bond with the local population, most accounts say he was instructed by God to face it and later commanded to change.

**"Those who were given the Book know."** **[Study Quran]** reports al-Ṭabarī's reading of the clause: they know that Makkah is the true qiblah for the Muslims — which must mean, it adds, that they know more generally that the Prophet is right, so that their opposition to the change is one more instance of their intransigence. **[Saʿdī]** puts the same, with the sting attached: the People of the Book and their learned know that you are on a clear truth in this matter — for their own Books describe it — so their denial is knowing. And **[Jalālayn]** notes the two readings of the final clause — "what you do," addressing the believers who obey the command, or "what they do," referring to the Jews' denial of the matter — while observing that God is not heedless either way.

**Reflection.** The verse is a glimpse into the intimacy of revelation: God announces that He has been watching the Prophet's face turn toward the sky, and grants the wish before it was asked. **[Maʿārif]**'s observation about the crowded, converging motives is worth keeping — the love of the ancestral House, the hope for a people's receptiveness, the weariness of a hostility that only hardened — because the verse does not treat the wish as a preference to be indulged or corrected, but as a longing that God Himself answers. And the second half gives the command its universality: "wherever you are" — the qiblah is not a place one must reach but a direction to which every place can be turned, and the House at the centre of the earth gathers a community that is itself placed in the middle.


## 2:145

*"And if you brought those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qiblah; nor are you a follower of their qiblah; nor are they followers of one another's qiblah. And if you followed their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would then be among the wrongdoers."*

**Meaning.** The verse closes the qiblah dispute with a statement about what more evidence can and cannot do [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Saʿdī]** begins from the Prophet's own state: out of the perfection of his concern for people's guidance he gave them the utmost of his counsel, was gentle in calling them, and grieved when they did not submit to God's command. But among the disbelievers were those who rebelled against God's command, grew arrogant toward His messengers and abandoned the truth deliberately and aggressively — among them the Jews and Christians, the People of the earlier Books, who disbelieved in Muḥammad knowingly, not out of ignorance. So God told him: if you brought them every sign — every proof and demonstration clarifying your word and what you call to — they would not follow your qiblah, that is, they would not follow you, since following the qiblah is the visible sign of following him and the dispute was precisely about the qiblah. And the reason they are like that is that they are obdurate: they know the truth and leave it. Signs benefit only the one who seeks the truth while it is still obscure to him, so that the clear proofs can clarify it; as for the one who has settled on not following the truth, there is no device against him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the same verse beside 10:96-97: "those against whom your Lord's word has been justified will not believe, even if every sign comes to them, until they see the painful punishment." **[Jalālayn]** notes the oath in the *lām* of "and if (*la-in*)," the categorical negation of the Prophet's desire that they become Muslims and of their desire that he return to their qiblah, and the third negation as well: the Jews and Christians do not follow one another's qiblah either.

**The mutual non-following.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports the ascription — al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd: the Jews are not followers of the Christians' qiblah, nor the Christians of the Jews' — and draws from it the verse's exposure of their condition: a declaration of their disagreement, their turning their backs on one another, and their straying. **[Maʿārif]** puts the same observation to work: their two groups display an equal malice even toward each other — the Jews adopted Bayt al-Maqdis, the Christians chose the East, and each rejects the other's direction. As for the Prophet ﷺ, he can accept neither, because the Muslims' new qiblah, the House of God, has been instituted by divine command and will never be abrogated; so there is no prospect of agreement between them and the Muslims in this matter. Bayt al-Maqdis was indeed once instituted by divine command, but that command has now been abrogated; and whoever follows an abrogated injunction while ignoring the new one that replaced it is disobeying God and acting on his own opinion and desire. It is therefore impossible for the Prophet ﷺ to follow their desires — and, he adds, the hypothetical in the last clause cannot arise at all, since as a prophet he is protected, and so cannot be among the unjust. **[Study Quran]** notes that "every sign" may also be read as "every kind of sign," cites the same 10:96-97 passage, and places the warning against following the caprices of other religious communities beside 2:120 and 5:48, 13:37 and 42:15. It observes that Jews traditionally face Jerusalem while Christian churches were historically oriented eastward toward the rising sun, and that the qiblah signifies more than physical orientation — it relates to identity and community, so that to follow someone else's qiblah is in effect to be excluded from the community or to be included in another. It records the ḥadīth: "Whoever prays our prayer and faces our qiblah and eats what we slaughter is a Muslim and is under the protection of God and the protection of His Messenger."

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammar: the oath-particle *la-in* is answered here with the answer proper to *law* — the two being, in effect, close enough that al-Farrāʾ and al-Akhfash judged the answer of one permissible for the other, the sense being "and were you (*law*) to bring them every sign..." — while Sibawayh held the meanings distinct and read the answer in the future: "and if you bring them every sign, they will not follow." The plural forms of *qiblah* are given: *qibal* in the broken plural, *qibalāt* in the sound plural, with the variants of vowelling. And on "nor are you a follower of their qiblah," he notes that the phrasing is a report which carries a command, meaning: do not lean toward any of that — and **[Saʿdī]** observes that the report form is more emphatic than a plain prohibition, since it states that the Prophet ﷺ is characterized by the opposite of following them, so that the act cannot occur from him at all.

**Reflection.** The verse is a hard answer to a reasonable expectation — that evidence should suffice. It says of a particular group, marking them as such, that no quantity of proof will move them, because their position is not the conclusion of an inquiry but a decision already made; and it adds the tell-tale sign: people who will not agree with one another on a direction will not agree with you either. The warning at the end is not addressed to the Prophet's own person, since he cannot do what it warns against, but to every reader who might be tempted by the thought that agreement could be purchased by a concession: after the knowledge has come, accommodation of another's desire is itself the wrong.


## 2:146

*"Those to whom We have given the Book recognize it as they recognize their children; yet a party of them knowingly conceal the truth."*

**Meaning.** The verse states what the previous one denied — that the evidence had never been lacking [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies those meant as the rabbis of the Jews and the scholars of the Christians, and reads the pronoun — "recognize *it*" — as the Sacred House: they know that the Kaʿbah is their qiblah and the qiblah of Ibrāhīm and of the prophets before you, as clearly as they know their own sons. **[Qurṭubī]** records both readings of the pronoun: Mujāhid, Qatāda and others took it as Muḥammad ﷺ — they recognize his prophethood and the truth of his mission; Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Jurayj al-Rabīʿ and Qatāda also held it to be the change of qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿbah, that it is the truth. And he explains why the comparison is with sons rather than with oneself, though a man is closer to himself: because a man passes through a stretch of his life in which he does not know himself, while no time passes in which he does not know his son. He records the exchange reported between ʿUmar and ʿAbd Allāh b. Salām: "Do you recognize Muḥammad ﷺ as you recognize your son?" He said, "Yes, and more: God sent His trustworthy one in His heaven to His trustworthy one on His earth with his description, and I recognized him — whereas my son, I do not know what came of his mother." That is the measure of the recognition the verse asserts. **[Jalālayn]** gives the same occasion with Ibn Salām's words, and reads the last clause as: a party of them conceal the truth — his description — while they know it. **[Saʿdī]** draws out the situation: the People of the Book had come to know, firmly and certainly, that Muḥammad ﷺ is God's Messenger and that what he brought is true, with a knowledge as distinct as their knowledge of their own sons; but most of those who disbelieved concealed this testimony although they were certain of it — and who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he holds from God? He notes that the verse contains consolation for the Prophet and the believers, and a warning against the harm and the doubts of such people — while some of them did not conceal the truth, and of those some believed and some disbelieved out of ignorance. And he draws the obligation the verse implies: the scholar's duty is to make the truth appear, clarify it and adorn it by every means of expression, proof and illustration he commands, and to nullify falsehood, distinguish it from the truth and make it repellent to souls by every route that serves that end — these concealers did the opposite, and their states were thereby reversed. **[Study Quran]** adjudicates between the readings: the recognition may be of the fact that the Kaʿbah is the true qiblah, following 2:144 where they are said to know; or of the Prophet himself, who is known not only through the prophecies in the Bible but also, in the Islamic view, through his presence, his character, the signs he brought and the truth of his message — so that recognizing the Kaʿbah's status depends on recognizing the Prophet's truthfulness rather than the reverse, since Jerusalem was a legitimate qiblah for a time. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes the proverb-like quality of the comparison — an Arabs' image for what is utterly plain — and cites the Prophet's ﷺ words to a man with a boy: "Is this your son?" "Yes, O Messenger of God, I bear witness to it." "Then he does not wrong you, nor you him." And on "they conceal the truth while they know it," **[Qurṭubī]** observes that the phrase makes their unbelief a matter of deliberate defiance — the same as "they denied them while their souls were certain of them" (27:14) and "when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it" (2:89).

**Reflection.** The verse denies the excuse of ignorance and names the offence precisely: not failure to see, but concealment of what is seen. **[Qurṭubī]**'s exchange between ʿUmar and Ibn Salām is the whole verse in two sentences — and its sting is the comparison: a father may not know what came of his son's mother, but about this matter there was no uncertainty at all. What the verse leaves its readers is a reversal of perspective: the dispute about the qiblah was never a dispute about evidence, and the party that appeared to be arguing was in fact hiding.

## 2:147

*"The truth is from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters."*

**Meaning.** The previous verse's charge of concealment is followed by a reaffirmation, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ and through him to the community [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense: know, O Muḥammad, that the truth is what your Lord has taught you and given you from Himself, not what the Jews and Christians tell you; and this is a report from God to His Prophet that the qiblah He turned him toward is the true qiblah, the one Ibrāhīm the friend of the Merciful was on, and the prophets after him — so work by the truth that has come to you from your Lord, and do not be among the doubters, that is, do not be among those who doubt that the qiblah you were turned toward is the qiblah of Ibrāhīm and of the prophets before you. **[Qurṭubī]** reads "the truth" as the facing of the Kaʿbah, not what the Jews told him of their own qiblah, and reports ʿAlī's reading of it in the accusative governed by "they know" — they know the truth — while permitting the accusative on the implied "cling to the truth," and the nominative as a new sentence or with an implied verb: "the truth has come to you." He also notes the address: it is to the Prophet ﷺ while the intended audience is his community. **[Saʿdī]** gives the reading that turns the verse into practice: this truth, which deserves the name of truth more than anything else because of what it contains of lofty aims, beautiful commands and the purification of souls — urging them toward their interests and away from their harms — has come from your Lord, whose very upbringing of you includes sending down this Qurʾān, which is the education of minds and souls and the whole of their benefit. So do not let the least doubt or misgiving settle in you; rather reflect on it and consider it until you arrive at certainty, since reflection upon it cannot but lead there. **[Jalālayn]** notes that the verse's clause is a fresh sentence in the nominative, and that the prohibition is a way of strengthening the heart — for the Prophet ﷺ is not a doubter, and the address is for the benefit of the community.

**Reflection.** The two verses together answer the concealers. The first says that they know and hide; the second says, to the one they hide from, that what he has is the truth and that he is not among those who vacillate. There is comfort in the pairing, and it is deliberately placed: the community is told that the opposition is not evidence against the revelation, and then told where certainty is to be found — not in the crowd's agreement but in reflection on what came from the Lord.


## 2:148

*"And each has a direction toward which he turns; so race to good deeds. Wherever you are, God will bring you all together; surely God is powerful over all things."*

**Meaning.** The verse turns the dispute about directions into an argument for action [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads "each" as each community: every follower of a creed has a direction he turns toward — the Jew has one and the Christian has one — while God has guided you, O community, to the qiblah that is the qiblah. He reports Mujāhid's and ʿAṭāʾ's glosses in the same sense: each community, each holder of a creed. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the language: *wijhah* is of the form *fiʿlah* from *muwājahah*, facing; and *wijhah*, *jihah* and *wajh* come to the same meaning, the qiblah — each has a direction, whether by right or by desire. And he gives the grammar of "he turns": the pronoun returns to the form of "each" rather than its sense, with the second object suppressed — he turns it, that is, he turns his face and himself toward it. **[Saʿdī]** draws the verse's lesson, and it is one of the most important observations in the passage: every people of a religion and a creed has a direction to which it turns in its worship, and the matter does not rest in facing the qiblah, since that is among the laws that change with times and conditions and into which abrogation enters, with movement from one direction to another. What the matter truly rests in is fulfilling the obedience of God, drawing near to Him and seeking standing with Him: this is the title of felicity and the patent of His friendship, and if souls do not take it on, their loss is in both worlds; while if they do, they are the true gainers. This much is agreed upon in every revealed law, and it is for this that God created people and commanded them. And then he notes the strength of the command to *race*: commanding that one race to good deeds is more than commanding that one merely do them, for racing includes doing them, completing them, performing them in the most perfect state and hastening to them — and whoever leads the race in this world to good deeds is the foremost in the next world to the Gardens; the foremost are the highest of creation in rank. And the "good deeds" include all the obligatory and supererogatory acts — prayer, fasting, alms, pilgrimage, *ʿumrah*, striving, and benefits that pass to others or remain with oneself. Because the strongest stimulus and the greatest incentive God has set for the souls is the reward He has arranged, the verse continues: "wherever you are, God will bring you all together" — He will gather you for the Day of Resurrection by His power and requite every doer for his deed: "that He may requite those who did evil for what they did, and requite those who did good with the best" (53:31). And from this noble verse, he says, one argues for performing every virtuous practice that attaches to a deed: prayer at the first of its time, hastening to discharge one's obligations for fasting, pilgrimage and *ʿumrah*, paying the alms, and performing the supererogatory acts and the courtesies of worship — what a comprehensive and useful verse this is.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn ʿĀmir, *muwallāhā* — "to which he is made to turn" — in the passive, and al-Rabīʿ's, ʿAṭāʾ's and Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of the sense in the active, with Ibn Jurayj and Mujāhid glossing "each" as each holder of a creed. **[Study Quran]** observes that the verse is understood to mean that all religious communities have a qiblah or direction of prayer, while the grammar also allows the reading "everyone has a direction toward which *He* directs him" — meaning that in the cases of the Kaʿbah and Jerusalem it is God who chooses the direction in which human beings pray — and that several commentators tie the command to race to the deeds specifically to timely performance of the canonical prayers, presumably because the qiblah is so closely associated with prayer; the same language of competing in good deeds appears elsewhere without the qiblah context, at 3:114, 5:48, 21:90, 23:56 and 35:32. **[Ibn Kathīr]** cites the same reports: Ibn ʿAbbās, that this speaks of the followers of the various religions, each nation and tribe having its own qiblah that they choose, while God's appointed qiblah is the one the believers face; and Abū al-ʿĀliyyah, that the Jew has his direction, the Christian his, and God has guided you, O community, to the qiblah that is the true qiblah — a statement also related from Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī and others. **[Maʿārif]** frames the same argument in the context of the change: it is an observable fact that every traditional community has had a religious orientation of its own, whether appointed by God or chosen by itself — so why should anyone object, or wonder, that God has appointed for the Islamic community a qiblah peculiar to it, considering that it is the last of all traditions, which makes a distinct qiblah all the more necessary? And once the divine command has been promulgated, the Muslims need not worry about the objections or the ridicule of others; they should give up fruitless controversy and strive to excel in good deeds, as defined by God and His Prophet ﷺ — for they must appear before God on the Day of Judgement.

**Reflection.** The verse relocates the whole quarrel. If every community has its direction, then the existence of different directions is not a scandal to be argued away; it is the human condition, and the verse lifts the discussion out of the geometry of prayer into the currency of deeds. **[Saʿdī]**'s distinction is the one the passage needs: the qiblah is a legislation that changes, while the race toward good is the constant; and the closing promise — that God will gather everyone wherever they are — gives the race its stakes, since the direction one faced will not be the question at the gathering, and what each has sent ahead of him will be.


## 2:149

*"And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord. And God is not heedless of what you do."*

**Meaning.** The command of the qiblah is repeated a second time, and now with the addition of travel [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the plain sense: from whatever place you leave for whatever destination, turn your face — turn it around — toward the Sacred Mosque; the turning itself is the *truth* that admits no doubt, from your Lord, so preserve it and obey God in facing it; and God is not unaware of what you do — He is not heedless of your deeds but is recording them, to repay you for them on the Day of Resurrection. **[Qurṭubī]** explains the repetition: it is emphasis upon the command and a sign of concern for it, because the change was extremely difficult for people to accept, so the command was stressed in order that they might see the importance and find it light and their souls settle into it. He reports the view of some, that verse 144 was directed to those present, verse 150 addressed the Muslims in all mosques everywhere, and this verse establishes the obligation of facing the Kaʿbah during journeys — and he states his preference for taking each verse by its proper sense, since verse 144 is particular and verse 149 adds the case of travel. **[Maʿārif]** sets out the division of labour among the three repetitions: the commands in the singular are addressed to the Prophet ﷺ himself and those in the plural to the Companions and the Muslims generally; thus verse 144 pertains to those who are in Madīnah or in their own town, and makes clear that the injunction is not particular to the Prophet's ﷺ mosque but applies to every town, village and quarter; verse 149 repeats the command with the phrase "from wherever you set out," which shows that the injunction now refers to the state of travel; and verse 150 repeats it again to cover the varied situations of a journey — unbroken travel for several days, or a short or long stay along the way. He adds a word about the term: verse 148 introduces the theme with *wijhah*, "the thing one turns one's face to," which Ibn ʿAbbās interpreted as the qiblah or religious orientation, and the reading of Ubayy b. Kaʿb has the word *qiblah* itself, leaving no ambiguity. **[Saʿdī]** notes that "from wherever you go out" is general, covering journeys and everything else; and that "it is the truth from your Lord" is reinforced by both *inna* and the *lām*, so that no one should entertain the least doubt about it, and so that no one should imagine it was on the footing of personal preference rather than obedience. And the closing clause is a summons to watchfulness: God sees you in all your states, so conduct yourselves with Him as those who are watched, by fulfilling His commands and avoiding His prohibitions, since your deeds are not neglected but will be repaid in fullest measure — if good, then good, and if evil, then evil. **[Jalālayn]** reads the repetition as intended to point out that the stipulation applies equally to being on a journey and to being settled at home.

**Reflection.** The law of the qiblah is stated once for the resident, once for the traveller, and once more for every circumstance a traveller can be in — and the effect is to remove the last place where an exception could be imagined. The verse's last clause completes the lesson: the direction of prayer is a matter of exact obedience, and the One who commanded the facing is not unaware of who turns.

## 2:150

*"And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it — so that the people may have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong. So fear them not, but fear Me — and so that I may complete My blessing upon you, and that you may be guided."*

**Meaning.** The command is given its third statement, and with it the reasons: to close the mouths of the disputants, and to complete a blessing [Saʿdī] [Study Quran] [Maʿārif]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the purpose clause as an answer to the whole dispute: God legislated facing the noble Kaʿbah so that people's argument against you might be cut off — the People of the Book and the idolaters alike. For had he remained facing Bayt al-Maqdis, the argument would have run against him: the People of the Book find in their Book that his settled qiblah was the Sacred House, and the idolaters counted this great House among their glories and as belonging to the religion of Ibrāhīm; so had Muḥammad ﷺ not faced it, their arguments would have pointed at him and they would have said, how can he claim to be on Ibrāhīm's religion and of his seed while he has abandoned facing his qiblah? By facing it, the proof was established against the People of the Book and the idolaters and their arguments were severed — all of them except the one among them who does wrong, that is, who argues from a position in which he is himself unjust and which has no support but following desire; such a one cannot be convinced by argument, and there is no point in making an object of the specious objection he raises, nor any reason to pay it attention. Hence: "so fear them not, but fear Me" — since their arguments carry no weight, and the command is God's. **[Study Quran]** identifies the parties the same way: the argument that the change cut off was the Jewish conceit that the Prophet was merely following their religion and their qiblah; and "except those of them who do wrong" refers to the idolatrous Makkans, who would not be silenced by the change, since one of their taunts had been precisely that the qiblah was other than the Kaʿbah — they might even have seen the change as a kind of victory, since they remained the custodians of the Kaʿbah, and grown more hopeful that Muḥammad would drift back into their religion. It notes that the message "fear them not, but fear Me" appears also at 3:175, 5:3 and 5:44, and that the fixing of the qiblah is presented as part of God's completion of His blessing for humanity — with similar passages connecting the completed blessing to pilgrimage (5:3) and to ablution (5:6), so that blessing is tied to ritual practice. **[Qurṭubī]** records the grammatical dispute over the exception: Abū ʿUbaydah held that *illā* here carries the sense of *wa* — and the wrongdoers too — citing al-Farazdaq's line, "there is no house in Madīnah but one, the house of the caliph, except the house of Marwān," where the sense is "and the house of Marwān"; but al-Zajjāj rejected this outright, calling it an error according to the skilled grammarians and a corruption of the meanings, and held instead that the exception is genuine: the argument is cut off from everyone except the wrongdoers, who keep a specious objection that deserves no attention. He also reports the alternative explanation of the purpose clause: that the people should not say to you, "you have been commanded to face the Kaʿbah and you cannot see it" — an objection removed by "wherever you are, turn your faces toward it," since the command is to face its direction, not to see it.

**The blessing completed.** "And so that I may complete My blessing upon you, and that you may be guided" [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Saʿdī]** traces the logic: since God's turning us toward the qiblah was a great blessing, and since His kindness to this community and His mercy keep increasing — every law He legislates for them being a great blessing — He said, "so that I may complete My blessing upon you." The root of the blessing is guidance to His religion by sending His Messenger and sending down His Book; the blessings that complete that root cannot be counted or limited, from the sending of the Prophet ﷺ until his departure drew near, when God gave him and gave his community what completed the blessing upon them all: "today I have perfected for you your religion and completed My blessing upon you and chosen for you Islam as a religion" (5:3). Praise be to God for a favour whose number we cannot reach, let alone give thanks for. And "that you may be guided" means that you may know the truth and act by it. He closes with the observation that God's mercy toward His servants has eased for them the paths of guidance to the utmost, alerted them to them and explained them most fully — so much so that among His means is that He raises up opponents against the truth to argue against it, whereby the truth becomes clear, its proofs and banners appear, and the vanity of falsehood is exposed as having no substance; for had it not been for the opposing of the truth, its condition might have remained unclear to most people. By their opposites things become clear: without the night the value of the day would not be known, without the ugly the merit of the beautiful, without darkness the benefit of light — and without falsehood the truth would not be so manifestly clear. Praise be to God for that. **[Maʿārif]** observes that the repetition of the same command teaches something about the Qurʾān's mode of expression, and that the revelation does not submit to the rules of human composition: reiteration of words and sentences is a regular mode of the divine Book, and where it occurs it does the work those being addressed require — here, closing each avenue of objection and removing each occasion for doubt.

**Reflection.** The verse gives reasons for a command, and the reasons are both polemical and pastoral. The change of direction was, in the end, an answer: it took away the last argument the older communities could use, that this prophet was a follower of their religion; and it took away the last excuse from the Muslims themselves, that the House was too far to be faced. What remains is the briefest possible statement of the alternative — fear them not, but fear Me — and a promise whose shape is worth noticing: the completion of a blessing is attached, not to a victory or a conquest, but to the community being guided, which is the sense **[Saʿdī]** gives the final clause, that they come to know the truth and act upon it.


## 2:151

*"Even as We have sent among you a messenger from among yourselves, reciting Our signs to you, purifying you, and teaching you the Book and the Wisdom, and teaching you what you did not know."*

**Meaning.** The verse names the blessing that includes all the others, and it is the answer to an earlier prayer [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif] [Jalālayn]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads it as the completion of the gift: God perfected His blessing upon them and guided them to the religion of His friend Ibrāhīm by granting the supplication Ibrāhīm had made — "our Lord, send among them a messenger from among themselves, who shall recite Your signs to them and teach them the Book and the Wisdom and purify them" (2:129). **[Maʿārif]** makes the same connection and draws the conclusion the Sūrah wanted: verse 151 repeats the second half of Ibrāhīm's prayer with which the whole discussion opened; the first prayer, for the founding of the Kaʿbah, has already been shown to be accepted in the qiblah discussion, and now the second request is declared granted as well — so that, since the Prophet ﷺ has been sent in answer to the prayer of the founder of the House, it is no wonder that the House should have been appointed as his qiblah. And it notes that the verse mentions the very attributes Ibrāhīm specified: he recites the verses; he teaches the Book and the Wisdom; he purifies; and he teaches what his hearers did not know and could not have found in the earlier Books or by individual reason. **[Jalālayn]** reads the opening *kāf* as connecting the verse to the previous one's "so that I may complete My blessing on you": the blessing was completed by the sending of Muḥammad ﷺ, who recites the Qurʾān to them, purifies them of idolatry, and teaches them the Book and the Wisdom — what the Book contains of rulings — and what they did not know. **[Qurṭubī]** reports the grammarians' analyses: al-Farrāʾ held the *kāf* to stand in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun — "that I may complete My blessing upon you with a completion like Our sending" — which Ibn ʿAṭiyyah judged the best view; others took it as a circumstantial clause; and ʿAlī and al-Zajjāj held that the sentence involves a transposition, the sense being "remember Me in the measure that We have sent among you a messenger..." — and al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm adopted this: as I have done this for you of the favours I have recounted, remember Me with thanks and I will remember you with increase.

**The four functions.** **[Saʿdī]** sets out what each means. "From among yourselves": one whose lineage, truthfulness, trustworthiness, completeness and counsel they knew — and the point of the phrase is that revelation arrived through a man with no strangeness about him. "He recites Our signs to you" — which includes the Qurʾānic verses and more: he recites the signs that distinguish right from falsehood and guidance from error, which first showed them God's oneness and perfection, then the truthfulness of His Messenger and the obligation of believing him, then all that he reported of the Resurrection and the unseen — until they obtained complete guidance and certain knowledge. "And he purifies you": he purifies your characters and souls, training them on noble traits and cleansing them of base ones — purification from idolatry to monotheism, from showing off to sincerity, from lying to truthfulness, from treachery to trustworthiness, from arrogance to humility, from bad character to good, from mutual hatred, estrangement and severing of ties to mutual love, connection and affection, and other kinds of purification. "And he teaches you the Book" — its words and its meanings — "and the Wisdom," which some call the Sunnah and others the knowledge of the secrets of the law and understanding it and putting things in their proper places; on the latter reading the teaching of the Sunnah is included in the teaching of the Book, since the Sunnah clarifies the Qurʾān, interprets it and expresses it. "And he teaches you what you did not know" — for before his mission they were in manifest error, with neither knowledge nor action, so that every knowledge and every deed this community attained came by his hand and through him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same arc: God reminds the believers of what He granted them by sending Muḥammad ﷺ — reciting His clear signs, purifying and cleansing them from the worst of manners, the diseases of souls and the practices of the Age of Ignorance, taking them out of darkness into light, teaching them the Book and the Wisdom, which is his Sunnah, and teaching them what they did not know. In the Age of Ignorance they used to utter foolish words; then, by the blessing of his mission, they were raised to the rank of God's friends and the standing of scholars — acquiring the deepest knowledge among people, the most devout hearts and the most truthful tongues. **[Study Quran]** notes that the verse describes the fulfilment of Ibrāhīm's prayer in 2:129 with the same elements of Book, Wisdom and purification, and reports the readings of the *kāf*: a continuation of the guidance mentioned in the previous verse, or an indication that the sending of the Messenger is itself part of the completion of the blessing.

**Reflection.** The verse gathers the whole of what a religious community receives and puts it in four words: signs recited, souls purified, a Book taught, a Wisdom given — and then adds the fifth, "what you did not know," which is the confession the community must keep making. **[Saʿdī]**'s list of transformations between the paired nouns is the verse's best commentary: each of the four verbs produces a substitution, and the substitutions are visible in a life before and after. And the historical observation with which the passage closes belongs to the Sūrah's argument: the community that inherited the House inherited it, not by descent, but by the sending of a messenger who answered a prayer made at its foundations.

## 2:152

*"So remember Me, and I will remember you; and be grateful to Me, and do not be ungrateful to Me."*

**Meaning.** The obligations follow the blessings [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains the remembering: remember Me, O believers, by obeying Me in what I command and forbidding what I prohibit, and I will remember you with My mercy and My forgiveness — as Saʿīd b. Jubayr put it: remember Me with obedience, and I will remember you with forgiveness. He records the other reading, that the remembering is by praise and commendation; al-Rabīʿ's summary — God remembers whoever remembers Him, increases for whoever thanks Him, and punishes whoever denies Him; and al-Suddī's: there is no servant who remembers God but that God remembers him — not a believer but He remembers him with mercy, nor a disbeliever but He remembers him with punishment. Then the second command: be grateful to Me for what I have blessed you with of Islam and of guidance to the religion I legislated for My prophets and My chosen ones, and do not be ungrateful to Me — do not deny My kindness to you, lest I strip from you the blessing I gave you; but thank Me for it, and I will increase it and complete My blessing upon you and guide you to what I was pleased with in My servants. For I have promised My creation that whoever thanks Me I increase, and whoever denies Me I deprive and strip of what I gave. He adds a grammatical note: the Arabs say "I gave you good counsel" and "I thanked *for* you," with the preposition, and only rarely without it — with the poet's line, "they gathered wretchedness and good fortune against you, so why did you not thank the people when you did not fight?" And on the two roots: *shukr* is praise of a person for his praiseworthy deeds, and *kufr* is covering a thing.

**The practice of remembrance.** **[Maʿārif]** explains what *dhikr* is and what its merits rest on. It pertains essentially to the heart, but since the tongue is the heart's interpreter, the oral recitation of a divine name or a verse of the Qurʾān is also called *dhikr* — with the qualification that oral remembrance is worth the name only when joined to the heart's remembrance; as Rūmī observes, the recitation of a divine name has no efficacy if the mind is on cows and donkeys meanwhile. He adds, however, that even a mechanical *dhikr* is not wholly futile, and reports from **[Qurṭubī]** the story that Abū ʿUthmān, hearing a man complain of precisely that condition, remarked that one should be grateful to God even for the favour of having drawn at least one organ of the body, the tongue, into His service. On the merits: what greater merit could one wish than the assurance that when a man remembers God, God remembers him? Abū ʿUthmān claimed to know the time when God remembers His servants; when they wondered how he could determine it, he answered that by the promise of the Qurʾān, when a Muslim remembers God, God remembers him — so anyone can know for himself that as soon as he turns to God and remembers Him, God remembers him. **[Study Quran]** gives the same reciprocity as a foundation of the Sufi practice of methodical remembrance, and cites the ḥadīth qudsī: "I am as My servant deems Me to be. I am with him when he remembers Me. Whoever remembers Me within himself, I shall remember him within Myself. Whoever remembers Me in company, I shall remember him in company better than them. Should he approach Me by a hand, I shall approach him by a cubit; and should he approach Me by a cubit, I shall approach him by a fathom; and should he come to Me walking, I shall go to him running."

**Thanksgiving.** **[Saʿdī]** works through the second command: thank Me for the blessings I have given you and for the kinds of harm I have turned away from you — and thanksgiving is of the heart, in acknowledgment and confession of the blessings; of the tongue, in remembrance and praise; and of the limbs, in obeying God, submitting to His command and avoiding His prohibition. In thanksgiving lies the preservation of the blessing one has and increase in the blessings one lacks — "if you are grateful, I will surely increase you" (14:7). And he observes the placement: the command to thank comes immediately after the mention of the religious blessings — knowledge, the purification of character, success in action — which shows that these are the greatest blessings, indeed the true blessings, which endure when others pass; and that those granted knowledge or action ought to thank God for it, so that He may increase them of His bounty and so that self-admiration may be repelled by their occupation with thanks. And since the opposite of thanksgiving is denial, the verse forbids the opposite: "and do not be ungrateful to Me" — the *kufr* meant here being the denial of blessings and the refusal to meet them with gratitude; while the wording may also be read more generally, in which case *kufr* has many kinds, the gravest being unbelief in God, and below it the several sorts of disobedience, from association with Him down to what is less.

**Reflection.** The verse makes worship a conversation: remembrance answered by remembrance, gratitude answered by increase — and it is worth noticing which side speaks first. God has just listed what He gave, and the response He asks for is not payment but attention: remember, and give thanks. **[Maʿārif]**'s observation that even a tongue without a heart is not nothing is a mercy worth keeping beside the ascetic warning of the Rūmī verse; and **[Saʿdī]**'s ordering of gratitude — heart, tongue, limbs — gives the command its full scope, so that "do not be ungrateful" covers every way of receiving a gift as though it were a payment or a right.


## 2:153
