*"O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer; surely God is with the patient."*

**Meaning.** The verse prescribes the remedy for a community under pressure [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** hears in it an incitement to God's obedience and to bearing what is disliked in body and property: seek help through patience and prayer in carrying out My obedience and discharging My obligations in the rulings I abrogate — and in turning away from what I abrogate toward what I bring newly for you of My obligations, and in submitting to My command when I bind its ruling on you and shifting when I shift you — even if hardship attaches to that. The plain sense is the passage's situation: a community wondering at changes and surrounded by opposition is told where strength comes from. **[Maʿārif]** states the context exactly: the enemies of Islam had been objecting to the change of qiblah to plant doubts, the earlier verses had answered them and removed every misgiving, but some persisted in hostility regardless — a situation likely to dishearten the Muslims, and so this verse nullifies such a reaction by prescribing the method of overcoming grief and anxiety. The method is turning to patience and prayer, with the assurance that God is with those who are patient — a promise that applies above all to those who pray, obligatory or supererogatory, since prayer is the supreme form of worship; and although the occasion was specific, the verse identifies the elixir for all the ills that are part of human existence, whether need and want, or anxiety and suffering.

**What patience is.** **[Saʿdī]** defines it as restraining the soul and holding it back from what it dislikes, and divides it into three: patience *upon* obeying God so that the obedience is performed; patience *against* disobeying God so that the sin is abandoned; and patience *under* God's painful decrees without resenting them. Patience, he says, is the great aid in every matter; there is no way for one who is not patient to reach what he seeks — especially continuous and difficult acts of obedience, which stand in desperate need of patient endurance and the swallowing of bitterness: if the doer holds to patience he succeeds, and if aversion and hardship turn him back from patience and perseverance he attains nothing and is left deprived. The same with sin, whose pull the soul presses hard toward while the servant has the power to commit it: it can only be left with great patience, holding back the heart's desires for God's sake and seeking God's aid for protection from it, since such enticements are among the great trials. And the same with severe affliction, especially if it continues: the powers of soul and body weaken, and resentment rises, unless the one afflicted resists it with patience for God's sake, reliance on Him, constant recourse to Him and perpetual need of Him. So the servant needs patience — is compelled to it — in every state, and that is why God commanded it and informed us that He is with the patient. "With" here is a special companionship that entails His love, His aid, His support and His nearness: a mighty distinction for the patient, such that if the patient had no merit but that they won this companionship of God, it would suffice them for honour and nobility. The general companionship, by contrast, is that of knowledge and power — "and He is with you wherever you are" (57:4) — which is common to all creation.

**āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes the underlying fact: the servant is either enjoying a blessing for which he should give thanks, or suffering a calamity which he should meet with patience — and he gives the ḥadīth: "Wondrous is the case of the believer: God does not decree anything for him but it is good for him. If good fortune comes to him and he is grateful, it is good for him; and if hardship comes and he is patient, it is good for him." And he records the categorization the commentators give patience: being resolute in avoiding sins, constant in meritorious actions, and content under affliction. **[Study Quran]** gives the same three kinds and points to the other places where recourse to patience and prayer is mentioned (2:45), where patience is made a matter of competition (3:200), and where people are enjoined to exhort one another to it (90:17; 103:3), as well as the verses in which God is said to be with the patient (8:46, 66). **[Qurṭubī]**, in the block that also carries his discussion of remembrance, gives the root of *dhikr* as the heart's alertness to the remembered thing and its waking to it, and reports Saʿīd b. Jubayr's rendering of the previous verse in the same spirit: remembrance is God's obedience, so that whoever does not obey Him has not remembered Him, however much he may praise Him with his tongue.

**Reflection.** The verse offers two instruments, and they are a pair: patience does the holding, prayer does the asking — the one keeps a person in place under weight, the other connects him to the One who carries the weight with him. **[Saʿdī]**'s threefold division matters because it refuses to let "patience" mean mere resignation: it is required in obeying, in resisting, and in suffering, which covers the whole of a life. And the promise attached is the reason both instruments work: not a general presence such as all creation has, but a companionship of love and support granted to those who endure — the honour that the verse holds out to a community being told that its enemies will not stop.


## 2:154

*"And do not say of those who are slain in the way of God that they are dead; rather they are alive, but you are unaware."*

**Meaning.** After the command to seek help through patience, the Sūrah names the hardest thing patience is asked for [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī] [Ṭabarī] and corrects the word with which it is spoken of. **[Ṭabarī]** puts the verse in the series: O believers, seek help through patience in obeying Me in the struggle against your enemy, in abandoning My prohibitions and in discharging the rest of My obligations — and do not say of one killed in God's way that he is dead; for the truly dead among My creation are those from whom I have taken life and whose senses I have voided, so that they taste no pleasure and perceive no bliss. But whoever of you, or of My creation generally, is killed in My way is alive with Me, in life and bliss, in pleasant living and abundant provision, rejoicing in what I have given them of My bounty and the honour I have conferred. He records Mujāhid's report of the sense of "alive": with their Lord, provided for, eating of the fruit of the Garden and catching its fragrance, though not yet within it. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the parallel at 3:169 — "do not reckon those killed in God's way dead; rather they are alive with their Lord, provided for" — where the rules concerning the martyrs are discussed; and he draws a theological point from this verse's wording: if God gives life after death to martyrs in order to provide for them, it is possible that He gives life to disbelievers in order to punish them — which contains a proof of the punishment of the grave. And he insists on the verb: the martyrs *are* alive now, not merely that they *will* be; if the verse meant only that they will live, there would be no difference between them and anyone else, since everyone will live — and the proof is the following clause, "but you are not aware," while the believers are perfectly aware that the others will be raised. **[Jalālayn]** gives the ḥadīth that fills in the manner of that life: their spirits are in the bodies of green birds flying freely wherever they wish in Paradise. **[Study Quran]** supplies that ḥadīth in full: the spirits of the witnesses are in the crops of green birds that alight upon lamps hanging from the Throne; their Lord turns to them and asks what they desire; they answer that He has given them what He has given no one else in creation; and when they see that the question will be repeated, they say that they wish to return to the world and to set out in His way and be killed for His sake again — because of the reward of martyrdom — and the Lord says, "I have written that they shall not return." Other reports describe their spirits as white birds eating the fruits of the Garden, or as birds perched on a tree there, remaining so until God returns them to their bodies at the resurrection — a state after death and before the Day of Resurrection, which belongs to the wider subject of the life of the grave. **[Saʿdī]** frames the verse as the chosen example of what patience is for: after commanding help through patience in all conditions, God mentions a sample — striving in His way, the most excellent of bodily acts of worship and the hardest upon souls, both because of its own hardship and because it leads to being killed and to the loss of the very life for whose sake people desire this world and everything in it. It is known that a rational person does not abandon something beloved except for something more beloved and greater: so God informed us that whoever is killed in His way — having fought so that God's word might be uppermost and His religion prevail, and for no other purpose — has not lost life but gained the greater one.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes the grammar: *amwāt* is in the nominative with an implied subject, and so is "alive" — that is, "they are dead; rather they are alive" — and that the verb "say" cannot govern them, since there is no correspondence between the two terms such as there is in "I said a word and a proof." And the closing "but you are not aware" is what marks the difference between the martyr's life and the general resurrection: everyone will rise, but the martyr's state now is hidden from perception, and the verse removes the excuse of judging by what the eye can see.

**Reflection.** The verse forbids a manner of speech as much as it corrects a doctrine. To say of the slain that they are dead is not a neutral error; it is to measure God's gift by what is visible, and the whole passage has been teaching a community under pressure to measure differently. **[Qurṭubī]**'s grammatical point is the theological one: the martyrs are alive in the present tense, and the reason we do not see it is our own limitation, not theirs — "but you are not aware" is stated as a fact about the observer, not an uncertainty about the observed.

## 2:155

*"And We shall surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and the loss of wealth and lives and fruits; and give glad tidings to the patient."*

**Meaning.** The trials are announced in advance, and the announcement is itself part of the mercy [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn] [Study Quran]. **[Saʿdī]** sets out the purpose: God informed us that He will certainly test His servants with trials, so that the truthful be distinguished from the liar and the impatient from the patient — this is His way with His creation, for if ease continued for the people of faith with no trial mixed in, there would be a confusion that is corruption; and God's wisdom requires that the people of good be distinguished from the people of evil. That, he says, is the benefit of trials — not that they remove the faith that is with the believers, nor turn them back from their religion; God would never let the faith of the believers be lost. And he attends to each term: "with something of fear" — from the enemies; "and hunger" — and only a little of either, since if He tested them with all fear or all hunger they would perish; trials sift, they do not destroy. "And loss of wealth" — which covers every depletion that befalls property: sky-borne calamities, drowning, ruin, and the taking of wealth by oppressive rulers, highwaymen and the like. "And lives" — the departure of loved ones: children, relatives, companions; and the various diseases of one's own body or of the body of one he loves. "And fruits" — grains, the fruits of palms and all trees and vegetables, by cold, hail, burning or sky-borne blight such as locusts. These things must occur, because the All-Knowing, All-Aware told us of them, and they occurred just as He told. And when they occur, people divide into two: the impatient and the patient. The impatient man suffers two calamities — the loss of the beloved, which is the affliction itself, and the loss of what is greater than it, namely the reward for obeying God's command to be patient — so he wins loss and deprivation, the faith he has is diminished, patience, contentment and gratitude pass him by, and resentment settles in, which is the mark of a severe deficiency. **[Jalālayn]** specifies each term in the same way: fear of an enemy, hunger by drought, diminution of goods by destruction, of lives by slaughter and disease, and of fruits by crop damage — and reads the verse as a test to see whether patience is practised, with the glad tidings being of Paradise for those who are patient in calamity. **[Study Quran]** expands the identifications: souls may mean friends, relatives and other loved ones, and fruits may mean food and crops but also children, who are "the fruit of the heart"; it points to 106:4, where the Quraysh are protected from hunger and fear, and to 16:112, where an ungrateful town is clothed in hunger and fear; and it records the allegorical reading some give — the fear of God, the hunger of the Ramaḍān fast, the loss of wealth in alms, loss of souls in sickness, loss of fruits in the death of children — with 9:120's note that when hunger befalls one in God's way, a righteous deed is recorded. It then gives the criterion for patience that the ḥadīth and the commentators supply: "Patience is at the first blow" — the proof of a steadfast heart is its state in the heat of the affliction, not when it is over, since by then anyone can be patient. And it records **[Qurṭubī]**'s qualification of the common definition: patience is not simply the absence of complaint, since Ayyūb said to God, "Satan has afflicted me with weariness and punishment" (38:41) — and yet God says of him, "We found him steadfast" (38:44).

**Reflection.** The verse tells a community about to be tested what the tests will be, and this is why the announcement precedes the ordeal: a trial named in advance is half endured. **[Saʿdī]**'s insistence that trials are for distinguishing and not for destroying answers the natural reading of such a list: the "something of" is deliberate — the pressure is measured, not total, and the point is not to break the believers but to show what they are. And the glad tidings are attached to the last word of the verse: not to those who feel nothing, but to those who endure — and, as the ḥadīth specifies, endure at the first blow, when the sting is fresh and the outcome still unknown.


## 2:156

*"Those who, when an affliction befalls them, say: 'Surely we belong to God, and surely to Him we return.'"*

**Meaning.** The verse defines the patient whom the previous verse's glad tidings address [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense: give glad tidings, O Muḥammad, to the patient — those who know that every blessing they have is from Me, so that they acknowledge My servitude over them, affirm My lordship, believe in the return to Me, submit to My decree, hope in My reward and fear My punishment. And when I test them with some of My trials, and afflict them with what I promised they would be afflicted with — fear, hunger, loss of wealth, lives and fruits, and the other calamities with which I test them — they say: we are our Lord's possessions and His creatures while we live; we are His servants; and to Him we shall go after our death — in submission to My decree and contentment with My rulings. **[Saʿdī]** makes the same division of the formula: "we belong to God" is that He owns us and disposes of us as He wills, and "to Him we return" is the Hereafter — so the servant acknowledges in two phrases both the ownership and the destination, and both are what make patience possible. **[Maʿārif]** supplies the reason the verses precede the trials with an announcement of them: afflictions are unnerving whatever their magnitude, but prior knowledge of them makes them easier to bear; and since the community is addressed, it should realize that the world is a place of hardship and labour, a place of ordeal, and that it does not amount to impatience for one to regard such accidents as neither strange nor a remote chance. And as the community generally displays the spirit of patience in its deeds, the reward of mercy is common to everyone who strives to be patient, while each will be rewarded individually according to the quality and degree of his patience. **[Jalālayn]** preserves the reports that grew around the formula: it is said that whoever pronounces the *istirjāʿ* — this sentence — when an affliction befalls him, God rewards him and compensates him with what is better; and that when the Prophet's lamp blew out he said the *istirjāʿ*, and ʿĀʾishah said, "It is only a lamp," and he answered, "Whatever bothers a believer is an affliction of sorts" — reported by Abū Dāwūd among the *mursal* reports.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** works through the vocabulary of affliction: *muṣībah* is everything that harms a believer and strikes him; the Arabic says a thing struck him (*aṣābahū*) and the noun forms include *muṣābah* and *muṣāb*; the plural *maṣāʾib* is regularly given the hamzah although its origin is a *wāw*, the Arabs assimilating the original to the augment, with the form *maṣāwib* also preserved. He also records the usage in which *muṣāb* is the act of striking itself, with the poet's line in address to Sulaym. **[Study Quran]** notes that this sentence, "truly we are God's, and unto Him we return," is the formula most Muslims recite when they learn of a death, and that it is connected with the loss of souls mentioned in the previous verse; the theme of the return runs throughout the Qurʾān, with human beings reminded that to God are all matters returned (2:210), and warned to be mindful of a day when they shall be returned to God (2:281), willingly or unwillingly (3:83), all together (5:48); while the sense of belonging is an extension of the many passages in which all that is in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him (2:116, 255, 284).

**Reflection.** Two clauses carry the whole weight of endurance: He owns us, so the thing taken was never ours to keep; and we are returning, so the loss is a step on the road home. **[Maʿārif]**'s observation about foreknowledge is the pastoral purpose of the whole passage — the trials are announced so that when they arrive they find a community that had already decided how it would answer — and **[Jalālayn]**'s small ḥadīth about the lamp gives the formula its domestic size: whatever bothers a believer is an affliction of sorts, and the sentence is for that too.

## 2:157

*"Upon those rest blessings and mercy from their Lord, and those are the rightly guided."*

**Meaning.** The reward of the formula is stated, and its terms are carefully chosen [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies those meant as the patient just described, and reads *ṣalawāt* as forgiveness — supporting it with the Prophet's ﷺ prayer over those who brought their alms, "O God, bless the family of Abū Awfā," where the blessing is God's forgiveness of His servants. So those who said the words in their affliction have upon them forgiveness and mercy from their Lord — and, the verse adds, "those are the rightly guided," that is, guided to the right road. **[Study Quran]** draws attention to the grammatical subtlety that gives the term its weight: *ṣalawāt* usually means prayer or worship, but when used with the preposition *ʿalā* — upon — it indicates something that comes from God toward human beings rather than something that goes from them toward God, as in 33:56, "truly God and His angels invoke blessings upon the Prophet; O you who believe, invoke blessings upon him and greetings of peace," and as in 9:99 and 9:103. **[Jalālayn]** renders the three gifts compactly: upon them rest blessings, forgiveness, and mercy and grace from their Lord, and they are the truly guided to rectitude. **[Saʿdī]** draws the point that the verse closes the passage with a reward compounded: the loss of the beloved is replaced by blessings, mercy and guidance — the guidance being, in his reading, guidance to the way of patience and submission, so that the afflicted are not merely compensated but taught. **[Maʿārif]** adds that since the community as a whole is asked to bear hardship with patience, the reward of mercy is common to everyone who strives for it, while the degrees of reward differ with the degrees of patience — each person rewarded in proportion to what he endured and how.

**Reflection.** The passage ends where religion usually ends in the Qurʾān: not with the removal of the trial but with what the trial produces. The afflicted who say the words are given three things — forgiveness, mercy, and guidance — and the third is the most surprising, since guidance is usually what one needs *before* the test. But the verse places it after: those who lived through the loss with that sentence on their lips have been shown the road, and the endurance has taught them what comfort could not. **[Study Quran]**'s grammatical observation makes the gift's direction visible: the blessings come *down*; nothing of it is the servant's own performance — which is why the passage that began with "seek help through patience and prayer" can end with the servant receiving rather than achieving.


## 2:158

*"Truly Ṣafā and Marwah are among the rites of God; so whoever performs the ḥajj to the House or the ʿumrah, there is no blame on him in going between them. And whoever volunteers good — surely God is Thankful, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** The verse removes a scruple that had kept some of the Companions from a rite, and declares the rite God's own [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Maʿārif]** sets it in the thread of the Sūrah: the subject of the Kaʿbah began at verse 124 with the testing of Ibrāhīm, opened with the House being made a place of convergence, a sanctuary and a centre of worship, and continued through Ibrāhīm's prayer to be shown the rites — which includes the ḥajj and the ʿumrah. Now the centrality of the House is manifest in two ways: it is the qiblah toward which all prayer is directed wherever it is performed, and it is the goal of the pilgrimage. And the present verse opens with the solemn declaration that the two hills adjoining the Kaʿbah in Makkah are tangible signs from God: pilgrims walk briskly between them after the circumambulation, an act called *saʿy* — and the practice had existed in the Jāhiliyyah, which made some Muslims doubt its propriety. It is exactly that doubt God aims to remove. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the report from al-Bukhārī that makes the situation concrete: ʿĀṣim b. Sulaymān said he asked Anas b. Mālik about Ṣafā and Marwah, and Anas said, "We used to think they were a matter of the Age of Ignorance, so when Islam came we held back from them; then God sent down: 'truly Ṣafā and Marwah are among the rites of God...'" — and the fuller report, from ʿUrwah, that he said to ʿĀʾishah, "I do not see any blame on a man who does not go between Ṣafā and Marwah, and I would not care if I did not," and she answered, "How badly you have spoken, son of my sister! The Messenger of God ﷺ went between them, and the Muslims went between them; the practice of holding back was only that of those who had consecrated themselves for Manāt, the idol at al-Mushallal, who would not go between Ṣafā and Marwah. Then God sent down: 'so whoever performs the ḥajj or the ʿumrah, there is no blame on him in going between them.' Had it been as you say, it would have read: *no blame on him not to go between them*." **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same exchange from Aḥmad and the report that the verse came down about the Anṣār, who had assumed the state of consecration for Manāt before Islam and used to hesitate to go between the two hills, and who then asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about it — "O Messenger of God, in the Age of Ignorance we used to hesitate to go between Ṣafā and Marwah" — and so the verse came down.

**Language.** **[Ṭabarī]** works through the two names: *Ṣafā* is the plural of *ṣafāh*, the smooth, bare rock — with the poet al-Ṭirimmāḥ's line, "the Possessor of strength and bounty refuses to let any hoof ever soften my rocks" — and while some held that *ṣafā* is a singular with the dual *ṣafawān* and the plurals *aṣfāʾ*, *ṣufiyy* and *ṣifiyy*, its likeness to *ʿaṣā* and *ʿiṣiyy*, *raḥā* and *ruḥiyy* was noted. *Marwah* is the small stone, or pebble. **[Jalālayn]** gives the sense of the rest: *shaʿāʾir* is the plural of *shaʿīrah*, the ritual ceremonies of His religion; "whoever performs the ḥajj to the House or the ʿumrah" — the original senses of *ḥajja* and *iʿtamara* being "to aim for" and "to visit" — and the original *tāʾ* of *yaṭṭawwafa* is assimilated, meaning to pace quickly between them seven times. It notes that the verse was revealed when the Muslims were averse to this pacing because the pagan Arabs used to pace between them with an idol atop each hill which they would stroke; and it records the difference over the obligation: Ibn ʿAbbās held that the pacing is not obligatory, on the ground that when no sin can be incurred the context implies free choice, while al-Shāfiʿī and others considered it a pillar of the pilgrimage rituals — and the Prophet ﷺ made its obligatory character clear when he said that God has prescribed for them the *saʿy*, as reported by al-Bayhaqī, and when he said, "begin with what God began," meaning Ṣafā, as reported by Muslim. **[Study Quran]** supplies the origin story: the two hills are between which pilgrims pass seven times, a practice traced to Hagar, who ran from one to the other seven times looking for water for Ismāʿīl after Ibrāhīm, at God's command, had left them there; and though the action was Hagar's, Muslims consider it part of the pilgrimage rites because it originated with Ibrāhīm, who built the House with Ismāʿīl once he had grown, and because the Prophet ﷺ continued the practice. It records the reports of the Companions' reluctance, the local legend that two people who fornicated in the Kaʿbah were turned to stone and slowly grew into the two hills, and the view that the verse answered those who thought the Kaʿbah alone should be circumambulated and that running to and fro had no place.

**The voluntary good.** "And whoever volunteers good — surely God is Thankful, Knowing" [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī]. **[Jalālayn]** reads the clause broadly: whoever performs a voluntary good deed — the pacing, or any other act of worship that is not incumbent on him — God is Thankful, that is, He appreciates and rewards him for it, and Knowing of it. **[Saʿdī]** places it as the natural close of a verse that has moved the rite from the column of blame to the column of honour: what was feared as a leftover of idolatry is announced as a rite of God, and over the whole passage the promise stands that what is offered voluntarily is not lost, since God knows it and will acknowledge it.

**The ruling read from the two texts.** **[Saʿdī]** argues the obligation from the joining of this verse with 22:32: if Ṣafā and Marwah are among God's rites, and God has said, "whoever magnifies the rites of God — that is from the piety of hearts," and piety is obligatory on every accountable person, then the *saʿy* between them is a duty of the ḥajj and the ʿumrah, as the majority hold — a position borne out by the Prophetic reports and by the Prophet's ﷺ own practice, with his instruction, "take your rites from me." He then reads the negation carefully: "no blame on him" removes an illusion, not an obligation — the Muslims were uneasy about the *ṭawāf* between the two hills because idols had been worshipped beside them in the Age of Ignorance, and God denied the blame to remove that unease, not because the act was optional. And he draws a fine legal point from the phrasing: the negation of blame is tied to one performing the ḥajj or the ʿumrah, which shows that the *saʿy* is not performed as a standalone voluntary act but only attached to a ḥajj or an ʿumrah — unlike the circumambulation of the House, which may be performed on its own as an act of worship. For the *saʿy*, the standing at ʿArafah and Muzdalīfah, and the pelting of the pillars follow the rite and belong to it; performed outside that frame they would be innovations — and he distinguishes two kinds of innovation: worshipping God by something He never legislated at all, and worshipping Him by something He legislated in a particular manner while performing it in a different manner. As for "whoever volunteers good," he reads it as any act of obedience done sincerely for God — ḥajj, ʿumrah, circumambulation, prayer, fasting and the rest — for it is good for him.

**Reflection.** The verse is a lesson in the weight of inherited habits. The Companions held back from a rite because their former enemies had performed it — and the Qurʾān does not answer with sentiment but with a divine title: these are the rites *of God*, and their history begins with the family Ibrāhīm was commanded to settle there. **[Qurṭubī]**'s report of ʿĀʾishah's argument from the wording is the sharpest thing in the passage: the verse says "no blame on him *in* going between them," which means the fear was about doing it, not about leaving it undone; the permission is for the scrupulous, not a licence for the negligent. And the closing line, about volunteering good, is what saves such a community from its scruples: where the doubt arose from a good impulse, the answer is that the good they perform — beyond obligation — is seen and acknowledged.


## 2:159

*"Truly those who conceal what We have sent down of the clear proofs and the guidance, after We made it clear to people in the Book — those are cursed by God and cursed by those who curse."*

**Meaning.** The Sūrah turns from the concealment it named earlier to its consequence [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies those meant as the scholars of the Jews and the Christians: they concealed from people the matter of Muḥammad ﷺ and left off following him, although they found him written in the Torah and the Gospel. The *bayyināt* they hid are what God made clear concerning his prophethood, his mission and his description in the two Books; the *hudā* is what He made plain to them of his affair in the scriptures He sent down to their prophets — and the charge is that they neither told people of it nor made known what God had clarified. **[Ṭabarī]**, **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Saʿdī]** all record the dispute over the verse's scope, and all three leave it open: it came down concerning the People of the Book and what they concealed of the Prophet's description and attributes, but its ruling is general for everyone marked by the concealment of what God has sent down. **[Saʿdī]** states the ground of the offence: God took the covenant from the people of knowledge to make clear to people what He had favoured them with of the knowledge of the Book and not to conceal it; so the one who casts that away commits two corruptions at once — concealing what God sent down, and defrauding God's servants. And he gives the punishment's fittingness: such people are cursed by God, that is, driven far away from His nearness and mercy, and cursed by the cursers — all creation — so that the curse falls on them from every quarter for their effort to defraud people, corrupt their religion and drive them from God's mercy. And he notes the reciprocity: as the one who teaches people good is blessed by God and His angels, and even by the fish in the depths of the water, for his service to creation and the reform of their religion, so the concealer of good is cursed by all.

**The ḥadīth and the rule.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports the Prophetic statement that gives the verse its practical edge: "Whoever is asked about knowledge he possesses and conceals it, God will bridle him on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire" — reported by Abū Hurayrah and ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ, and recorded by Ibn Mājah. He notes that the Muslim rulers compelled the People of the Book to disclose what they had of the description of the Prophet, and that the verse therefore strikes at any scholar who hides what people need of the knowledge of God's religion. **[Study Quran]** reads the verse's scope the same way: it may be general, so that it is sinful for anyone to obscure a truth of religion; or specific to the People of the Book around the Prophet ﷺ, with the report that some Muslims asked a group of them to point out the Prophet described in their Book and they refused; or it may mean that they conceal the truth of Islam itself, undercutting it, calling it false and failing to make known the foretelling of the Prophet's coming — and it points to the same theme at 2:174, 3:187 and 5:15. On the "cursers," it reports the views: the beasts of the earth; or the angels and the believers, as in 2:161; or that the denizens of Hell, who blame them for their own state, will curse them too.

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** gives the two terms compactly: the verse came down concerning the Jews, who concealed the clear proofs and the guidance — such as the verse of stoning and the description of Muḥammad ﷺ — after God had shown them clearly in the Torah; they shall be cursed by God, that is, He will distance them from His mercy, and by the cursers — the angels, the believers, or every single thing when it supplicates that they be cursed.

**Reflection.** The verse makes the scholar's office a trust and names the failure of it a curse, and **[Qurṭubī]**'s ḥadīth gives the offence its picture: knowledge held back from people who need it is not a private possession but a bridle of fire. **[Saʿdī]**'s pairing of the two corruptions is the verse's moral anatomy — what is concealed is hidden from God's servants as well as withheld from God's due — and his comparison of the cursers and the blessers is the passage's most sobering line: the same creation that blesses the teacher of good curses the one who keeps good to himself, and the fish in the water are on one side or the other.

## 2:160

*"Except those who repent, and make amends, and make clear — those, I shall relent toward them; and I am the Relenting, the Merciful."*

**Meaning.** The curse is not the last word, and the verse states the way back [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads the exception as an opening for the very people the previous verse described: those who concealed from people what they knew of the Prophet's prophethood and description, as God set it out in the Book and made clear to people, are cursed — except those among them who turn back from that concealment, return in repentance by believing in Muḥammad ﷺ and affirming his prophethood and accepting what he brought; who set their own state right by drawing near to God with good deeds that please Him; and who make clear what they knew of God's revelation which He entrusted to them in His Books and did not conceal it but made it known. Those are the ones I shall relent toward, making them people of return to My obedience and of turning toward My good pleasure. **[Jalālayn]** gives the three verbs with their objects: those who repent — turning back from such deeds; and make amends — in their actions; and make clear what they were concealing — them I shall relent toward, accepting their repentance; I am the Relenting, the Merciful. **[Study Quran]** observes that here, as elsewhere, "repent" and "relent" translate the same verb, whose root means to turn, used with different prepositions: the servant turns and God turns toward him — the reciprocity that runs through the Qurʾānic vocabulary of *tawbah*. It notes that "make amends" carries the sense of putting things right, and that "make clear" is understood to mean that they should address and clarify what they had concealed, with the cross-references to the discussions of repentance at 2:37, 2:128 and 4:17-18.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** reads the sequence as the passage's design: the text has been dealing with those who not only concealed the truth but went further in obstinacy; the ultimate fate of such persistence is obvious, and yet God still extends the promise of His mercy and forgiveness to those who repent, reflect on what they did and retrace their steps — and it notes that the exception contains all three conditions, so that a repentance which leaves the damage unrepaired and the truth still hidden is not the repentance this verse describes. **[Saʿdī]** draws the same point from the order of the verbs: turning back, then setting things right, then disclosing what was hidden — three acts covering the heart, the conduct and the public record.

**Reflection.** The verse is a door built into a wall of curse, and the three conditions make it precise. It is not enough to stop concealing; the concealed thing must be produced. The repentance that the verse accepts repairs the very harm that the offence caused — knowledge restored to those from whom it had been kept — and the closing names are the reason such a door exists at all: the One who relents is the One who is *al-Tawwāb*, the ever-turning, and *al-Raḥīm*.


## 2:161

*"Truly those who disbelieve, and die while they are disbelievers — on them is the curse of God, and of the angels, and of people all together."*

**Meaning.** The verse states what the concealment of the previous verses becomes when its owner persists to the end [Ṭabarī] [Study Quran] [Maʿārif]. **[Study Quran]** gives the sense of the key term: the curse is commonly understood as being distanced from God and driven away from His mercy; the curse of the angels and the believers is their invocation of God's curse upon the disbelievers, as Ṭabarī put it. And "people" may cover all human beings, or only some, as often in the Qurʾān; or it may mean that a man's own allies curse him in the Hereafter for misleading them — and since all human beings curse what is intrinsically vile, those who die in disbelief come to have the curse of all fall upon them one way or another. **[Jalālayn]** reads "while they are disbelievers" as a circumstantial clause, meaning that they died in that state, and glosses the curse as something they deserve in this life and the next, with "people" meaning either people generally or the believers in particular.

**Rulings — whom may one curse?** **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Maʿārif]** draw from the verse's condition a rule about the tongue. The verse ties the curse to dying in disbelief, and since no one can know how a particular person will die, a specific disbeliever may not be cursed by name: one cannot make his death in disbelief a settled matter. That the Prophet ﷺ did curse certain disbelievers by name is explained by the fact that their end was divinely disclosed to him. As for the disbelievers as a class — the tyrants and the unjust among them — cursing them without particularization is correct. **[Qurṭubī]** adduces the Prophetic instruction, "do not be a helper of Satan against your brother," in the case of Nuʿaymān after the fixed penalty had been carried out on him: one who has been punished by God's limit should not be cursed, whereas one who has not yet been punished may be — because the Prophet ﷺ cursed only those on whom the curse was due while they remained in the state that made it due; once such a person repents, desists, and is cleansed by the penalty, no curse attaches to him. **[Maʿārif]** makes the same point and presses it further: if cursing is disallowed even for an infidel whose death in disbelief is uncertain, how much more so for a Muslim — and it observes that careless speech of this kind, which treats the curse as ordinary vocabulary for one's dislikes, is a common failing in ordinary conversation, and it should be understood for what worship it is. It notes also the report of the Prophet's practice of cursing which al-Qurṭubī records, and its explanation. **[Study Quran]** adds al-Qurṭubī's further argument, that the curse in this passage concerns the Hereafter: a curse is meant as a prodding away from disbelief and a communication of disapproval, and so is of no use in the case of someone who is dead or insane — hence the verse and its like are read as a description of the Hereafter rather than as a command to action in this world, with 29:25 in the background: "then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another, and you will curse one another." **[Ṭabarī]**'s gloss of the divine curse as expulsion from mercy, and of the angels' and people's curse as their supplication for it, underlies all these discussions.

**Reflection.** The verse describes a settled condition, not a momentary one: the man who disbelieves and stays in it till death, and then finds that the whole of creation — God, the angels, and people — is against him. And the legal discussion the commentators attach to it is a useful check on the way such verses are used: the curse belongs to God, its content is distance from mercy, and the servant's share in it is supplication, not invective — which is why **[Qurṭubī]**'s precaution about naming individuals follows so directly from the verse's own wording: the condition it states is not a thing a human being can certify about anyone's future, and language that treats it as known has exceeded the verse.

## 2:162

*"Abiding therein; the punishment shall not be lightened for them, nor shall they be given respite."*

**Meaning.** The last clause of this passage is a sentence of permanence [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** settles the grammar: *khālidīn* — abiding — is in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in "on them," so that the sense is: those are they whom God, the angels and people all together curse, abiding in it. He notes that an alternative reading has the sentence end differently, with "the angels and people all together" in the nominative, and that while this is permissible in Arabic in itself, it is not permissible to recite it, because it contradicts the codices of the Muslims and the reading that has come down from them in wide transmission — and the anomalous reading cannot be used as an argument against what is firmly established. **[Jalālayn]** identifies what they abide in: the curse and the Fire, the latter indicated by what follows — and explains the two negations: the punishment is not lightened for them, not even for the blink of an eye; and they are given no respite, no delay in which to repent or to offer excuses. **[Study Quran]** notes that the same statement about the punishment not being lightened recurs at 2:86, at 3:88 in the same wording, and at 16:85, 35:36 and 43:75, and refers the reader to the discussion of the abiding in the Fire and its duration at 2:80-82 and to the essay on death, dying and the afterlife in the Qurʾān.

**Belief.** The pair of negations is deliberate, and the tradition's reading of them names the two things a condemned person hopes for: an easing of the sentence, and a delay. **[Jalālayn]** closes both doors — no lightening, however brief, and no postponement for repentance or excuse — and **[Study Quran]**'s parallel passages show how consistently the Qurʾān repeats the formula. **[Ṭabarī]**'s editorial point about the reading is worth noting in its own right: he treats the canonical recitation as a settled authority that even a grammatically admissible variant cannot displace, which is the same instinct that makes him refuse to treat a general verse as particular without evidence, and it belongs to the same discipline with which he handles the abrogation and the qiblah.

**Reflection.** The verse ends the passage on concealment with the two things no one can bargain for: time and relief. Everything the Qurʾān asks of a human being is asked within the span in which both are still possible — the truth still publishable, the sentence still commutable by repentance — and the finality of these lines is what gives the earlier verse's "except those who repent" its urgency. The passage has run from a curse, to a door, to a closed door — and the closing of the door is stated only so that no reader will wait for a time that does not come.


## 2:163

*"And your God is one God; there is no god but He, the Compassionate, the Merciful."*

**Meaning.** After the warnings about concealing the truth, the Sūrah states what must not be concealed [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Qurṭubī]** draws the connection: when God had warned against hiding the truth, He showed that the first thing that must be made known and may not be concealed is the matter of divine oneness — and He joined it to the mention of the proof and the way of reflection, namely thought upon the wonders of creation, so that it be known that the world must have a maker who resembles nothing. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the terms: *ulūhiyyah* is being worshipped; and the sense of the verse is that the One who deserves your obedience, O people, and has a claim on your worship, is one God and one Lord — so do not worship another, and do not associate anything with Him, since whatever you associate with Him in worship is a creature of your God, like yourselves; your God is one, with no like and no peer. He records the dispute over the meaning of God's oneness: some held it is the negation of likenesses and similitudes, as when one says a man is "the unique one of his people," meaning he has no peer among them — so "God is one" means God has no like and no equal. **[Saʿdī]** unfolds the same in its four dimensions: He is one, alone and unique in His essence, His names, His attributes and His acts — no partner in His essence, no namesake, no equal, no likeness, no parallel, no creator or disposer other than Him; and being so, He alone is entitled to be deified and worshipped with every kind of worship, and no creature may be associated with Him. And the two names at the end supply the reason: He is *al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm*, possessed of a mercy so great that no one's mercy resembles it — it has encompassed everything and reached every living being; by His mercy creatures exist, by it they obtain every perfection, by it every harm is repelled from them; and by His mercy He made Himself known to His servants through His attributes and His bounties, and explained to them everything they need of the interests of their religion and their world by sending messengers and sending down books. So when one knows that every blessing anyone has is from God, and that no creature benefits another, it is known that God alone deserves every kind of worship and is to be singled out for love, fear, hope, reverence, reliance and the rest of the acts of obedience — and that there is no injustice viler or uglier than to turn from His worship to the worship of slaves, and to associate creatures made of dust with the Lord of lords, or to worship the creature — incapable in every respect — alongside the Creator, powerful and disposing, who has subdued everything and to whom everything submits.

**Context and merit.** **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Jalālayn]** give the occasion: the disbelievers of Quraysh said, "O Muḥammad, describe your Lord to us, give us his lineage" — and God sent down Sūrat al-Ikhlāṣ and this verse; and the idolaters had three hundred and sixty idols, while God declared that He is one. **[Maʿārif]** notes the puzzlement the verse produced among the associators, who found it hard to see how one single object of worship could be for the whole wide world, and that the following verses embody the proof in brief. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the ḥadīth of Asmāʾ bint Yazīd b. al-Sakān, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "God's greatest name is contained in these two verses" — this one and the one following. And **[Qurṭubī]** observes the structure of the central phrase: "there is no god but He" is negation and affirmation, its first half unbelief and its last faith. **[Study Quran]** notes that the verse is among the most often recited in the Qurʾān, and that God is rendered by *ilāh*, the general noun for a god or divinity, rather than the supreme personal name *Allāh*; that *wāḥid*, one, includes the sense of being unique, not composed of parts, without equal or like.

**Reflection.** The verse's placement is the point: having spent a long passage on those who concealed the truth about a prophet, the Sūrah states the truth about God — the thing the concealment was for. And the argument runs in the order **[Saʿdī]** lays out: oneness names what worship is owed, and mercy names why; the God who has no peer is the God whose mercy has reached everything, so that the worship of anything else is not merely error but the ugliest of injustices — turning from the Lord of lords to slaves made of dust.


## 2:164

*"Surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ships that run upon the sea with what benefits people, and the water God sends down from the sky, reviving the earth with it after its death and scattering in it every kind of creature, and the shifting of the winds, and the clouds subdued between the sky and the earth — surely there are signs for a people who understand."*

**Meaning.** The verse supplies the proof the previous declaration of oneness would need, and it takes the proof from what everyone can see [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** frames the argument: if you are ignorant of, or doubt, the truth of what I have told you — that your God is one God, apart from the rivals and idols you claim as deities — then reflect on My proofs and think them through. Among My proofs are the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the ships that run upon the sea with what profits people, the water I send down from the sky reviving the earth after its death, the creatures I have scattered through it, and the clouds subdued between the sky and the earth. If the idols and rivals you worship — all of them gathered together, or each one separately — could create the like of any single thing I have named, then you would have an excuse in worshipping them; but if not, there is no excuse for taking any god besides Me, and no god exists for you or for what you worship other than Me. He adds that the thoughtful should observe how God compresses His argument against all who disbelieve in Him, in this verse and the one after it, into the fewest words, the most compelling proof and the finest meaning, bringing them to the edge of knowing the excellence of His wisdom and His eloquence. **[Qurṭubī]** and **[Jalālayn]** give the occasion: ʿAṭāʾ said that when "and your God is one God" was revealed, the disbelievers of Quraysh said, "How can one god suffice all people?" and this verse came down; and Sufyān, from his father, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā, that they said, "Is there any proof for that?" and God sent down "surely in the creation of the heavens and the earth" — so that they asked for a sign, and God showed them the proof of oneness and that this world, this wondrous structure, must have a builder and a maker.

**The signs, one by one.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes the plural of heavens and the singular of earth: the heavens are different kinds, each of a kind other than the next, while the earth is all dust. The sign in the heavens is that they stand raised without pillars beneath them or supports above them — which points to power and to the breaching of the ordinary course of things, since a prophet who challenged others to suspend a mountain in the air without support would be working a miracle; and then the second sign is what the heavens contain: the sun, the moon, the moving stars and shining planets, rising and setting, luminous and effaced. The sign in the earth is its seas, rivers, minerals, trees, plains and mountains. **[Saʿdī]** works each element into the argument. In the creation of the heavens: their height, expanse, firmness and perfection, and what God placed in them of sun, moon and stars ordered for people's interests. In the creation of the earth: that it is spread out as a cradle for creation so that they may settle on it and draw benefit from it and take lesson — and all of this points to God's being alone in creation and disposal, to the greatness of the power by which He made them, the wisdom by which He perfected and ordered them, the knowledge and mercy by which He stored in them what He stored of benefits, interests and necessities. That is the fullest proof of His perfection and of His deserving to be worshipped alone, since He is alone in creating, disposing and managing the affairs of His servants. In the alternation of night and day: their constant taking one another's place, one following as the other leaves, and their variation in heat, cold and temperateness, in length, shortness and the mean between — and the seasons that arise from that, by which the interests of human beings and their animals are ordered, and all that is on the face of the earth of trees and vegetation; all of it in such order, disposal and subjection as dazzles minds and defeats even the most capable men from grasping it. In the ships that run upon the sea: God inspired His servants to make them, created for them the inner and outer instruments that enabled them, and then subjected to them this great sea, and the winds that carry them with their passengers, wealth and goods, which are among people's benefits and by which their interests and livelihoods are ordered — and who is it that inspired them to build, if not the One whose power sustains it? In the water sent down from the sky, reviving the earth after its death and scattering in it every kind of creature: the life of hearts and bodies together. In the shifting of the winds, and the clouds subdued between sky and earth: the winds are dispatched between the hands of His mercy, and the clouds are driven and held between two spaces by His command. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gathers the same: the sky with its height, intricate design, vastness and the orbiting bodies in it; the earth with its density, lowlands, mountains, seas, deserts and valleys and the beneficial things it holds; and the alternation of night and day, one coming and going while the other follows without delay, just as "it is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each floats in an orbit" (36:40). **[Study Quran]** notes that such lists of natural and cosmic phenomena as signs appear throughout the Qurʾān, sometimes singly and sometimes in series, as at 30:20-27, and that the elements here recur elsewhere: the variation of night and day (3:190; 10:6; 23:80; 45:5), the creation of the heavens and the earth (3:190; 30:22; 42:29), ships that sail upon the sea (14:32; 17:66; 31:31; 42:32), the revival of the earth (16:65; 30:19; 57:17), winds as signs and blessings (7:57; 15:22; 25:48; 30:46), and the clouds made to course and held subdued. It observes that ships are significant as the only human-made item in the list, yet so intimately connected with the natural world, and so fragile next to the sea, that the very possibility of seafaring and its precariousness are a reminder of God — and it notes that in other passages it is during a storm at sea that human beings turn to God sincerely, only to lapse when the storm has passed (29:65; 31:32). And it points out that the word for wind, *rīḥ*, shares a root with *rūḥ*, spirit. **[Maʿārif]** notes that the series of signs can be grasped by the learned and the ignorant alike: who can bypass the wonder of the creation of the heavens and the earth, or ignore the constant alternation of night and day? Their origination and their perpetuity are the work of perfect power alone. And it draws attention to the wonder in the water: that a substance so fluid was given the property of carrying on its back ships bearing tons of weight from East to West — if water had not been given a state in which its molecules move freely among themselves while remaining one mass, all this maritime activity would not exist. **[Jalālayn]** gives the same inventory compactly, closing as the verse does: surely in these there are signs indicating His oneness and His power for a people who comprehend, that is, who contemplate.

**Reflection.** The verse answers a demand for a sign by pointing at everything. Its argument is not a syllogism but an inventory: the sky, the calendar, the shipping lane, the rain, the creatures it wakes, the wind and the cloud — and then the claim that all of this could not be the work of anything but one disposing will, since the gods they set beside Him cannot make the like of a single item on the list. And the phrase at the end, "a people who understand," is the verse's own limit: **[Saʿdī]** observes that the signs profit a person according to the mind God has given him and his use of it, since these proofs are not for those who look without considering, but for those who work their minds on what the world was made to teach.


## 2:165

*"And among people are those who take equals besides God, loving them as God is loved; but those who believe are more ardent in their love of God. If only those who do wrong could see, when they see the punishment, that power belongs altogether to God, and that God is severe in punishment —"*

**Meaning.** After the proofs of oneness, the Sūrah names the fact that defeats them in practice [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** opens with the fit of the passage: what a fine connection this verse has with the one before it — for when God had explained His oneness and its decisive proofs and shining demonstrations, leading to certainty and removing every doubt, He stated here that among people, *despite* that complete clarification, there are those who take from among creatures "equals" for God: peers and counterparts whom they equate with Him in worship, love, reverence and obedience. And whoever is in that condition after the proof has been established and oneness made clear is known to be either an obstinate opponent of God and a breaker with Him, or someone who has turned away from reflecting on His signs and pondering His creatures — in which case he has not the least excuse; the word of punishment is due upon him. He then draws the distinction on which the whole verse turns: these people do not equate their rivals with God in creation, provision or disposal — they equate them with Him in *worship*, worshipping them that they may bring them near. And the very word "take" (*ittakhadhū*) is evidence that God has no equal: the idolaters made certain creatures into equals for Him, a mere naming, a word empty of meaning — as the Qurʾān says elsewhere, "they have ascribed to God partners; say: name them — or do you inform Him of something He does not know in the earth? — or is it but a saying?" and "they are nothing but names you and your fathers have named; God has sent down no authority for them; they follow nothing but conjecture" (53:23, 28). The creature is not a peer of God, since God is the Creator and everything else is created; the Lord is the Provider and all besides Him is provided for; God is the Rich and you are the poor; He is complete in every respect and the servants are deficient in every respect; God benefits and harms, while the creature has no part in benefit, harm or command. So it is known with certainty that the position of those who take gods and equals besides God is void — whether the object be an angel, a prophet, a righteous man, an idol or anything else — and that God alone deserves complete love and total humility. Therefore God praised the believers: "those who believe are more ardent in their love of God" — more ardent than the people of equals are in their love of their equals: because the believers have made their love purely for Him, while those have associated others in it; because the believers love the One who truly deserves love, whose love is the very substance of the servant's soundness, felicity and success; while the idolaters love what deserves no love at all, and whose love is the very substance of the servant's misery, corruption and disarray. And so the threat: "if only those who do wrong could see" — by taking equals and by subjecting themselves to other than the Lord of servants, and wronging creation by blocking God's way and working toward their own harm — "when they see the punishment" — that is, on the Day of Resurrection, with their own eyes — "that power belongs altogether to God, and that God is severe in punishment." Then they would know with certainty that strength and power belong to God entirely, and that their equals have no strength in them at all; their weakness and incapacity would become clear to them on that day.

**Who the equals are.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains *andād* as peers and equals, and reports the early authorities on what these were: Qatāda and Mujāhid said they are the idols and gods the disbelievers worshipped besides God, with Mujāhid adding that they loved them in rivalry and counterfeiting of the truth — and Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Suddī said the *andād* are the leaders, obeyed as God should be obeyed. **[Qurṭubī]** gives both readings of the phrase "loving them as God is loved": al-Mubarrad read it as the idolaters loving their idols in falsehood in the measure that the believers love God in truth; al-Zajjāj, that they love them though they are powerless, while the believers love God who is powerful. **[Study Quran]** lays out the possibilities the wording permits: that they love their idols as the believers love God; that they obey their leaders as they should obey God; that they love these equals as they themselves love God, dividing their love between God and the idols; that they love them as God ought to be loved; and that they glorify and obey their idols, or their human leaders, or other human agencies, as they should God. It explains why the believers' love is called more ardent: it is directed undividedly at the one true object of love, whereas the idolaters direct love toward idols in ordinary times and toward God in times of need — as when they call out to Him when a ship is buffeted by the waves. And it gathers the Qurʾān's use of *ḥubb*: the human love of God at 2:165, 3:31 ("say: if you love God, follow me"), 5:54 ("God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him") and 9:24; the ḥadīth in which a man told the Prophet ﷺ that he had not prepared much in the way of prayer, fasting or alms, but that he loved God and His Messenger, and was told, "you will be with those whom you love"; and the dozens of places where the word describes what God loves — the virtuous, the repentant, the reverent, the patient, those who trust, the just, those who strive in His way, those who purify themselves — and what He does not love: disbelief, transgression, sin, wrongdoing, vainglory, corruption, prodigality, treachery and exultation. **[Maʿārif]** puts the contrast in one sentence: a polytheist may turn away from his self-made god at the first impending loss, while a true believer reposes total confidence in God in gain and loss alike, holding His love and pleasure as his lasting possession. And it observes the verse's subtle suggestion about the wrongdoers: the opportunity to correct their position had been there, since their own frustrations with their gods could have taught them that these were helpless and that real power rested with God — but they missed it, and now they must learn the hard way.

**Language.** **[Jalālayn]** works through the syntax of the closing sentence: *idh* here is effectively *idhā*, "when"; the verb "they see" is read both in the active and in the passive; the "that" clause — that power belongs altogether to God, and that God is terrible in chastisement — stands in place of the objects of the verb; and the answer to the opening conditional is left unstated, to be understood: were they to see this, they would not have taken equals. **[Study Quran]** gives the same alternative: "if *you* saw those who do wrong when they see the punishment, [you would see] that power belongs wholly to God." **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that the verse is followed directly by the scene in which the followed disown the followers, and the Fire is shown as the end of both.

**Reflection.** The verse weighs loves, and its criterion is not intensity but integrity. The idolater's affection for his equals can look strong, but it is distributed, and it collapses under pressure; the believer's love of God is called more ardent because it holds when nothing else does. **[Saʿdī]**'s argument about the word "take" is the philosophical core: an equal that must be manufactured by the worshipper was never an equal — the creature is created, provided for, poor, deficient and powerless, and the sentence against its deification is written into what it is. And the unfinished conditional at the end is the verse's art: the sight that would have prevented the whole business is exactly the sight they refused in this world, and the verse leaves it hanging as a door that was open and is now being closed.


## 2:166

*"When those who were followed disown those who followed them, and they see the punishment, and the ties are cut from them."*

**Meaning.** The verse opens the scene into which the unfinished conditional of the previous verse was pointing [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** reports the identification: Qatāda said those who were followed are the tyrants, the leaders and the heads in the ways of association with God, and those who followed are the weak followers; al-Rabīʿ said the leaders disown the followers on the Day of Resurrection; and ʿAṭāʾ, in Ibn Jurayj's report, that their chiefs, commanders and masters disown those who followed them. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same, and adds the further reading of Qatāda and al-Suddī that the followed are the devils who led astray, disowning human beings — while others held the verse general in every followed one, whatever he may be. On "and they see the punishment," he notes that the seeing belongs to both parties, and if it is asked whether this is the certainty of it at death or the sight of it in the Hereafter, both are included: at death they perceive the humiliation to which they are going, and in the Hereafter they taste the painful punishment and the exemplary retribution. And "the ties are cut from them": Mujāhid and others said these are the connections by which they joined one another in the world — kinship and the like; al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd said they are their deeds. The singular is *sabab*, and its original sense is a rope with which one binds a thing and draws it, so that everything that draws something else came to be called a *sabab*; and it also means a direction or side, as in Zuḥayr's line, "whoever fears the approaches of deaths — they will reach him, even if he seeks the rope-ladders to the sky."

**The scene.** **[Study Quran]** lists the possible referents: the leaders of idolatry and their minions and adherents; or the satans and the human beings who followed them; or generally all who led and followed in the ways of error in the life of the world. On "recourse" — *asbāb* — it gives the meanings the term carries: a rope, a means by which to obtain something, or a cause; here understood as the bonds, love, friendships and blood ties they shared in the world, all of which will be severed from them as a means of help in the Hereafter — with the further interpretation that the recourse is their deeds in this life, which remain sound in the Hereafter if they are righteous and are cut off when they are evil; and the sense that they will have no way of staving off the punishment or escaping the consequences of what they did. **[Ibn Kathīr]** supplies the Qurʾānic parallels for the disowning: the angels they used to claim to worship declare their innocence of them on that day — "we declare our innocence before You; it was not us they worshipped" (28:63) — and "glorified be You! You are our protector, not they; rather they used to worship the jinn" (34:41); and the verse runs on from there into the followers' cry, in 2:167. **[Maʿārif]** draws the scene's human analogy: the severity of the threatened punishment unfolds when the leaders disown their votaries, and both the leaders and the led witness the punishment while whatever bonds of leading and following existed between them are snapped apart — very much as happens in this world when people share in an illegality and then wriggle out when apprehended, to the point of refusing to recognize their own accomplices. **[Jalālayn]** notes the syntax: the *idh* here continues the *idh* of the previous verse; the leaders disown their followers, denying that they misled them; and the cords — the bonds of affection and kinship that were between them in the world — are cut away from them, the cutting being joined to the disowning as a second act of the same moment.

**Reflection.** The verse is the exact reversal of the relationship the previous verses described. In this world, the followed were the powerful ones, the makers of opinion, the objects of a loyalty that imitated the love owed to God; in the next, the loyalty runs one way only, and the leaders — whether idols, chiefs or devils — are the first to disclaim. **[Qurṭubī]**'s gloss of *asbāb* as ropes is worth keeping: everything the followers depended on was a cord, and the verse says the cords were cut. And this is the fate of every structure in which the many obey the few against the truth, which is why the passage lets the followers speak next.

## 2:167

*"And those who followed say: 'If only we had another turn, we would disown them as they disowned us.' Thus God shows them their deeds as regrets for them, and they shall never leave the Fire."*

**Meaning.** The followers answer, and their answer is a wish for a second chance [Jalālayn] [Study Quran] [Maʿārif]. **[Jalālayn]** gives the construction: the "if only" is optative, and its answer is "we would disown them" — that is, if only we might return to the world, we would disown the ones who were followed, as they have disowned us. And just as God showed them the severity of His chastisement and their mutual disowning, so He shows them their evil deeds as anguish — regrets for them, a circumstantial qualification of the showing. And the last clause closes the door: never shall they leave the Fire once they have entered it. **[Study Quran]** explains "another turn" as the chance to return to the world, and the regret as concerning both the sins committed and the good deeds omitted: they see what they would have had in the Hereafter had they acted righteously, and are tormented by it — with another interpretation that they will see the dwellings of the Garden and wish for them while its inhabitants see them and wish that God would bless them. It sets the scene beside 29:25, "then on the Day of Resurrection you will disown one another, and you will curse one another," and the conversations among the denizens of Hell at 7:38-39, and Satan's address on the Day of Judgement in 14:22: "God made you a promise of truth, and I made you a promise, and I failed you." And it reports al-Ṭabarī's reading of the closing clause: their regret and their desire for another chance will not remove them from the Fire — which he takes as evidence that the disbelievers remain in it everlastingly. **[Maʿārif]** gives the scene its psychology: when the so-called people of their leaders see the turnabout, they fret and fume but can do nothing except wish for a return to the world where they might square things with their smooth-tongued leaders — and this time, they think, they would refuse the allegiance and do to them what they had done to us.

**The showing of deeds.** The phrase "thus God shows them their deeds" is the verse's quiet centre: the punishment is not an arbitrary infliction laid over the guilty, but their own record, produced and displayed, so that their torment is what they see of what they did. **[Saʿdī]**, reading these verses together, had made the same point from the opposite end — the reckoning on that day is each man's own work, and neither lineage nor following will be asked about. And **[Jalālayn]**'s "regrets for them" makes the display an instrument: what is shown is shown *as* regret, which is the only form in which a dead act can still be experienced.

**Reflection.** The two verses together are a study in the structure of influence. The followers did not invent their error — they inherited it from those they venerated, and the Qurʾān will not let them off; but neither will it let the leaders off, and the disowning cuts both ways. What the passage denies is the notion that one can hide behind another on that day: the ties are cut, the loyalty reversed, and the record shown. And the wish to return is stated precisely in order to be denied: they want to do to their leaders what their leaders did to them — which is the same act they are being punished for, only this time aimed at the right target; and the verse answers that the time for choosing whom to disown has passed.


## 2:168

*"O people, eat of what is lawful and good in the earth, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan; surely he is a manifest enemy to you."*

**Meaning.** The verse turns from the claims of the followers to the everyday matter of what one may eat [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** notes that the address is to all people, believer and disbeliever alike: God favours them by commanding them to eat of all that is in the earth — grains, fruits, produce and animals — *lawful*, that is, permitted to them, not seized or stolen, not acquired by a forbidden transaction, not eaten in a forbidden manner nor used to aid something forbidden; and *good*, that is, not foul like carrion, blood, swine's flesh and the other repugnant things. From the verse he draws two principles: that the default in things is permissibility, in eating and in use; and that the forbidden is of two kinds — what is forbidden in itself, the foul that is the opposite of the good, and what is forbidden for an extrinsic reason, namely a right of God or of His servants attached to it, which is the opposite of the lawful. He also draws the inference that eating enough to sustain the body is obligatory, and that one who abandons it sins, because the command is in the imperative. And since God has commanded what is their very welfare, He forbade them the following of the footsteps of Satan — his paths and the ways he commands, which are all the acts of disobedience: disbelief, sinfulness and wrong. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the historical application: eat of what I have made lawful for you through My Messenger ﷺ, which you forbid yourselves of the *baḥīrah*, the *sāʾibah*, the *waṣīlah* and the like which I did not forbid — as opposed to what I did forbid, which I have made foul: carrion, blood, swine's flesh and what is dedicated to other than Me — and leave the footsteps of Satan, who destroys you, brings you to the watering-places of ruin, and forbids you your own property. **[Qurṭubī]** reports the occasion: the verse came down concerning Thaqīf, Khuzāʿah and Banū Mudlij, in what they had forbidden themselves of livestock, while the wording is universal. And he gives the difference over *ṭayyib*: Mālik held that the good here is the lawful, so that the two words are an emphasis of one sense with different wording; al-Shāfiʿī held that the good is the pleasant, so that the two are a division, which is why the eating of repugnant animals is forbidden. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the verse in its context: after declaring that there is no god but He and that He alone created, God stated that He is the sustainer of His creation and mentioned a favour He granted them — that He has allowed them to eat of the pure, lawful things of the earth which do not harm body or mind — and forbade them the following of Satan's ways and methods with which he misguides his followers, such as forbidding the *baḥīrah* and the *sāʾibah*. **[Study Quran]** notes the same occasion and the same universal import, explains *ḥalāl* as what the Law deems permissible from a root with the senses of untying, setting free and unbinding, and *ṭayyib* as pleasant and delicious; traces the image of following Satan's footsteps elsewhere (2:208; 6:142; 24:21), where the commentators gloss it as submitting to temptation and committing evil; and notes that Satan is called a manifest enemy in many places (7:22; 12:5; 17:53; 28:15; 36:60; 43:62). It mentions the related matter of oaths — some relating the verse to the practice of swearing to refrain from something, oaths not being valid in anger and requiring expiation when taken so, with the discussion of carelessness in oaths belonging to 2:225 — and it records the ḥadīth qudsī, "I created My servants as ḥanīfs; then the satans came to them and diverted them from their religion and forbade for them what I had made lawful," and the exchange in which a Companion asked how his supplication might be answered and was told, "make your food wholesome, and your supplication will be answered; a man puts a forbidden morsel in his mouth and his supplication is not accepted for forty days." **[Maʿārif]** notes the root sense of *ḥalāl* — the opening of a knot, so that the permitted is what has been released from restriction — and reports Sahl b. ʿAbdullāh's saying that salvation depends on three things: eating the lawful, fulfilling divine obligations, and following the Sunnah; it explains *khutuwāt* as the distance between the feet in striding, so that Satan's footsteps are his deeds; and it lists the polytheistic practices the verse addresses, such as releasing animals in the names of idols. **[Jalālayn]** gives the occasion in brief — the verse came down when some declared it unlawful to take a released she-camel — and reads *ṭayyib* as an adjective of emphasis: that is, what is delicious.

**Reflection.** The verse is a small charter of the ordinary: what one eats is God's gift, subject to two filters, the lawful and the wholesome, and the enemy's first move is not to make people sin but to make them forbid themselves what God permitted. **[Ṭabarī]**'s picture — Satan forbidding you your own property — is the exact mechanism the passage has been describing in the *baḥīrah* and the *sāʾibah*, and **[Study Quran]**'s ḥadīth qudsī states the same in God's own words: the servants were created ḥanīf, and the satans came and forbade what God had made lawful. Against that, the verse's two words do the work of religion in the kitchen: permission received, and goodness required — with the reminder that the God who forbade the foul did not intend the rest to be renounced.

## 2:169

*"He only commands you to evil and indecency, and that you should say of God what you do not know."*

**Meaning.** The verse names what the footsteps of the previous verse lead to, and the three terms climb [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** explains each: the *sūʾ* — evil — is sin, from the root by which one says a thing saddened him; it is called evil because of what its end will make of its doer, since its consequence with God is grief. The *faḥshāʾ* is everything whose mention is abhorrent and whose hearing is ugly, and it is said to be specifically fornication, so called because of the ugliness of speaking of it and the hatred of what the doer is remembered by.
