And the third and last command of the devil is that you should say of God what you do not know. **[Jalālayn]** fills that clause in: such as forbidding what He has not forbidden. **[Saʿdī]** reads the sequence as the satanic programme in full: the footsteps of Satan are all the acts of disobedience, from disbelief and sinfulness to wrongdoing — and the verse identifies the three ranks the enemy works along: the doing of evil, the commission of what is shameful, and the speech that legislates for God without knowledge. **[Study Quran]** notes that Satan's command of indecency is mentioned also at 2:268 and 24:21, and that elsewhere both God and the prayer are described as forbidding and preventing indecency (7:28; 16:90; 29:45); it records al-Ṭabarī's connection of the indecency here to the sacrificial practices spoken of in 5:103 — "God has not established the *baḥīrah*, the *sāʾibah*, the *waṣīlah* or the *ḥām*" — with the comment that those who disbelieve fabricate lies against God and most of them do not understand. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the verse as the explanation of the previous one: Satan commands what is evil and shameful, and that people should say about God what they do not know.

**Reflection.** The order of the three clauses is deliberate, and its climax is not the immoral act but the untutored pronouncement about God. Something may be permitted or forbidden — that is not settled by taste, custom, or the authority of the ancestors, but by revelation; and the one who invents such rulings in God's name has moved from being a follower of his appetites to being their lawgiver. The whole passage about the *baḥīrah* and the *sāʾibah* is compressed here: the devil's final service to himself is not to make a man sin, but to make him legislate.


## 2:170

*"And when it is said to them, 'Follow what God has sent down,' they say, 'Rather we follow what we found our fathers practicing.' What — even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?"*

**Meaning.** The verse reports the answer the call habitually receives and then dissolves it [Ṭabarī] [Maʿārif] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** notes two readings of the pronoun in "to them": it may return to the "one who takes equals" of 2:165, so that the verse continues that portrait — the man who takes rivals besides God is the man who, when told to follow what God sent down, answers that he follows his fathers; or it may return to "people" in the address of 2:168, the speech passing from direct address to report of the absent, as is ordinary in the Qurʾān. **[Qurṭubī]** records the identifications: the disbelievers of the Arabs, per one view; the Jews, per Ibn ʿAbbās; or the "people" of 2:168, per al-Ṭabarī; and he gives the lexical note that *alfaynā* is "we found," with the poet's line, "I found him one who gives no cause for blame and remembers God but little." **[Study Quran]** places the verse among the many in which recourse to mere custom is refused as an excuse: "sufficient for us is that which we found our fathers practicing" (5:104) — followed by the same rebuke, "what, even if their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?" — and the similar addresses to the Children of Ādam (7:28), to the Egyptians (10:78), to Ibrāhīm's people (21:53-54) and to people generally (31:21; 43:24). It notes that commentators connect the verse either to the norms of lawful and forbidden discussed just before, or take it as addressed to the idolaters and the People of the Book, or to people in general. **[Ibn Kathīr]** states the reference of the imitation: they mean the worship of idols and false deities, and God refuted them by asking whether they would do so even if those they followed and imitated had no understanding and no guidance. **[Maʿārif]** sets out the logic the verse dismantles: the idolaters refused the revealed injunctions on the ground that they would rather follow the customary practice inherited from their fathers, assuming that those models were divinely appointed to their way; and God's answer destroys the assumption by the single question — how could they follow those ways in all conditions, to the exclusion of every other, even if the fathers understood little of the true faith and were never given guidance by their Lord? **[Jalālayn]** reads the answer as naming what was inherited — idolatry, declaring the released camel lawful or unlawful, and the slitting of the camel's ear — and the rebuke as addressed to the practice of following the unguided.

**Reflection.** The verse is the Sūrah's most economical statement of a principle that recurs in the Qurʾān's dealings with every community: the authority of the ancestors is not an argument, and to answer a command of God with "this is what we found our parents doing" is to answer a proof with a habit. Its question, "even if their fathers understood nothing and were not guided?", identifies the fatal defect in such transmission — not that it is old, but that nothing in it can be demonstrated to a living mind. What the verse leaves standing is not the rejection of inheritance as such but of inheritance as a substitute for understanding; and the parable that follows describes the position of those who keep the habit without the understanding.

## 2:171

*"And the likeness of those who disbelieve is as the likeness of one who cries out to what hears nothing but a call and a cry. Deaf, dumb, blind — so they do not understand."*

**Meaning.** The parable is drawn, and its point is the gap between sound and sense [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** reports the two lines of interpretation. Some took the likeness to be the disbelievers' own manner of understanding: like a beast that hears the voice when it is called — ʿIkrimah said like a camel or a donkey, from another report like a sheep — and does not grasp what is said to it; so the disbeliever hears what is recited to him from God's Book without comprehending it, and hears what he is called to of God's oneness and admonition without good acceptance. Others took the likeness as the calling itself: the idolaters call upon idols that hear nothing — the one who cries out being the worshipper and the cry reaching what cannot hear it. **[Study Quran]** gives both senses: the verse suggests that calling to disbelievers is like calling to sheep — they hear, but only the sound and not the meaning of the call — while it may also refer to the prayers the idolaters offer to idols, which the insensate idols cannot hear; and it notes that insensibility to the wisdom of revelation is described with animal metaphors elsewhere, as at 62:5, "the parable of those who were made to bear the Torah and did not bear it is that of an ass bearing books," and 7:176's dog, while being deaf, dumb and blind is attributed to the disbelievers also at 2:18, 8:22 and 17:97. **[Saʿdī]** reads the parable in its context: once God had shown their refusal to submit to what the messengers brought and their rejection of it in favour of imitation, it was known that they were not receptive to the truth or answerable to it — indeed it was evident to everyone that they would not leave their obstinacy. So God informed us that their likeness, when a caller calls them to faith, is the likeness of livestock whose herdsman calls to them: they hear the bare sound that establishes the proof against them, but they do not grasp it with a grasp that profits them. Therefore they are deaf — not hearing the truth with a hearing of understanding and acceptance; blind — not looking with a look of consideration; dumb — not saying what would be good for them; and the cause of all of it is that they have no sound reason, but are the most foolish of the foolish and the most ignorant of the ignorant. **[Maʿārif]** gives the same progression through the three epithets: they hear the call but not what is meant to correct them, so they are called deaf; they are tight-lipped about accepting the truth, so they are called dumb; and since they do not see their own benefit or loss, they are called blind — with the senses so dulled that the whole person seems less than what he was made. **[Jalālayn]** reads the likeness as the calling shepherd and his flock: the disbelievers, when they listen to admonition, are like cattle that hear the shepherd's cry but do not understand what he is saying — and it applies the three words as the verse does: deaf, dumb, blind, not comprehending any admonition.

**Reflection.** The parable identifies the precise failure of the previous verse's imitators: they are not accused of refusing to hear, but of hearing only the noise. Everything the caller says reaches them as sound — the proof is established, the call is delivered — and nothing arrives as meaning, which is why the verse ends with "so they do not understand" rather than "so they do not obey." And the three adjectives name what has been lost in each direction: the ear that takes in words, the tongue that could state a case, the eye that could look and consider. The passage has been showing a community that answered revelation with inheritance; the parable shows what the answer means — a man who has kept the voice and let go of the sense.


## 2:172

*"O you who believe, eat of the good things with which We have provided you, and give thanks to God, if it is He whom you worship."*

**Meaning.** The command to humanity is renewed, and now for the believers specifically [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Qurṭubī]** reads the verse as an emphasis of the earlier command, with the believers singled out here by way of honour; and he notes that the "eating" meant is benefiting in every way, though it is said to be the ordinary act of eating. **[Saʿdī]** explains why the address is narrowed: these are the ones who truly benefit from commands and prohibitions, because of their faith — so God commanded them to eat of the good things of the provision given them, and to give thanks to God for His favour by using it in His obedience and by taking strength from it for what leads to Him. He observes that God gave the messengers the same command — "O messengers, eat of the good things and act righteously; surely I know what you do" (23:51) — and that in that verse the thanks is righteous action, so that here too the thanks of the verse is not merely a word but a life. And the condition with which the verse closes, "if it is He whom you worship," is the mark of what thanksgiving is: the one who claims to worship Him is the one whose worship shows itself in the way he receives His gifts. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense of the command's object: eat of the lawful provision I have made lawful for you — which became good for you by My permitting it — of the things you had been forbidding yourselves that I had not forbidden. **[Maʿārif]** sets the verse in its moment: the earlier passage corrected the associators who made unlawful what was good and permissible, and here the believers are warned against falling into the same error, with the reminder of God's blessings and the teaching of gratitude; while the verse that follows makes the complementary point — that the prohibited must remain prohibited and must never be treated as lawful, as the associators did when they ate carrion or animals slaughtered in a name other than God's — and, implicitly, that it is an error to declare any animal unlawful beyond those specified.

**The effects of the lawful and the unlawful.** **[Maʿārif]** develops the practical observation that lies behind the verse's emphasis: eating the unlawful promotes evil instincts, kills the taste of worship and renders prayer ineffective, while eating the lawful generates inner light, creates a distaste for evil deeds and leads toward high moral character and a state of watchfulness. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the ḥadīth in Muslim that states the same with an image: the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "O people, God is good and accepts only what is good; God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers: 'O messengers, eat of the good things and act righteously' and 'O you who believe, eat of the good things with which We have provided you.'" Then he mentioned the man who travels far, dishevelled and dusty, stretching his hands toward the heaven, "O Lord, O Lord" — while his food is unlawful, his drink unlawful, his clothing unlawful, and he is nourished on the unlawful: how should such a one be answered? **[Ibn Kathīr]** draws the same conclusion in a sentence: eating from pure sources is a cause for the acceptance of supplications and acts of worship.

**Reflection.** Two addresses stand side by side: the first invited all people to the lawful and good, and this one binds the believers to the same table with a new obligation — gratitude. **[Saʿdī]**'s identification of thanks with righteous action is what gives the verse its edge: the food is not the reward of belief but its instrument, and the worshipper is known by what he does with what he is given. And **[Maʿārif]**'s observation about the inward effects of the two kinds of food supplies the reason the Qurʾān cares about the subject at all: what a man eats is not a private matter of taste but part of what forms the person who prays — which is why the verse that follows intends to fence the prohibited carefully, and the one before it refused to add to the fence.


## 2:173

*"He has forbidden you only carrion, and blood, and the flesh of swine, and what has been dedicated to other than God. But whoever is compelled, neither coveting nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him; surely God is Forgiving, Merciful."*

**Meaning.** The verse names what is actually forbidden, in answer to those who had made their own categories [Qurṭubī] [Maʿārif] [Ṭabarī]. **[Ṭabarī]** sets the address first: do not forbid yourselves, O believers, what I have not forbidden you — the *baḥīrah*, the *sāʾibah* and the like — but eat them, for I have forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine and what is dedicated to other than Me. **[Qurṭubī]** explains the force of *innamā*: it is a word of restriction, comprising negation and affirmation — affirming what the address contains and negating what lies beyond it — and here it restricts the prohibition, especially since it comes directly after the permission of 2:172, with the result that the two verses between them exhaust the two categories: no forbidden thing falls outside this verse. And he records Ibn al-ʿArabī's observation that the verse is Madinan while the latter statement — "say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to one who eats it..." (6:145) — was revealed at ʿArafah, so that the clarification was completed first and last. **[Maʿārif]** faces the difficulty that this restriction presents, since many other things are forbidden by other verses and by ḥadīth, and answers it: lawful and forbidden are not being discussed here in the absolute sense, but with reference to those particular animals which the polytheists of Makkah treated as lawful or forbidden according to their pagan beliefs — the previous verse having censured them for declaring lawful animals unlawful, and this verse addressing the complementary fault, that they did not keep away from animals God had forbidden. The restriction, then, is relative, in opposition to the polytheists' categories rather than a total inventory of the forbidden. And **[Ṭabarī]** notes the grammatical point that makes the restriction what it is: *innamā* is a single particle, which is why "carrion and blood" stand in the accusative after it; were it two separate words, the nouns would be nominative. He also reports a reading that takes it as two words, and states that he does not permit himself to recite it, though it has a clear sense in Arabic, because the authoritative reciters are agreed on the other — and, he says, it is not permissible for anyone to object to what they have transmitted in consensus.

**The four, one by one.** **[Saʿdī]** gives the reasons and the qualifications. Carrion is what died without a lawful slaughter: it is foul and harmful in itself, and in most cases the animal died of disease, so eating it adds disease to disease; and the Lawgiver excepted from this generality the carrion of locusts and fish, which are lawful and good. Blood means the blood poured forth, as the qualification in 6:145 makes clear — "or poured-out blood" — so that the blood remaining in the flesh after slaughter is not meant. The flesh of swine is specified although the whole animal is included, because the flesh is the part people mostly seek. And "what has been dedicated to other than God" is what has been slaughtered in a name other than His: *ihlāl* is the raising of the voice, which they used to do when sacrificing to their gods. **[Jalālayn]** adds the traditions' qualifications: the Sunna adds to the category of carrion whatever has been severed from a living creature; fish and locusts have a special status exempting them; and the dedicating of an animal to other than God is the slaughter performed in a name other than His. **[Maʿārif]** lists the four in the same order and notes that the prohibition here is a fence against both errors at once: against adding to God's prohibitions, and against treating His prohibitions as lawful.

**The dispensation of necessity.** "But whoever is compelled, neither coveting nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him" [Study Quran] [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī]. **[Study Quran]** explains the situation: one may be compelled by hunger to eat what is normally forbidden in order to survive or protect one's life, but this must be done neither coveting — *bāghin*, which carries the sense of rebellion — nor transgressing — *ʿādin* — meaning not with the intention of bypassing God's commandments in order to enjoy what is forbidden. It records the further sense some give to *ʿādin*: the practice of highway robbery, going against the authorities, or setting out to disobey God — so that it is not permissible to pursue food in such ways even in need. **[Jalālayn]** reports that the aggressor and the transgressor are excluded from the dispensation, and that to these two categories some add everyone who sets out on a journey in disobedience — the fugitive, or the tax collector exacting unjustly — for whom eating of the forbidden would remain unlawful unless they repent of their disobedience; this being al-Shāfiʿī's view. **[Saʿdī]** puts the mercy of the clause in its place: the servant is not abandoned in extremity, but the permission is bounded by the man's own state — the one who eats out of need is excused, and the one who eats as a rebel or an aggressor is not. And the verse closes with the two names that make the dispensation intelligible: God is Forgiving to those who fall into it, Merciful to those who obey Him, having granted them room in this matter [Jalālayn]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** keeps the passage tied to the previous verse's teaching by citing the ḥadīth: God is good and accepts only what is good; and the man who travels long, dishevelled and dusty, raising his hands to the sky and calling, "O Lord, O Lord," while his food, drink and clothing are unlawful and he was nourished on the unlawful — how should he be answered?

**Reflection.** The passage closes the argument about food by doing two things at once: it limits the forbidden to a short and unambiguous list, and it provides an escape hatch for extremity. Both are directed at the same vice — the human tendency to make religious law out of taste, and then to observe it in the wrong direction. **[Maʿārif]**'s resolution of the apparent narrowness is worth keeping: the restriction is aimed at a people who had invented prohibitions, and the verse tells them that God has not forbidden what they forbade while they ate what He had; and the dispensation tells them that even the short list bends for the man in danger, so long as he is in need and not in rebellion. What is left is neither licence nor scrupulosity, but a boundary drawn by revelation and a mercy built into the edge of it.


## 2:174

*"Truly those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and sell it for a paltry price — those are they who eat nothing into their bellies but fire. And God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them; and theirs is a painful punishment."*

**Meaning.** The passage returns to the concealers, and this time the exchange is named [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** identifies them as those who conceal what God sent down in the Book concerning Muḥammad ﷺ for the paltry bribe they are given, distorting God's verses for it and changing their meanings; and what they eat into their bellies by the bribes and fees they take for that is nothing but what will bring them to the Fire and roast them in it. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same identification — the scholars of the Jews concealing what God sent down in the Torah of the Prophet's ﷺ description and the truth of his mission — and adds the lexical point that *anzala* here means "made manifest," as in "I shall send down the like of what God has sent down" (6:93), meaning "I shall make manifest"; and that the price is called paltry because its term is cut off and its outcome is evil. **[Jalālayn]** supplies the motive: they sold it for a little price in this world, taking that price in its place out of fear of losing standing if the truth about Muḥammad ﷺ were made manifest. And the sentence about eating is glossed: they shall consume nothing in their bellies but the Fire, because that is their journey's end.

**The three sentences of the punishment.** "God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them" [Study Quran] [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif]. **[Study Quran]** places the clause beside its twin at 3:77 — "God will not speak to them, nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them; and theirs is a painful punishment" — and then handles the difficulty raised by the verses in which God does speak to human beings on that day: "so by your Lord, We shall question them all concerning what they used to do" (15:92-93); "then We shall surely question those to whom Our message was sent, and We shall surely question the messengers" (7:6); and "be gone therein, and speak not to Me" (23:108). Al-Rāzī's resolution is that the plain sense of this verse and 3:77 is that He will not speak to them at all, but that in light of those other verses it is to be understood as a description of a punishment — that He will not speak words of peace and welcome; and he compares it to intimacy with a king, who shows his displeasure by imposing exile and cutting off contact, and suggests that on that day it will be the angels who speak to people. Al-Ṭabarī gives a similar reading: God will not say things agreeable to them. Al-Qurṭubī points out the idiom that makes the phrase so heavy: it is said of a person with whom one is angry, "he did not speak to him." On "nor will He purify them," it reports the explanations: that He will not praise them for good or call them purified; that He will not set their evil deeds right; or that He will not accept their deeds as He accepts those of the purified — with the note that the verb *zakkā* can mean both to purify and to deem purified, as at 53:32, "so do not deem yourselves purified." **[Saʿdī]** reads the three clauses as one ascending severity: they eat nothing but fire, because the price they gained was acquired by the most abominable of earnings and the gravest of the forbidden things, so their recompense is of the kind of their deed; then God will not speak to them on that day but has become angry with them and turned away — and that, he says, is greater upon them than the punishment of the Fire; and He will not purify them, that is, will not cleanse them of base character, and they have no deeds fit for praise, approval or reward — the reason being that they corrupted the knowledge they were entrusted with. **[Maʿārif]** sets the passage in the sequence of the Sūrah: the earlier verses dealt with forbidden things that are tangible, and these verses take up the forbidden deeds that are intangible, inward and outward — the scholars among the Jews who gave false verdicts for those who bribed them and went to the length of distorting the Torah to suit their client. And it draws the warning that travels with the passage: there is in it a veiled admonition to the scholars of the community of the last Prophet, that they keep away from such practices and never fall short in disclosing the true rulings of God for any material reason or private interest.

**Reflection.** The verse holds a bargain up to the light: a description concealed, a bribe received, and the price called paltry — while what was purchased with it is described in the only currency that will matter, as food. **[Study Quran]**'s handling of "God will not speak to them" preserves both the severity and the coherence of the Qurʾān: the punishment of that day is stated in terms of the withdrawal of address, which the commentators recognized as the idiom of a relationship ended rather than a philosophy of silence. And **[Maʿārif]**'s application of the passage to the scholars of this community is the natural one: the verses were revealed about people who sold their learning, and the warning they carry does not expire with the seller.

## 2:175

*"Those are they who bought error at the price of guidance, and punishment at the price of forgiveness. How patient they are for the Fire!"*

**Meaning.** The verse states the exchange once more and then closes with an exclamation [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense of the barter: those are they who took error and left guidance, took what brings them God's punishment on the Day of Resurrection and left what brings His forgiveness and good pleasure — the cause being left unstated because the hearers understand what each of the two purchases brings. **[Jalālayn]** reads the second clause as a question of astonishment: what makes them so patient for the Fire? — that is, how great is the extent of their patience, the statement being intended to provoke the believers' amazement at the way these people commit the sins that necessitate their punishment with complete indifference. And it adds the correction that in reality they would have no patience whatever to endure the Fire. **[Study Quran]** records the readings of the exclamation: for some it means, "what drove them to the deeds that brought them closer to the Fire?" — so that it is not patience that helps them endure it; for others, "what gives them patience in relation to the Fire, that they should abandon truth for falsehood?" — and in a general sense it can be understood as a way of saying, "What made them do this?" **[Saʿdī]**, reading these two verses together, supplies the frame: this is a severe warning to those who concealed the knowledge God sent down, whose keepers were bound by God's covenant to make it clear to people and not to hide it — so that whoever took a worldly scrap in exchange for it and cast off God's command has his recompense stated in the only terms his bargain deserves, and the anger and turning-away of God described in the previous verse is upon him.

**Language.** The exclamation turns on the verb *ṣabara*, to be patient or to endure: the Qurʾān uses its intensive exclamatory form to say, in effect, "how much endurance they have!" — and the whole point is the impossibility it exposes. They have shown themselves to be, in this life, extraordinarily patient in doing the things that lead to the Fire, and in that sense their patience is real; but the patience the phrase attributes to them cannot possibly hold once the Fire is actually there, as **[Jalālayn]** says. The irony is the verse's judgment: the same people who would not tolerate a moment of the Fire have been patient through a lifetime of what earns it.

**Reflection.** The two verses close the passage on concealment with an accounting stated as a trade: guidance went one way, error came back; forgiveness went one way, punishment came back; and the exclamation at the end measures the absurdity of the transaction without a sentence of condemnation. It is the same figure the Sūrah has used since 2:16 and 2:86 — buying this world with the next — and, like those, it leaves the reader to do the arithmetic: if the price was paltry and the merchandise is fire, there is no way of stating the loss that the verse's astonishment does not state better.


## 2:176

*"That is because God sent down the Book in truth; and truly those who differ concerning the Book are in extreme schism."*

**Meaning.** The verse gives the reason for the punishments just described, and states the state of those who quarrel over revelation [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** reports the readings of "that": it refers to their conduct — their audacity in the face of the Fire, their defiance of God's command, and their concealment from people of what God sent down in His Book and commanded to be made clear concerning Muḥammad ﷺ and his religion — and the reason is that God sent down the Book in truth; the sending of the Book in truth being His report concerning them, and His establishing the truth by it so that the one who follows it is guided and the one who turns from it perishes. **[Qurṭubī]** works through the grammar: "that" stands in the nominative, pointing to the judgment, as though to say, that judgment of the Fire; al-Akhfash held its predicate is suppressed, meaning "that is known to them"; and others took the place of the phrase to be accusative, meaning "We did that to them." On "the Book": the Qurʾān is meant here, and "in truth" is "in truthfulness" or "with the proof." And the differing: they differed concerning the Book, that is, the Torah — alleging one thing about it and denying another — or they differed from their forefathers in holding to it, or they differed over what the Torah contains of the Prophet's ﷺ description; while others read the verse of the Qurʾān and of the disbelievers of Quraysh, some calling it sorcery, some the tales of the ancients, some an invention. **[Jalālayn]** puts the connection simply: what has been mentioned of their eating the Fire and what follows it is because God revealed the Book with the truth, while they are at variance over it — believing in parts and disbelieving and concealing others — and those at variance over the Book, whether the Jews or the idolaters who called the Qurʾān poetry, sorcery or divination, are in schism, in disagreement far removed from the truth. **[Saʿdī]** reads the phrase as showing that even the punishment is the working of truth: the matter mentioned — the requital in justice and the withholding of the means of guidance from the one who refused and chose otherwise — is because God sent down the Book in truth; and part of the truth is that the doer of good be requited with his good and the doer of evil with his evil. **[Study Quran]** notes that "that is because" ties the punishment to their treatment of God's Book, reaching back to 2:174; that schism (*shiqāq*) recurs at 22:53, 38:2 and 41:52, and was treated at 2:137; and that the Book could mean the Torah and the Gospel, which in the Islamic understanding attest the Prophet's truth — with the differing being over interpretation and distortion — or the whole of God's scriptures, including the Qurʾān, taken together. **[Ibn Kathīr]** keeps the identification of the first party: the Jews who concealed their Book's description of Muḥammad ﷺ, and then differed over it after the knowledge had come to them.

**Reflection.** The verse supplies the logic that the passage's imagery has been carrying: the Book was sent in truth, so disagreement with it is not an opinion but a rupture — which is why the Qurʾān's word for the disputants is not "mistaken" but *shiqāq*, a splitting apart, a taking of sides against. And the placement matters: the people being described are those who knew the Book well enough to sell their knowledge of it, which makes their quarrel a quarrel with what they had already found in their hands.


## 2:177

*"It is not piety that you turn your faces toward the east and the west; but piety is he who believes in God, and the Last Day, and the angels, and the Book, and the prophets; and who gives wealth, despite his love for it, to kinsfolk, and orphans, and the indigent, and the traveller, and the beggars, and for the ransoming of slaves; and who performs the prayer and gives the alms; and those who fulfil their covenant when they make it, and are patient in misfortune and hardship and moments of peril. Those are the truthful, and those are the reverent."*

**Meaning.** The Sūrah turns from the disputes about direction to the substance of religion, and the turn is one of its hinges [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī]. **[Maʿārif]** marks the place: from the beginning to this point the message was mostly addressed to those who denied it, while the second half of the Sūrah is given to educating the Muslims in the principles and branches of their religion, and it opens with the cardinal concept of *birr* — an umbrella word for all that is good. **[Qurṭubī]** reports the occasions: Qatāda said a man asked the Prophet ﷺ about piety, and God sent down this verse — and before the obligations were revealed, a man who bore witness that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is His servant and messenger and died on that had the Garden assured to him, until this verse came down and set out the whole of it. Al-Rabīʿ and Qatāda also held the address to be to the Jews and Christians, who had quarrelled about facing: the Jews facing the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis, the Christians the east, each praising its own orientation — so they were told that piety is not what you are in, but rather the one who believes in God. **[Ṭabarī]** gathers the reports to the same effect: Ibn ʿAbbās, that the verse means not the prayer alone without works — "not piety that you pray and do nothing else," which is the sense after the migration, when the obligations came down and the limits were fixed, so that God commanded the obligations and acting by them; and Mujāhid, that piety is what is established in the hearts of obedience to God. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the setting in the qiblah controversy: the change from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Kaʿbah was hard for some of the People of the Book and even for some Muslims, so revelation clarified that the object is obedience to God and adherence to His commands, facing wherever He commands, and implementing whatever He legislates — and that this is piety, reverent fear and complete faith, while facing east or west carries no righteousness in itself unless God legislates it. He notes that the verse contains many great wisdoms, encompassing rulings and correct beliefs.

**The contents of the verse.** The verse then sets out its inventory, and **[Saʿdī]** works through it. Piety is the one who believes in God — as one God, described with every perfection and free of every defect — and in the Last Day, that is, everything God or His Messenger told of what comes after death; and in the angels as God and His Messenger described them; and in the Book, that is, the scriptures God sent down to His messengers, the greatest of which is the Qurʾān, believing what it contains of reports and rulings; and in the prophets generally, and most particularly in their seal and best, Muḥammad ﷺ. Then: "and gives wealth, despite his love for it" — wealth being all that a person counts as property, little or much, given out while the soul loves it and clings to it, so that parting with it becomes the proof of the giver's faith. And **[Saʿdī]** observes that giving it out of love of God includes giving while healthy and stingy, hoping for wealth and fearing poverty, and that giving out of scarcity is better still, since the soul then loves to hold back; and that it includes giving what is precious, as the Qurʾān says, "you shall not attain piety until you spend of what you love" (3:92). Then the recipients, in the order the verse gives them: the kinsfolk — whose sufferings grieve one and whose joys gladden — with kindness in word and wealth according to their nearness and need; then the orphans, who have no earner and no strength, and whose care is a mark of God's mercy to His servants — for God has prescribed in people's wealth kindness toward those who have lost their fathers so that they become as though they had not, and because the recompense is of the kind of the deed, whoever shows mercy to another's orphan will have his own orphan shown mercy; then the indigent, whom need has made still and humble; then the traveller, the beggars, and the freeing of the enslaved — the captive and the one purchasing his own freedom. Then the two rituals: performing the prayer and giving the alms — and **[Qurṭubī]** notes that the wealth spoken of earlier must be other than the alms, since the alms is named separately afterward. Then character: those who fulfil their covenant when they make it, and those who are patient in misfortune — abject poverty — and hardship — illness — and at the moments of peril, that is, in battle when the enemy is met. And the verse closes with its two verdicts: those are the truthful — in their faith and in their claims to piety — and those are the reverent [Jalālayn] [Saʿdī].

**Language and structure.** **[Qurṭubī]** records the readings: Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ read *al-birra* in the accusative, since *laysa* belongs to the family of *kāna*, after which two definite nouns may come and either may be made the subject or the predicate — and the infinitive is the more suitable subject here, since it is not made indefinite. **[Jalālayn]** notes the alternative reading *al-barr*, meaning the dutiful person, so that the verse reads: the dutiful is he who believes — and it explains *ʿalā ḥubbihi* as "despite its being cherished by him," and lists the terms: kinsmen, orphans, the needy, the traveller, the beggars, the ransoming of slaves both the captive and the one manumitting himself by contract; the prayer and the alms, both obligatory and what the believers gave before alms was prescribed; the fulfilment of covenants made with God or with people; and patience at misfortune, illness and the height of battle. **[Study Quran]** notes that faith in God, the Last Day, the angels, the Book and the prophets are the five principal articles of faith on which all Islamic creedal formulations rest, appearing also at 4:136 and in the ḥadīth of Jibrīl; that "despite loving it" is explained as parting with wealth when one fears poverty or yearns for its benefits, and appears again at 76:8, while some read it as "because of love for Him," the pronoun referring to God — with many arguing that this wealth must be other than the alms, since the alms is listed later as one of the things to which one contributes; that the recipients recur at 2:215 and 4:36, are given a share of the spoils at 8:41 and 59:7, and are each treated singly elsewhere in the Qurʾān; and that *baʾsāʾ*, *ḍarrāʾ* and *ḥīn al-baʾs* are explained as poverty, sickness, and the meeting of the enemy respectively. **[Maʿārif]** observes that the verse has gathered the whole of religion in its four dimensions: belief, worship, dealings with people, and the character of the self.

**Reflection.** The verse answers a quarrel about which way to face by describing a man — and the description is deliberately made of parts that no orientation can replace. It is worth noticing the proportion: five items of belief, six classes of people to be helped, two acts of worship, and then the qualities that hold them together — truthfulness in promises and patience under pressure. **[Saʿdī]**'s reading of "despite his love for it" is the verse's moral centre: religion is what a person does with what he would rather keep. And the final verdict, "those are the truthful, and those are the reverent," is the passage's answer to the whole long dispute over directions, claims and lineages: piety is not a position one occupies but a man one becomes.


## 2:178

*"O you who believe, retribution is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother for anything, then let the pursuit be honorable and the payment to him be with goodness. That is an alleviation from your Lord, and a mercy. And whoever transgresses after that shall have a painful punishment."*

**Meaning.** From the definition of piety the Sūrah turns to the first of the injunctions that piety consists of [Maʿārif] [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Maʿārif]** frames the transition: from the brief introduction to the nature of righteousness, the text now enters the description of the related subsidiary injunctions, and the first is the law of *qiṣāṣ* — that the killer is killed, irrespective of the status of the parties. **[Ṭabarī]** addresses the wording, because "prescribed" might mislead: the *qiṣāṣ* is not an obligation of the rank of prayer and fasting, which one may not abandon; what is prescribed is that the killer's blood equals the slain man's blood — that the retaliation fall on the killer and not beyond him; and therefore the heir is free to retaliate, to forgive, or to take the blood money. The prohibition is of excess: it is forbidden to kill, in place of the killer, someone who did not kill. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as a favour declared: God imposed the law of equality in the slain, so that the killer is killed in the manner and measure with which he killed, establishing justice among servants. And he draws a proof from the address: the command being to all believers shows that all of them — even the killer's own kin, even the killer himself in a sense — are obliged to assist the heir of the slain when he seeks retaliation, and to enable him to reach the killer; they may not stand between the heir and this right, nor shelter the offender, as was the custom of the Jāhiliyyah and of those who imitate it by harbouring criminals.

**The context of the law.** **[Study Quran]** sets out the social world the verse was reforming: the tribal feuds and vendettas of Arabia, which the commentators describe as often escalating far beyond the original crime. One tribe might retaliate for the killing of a man by killing not only his murderer but many other members of his tribe, serving to exact revenge for past crimes and to sustain the tribe's status and esteem; and a tribe bent on maintaining or raising its position would often target a person of higher social standing than the one originally killed — killing a free person for the death of a slave, a man for the death of a woman, a notable for the death of a person of low station. Like vendettas in other cultures, the original crime often became irrelevant to the conflict, which was fueled by the most recent act of retaliation. The verse, it says, is explained as a limitation on such disproportionate revenge and an injunction to carry out remedies straight. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same picture with the reports: al-Shaʿbī, Qatāda and others said the people of the Jāhiliyyah were marked by aggression and obedience to Satan, so that when a tribe had power and strength and one of its men was killed by a weaker tribe, it would refuse equality and would not accept retaliation against the killer unless it could kill a more noble victim; and he records the Prophet's ﷺ warning that among the most insolent of men against God on the Day of Resurrection are three: a man who kills other than his killer, a man who kills within the sacred precinct, and a man who takes up the blood-feuds of the Age of Ignorance. **[Ibn Kathīr]** traces the law's background to a specific rivalry: Banū al-Naḍīr had overcome Qurayẓah in the Jāhiliyyah, and the settlement they imposed was that when a man of al-Naḍīr killed a man of Qurayẓah he was not killed for him, but only a blood-money payment was made — while the reverse was retaliation — until Islam came and made the law equal. **[Qurṭubī]**, from al-Bukhārī and al-Nasāʾī and al-Dāraquṭnī, gives Ibn ʿAbbās's report of the wider history: among the Children of Israel there was retaliation but no blood money, and God said to this community, "retribution is prescribed for you in the matter of the slain..." — so that the forgiveness means accepting the blood money in the case of intentional killing, and "that is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy," compared with what was prescribed for those before you.

**The pardon and the pursuit.** "But whoever is pardoned by his brother for anything..." [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** explains the mechanics: if the heir of the slain pardons the killer in exchange for blood money, or if only some of the heirs pardon, the retaliation falls away and the blood money becomes due — the choice between retaliation and the blood money lying with the heir. When the pardon occurs, the heir must pursue the killer "honourably": without harassing him, without demanding what he cannot bear, good-naturedly and without putting him in a corner. And the killer must pay "with goodness": without delay, without shortfall, without injury in word or deed. Is the reward of the kindness shown him in pardoning anything but kindness in good repayment? And this, he says, is the command in every obligation standing against a person: the one owed is told to pursue honourably, and the one owing to pay with goodness. He notes too the gentleness of the verse's wording — "pardoned by his brother" — where the killer is called the heir's brother, a conciliatory phrase and an exhortation to forgive, and a declaration that killing should not sever the bonds of religious brotherhood. **[Jalālayn]** gives the finer points: the indefiniteness of "anything" implies the waiving of retaliation through a partial pardon by the heirs; the "brother" is a conciliatory entreaty; and it reports the legal dispute over the effect of the pardon — whether retaliation remains the duty and the blood money is merely compensation for forgoing it, so that a pardon that does not specify the money has no effect (the preferred view) — or whether the pursuing of the payment becomes the duty once the pardon is given, which is one of al-Shāfiʿī's two opinions. It also notes that while the verse's wording brings in the pairs — free for free, slave for slave, female for female — the Sunnah clarifies that a male may be killed for a female, that religious affiliation is considered so that a Muslim is not killed in retaliation for a disbeliever even if the former is a slave and the latter free, and that parents are not killed for their children. **[Saʿdī]** works the same qualifications and notes why: it is not justice that a Muslim be killed for the enemy of God, and not according to the order of equality when the verse's own premise — the equality of the parties — fails. And the closing warning: whoever transgresses after that, killing after being pardoned, or killing other than the killer — his is a painful punishment, whether in this world by being killed, or in the next by the Fire [Jalālayn].

**Reflection.** The verse is a fence built around the most dangerous of human instincts. The ancient law of revenge is not abolished here but limited and equalized: the same life for the same life, the killer for the killing, and no extension of the feud beyond the guilty. And the second half of the verse opens the door the previous systems had left closed — one may pardon, and the blood money stands as the compensation — a door that the verse itself calls an alleviation and a mercy. **[Saʿdī]**'s observation about the "brother" is the passage's spirit: even in the law of killing, the Qurʾān keeps addressing the killer as kin, so that justice may be done between brothers rather than between tribes.


## 2:179

*"And there is life for you in retribution, O possessors of understanding, that haply you may be reverent."*

**Meaning.** The verse seals the law with a statement that has been counted among the most concise of the Arabs' aphorisms [Qurṭubī] [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense: for you, O possessors of minds, in what I have prescribed and made obligatory between you of retaliation for lives, wounds and head-injuries, there is what restrains some of you from killing others and checks one from another, so that by it you live — and in My rule between you there was life. He records Mujāhid's compression of the same idea: a deterrent, a stopping. **[Qurṭubī]** calls the sentence a piece of the most eloquent and concise speech, and explains it: it means that you do not kill one another. The mechanism is that when retaliation is established and the ruling carried through, the man who intends to kill another is deterred by fear of being retaliated against — and so both of them live together. And he draws the contrast with what the verse replaced: when a man was killed among the Arabs, his and the killer's tribes would rise and fight, and that drew them into killing great numbers, so that what had been one death multiplied. **[Jalālayn]** puts the same in a single line: in retaliation there is great longevity, because if the would-be killer knew that he would be killed in retaliation he would refrain — and by refraining he would have given life both to himself and to the one he intended to kill; so retaliation was stipulated by the Law that you might fear killing. **[Study Quran]** draws out the two ways the statement is true: the exemplary punishment serves as a deterrent for future crimes, and by fixing the maximum revenge at the execution of the perpetrator and forbidding vendettas, it preserves life — while the transaction also places a concrete value on human life. And it explains the address: *ūlu'l-albāb* literally means possessors of kernels, using the symbolism of the nut to show that wisdom lies deeper than the shell, that one needs to grasp and be nourished by the inner truth of things. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the fitting crown of the statute: God's law of equality in the slain is itself a gift of life, since the safety of a society depends on the certainty of the penalty, and the verse's address to the people of understanding is an invitation to see the mechanism — the law that seems to take life is what makes life possible. **[Maʿārif]** makes the same observation in its most pointed form: wise people should have no difficulty seeing that even retaliation does not take life but gives it, since such a deterrent law will make people fear the punishment of killing and thus lives will be saved. **[Qurṭubī]**'s report of the tribal escalation gives that claim its historical ground: in the disorder the law displaced, one killing produced a war, and under the law of equality one killing produces one penalty.

**Language.** Two small details carry weight. The first is the form of the sentence: a nominal phrase without a verb, "and for you in retaliation is life" — which is why **[Qurṭubī]** counted it among the most concise of expressions, since it states a complete and complex truth in five words. The second is the closing clause, "that haply you may be reverent": the law is not presented as a trap for offenders but as a training in *taqwā* — the restraint that the penalty teaches from the outside is meant to become the restraint that reverent fear produces from within.

**Reflection.** The verse is the best-known half-line in the Sūrah's legal section, and its paradox is the point: a law of killing is a law of life. The Qurʾān does not pretend that the sword is gentle; it says instead that a society in which murder is repaid in kind is a society whose members survive — because the certainty of the penalty does what the severity of the crime cannot, and deters the hand before it moves. **[Qurṭubī]**'s picture of feuding tribes is the necessary backdrop: the alternative to measured retaliation is not forgiveness but escalation, and it is against the arithmetic of the vendetta — where one death begets many — that the verse sets its own arithmetic, where one life answers one life and the rest of the living are left to live.


## 2:180

*"It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves some good, that he make a bequest for parents and near kin, in an honourable way — a duty upon the reverent."*

**Meaning.** The Sūrah moves from the law of the slain to the law of the dying [Saʿdī] [Maʿārif] [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as an obligation laid on the believers: when death approaches one of you — that is, its causes, such as a disease bringing a man to the edge of destruction — and he leaves *good*, meaning wealth in the customary sense of the word, he must make a bequest for his parents and those nearest to him, in the honourable manner: according to his own measure, without extravagance and without restricting the bequest to the farthest at the expense of the nearest, but arranging them by nearness and need — which is why the verse uses the comparative form, "the nearest." And the closing "a duty upon the reverent" proves the obligation, since a *ḥaqq* is what is established, and God has made this one of the requirements of reverent fear. **[Jalālayn]** supplies the sense of "honourably": justly, not exceeding the allotted third, and not preferring the richer over the poorer; and it reads "a duty" as emphasizing the obligation, laid upon those who fear God. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the grammar of the clause and its difficulty — the nominative *al-waṣiyyatu* after *kutiba*, and the two analyses of how it attaches to the conditional — and observes that this is the Qurʾān's one full treatment of the will, the mentions at 4:12 and 5:106 being brief allusions to it. **[Maʿārif]** explains what a *waṣiyyah* is: literally an order to do something, in one's lifetime or after death, but in usage what must be done after death; and it gives the three elements the verse carried in early Islam: that before the shares were fixed, the heirs other than children received nothing by right and their portions were determined by the dying man's will; that making a will for such relatives was obligatory; and that a bequest beyond a third was not permissible.

**The abrogation question.** On this the commentators divide, and the division is one of the passage's most instructive [Ibn Kathīr] [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī]. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the majority position: the verse commanded that parents and relatives be included in the will, and this was obligatory before the verse of inheritance came down; when the inheritance verses came, this verse was abrogated, since God legislated fixed shares for those entitled to them, so that the deserving heir now takes his fixed share without needing to be included in the will or reminded of the testator's favour. He cites the ḥadīth reported in the Sunan, from ʿAmr b. Khārijah, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said in a sermon, "God has given every possessor of a right his right; so there is no bequest for an heir" — the wording being the tradition's own statement that the will no longer displaces the shares. **[Jalālayn]** records the same: the verse is abrogated by the inheritance verse and by the ḥadīth, "do not make bequests for one already inheriting," as reported by al-Tirmidhī. **[Ṭabarī]**, however, argues the other side and states his principle: a group of scholars said the verse is abrogated, and another group said it stands and is not abrogated; and where the learned disagree over whether a verse is abrogated, we may not pronounce it abrogated without a proof that commands assent, since it is not impossible for the ruling of this verse and the ruling of the inheritance verses to hold together soundly without either contradicting the other — while abrogation is only established where two rulings cannot possibly coexist. He compares the obligation to that of fasting: no one doubts that one who is able to fast and leaves it off has lost an obligation God laid on him, and so it is with the will — one who leaves the bequest for his parents and near kin, having something to leave, has lost a duty of God. And he reports that a group of the earlier and later scholars held this. **[Saʿdī]** offers the resolution that has recommended itself to many: the verse's bequest was left general and referred to the prevailing practice, and then God fixed the honourable portions for the inheriting parents and relatives in the inheritance verses; what remains of the verse is the case of parents and relatives who do not inherit — those excluded by a specific person or by a description — for a man is commanded to make a bequest for them, and they are the most deserving of his kindness. The nation agrees on this, he says, and by it the two earlier positions are joined, since each of those who held them looked at one aspect and the cases differ. **[Study Quran]** sets out the legal frame: the two main restrictions on bequests in Islamic law are that they amount to no more than a third of the estate, and that they not be designated for a person who automatically inherits under the Qurʾānic shares; it notes that some consider the verse abrogated completely, others partially — continuing to apply to those who are not legal heirs — while others, including the Shīʿah, hold that it was not abrogated at all and does not contradict any other verse; and it notes **[Qurṭubī]**'s point that accepting the ḥadīth as binding here shows the Sunnah abrogating the Qurʾān, a question treated at length in the discussion of naskh. **[Maʿārif]**'s summary is the same in three parts: of the three injunctions noted, the first was abrogated by the verse of inheritance as most of the Companions held, while the obligation of a bequest within a third for those who do not inherit remained.

**Reflection.** The verse is a reminder of how the Sharīʿah grew: a community was first taught to dispose of its wealth at death by an honourable standard of nearness and need, and when the shares were later fixed by revelation, the practice was not so much abolished as completed — the obligatory bequest gave way to determined rights, and what remains is the freedom to leave something, within a third, to those whom the fixed law would pass by. **[Saʿdī]**'s reading of the joining of the two positions is the most satisfying of the solutions, since it preserves both the force of the verses and the integrity of the will; and **[Ṭabarī]**'s refusal to affirm abrogation without proof stands as a methodological note worth hearing, in a Sūrah that has already made abrogation one of its subjects.


## 2:181

*"Then if anyone alters it after hearing it, the sin shall be upon those who alter it. Truly God is Hearing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** The will, once made by the honourable standard of 2:180, is not to be played with [Saʿdī] [Ṭabarī] [Jalālayn]. **[Saʿdī]** reads it as the counterweight to the preceding verse: since a testator might be tempted to refrain from making a bequest for fear that those who survive him will change what he has bequeathed, God says: whoever alters his bequest after hearing it — that is, after having understood it, and knowing the ways and means of executing it — the sin of the alteration falls on those who alter, and not on the one who made the will. **[Jalālayn]** narrows it: whether the changer be a witness or a trustee, the sin rests on those who change it — the plural standing where the implicit singular might have been, to fix the blame on the class of those who do it — and the closing "surely God is Hearing of the testator's words, Knowing of the deeds of the trustee, requiting each accordingly." **[Ṭabarī]** supplies the grammatical key, that the pronouns be read correctly: the *hāʾ* in "whoever alters it" returns to something omitted but indicated by the context — the dying man's charge, and his committing it to the one entrusted with it, for the benefit of the one for whom it was made; the *hāʾ* in "after hearing it" returns to the first; and the one in "its sin" stands for the alteration itself. His argument is precise: the *hāʾ* cannot go back to the command of God to make a will, since no one can alter God's command; it must go back to the will itself. He reports the early readers: Mujāhid said, "the bequest"; and ʿAṭāʾ, Sālim b. ʿAbd Allāh and Sulaymān b. Yasār held that the bequest is carried out for the one to whom it was made. **[Maʿārif]**'s point on the verse is that the obligation to alter an invalid will is not a sin but a duty: reducing a bequest above the third, for example, is not *tabdīl* but rectification, which is why 2:182 follows with its exemption for the one who sets things right.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** draws four matters from the verse. First, the wording is a conditional and its answer, with *mā* preventing *inna* from governing, "its sin" raised as subject and the prepositional phrase as predicate; and the pronoun in "altered it" returns to the *īṣāʾ* — the act of bequeathing — since the will is, in sense, the bequeathing, as in "if a sermon comes to him from his Lord" meaning an admonition, and "when the division is attended" meaning the property. Second, the verse is evidence that a debt bequeathed by the dead man leaves his own liability and becomes a claim against the executor, who has a reward for discharging it and a burden for delaying it — and al-Qāḍī Abū Bakr Ibn al-ʿArabī qualifies this: it holds only if the dead man did not fall short in its payment at the time he was able, for if he was able and neglected it and then bequeathed it, the executor's neglect does not lift it from his own neck. Third, there is no disagreement that an invalid bequest — wine, swine, or anything among acts of disobedience, or more than a third — must not be carried out and may be altered; Abū ʿUmar said this. Fourth, "God is Hearing, Knowing" are two attributes, so that nothing of the testators' injustice nor the altering of the transgressors is hidden from Him. **[Study Quran]**'s note is the same in modern legal phrasing: one may not alter a bequest, although an inherently invalid bequest can be cancelled or modified — a bequest above a third reduced to a third, and a bequest of a forbidden substance such as wine nullified.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The verse was not left to be applied by memory alone [Ibn Kathīr]. Ibn Kathīr records from the Ṣaḥīḥayn, Ibn ʿUmar's report that the Prophet ﷺ said, "It is not for a Muslim who has anything to bequeath to let two nights pass without his will being written and kept with him" — and Ibn ʿUmar said, "Since I heard this from the Messenger of God ﷺ no night has passed but my will was with me." Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ asked the Prophet ﷺ: "I have wealth, and only a daughter inherits from me; should I bequeath all of it?" — "No." "Half?" — "No." "A third?" — "A third, though a third is much; it is better to leave your heirs wealthy than to leave them poor, stretching out their hands to people." And al-Bukhārī records from Ibn ʿAbbās that he preferred that people reduce the bequest to a fourth rather than a third, because the Prophet ﷺ said, "A third — and a third is much, or a third is enough." **[Ibn Kathīr]** also reports, from ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Abū Hurayrah's version with the reminder that closed the Prophet's sermon: "God has given every possessor of a right his right, so there is no bequest for an heir." The same chapter of tradition includes the warning reported from Abū Hurayrah that a man may do the works of the people of good for seventy years, then become unjust in his will, and his life's work is sealed with the worst of his deeds, and he enters the Fire; and a man may do the works of the people of evil for seventy years, then be just in his will, and his life is sealed with the best of his deeds, and he enters the Garden. Abū Hurayrah then said, "Recite if you wish: *These are God's limits, so do not transgress them*" (2:229). **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the tradition as the reason the following verse was revealed, and he explains the relation: what a testator does with *janaf* — a mistaken leaning from the truth of the will — is one thing; what the executor does by deliberate alteration is another, and only the second is the sin the verse lays on those who change.

**Reflection.** Two verses have turned a private act into a public law: a Muslim's wealth at death is disposed of by an honourable standard, written and witnessed, and its executor holds a trust that is answerable to God before any heir or judge. **[Saʿdī]** sees the fairness of it: the dying man is spared the fear that his will will be undone, and the living are warned that the change is theirs and not another's. And **[Qurṭubī]**'s third matter supplies the necessary brake — not every alteration is a crime, for a bequest of wine or of more than a third is not to be fulfilled but corrected, which the next verse will expressly excuse.


## 2:182

*"But whoever fears from a testator a leaning or a sin, and sets things right between them — no sin shall be upon him. Truly God is Forgiving, Merciful."*

**Meaning.** The exception to the prohibition of alteration [Saʿdī] [Qurṭubī]. **[Saʿdī]** distinguishes the two wills: the just will stands, and he who changes it sins; but a will in which there is *ḥayf*, *janaf* and *ithm* is another matter. Whoever attends the testator while he is dictating should counsel him toward what is best and most just and forbid him the injustice — and *janaf* is a leaning from the right course by mistake and without intent, while *ithm* is the deliberate doing of it. If counsel does not avail, one should reconcile between those bequeathed to, arriving at justice among them by mutual consent and by admonition to clear the dead man's account; such a person has done a great good, and no sin is on him, unlike the one who alters a valid will — which is why the verse closes with "God is Forgiving, Merciful," forgiving all slips and pardoning claims against those who repent; and among His forgiveness is that He forgives the man who forgoes some of his right for his brother, for whoever is lenient is shown leniency. **[Jalālayn]** makes the fear the reader's own: if one apprehends from a testator a straying from right — or a sin, because he has deliberately raised a share above a third or named a rich man in particular — and then puts things right between testator and trustee by commanding justice, no sin attaches; God is Forgiving, Merciful. **[Study Quran]** gives the concrete abuse in view: a testator might manipulate bequests to prejudice his heirs, for example bequeathing to a daughter-in-law with the intent of enriching his son, which would violate the rule that legal heirs cannot receive bequests; and where such intent to circumvent the Qurʾānic shares is clear, it is the community's duty to adjust or cancel the bequest.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** parses the verse word by word. "Whoever fears" — *man* is conditional, and *khāfa* carries the sense of *khashiya*, apprehension; some said it means "knows." The root is *khawafa*, the *wāw* turned to *alif* because of the vowelling of what precedes. The people of Kūfah give the word a leaning pronunciation to indicate the *kasrah* of *faʿilat*. "From a testator" — Abū Bakr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read it with the doubled *ṣād* (*muwaṣṣin*), the rest with it lightened (*mūṣin*), and the lightening is clearer, since most grammarians make the doubled form the intensive, though it may also be as *karrama* beside *akrama*. "Janaf" is from *janifa yajnafu* when he inclines away, the noun being *janaf* and *jānif*; the *Ṣiḥāḥ* gives *janaf* as inclination, and the poet's "my she-camel bends aside from the Ḥijr of al-Yamāmah" and "they are the patrons, though they lean against us" carry the same sense. **[Ṭabarī]** gathers the reports on what the leaning is: Mujāhid and ʿAṭāʾ are quoted through Ibn Jurayj — a man leans or sins at his death, giving to some of his heirs and not others, and no sin falls on the one who reconciles them; Ibn ʿAbbās, through ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥah, says if the dying man erred in his will or leaned in it, there is no blame on the relatives for returning his error to what is right; Qatādah says the guardian of the dead man, or an imām among the imāms of the Muslims, returns it to the Book of God and to justice. And there is a particular class of case: a man bequeaths to those who do not inherit him in a way whose benefit returns to an heir — Ibn Ṭāwūs reports from his father that his *janaf* and *ithm* is that a man makes a bequest to his son's sons so that the property may come to their father; Ibn Jurayj says the same, that a man bequeaths to his daughter's husband so that the wealth may reach his daughter, or to his son's son so it reaches his son.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** draws the governing principles in his six matters. The address is to all Muslims: if you fear a testator's inclination from the truth, his falling into sin, and his not carrying the bequest out honourably — bequeathing to his daughter's husband or his daughter's son so the wealth may pass to the daughter or the son, or bequeathing to a distant relative while leaving the near one — then hasten to reconciliation between them; when the settlement occurs, the sin falls away from the reconciler. Reconciliation is a *farḍ kifāyah*, an obligation of the community: when one of them performs it the rest are relieved, and if none does, all have sinned. And the reports collected by **[Ṭabarī]** and **[Qurṭubī]** agree that the correction may be *after* the testator's death: Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah and al-Rabīʿ hold that whoever comes to know after the death that the testator leaned and deliberately harmed some of his heirs, and then reconciles what had fallen into dispute among them, incurs no sin — even though his act is in the nature of a change, it is an alteration made for a good purpose; and the alteration that carries sin is only the alteration of caprice. Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī was asked about a man who bequeathed more than a third, and said, "Return it," then recited this verse. **[Study Quran]**, following **[Qurṭubī]**, names the same examples, and adds the tradition, "Injustice in the matter of bequests is a major sin" — the very word *janaf* of the verse.

**Belief.** The two names that close the verse are the guarantee of the whole arrangement [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī]. God is *Ghafūr*, forgiving the testator when admonition works in him and he turns back from the harm he intended, and forgiving the heirs when they relinquish part of what is theirs so that their dead man's account may be cleared; and He is *Raḥīm* toward His servants, in that He has legislated for them every matter by which they show mercy and compassion to one another. **[Saʿdī]** sums up the three verses as a whole: the passage urges the making of the will, names those for whom it is to be made, warns the one who alters a just will, and invites the correction of an unjust one.

**Reflection.** The Sūrah has just delivered a heavy law of retaliation; now it treats the last transaction of a life, and it does so in the same spirit — rights must be paid, but where a mistake can be mended without harm, the Law prefers the menders to the litigants. The instruction is not to enforce the letter of a dying man's prejudice but to sit between the heirs and the legatees and bring them to a settlement they accept, so that a grave may not become a courtroom and a family's grief not be sharpened by a grudge. It is a small passage in a long Sūrah, but it teaches the community how to be a community: **[Qurṭubī]**'s *farḍ kifāyah* means that here, as at the beginning of the Sūrah, no one may leave the work of setting things right entirely to someone else.


## 2:183

*"O you who believe, fasting is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you, that haply you may be reverent."*

**Meaning.** With the seventh month of the second year the Sūrah turns to a new institution, and it begins with the same verb that opened the laws of retaliation and bequest: *kutiba* [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Study Quran]. **[Ṭabarī]** fixes the sense: *kutiba* means *furida* — laid on you as an obligation; and the address "O you who believe" is to those who believe in God and His Messenger and affirm them both. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the order of the laws: having mentioned what was written upon the legally responsible in retaliation and bequest, God mentions that fasting too was written upon them and made binding and obligatory, and there is no disagreement on this — the Prophet ﷺ said, "Islam is built on five: testimony that there is no god but God and that Muḥammad is the Messenger of God, establishing the prayer, giving the alms-tax, the fast of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage." **[Ibn Kathīr]** states what the fast is: abstaining from food, drink and sexual activity with the intention of doing so sincerely for God alone, since fasting purifies the soul and cleanses it of the ill that mixes with it; and God has mentioned that He ordained it for this community as He ordained it for those before them, that they be an example, so let them perform this obligation more eagerly than the nations who preceded them. **[Study Quran]** sets the passage's frame: fasting is the subject of vv. 183–187, and the obligatory fast of Ramadan is held by all schools of law to be one of the five pillars; the fast of Ramadan was imposed shortly before the Battle of Badr (2/624, that is, 2 A.H.).

**Who are the first and last.** **[Ṭabarī]** reports the disagreement, and it is worth hearing because it colors the whole passage. One group said the comparison is drawn with the Christians: al-Shaʿbī, whose statement opens the reports, is said to have declared, "If I fasted the whole year I would break on only that day about which there is doubt, when it is said it is from Shaʿbān and it is said it is from Ramaḍān" — his reason being that the Christians were charged with Ramaḍān just as we are, but they moved it to a fixed season because of the heat or the cold. Al-Suddī's report fills out the story: the fast of Ramaḍān was written on them, with the added rule that they might not eat or drink after sleeping and might not approach women during the month; it became hard for them, being turned round upon them in winter and summer, so they gathered and made it a fixed season, and then the penance was added — eat, drink and come near, and fast thirty days, and feed a poor man for each day you miss; and then a later generation, trusting their own strength, fasted a day before and a day after, and this continued until the fast reached fifty days. The reference of "*as it was prescribed for those before you*" is "[those before you in respect of our fast and the fast of those before us]." A second group held that the likeness is precisely that their fast ran, as the believers' fast first ran, from the night prayer to the night prayer. **[Maʿārif]**, though, prefers the general sense: the words "those before you" include all religious communities from Adam to the last of the prophets, so that fasting, like prayer, was enjoined upon the community of every prophet without exception; those who restricted it to the Christians took them as an instance, not as a limit. And he adds the corollary that the verse does not require the fasts themselves to be identical in every respect — differences in number and timing there certainly were. **[Study Quran]** reports the same three readings: the Christians, the People of the Book, or all people in general.

**Language.** The root carries a broader sense than eating and drinking [Ṭabarī] [Qurṭubī] [Ibn Kathīr] [Maʿārif]. **[Ṭabarī]** derives it from *ṣumtu ʿan kadhā* — I held back from it; the *ṣiyām* is the holding back from what God has commanded to be held back from, and hence the poet's *khaylun ṣiyām* — horses held in under the dust of battle, one of them champing the bit, and hence the Qurʾānic "I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast" (19:26) which means silence from speech. **[Qurṭubī]**'s survey is fuller: in the language it is *al-imsāk*, holding back, and forsaking movement from one state to another; silence is called *ṣawm* because it is a holding back from speech; the *ṣawm* of the wind is its stillness, its holding back from blowing; the beast's *ṣāmat ʿalā āriyyihā* means it stood at its halter and did not feed; the day's *ṣāma* means it stood at the meridian; and the sun's *maṣām* is where it stands still at noon. **[Maʿārif]** gives the legal definition that has entered the textbooks: abstaining from eating, drinking and sexual intercourse continuously from dawn to sunset, with an intention — so that one who eats a minute before sunset has no fast, and one who abstains all day without the intention has no fast either.

**Rulings and the fruits of the fast.** The purpose clause is the pivot [Qurṭubī] [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn] [Ibn Kathīr]. **[Jalālayn]** reads "that haply you may be reverent" as "so that you may guard yourselves against acts of disobedience, for the fast curbs the desires that prompt them." **[Saʿdī]** unfolds the same into a list: fasting is among the greatest causes of *taqwā*, since it is obedience to God's command and avoidance of His prohibition; and among the things it contains of reverence are that the faster leaves the food, drink and intercourse that his own soul inclines to, drawing near to God by renouncing them and hoping for His reward; that he trains himself to watch God, leaving what his soul desires although he is able to take it, because he knows God sees him; that fasting narrows the courses of Satan, for he runs in the son of Adam as the blood runs, and by fasting his penetration weakens and the acts of disobedience decrease; that the faster's acts of obedience ordinarily multiply, and obedience is of the character of reverence; and that when the rich man tastes the pain of hunger it obliges him to console the destitute poor. **[Qurṭubī]**, in his second matter, explains why God singled out fasting for the honor of attribution: the well-known holy tradition in which God says, "Every deed of the son of Adam is his except fasting: it is Mine, and I reward for it" — and this is not because the other acts of worship belong to anyone else, but because the fast is distinguished by two things. It prevents the soul from its pleasures and appetites as no other act of worship does; and it is a secret between the servant and his Lord, invisible to people, whereas the other acts are visible and may be done for show — and for this reason it became the most particularly God's. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s summary is that the fast of the former nations is invoked as a goad to emulation, and quotes the verse that puts the diversity of law in God's own design: "To each of you We have given a law and a way" (5:48).

**Reflection.** The verse defines the believer's year with a discipline that no one can verify for another: no posture, no coin, no pilgrimage — nothing external to be seen, only the interior refusal of what is permitted. That is the reason the tradition insists the fast is God's own, and the reason **[Saʿdī]** lists *murāqabah* — the awareness that God observes — as its chief fruit. And by addressing the believers as a community whose obligation was never theirs alone, the verse relieves the sense of hardship with the sense of a road already walked: **[Maʿārif]**'s observation that the same inconvenience was faced by the earlier communities, and that "if an inconvenience is faced by a large number of people, it becomes easier to bear," is a piece of practical wisdom that the verse itself implies.


## 2:184
