Yet they disbelieved My proofs, belied My messengers, changed My blessings toward them, and substituted My covenant and My charge to them. **[Jalālayn]** names the signs: how many a manifest proof, such as the parting of the sea and the sending down of manna and quails, which they met with unbelief; and the verse's second half states the general rule: whoever alters God's grace — that is, what God has blessed him with of signs, since these are the causes of guidance — after it has come to him, out of unbelief, then God is severe in retribution against him. **[Maʿārif]** gives the sequence of the Israelites' history that the verse calls up: the Torah came to them and deserved acceptance, but they denied it and were threatened with the mountain looming over them; they heard the word of God and should have loved and respected it, but they mixed it with doubts and were struck dead by lightning; they were delivered from Pharaoh through a passage made by the parting of the sea, but showed no gratitude and took the calf, for which they were killed; they should have been grateful when manna and quails were sent, but they disobeyed and corruption set in, and when they showed their distaste the food stopped coming and they were thrown into the toil of farming. **[Study Quran]** adds that the clear proofs are, in the commentators' view, the miracles of Moses — the casting of the staff, the white hand, the parting of the waters and the drowning of their enemies — while the "blessing" is interpreted as the trust and covenant God made with the Jews, and "altering" it as denying it or disbelieving in it; it notes that *baddala* can also mean "to substitute," and that some commentators connect the verse with the accusation that the Jews engaged in distortion of their scripture, treated at 2:75. **[Qurṭubī]** opens with a grammatical note on the imperative *sal*, read with the *hamzah* lightened — the *wāw* of connection dropping it in "ask the Children of Israel" and restoring it in "ask the village" (12:82) and "ask God of His bounty" (4:32) — and Abū ʿAmr's reading *isʾal* according to the original form.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** extracts the principle beneath the historical case. The Children of Israel were certain of the signs and knew them, yet did not rise to the gratitude that such a blessing required; rather they disbelieved in it and exchanged God's blessing for unbelief, and so deserved that God send His punishment upon them and deprive them of His reward. And God named the ingratitude toward the blessing an alteration of it — because whoever is given a blessing, religious or worldly, and does not give thanks for it or fulfil its due, the blessing dissolves away from him, departs, and is replaced by unbelief and disobedience, so that unbelief takes the place of the blessing; whereas whoever thanks God and fulfils the blessing's right, it is confirmed and continues, and God increases him in it. **[Study Quran]** notes the same logic in the legal register: the blessing is the covenant, and its alteration is disbelief.

**Reflection.** The verse turns the Sūrah's recurring theme of the Israelites into a general law: signs are not merely information, they are trust, and a blessing unthanked is a blessing lost. **[Saʿdī]**'s formulation — that ingratitude is itself the alteration, since the blessing is exchanged for its opposite — explains why the verse closes not with an account of Israel's punishment but with the attribute: "God is severe in retribution." The command "ask" gives the Prophet ﷺ his evidence in the history of the people who had the proofs before him.


## 2:212

*"Decked out fair to the disbelievers is the life of this world, and they mock those who believe; but those who are reverent shall be above them on the Day of Resurrection. And God provides for whom He wills without reckoning."*

**Meaning.** The Sūrah turns from the covenant-breaking of Israel to the sneer of Mecca's wealthy [Ṭabarī] [Saʿdī] [Jalālayn] [Qurṭubī]. **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse of the disbelievers' love of the present life, made attractive to them so that they seek in it increase and boasting, offices and display, and grow too proud to follow you, O Muḥammad, or to acknowledge what you have brought from God — magnifying themselves over those who believe you and follow you — and mock those of the believers who follow you, for their abandonment of rivalry and boasting over the world's ornament of goods and wealth, and for their pursuit of what is with God by casting off the world and leaving its adornment; while those who worked for God and turned to His obedience, and rejected the world's pleasures and appetites, following you and seeking what is with Him, fearing Him by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions — those are above the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, by the entrance of the reverent into the Garden and the disbelievers into the Fire. Ibn Jurayj's report, from ʿIkrimah, gives the mockery its words: the disbelievers said, "If Muḥammad were a prophet as he claims, the nobles and chiefs among us would have followed him; by God, only the needy follow him — people like Ibn Masʿūd!" **[Jalālayn]** names them: Bilāl al-Ḥabashī, ʿAmmār b. Yāsir and Suhayb al-Rūmī, mocked and treated condescendingly by the men of wealth; and it reads the promise as the reversal: those who feared idolatry are above them on the Day of Resurrection, and God sustains whom He wills without reckoning. **[Study Quran]** reports the disagreement about the verse's first audience — the idolaters of Mecca, the hypocrites of Madīnah, or the Jewish leaders of Madīnah who belittled the Muslim community for being made up of the poor and weak — and gives the ḥadīth of Abū Dharr: the Prophet ﷺ said, "Abū Dharr, look around and find the most exalted man you can see in the mosque" — and he looked and there was a man in fine clothes, and he said, "That one" — and then, "Look around and find the lowliest man you can see in the mosque" — and there was a weak man in tattered clothes, and he said, "That one" — and the Prophet ﷺ said, "By Him in whose hand is my soul, that latter is better in God's sight than a world full of that former's kind."

**Language and rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes that "decked out" is passive, with the subject unstated, and the men meant are the chiefs of Quraysh; Mujāhid and Ḥumayd b. Qays read it with the active verb, which al-Naḥḥās called anomalous since no agent had been mentioned before. Ibn Abī ʿAblah read *zuyyināt* with the feminine marker shown, permissible because the feminineness is not real. The beautifier, he says, is God who created and originated it and created the disbelief, and Satan too beautifies it by his whispering and misguidance — but God singled out the disbelievers for mention because they accepted the adornment wholesale, turning to the world and away from the Hereafter because of it. He adds that God made what is on the earth an adornment for it in order to test which of His creatures acts best; the believers, who walk by the Sharīʿah's paths, were not seduced by the adornment, while the disbelievers were possessed by it because they believe in nothing else. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes the charge against the wealthy disbelievers: they gather wealth but hold it back from spending where it would earn God's pleasure, and instead mock the believers who ignore this life and spend what they earn for what pleases their Lord — and so the believers have gained the ultimate happiness and the best share. **[Study Quran]** gives the range of "without reckoning": that God gives no account to anyone of what He does; or that, being infinite, He needs no reckoning of what He gives, as though fearing it would dwindle; and that the giving may be in this world or in the Hereafter.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the two lessons the verse is built to teach. The disbelievers' scorn is of a piece with their narrow sight: the world is the abode of trial and testing, and the true reckoning and the real preferment belong to the abode that remains — hence the reverent, in the highest degrees, enjoying every kind of bliss and joy, with the disbelievers beneath them in the lowest depths — which makes the verse a consolation for the believers and an indictment of the disbelievers. And since all provision, of this world and the next, comes only by God's decree and will, the closing clause distinguishes what is given to whom: the provision of this world reaches believer and disbeliever alike, while the provision of the heart — knowledge, faith, love of God, fear of Him and hope in Him — is given only to those whom He loves. The mockery of the poor, in other words, is itself a symptom of a poverty no wealth can cure.


## 2:213

*"Mankind was one community, and God sent the prophets as bearers of glad tidings and warners, and He sent down with them the Book in truth, to judge among mankind in what they differed over. And none differed over it except those who had been given it, after the clear proofs had come to them, out of envy among themselves. Then God guided those who believed to the truth of what they differed over, by His leave; and God guides whom He wills to a straight path."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the exegetical dispute that the verse's first clause has always carried. Some said the one community were those between Ādam and Nūḥ — ten generations, all on a law of truth, who then differed, whereupon God sent the prophets as bearers of glad tidings and warners; that is Ibn ʿAbbās's report through ʿIkrimah, and it is corroborated by ʿAbdullāh's reading, "Mankind was one community, and they differed, so God sent the prophets." Qatādah said they were all upon guidance, then differed, and the first prophet sent was Nūḥ. Others said the "community" was Ādam himself: Mujāhid reported that "mankind" here is Ādam, who was an *ummah* alone, and that between Ādam and Nūḥ were ten prophets; Ṭabarī explains why a single man could be called by the name of a congregation — because the good character that is found scattered among a group was gathered in him, as the Arabs say, "so-and-so is an *ummah* by himself," meaning he stands in the place of a community — and adds that it may be because Ādam was the cause of the gathering of those of his offspring who gathered upon his religion until they differed. Yet others said the people of that first community were upon misguidance, and that God sent the prophets to them as warners; and others still located the verse at the day God drew forth the offspring of Ādam from his loins and presented them to him (cf. 7:172). Ṭabarī settles the lexical point that supports Ibn ʿAbbās: *ummah* here means the religion, as al-Nābighah's line asks, "Does one of *ummah* — that is, of religion — sin while he is obedient?" — and so the sense is that people were a single community on one religion until they differed.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** collects the readings: Ubayy b. Kaʿb read "the humans were one community"; Ibn Masʿūd read "mankind was one community, and they differed, so He sent" — supplying the elided clause, which the verse's own later words confirm: "and none differed over it except those who had been given it." He notes the possibility that *kāna* here is the *kāna* of permanence, not of past time, and that the verse may be informing us about mankind as a genus — that they were one community in their emptiness of revealed laws and their ignorance of realities, were it not for God's favor in sending the messengers. He gives the derivation of *ummah* from *amm*, meaning purpose, since people purpose toward it — and one view that *ummah* is the blessing itself, another that it is a leader, "because people aim at what he does." He gives the counts: the prophets in sum are 124,000, the messengers among them 313, those named in the Qurʾān 18; the first messenger, on the ḥadīth of Abū Dharr, was Ādam, though others said Nūḥ, since on the Day of Intercession people will say to him, "You are the first of the messengers," and others said Idrīs. "And He sent down with them the Book" — a generic noun meaning the Books; al-Ṭabarī held that the definite article refers to the known book, the Torah. "To judge" is ascribed to the Book in the majority's view — metaphor on the pattern of "this Our Book speaks against you in truth" (45:29), and if the prophet judges by the Book it is as though the Book judges; ʿĀṣim al-Jaḥdarī's reading, "that judgment be given among the people," is anomalous since the Book has already been mentioned.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the celebrated report of Abū Hurayrah on the words "God guided those who believed to the truth of what they differed over": the Prophet ﷺ said, "We are the last and the first on the Day of Resurrection. We are the first of the people to enter the Garden, though they were given the Book before us and we were given it after them. God guided us to the truth of what they differed over: this is the day they differed over, and God guided us to it — so the people follow us; tomorrow is for the Jews and the day after tomorrow for the Christians." Ibn Zayd gives the catalogue of the disputes: the day of congregation — the Jews made it Saturday and the Christians Sunday, and God guided this community to Friday; the *qiblah* — the Christians faced east and the Jews faced Bayt al-Maqdis, and God guided us to the Kaʿbah; the prayer — some bow without prostrating and others prostrate without bowing, some pray while talking and some while walking; the fast — some fast for part of the day and others from certain foods; and Ibrāhīm — the Jews said he was a Jew and the Christians said a Christian, and God made him a ḥanīf, a muslim; and ʿĪsā, whom the Jews rejected and slandered his mother, while the Christians made him God and the son of God. **[Study Quran]** gives the range of interpretations of "one community": the period between Ādam and Nūḥ; a unity in submission to God before deviation set in; Ādam himself, on the analogy of "Ibrāhīm was a community" (16:120); and the pretemporal covenant of 7:172 — with al-Ṭabarī's observation that the exact dates are not significant to the meaning.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** makes the verse a lesson in how difference is to be handled: everything the Books contain is truth that judges between those who dispute in the principles and the branches of religion, and this is the duty when disagreement and contention arise — to return the dispute to God and to His Messenger; had His Book and His Messenger's Sunnah not decided the contention, He would not have commanded the return to them. And the very favor of sending the Books down to the People of the Book required their agreement upon them and their unity around them, yet God informed that they transgressed against one another, contention and enmity arose, and they differed over the very Book that should have been the first thing to unite them — and that after they had known it and become certain of it through clear signs and decisive proofs. And so God guided this community, the believers, to the truth wherever the People of the Book had differed and erred, by His permission, ease and mercy.

**Reflection.** The verse is the Sūrah's account of religious history in miniature: unity, then difference, then revelation to adjudicate the difference, then a second and worse difference — over the revelation itself — born of *baghy*, the envy and mutual aggression of those who had been given it. **[Maʿārif]** draws three lessons from it: that the coming of prophets and Books was never the source of division, since all prophets aimed at gathering people around one true faith; that the Qurʾān's identification of nationhood by religion rather than by country of origin is grounded here, in the original unity of those who followed the truth and the cutting off of those who rejected it; and that the enmity of the evil toward every prophet is the customary way of the world, so that the faithful should not feel wronged by it, but should keep to the practice of their elders, the prophets, in patience and in calling to the truth with wisdom and good counsel — which is why the verse is followed by the counsel of forbearance in the next.


## 2:214

*"Or did you suppose that you would enter the Garden without there having come to you the like of what came to those who passed away before you? Misery and hardship touched them, and they were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, 'When will God's help come?' — Yea, surely God's help is near."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** notes the grammar of the opening: the "*am*" begins a question though no interrogative particle precedes it, because a statement to which it connects has come before — the preceding verses on the difference of the People of the Book and the guidance of the believers. **[Qurṭubī]** renders *ḥasibtum* as "you thought," and collects the occasions. Qatādah, al-Suddī and most of the commentators said it came down at the Battle of the Trench, when there struck the Muslims the weariness and severity, the heat and the cold, the hardship of living and every kind of tribulation that God described — "and the hearts reached the throats" (33:10). Others said it was at Uḥud, with the parallel in Āl ʿImrān, "or did you suppose that you would enter the Garden while God has not yet known those among you who strive" (3:142). And a party said the verse was sent down as consolation for the emigrants, who had left their homes and their wealth in the hands of the idolaters and preferred the pleasure of God and His Messenger, while the Jews showed enmity to the Prophet ﷺ and some of the wealthy concealed hypocrisy — so God sent down "or did you suppose" to make their hearts sound. *Am* here is *munqaṭiʿah*, in the sense of *bal* — rather. He notes the readings of "until the Messenger says" — *yaqūla* with the accusative and *yaqūlu* with the nominative, the first implying the speech is contemporaneous with the shaking, the second, that the saying follows the extreme hardship. **[Jalālayn]** gives the sequence plainly: the verse was sent down after the Muslims suffered a trying experience; "or did you suppose that you should enter Paradise without there having come upon you the like of what came upon those believers who passed away before you?" — that is, trials and afflictions, so that you may be patient as they were; they were afflicted by misery, extreme poverty and hardship, illness, and were convulsed by every kind of tribulation, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, not expecting to see help because of the extremity — "When will God's help come?" — and God answered, "Yea, surely God's help is near."

**The occasions and the trials.** **[Study Quran]** notes the connection some make with the Battle of the Trench and others with Uḥud, and the report that the burden of being exiled and living without the property they had left behind in Mecca was itself a hardship for the emigrants, who suffered the taunts and insults of the locals and the hypocrites asking how long they would sacrifice themselves and their property for a seemingly losing cause. The Messenger here is not identified: some interpret it as Muḥammad ﷺ, others say that because all prophets encounter severe trials it could be a general description of them all — and, **[Study Quran]** adds, perhaps to protect the idea of the prophets' perfect faith, some interpret the question "When will God's help come?" as meaning that although the Messenger knew the help was coming he was seeking to hasten it. It cites the Qurʾān's own examples of prophets troubled: "the messengers despaired and thought they were deemed liars" (12:110), "We know that your breast is straitened" (15:97), "perhaps you torment yourself that they are not believers" (26:3) — the station of prophethood in the Qurʾān not precluding the prophets' human vulnerability to fear, sadness and discouragement.

**Rulings and belief.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the abiding law from the verse: God informs that He must test His servants with ease and hardship and difficulty as He did with those before them, a sunnah that neither changes nor alters — whoever stands up for God and His law must be tried; if he is patient in God's command and does not care for the hardships standing in his way, he is the truthful one who has attained the perfection of felicity and the instrument of mastery; while whoever makes the trial of people into a punishment from God, so that hardships turn him back from his purpose, is the liar in his claim of faith — for faith is not pretense, wish and mere claim, until deeds either confirm or deny it. The ancient nations were touched by *baʾsāʾ*, poverty, and *ḍarrāʾ*, illness of the body, and were "shaken" by every kind of fear — threats of killing, banishment, seizure of property, the slaying of loved ones and every sort of harm — until their state reached the point that they sought to hasten God's help despite their certainty of it, though it was only the severity of the situation and its straitness that made them ask, "When will God's help come?" And since relief lies at the point of severity, and the tighter the situation the closer the opening, God answered, "Yea, surely God's help is near." So it is for everyone who stands up for the truth: whenever it grows severe he perseveres, and the trial turns for him into a gift, and the hardships into ease, and there follows victory over the enemies and healing for the disease in his breast. **[Saʿdī]** cites the parallels — "or did you suppose that you would enter the Garden while God has not yet known those among you who strive and known the patient" (3:142) and "did people suppose that they would be left to say, 'We believe,' and not be tried? We tried those before them, so God will surely know those who are truthful and surely know the liars" (29:2–3) — and closes with the proverbial line: in the trial a man is honored or humiliated.

**Reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** raises the objection the verse seems to raise and answers it. On the surface it indicates that no one enters Paradise without passing through hardships and suffering, though Qurʾānic statements and sayings of the Prophet ﷺ prove that many sinners will enter Paradise simply by God's grace, mercy and forgiveness, and will undergo no hardship; the resolution is that hardship and suffering have degrees: the lowest is to resist one's own desire and Satan, or to strengthen the foundations of belief against the forces working against the faith, and this degree is within the grasp of every Muslim, with middle and higher degrees above it. He also draws the verse's placement: the previous verse told how hostile the disbelievers have been to the prophets and the believers, comforting the Muslims with the news that there is nothing new in this antagonism — and the present verse recounts the great suffering of the past prophets and their followers at hostile hands, consoling the Muslims to be patient against hostility, since ideal happiness is reached only by preparation and hard work for the Hereafter.


## 2:215

*"They ask you what they should spend. Say: whatever of good you spend, it is for parents and kinsfolk, and orphans, and the poor, and the traveller. And whatever good you do — God knows it."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the question as covering both halves: your companions ask you, O Muḥammad, what of their wealth they should spend, and upon whom they should spend it — and the answer supplies both: whatever you spend of your wealth and give in charity, give it to your fathers and mothers, your nearest kin, the orphans among you, the poor and the traveller; and whatever good you do, God knows it and counts it for you until He repays you your reward on the Day of Resurrection. He notes that "good" in the verse is wealth, and that the command is not to a fixed amount but to the good itself. **[Saʿdī]** reads the answer as a settlement of priorities: the first among people to deserve your spending, the most entitled of them to precedence, are those with the greatest right over you — the parents, whose kindness is obligatory and whose ill-treatment is forbidden, and among the greatest acts of kindness to them is spending on them, just as one of the greatest acts of defiance is to leave them unprovided for; hence spending on them is obligatory upon the well-off child. After the parents come the nearest kin, each level ahead of the next according to nearness and need, and spending on them is both charity and the maintenance of kinship; then the orphans, meaning the small ones who have no earner; then the poor; then the traveller. And the closing clause — "whatever good you do, God knows it" — includes all the kinds of obedience and nearness, since they enter under the name of good, and God will reward each according to his intention and sincerity, and according to his spending, little or much, and the severity of the need met and the greatness of its effect.

**Context and occasion.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the four matters his commentary raises on the verse. First, its sent-down occasion: ʿAmr b. al-Jamūḥ, a very old man, said, "Messenger of God, my wealth is much — on what should I give charity, and on whom should I spend?" — and so the verse came down. Second, the grammar of "what": either *mā* is in the nominative as subject and *dhā* its predicate meaning "the one which," with the pronoun elided because the noun is long, so that the sense is "what is the thing they spend?"; or *mā* is in the accusative governed by "they spend," and *mā dhā* together are like a single word needing no pronoun. He gives the poet's line as the exception where *ʿasā* does not govern it, keeping it in the nominative though compounded. Third, the questioners were the believers, asking what they should spend. He also notes the lightening of the *hamzah*: *yasalūnaka*, with its vowel transferred to the *sīn* so that it opens. **[Jalālayn]** names the questioner and marks the two halves of the answer: the open question "what" is answered with respect to the spender — "whatever you spend of good," covering small and large amounts — and the unspoken question "upon whom" is answered with respect to the recipient — parents, nearest kin, orphans, the poor and the traveller are the most deserving of it. **[Study Quran]** notes that the verse is said to have been revealed before the institution of the formal alms, and so refers to ordinary charitable giving, and that the list of recipients is familiar and appears in one form or another throughout the Qurʾān.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports that Muqātil b. Ḥayyān said the verse was revealed about voluntary charity, and that Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid said its sense is that they ask how they should spend. He cites the ḥadīth that ranks the deserving: "your mother, your father, your sister, your brother, then the nearest and then the nearest" — that is, those closest to you and then those further. And he reports Maymūn b. Mihrān reciting this verse and commenting: "These are the areas of spending. God did not mention among them the drum, the pipe, or the carved image" — a warning against spending on idle and forbidden things, which are excluded by the verse's own list.

**Rulings and reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** observes that this verse opens a section of detailed answers to questions the Companions put to the Prophet ﷺ, and that the rulings come directly from God through the Prophet — a *fatwā*, so to speak, given by God Himself, as the Qurʾān itself says, "God decides for you concerning them" (4:127); whether taken as God's own answer or as the Prophet's answer revealed to him, the point is that the injunctions of this section are answers to questions, and after the commands of entering Islam wholly, resisting the enemies, spending wealth and striving in God's way, and standing firm in hardship, the Sūrah now turns to the details of that obedience concerning wealth, life, marriage and divorce, all under the general theme of righteousness. The verse's own order — parents first, then the nearest, then the orphans, the poor and the wayfarer — sets the map by which the rest of the section's rulings on wealth are given.


## 2:216

*"Fighting is prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But it may be that you hate a thing while it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing while it is evil for you. God knows, and you do not know."*

**Meaning.** **[Qurṭubī]** opens with the word: *kutiba* means *furiḍa*, made obligatory; and some read it "killing" — the poet's line runs, "Killing and fighting were written upon us, and upon the singing girls the trailing of skirts." This is the obligation of *jihād*, and God has shown that it is one of the things by which they were tested and made a means to the Garden. What is meant is fighting the enemies among the disbelievers, and this was known to them from the indications of the situation: permission for fighting was not given to the Prophet ﷺ during his stay in Mecca, and when he emigrated he was permitted to fight those who fought him — "permission is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged" (22:39) — and afterward he was permitted to fight the idolaters generally. He explains what the hatred was: *jihād* was hateful because it meant spending wealth, leaving homeland and family, exposing the body to wounds and gashes, the cutting off of limbs and the loss of life; what they hated was that, not God's obligation. ʿIkrimah said of the verse that they hated it and then loved it and said, "We hear and we obey" — since obeying an order involves hardship, but when the reward is known, enduring hardships becomes easy beside it. **[Qurṭubī]** offers the worldly analogy: it is like removing what pains a man and what he fears — amputating a limb, pulling a tooth, cupping and bloodletting — in pursuit of well-being and lasting health; and no bliss is better than the eternal life in the abode of permanence and honor in a seat of truth. **[Jalālayn]** gives the same sense in brief: the fighting of the disbelievers is prescribed though hateful by nature because of the hardship involved; and the verse's second part explains why: the soul inclines to desires that destroy it and rejects obligations that would bring it happiness — perhaps you find much good in fighting through victory, booty, martyrdom or reward, while refusing it brings subjugation, poverty and the loss of reward. God knows what is good for you and you do not know, so strive in what He commands.

**Rulings.** **[Ṭabarī]** records the dispute over whom the verse addressed. Some said it meant the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ specifically and no others: Ibn Jurayj asked ʿAṭāʾ whether military expedition was obligatory on people because of this verse, and he said no — "it was written on those at that time." Ibn ʿAbbās, in one report from ʿIkrimah, said the verse was abrogated by "they said, 'We hear and we obey'" (2:285) — and Ṭabarī rejects this flatly: abrogation of rulings comes from God, not from the servants, and that verse is God's report of the believers' saying it, not an abrogation from Him. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives al-Zuhrī's formulation of the obligation's scope: *jihād* is required of every person, whether he actually joins the fighting or remains behind — whoever stays behind is required to give support if support is warranted, to provide aid if aid is needed, and to march out if he is commanded to do so; and if he is not needed, he remains behind. He cites the ḥadīth of the Ṣaḥīḥ: "Whoever dies without having fought or having sincerely resolved upon fighting dies a death of *jāhiliyyah*" — and the Prophet's ﷺ words on the day of the conquest: "There is no emigration after the conquest, but *jihād* and intention; and when you are called out, then go out." **[Study Quran]** gives the historical discussion the verse has carried: some early commentators held that "fighting has been prescribed for you" referred only to the Companions, fighting alongside the Prophet ﷺ being an individual responsibility for each of them, which later became a communal responsibility — since after Islam's precarious beginnings in Mecca, where warfare was forbidden, and the initial phase in Madīnah, the community was no longer in danger of eradication and the universal prescription was lifted; some of the early generations, such as Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab, deemed fighting in God's way an everlasting obligation, while others, such as Sufyān al-Thawrī, considered it voluntary; and al-Rāzī reports the consensus that when fighting is called for it is a communal responsibility, except when Muslim lands are invaded, in which case it becomes an individual responsibility. It also reports ʿAbdullāh b. ʿUmar's answer when he was challenged for not fighting during the First Civil War: "We did that during the time of the Prophet, when Islam was small, when a man would be tried in his religion and would be killed or tortured; but then Islam became great and there was no trial."

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the general law that the verse states as a principle, not a special pleading: the acts of good that the soul hates because of their hardship are good beyond doubt, and the acts of evil that the soul loves because of the rest and pleasure it imagines in them are evil beyond doubt. The particulars of worldly affairs do not always run so plainly, but the servant who loves something and finds God turning it away from him should be content and thank God, believing good to lie in what happened, since God is more merciful to him than he is to himself, more able to secure his interest and more knowing of it than he is — as the verse says, "God knows, and you do not know." What befits the servant is to walk along with God's decrees, whether they please him or grieve him. And the negative instance is exact: shrinking from *jihād* in search of comfort is evil, for it brings abandonment, the enemies' domination over Islam and its people, humiliation and contempt, the loss of great reward and the incurring of punishment.

**Reflection.** The verse's most-remembered words are its middle clause, and they are placed there as the answer to reluctance: not a denial that fighting is hateful, nor a pretense that it is pleasant, but a claim about the limits of human judgment. **[Qurṭubī]**'s medical analogy — that a man endures the surgeon's knife for the sake of health — states the verse's logic in the register of ordinary life, and **[Saʿdī]**'s closing line carries it into providence: the servant who knows that God is more merciful to him than he is to himself can walk with the decree whether it pleases or grieves him. The obligation is heavy, and the verse says so; what it denies is that the weight is the measure of the good.


## 2:217

*"They ask you about the sacred month — about fighting in it. Say: fighting in it is grave; but barring from the way of God, and disbelief in Him, and barring from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is graver in God's sight. And strife is graver than killing. And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies a disbeliever — their deeds have come to nothing in this world and the Hereafter, and they are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein."*

**Context: the raid at Nakhlah.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives Ibn Isḥāq's account, from al-Zuhrī and Yazīd b. Rūmān, from ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr: the Messenger of God ﷺ sent ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh in Rajab, on his return from the first Badr, with eight men of the emigrants — among them Abū Ḥudhayfah b. ʿUtbah, ʿAkkāshah b. Muḥṣin, ʿUtbah b. Ghazwān, Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ, ʿĀmir b. Rabīʿah, Wāqid b. ʿAbd Allāh and Suhayl b. Bayḍāʾ — none of the Helpers among them, and he wrote him a letter and commanded him not to look into it until he had traveled two days, and not to compel any of his companions. When he had gone two days he opened the letter: "When you look into this letter of mine, journey until you alight at Nakhlah, between Mecca and Ṭāʾif, and lie in wait there for Quraysh and bring us news of them." He said, "Hearing and obedience" — then told his companions that whoever desired martyrdom and longed for it should go, and whoever disliked it should return, and that he himself was going on the Messenger's command. All of them went with him. Saʿd b. Abī Waqqāṣ and ʿUtbah b. Ghazwān fell behind searching for a camel of theirs, and the rest came to Nakhlah, where a caravan of Quraysh passed carrying raisins, leather and trade goods, with ʿAmr b. al-Ḥaḍramī and ʿUthmān and Naufal, sons of ʿAbd Allāh b. al-Mughīrah, and al-Ḥakam b. Kaysān. ʿAkkāshah b. Muḥṣin, who had shaved his head, appeared to them, and seeing him they felt safe and said, "Pilgrims! No harm from them." The party took counsel — it was the last day of Rajab, and they said: "If you leave these people tonight they will enter the sanctuary and be protected from you; and if you kill them you will have killed in the sacred month." They hesitated, then took courage, agreed to kill whom they could and take what they had. Wāqid b. ʿAbd Allāh shot ʿAmr b. al-Ḥaḍramī dead; ʿUthmān and al-Ḥakam were taken captive and Naufal escaped. They came to Madīnah with the caravan and the two captives. The Prophet ﷺ said, "I did not command you to fight in the sacred month," and withheld the caravan and the captives and refused to take anything from it. The people's hands fell, they thought they had perished, and the Muslims reproached them: "You did what you were not commanded, and fought in the sacred month without being commanded to fight." Quraysh said, "Muḥammad and his companions have made the sacred month lawful: they shed blood in it, took property in it and made prisoners of men." Some Muslims in Mecca answered that it had happened in Jumādā. And the Jews of Madīnah read it as an evil omen against the Prophet: "ʿAmr b. al-Ḥaḍramī — killed by Wāqid b. ʿAbd Allāh! ʿAmr, so war flourished; al-Ḥaḍramī, so war attended; Wāqid, so war was kindled" — and God made it fall upon them. Then, when talk multiplied, God sent down, "They ask you about the sacred month — about fighting in it." **[Study Quran]** adds the sequel: the Prophet ﷺ refused the portion of spoils brought to him, and the Quraysh condemned the breach and accused him of transgressing the accepted norm of the sacred months; in the end the matter was settled by a prisoner exchange and the payment of blood money for ʿAmr b. al-Ḥaḍramī. It notes that the Companions claimed to have thought it was the last day of Jumādā al-Ākhirah, not knowing it was the first of Rajab, since the calendar depended on sighting the crescent.

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the answer as a comparison of two transgressions: fighting in the sacred month is grave — but if you killed in the sacred month, they had barred you from God's way together with disbelief in Him, barred you from the Sacred Mosque, and expelled you from it while you were its people and its guardians; that is greater in God's sight than killing those you killed; and the *fitnah* — their turning the Muslim from his religion until they brought him back to disbelief after his faith — is greater in God's sight than the killing. And "they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion if they are able": they persist in the worst and greatest of it, unrepentant and unyielding. Then, when the Qurʾān settled the matter and God relieved the Muslims of the fear they were in, the Messenger ﷺ took the caravan and the two captives. Ṭabarī also rejects al-Farrāʾ's grammatical claim that "and the Sacred Mosque" is coordinated with "fighting" — as though they had asked about the Sacred Mosque as well as the sacred month — because the people were in no doubt about the enormity of what the idolaters had done in expelling the Muslims from their homes in Mecca, and no one disputed it; they asked only about what they doubted, the killing of Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī. He notes that there is no disagreement among the interpreters that the verse came down on account of that killing. **[Jalālayn]** gives the reading: "fighting in it" is an inclusive substitution for "the sacred month"; "fighting in it is grave" — that is, heinous as sin; "but barring from God's way, and disbelief in Him, and barring from the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is graver" — and "strife is graver than killing," meaning your idolatry is graver than your slaying in it.

**Rulings: the sacred months.** **[Maʿārif]** reports the majority position that the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months was abrogated by "slay the disbelievers wherever you find them" (9:5), taking *ḥaythu* in the sense of "whenever," or by "fight the idolaters all together" (9:36); some hold that the abrogator was the Prophet's own practice, since he besieged Ṭāʾif in the sacred months and sent ʿĀmir al-Ashʿarī on the expedition of Awtās then; and on these grounds the jurists in general regarded the prohibition as abrogated — al-Jaṣṣāṣ calls it the position of the majority of jurists, and Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and al-Bayḍāwī report the consensus of the community on the abrogation. He then gives al-Mazharī's answer: the sanctity of the sacred months is clearly present in the Verse of the Sword itself, "the number of months with God is twelve, in the Book of God, the day He created the heavens and the earth; four of them are sacred" (9:36) — so the sanctity stands, and the prohibition concerns initiating fighting, while defensive fighting is permitted in the sacred months as it is in the sacred precinct. **[Saʿdī]** holds the same distinction: the majority hold the prohibition abrogated by the command to fight the idolaters wherever they are found; some say it was not abrogated, since the unrestricted text is carried upon the restricted, and this verse restricts the general command to fight; and the greatest of the sacred months' distinctions, indeed their greatest merit, is this prohibition of fighting in them — which applies to initiating fighting, while fighting in defense is permitted in the sacred months as it is in the sacred city.

**Apostasy and the aim of the enemy.** **[Saʿdī]** reads "and they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able" as the disclosure of the enemy's true object: their purpose is not your wealth or your lives but to make you disbelievers after your faith, so that you join the people of the Blaze; they spend their power on that and strive with all they can, and God will not let it be but that His light be perfected, however much the disbelievers hate it. He notes that the description is general for all the disbelievers, and especially the People of the Book, who have deployed societies and sent out missionaries, published doctors and built schools to draw nations to their religion and to insinuate doubts against the faith — and the hope is from God, who has favored the believers with Islam, chosen for them His upright religion and perfected it for them, that He complete His favor upon them and abandon everyone who wishes to extinguish His light. On the apostasy clause, he notes the condition: whoever chooses disbelief and continues in it until he dies a disbeliever — his deeds are void in the world and the Hereafter, for their condition, which is Islam, is absent; while the verse's implication indicates that one who apostatizes and then returns to Islam has his earlier deeds restored to him, as does the one who repents of sins. **[Jalālayn]** states the same point with al-Shāfiʿī's example: the specification of death as the condition is because if the person returned to Islam his original deeds would not be invalidated and he would be rewarded for them, and would not have to repeat them — acts such as the pilgrimage. **[Study Quran]** notes that the Qurʾān elsewhere says, "It is the truth from your Lord; so whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve" (18:29) and "there is no coercion in religion" (2:256), and that the verb *irtaddā*, often translated "apostasy," can be misleading.

**Rulings and āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** opens with Ibn ʿAbbās's testimony: "I have not seen a people better than the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ; they asked him only about thirteen matters, all of them in the Qurʾān — they asked about the menstruation, the sacred month, the orphans — they only asked about what benefited them." **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the report of Jundub b. ʿAbdullāh: the Messenger of God ﷺ assembled a group under Abū ʿUbaydah b. al-Jarrāḥ, and when he was about to set out he wept at the thought of being parted from the Messenger of God ﷺ; so the Prophet ﷺ appointed ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh in his place, gave him written instructions, and commanded him not to read them until he reached such-and-such a place, and told him, "Do not compel any of your companions to march with you." When ʿAbd Allāh read the letter he recited the words of return — "Truly to God we belong and truly to Him we return" — and said, "I hear and obey God and His Messenger."


## 2:218

*"Those who believe, and those who emigrate and strive in the way of God — those hope for the mercy of God. And God is Forgiving, Merciful."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** gives the occasion: when the raiding party of ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh thought that although they had been released from the sin of having slain in the sacred month they would receive no reward, the verse was sent down — "those who believe, and those who emigrate and strive in God's way, those have hope of God's compassion" — His reward; and God is Forgiving of believers, Merciful to them. **[Ṭabarī]** records the reports in full. Jundub b. ʿAbdullāh relates that when the matter of ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh and his companions and the affair of Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī had played out, some of the Muslims said that if they had not incurred a sin in their journey, then they had no reward in it — and God sent down the verse. From ʿUrwah b. al-Zubayr comes the sequel: when the Qurʾān came down as it did and God relieved the Muslims in the affair of ʿAbd Allāh b. Jaḥsh and his companions, and the anxiety they had been in was lifted, they aspired to reward and said, "Messenger of God, may we hope that this will count for us as a raid in which we are given the reward of the strivers?" — and God sent down concerning them, "Those who believe, and those who emigrate and strive in the way of God — those hope for the mercy of God; and God is Forgiving, Merciful." Ṭabarī notes the phrase: "and God set them, in that, upon the greatest hope." Qatādah's report reads: God praised the companions of His Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ with the best of praise — "these are the best of this community" — and then made them people of hope; and whoever hopes, seeks; and whoever fears, flees.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** takes the three works the verse names — faith, emigration, striving — as the marquee of felicity and the axis of servitude, the measure by which a man's profit and loss are known. Of faith no one need ask its merit: it is the divider between the people of felicity and the people of misery, between the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire; with it in a servant, his good deeds are accepted, and when it is absent from him, no obligatory act and no voluntary act is accepted from him. Emigration is the leaving behind of the abodes of the disbelievers — abandoning the worshipers of idols, widening the circle of Islam, securing the Muslims' lives, property and children. And whoever stands up to these three works despite their difficulty will be all the more capable of the rest and more complete in them — so well may these be the ones who hope for God's mercy, since they have brought the cause that obliges mercy. This, he notes, is the proof that hope has no substance unless the causes of felicity are undertaken: hope joined to laziness and the neglect of means is incapacity, wishful thinking and delusion, betraying a weak resolve and a deficient mind — like one who hopes for a child without marriage, or for a harvest without sowing and watering. And "those hope for the mercy of God" also signals that a servant, however much he does, should not rely upon his deeds and hang his trust on them, but hope for his Lord's mercy, for the acceptance of his works, the forgiveness of his sins and the covering of his faults — which is why the verse closes with the two names: "God is Forgiving" — of the one who repents sincerely — "Merciful," whose mercy encompasses all things and whose generosity and goodness extend to every living being. And there is more: their very works are among God's mercy to them, since without His granting them success they would not have wanted them, without His enabling they could not have performed them, and without His grace He would not have perfected them and accepted them from them — so the favor is His, first and last.

**Reflection.** **[Study Quran]** notes the notion of hope the verse sets at its close: it reflects the idea that no reward is certain, that everything lies in God's hands and one might still die a disbeliever; it may also be understood as a descriptive statement — that believers should approach God with an attitude of hope and fear — an idea connected by some with 2:46, where hoping and reckoning are descriptions of what believers do. **[Saʿdī]**'s reading sharpens the point: the verse does not say they possess mercy, but that they hope for it — and that hope is anchored in three deeds so heavy that only men who have taken the means could utter it. The chapter of the Sūrah that runs from 2:153 to this verse — testing, trial, the trial of the sacred month, the fear of having lost the reward of patience — closes with a promise that keeps the balance: hope, and the two names of forgiveness.


## 2:219

*"They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: in them both there is great sin, and benefits for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit. And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus. Thus God makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** begins with the words. *Al-khamr* is every drink that covers the intellect and veils it — from *khamartu al-ināʾ*, when you covered a vessel, and from the woman's *khimār*, since it covers her head; a man is "in the *khumār* of the people" when he has entered among them, and the hyena is called to as "cover yourself." Whatever disease or drunkenness steals over the intellect and mixes with it, covering it, is *khamr*. He cites al-ʿAjjāj describing an army: "in the flashing of the banners, he does not come by stealth," walking openly with armies rather than lurking. *Al-maysir* he derives from the phrase *yasara lī hādhā al-amr*, when a thing became due to me — since the share of the man with the arrow becomes due to him when his arrow comes out. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same root for *khamr* and notes that the questioners were the believers. Both note the readings of the phrase: the many-read *ithm kabīr*, great sin, with Abū ʿAmr reading *kathīr*, much or abundant.

**Context: the three steps.** **[Maʿārif]** tells how the question arose: ʿUmar al-Fārūq and Muʿādh b. Jabal with some of the Anṣārī companions came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him how wine and gambling spoil a man's reason and cause financial loss, and sought his counsel — and in answer this verse came down, the first verse in which the elementary step was taken to stop the Muslims from the two. He explains what it says and does not say: drinking was not clearly declared unlawful here; its evils were pointed out, which amounts to good counsel urging abandonment — and so some noble Companions took the counsel seriously and stopped drinking then and there, while others reasoned that the verse had not made wine unlawful but had named it a cause of sin, and that if they could keep themselves immune from the evils there was no harm in continuing. **[Ibn Kathīr]** supplies the reports that trace the rest of the sequence through ʿUmar: Imam Aḥmad records from Abū Maysarah that ʿUmar said, "O God, give us a clear ruling about *al-khamr*!" — and the verse of al-Baqarah came down; ʿUmar was summoned and it was recited to him, and he said again, "O God, give us a clear ruling about *al-khamr*!" Then came the verse of al-Nisāʾ, "O you who believe, do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated" (4:43) — and when the prayer was called, a herald would announce on behalf of the Messenger of God ﷺ that no drunk person should attend the prayer; ʿUmar was summoned and it was recited to him, and he said again, "O God, give us a clear ruling about *al-khamr*!" Then came the verse of al-Māʾidah, and ʿUmar was summoned and it was recited to him until it reached "will you not then abstain?" — and he said, "We have abstained, we have abstained." **[Maʿārif]** gives the middle step in narrative form: the Companions drank on until ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf invited some friends, and when dinner was over and they had drunk, the time of Maghrib came, they stood for prayer and chose one to lead them, and the imam, drunk, recited Sūrat al-Kāfirūn all wrong — whereupon the second step was taken, the revelation of 4:43, which made drinking unlawful at the time of prayer. And then the final step, the verses of al-Māʾidah that declare wine and gambling and the stone altars and the divining arrows an abomination of Satan's handiwork, and ʿUmar's "we have abstained." **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that Ibn ʿUmar, al-Shaʿbī, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ b. Anas and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Aslam all said this verse was the first revealed about *khamr*.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives it as a mark of God's honor to this community that He did not impose the laws all at once but one stage after another — and the prohibition of wine follows the same pattern: this verse first, then "do not approach the prayer while intoxicated" (4:43), then the verses of al-Māʾidah. He records the disagreement over intoxicants from things other than grapes, and answers the view that what intoxicates in quantity is lawful in small quantity: that position, he says, is weak, refuted by both reasoning and report. On the verse's other question, "what should they spend?" — the answer is *al-ʿafw*, the surplus; the majority read it in the accusative, Abū ʿAmr alone and, in one report, Ibn Kathīr in the nominative, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Ibn Abī Isḥāq likewise. Al-Naḥḥās and others explain: if *dhā* is taken in the sense of "the one which," the nominative is preferable — "the thing they spend is the surplus" — and the accusative is also permitted; but if *mā* and *dhā* are taken as a single word, the accusative is preferable — "say: they spend the surplus." He notes the second matter: since the earlier question "what should they spend?" (2:215) was about *to whom* the spending goes — as the answer made clear — the second question here is about *how much*, and the scholars said its answer is the surplus above one's needs. **[Jalālayn]** states that sense plainly: "the surplus of your need — and do not spend what you need, ruining yourselves." **[Study Quran]** explains *maysir* for the reader: it denotes one type of gambling in particular, known generally as *qimār* — in *maysir* people drew arrows over meat, rather like drawing straws, the loser paying for the meat without getting any and being mocked, while the winners gave their portions to the poor as a display of generosity. It notes that in Islamic law gambling in the form of wagering is forbidden, while games such as chess and backgammon are frowned upon by many as a spiritual distraction, usually without being forbidden outright.

**Belief and reflection.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the two sides of the verse side by side: the harm that wine and gambling cause touches the religion, while the benefit is material — digestion of food, the passing of waste, a sharpening of the mind, a feeling of joy, financial gain from trade in wine, and the earnings one takes through gambling to spend on family and self — yet these benefits are outweighed by the clear harm to mind and religion, which is why God said, "their sin is greater than their benefit." **[Maʿārif]** draws out the meaning of *ithm*: it includes everything that becomes a preliminary to sin. Wine dulls the senses and weakens the power of reason, which is the very basis of human excellence and the brake against evil deeds; once reason is blotted out, the door opens to every kind of evil. The verse, then, is a counsel before it is a prohibition — and the counsel was the first step of a graduation completed only in al-Māʾidah: this is how the Qurʾān removed from the community a practice woven into its daily life, not by a single stroke but by turning its members' own reasoning against it, until the questioner himself, three revelations later, said of the final verse, "We have abstained."


## 2:220

*"...reflecting upon this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you about orphans. Say: setting their affairs aright is best; and if you intermix with them, they are your brothers. And God knows the corrupter from the setter-aright. And had God willed, He would have put you to hardship. Truly God is Mighty, Wise."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** ties the verse's opening to the previous: reflection upon the matters of this world and the Hereafter, and following what is best for you in both. Then the question about orphans and the distress their affair caused the guardians: if they became intimate with them they might slip into taking from them, while if they set aside the money due to them and prepared their meals separately it distressed them and the orphans. The answer: to set their affairs aright — in respect of their funds, by looking after them, and in respect of your mingling with them — is better than leaving it; and if you intermix your funds with theirs, they are your brothers in religion, and it is only natural that a man mix his affair with his brother's. God knows well the one who works corruption in their property while intermixing from the one who sets it aright, and He will requite both. Had He willed, He would have harassed you and made it difficult by prohibiting the intermixing — but God is Mighty, victorious in His affair, Wise in His actions.

**Context: the scruple and the licence.** **[Ṭabarī]** records the reports of the occasion. Ibn ʿAbbās says: when God sent down "do not approach the orphan's property except in the way that is best" (6:152) and "those who devour the property of orphans unjustly only devour fire into their bellies, and they will roast in a blaze" (4:10), whoever had an orphan with him set his food apart from his own and his drink from his own; whatever was left over of his own food he would hold back for the orphan until he ate it or it spoiled. The practice grew hard upon them, and they mentioned it to the Messenger of God ﷺ — and God sent down, "And they ask you about orphans. Say: setting their affairs aright is best; and if you intermix with them, they are your brothers" — so they mixed their food with their food and their drink with their drink. **[Qurṭubī]** gives Abū Dāwūd's and al-Nasāʾī's version of the same report, and notes that the verse is connected to what precedes because the mention of wealth brought with it the command to guard the orphans' wealth. He notes the report that the questioner was ʿAbd Allāh b. Rawāḥah. **[Study Quran]** adds that an orphan's inheritance would often have taken the form of fruit trees and livestock, and it is precisely through using them — picking the fruit, riding and breeding the animals — that their value is maintained; the custodians' scruple ruined both the property and the children's interests, and the verse removes the difficulty. It also notes the reading that joins the end of the previous verse with this one: "Thus does God make clear, in this world and the Hereafter, the signs" — and the connection of the theme to wine and gambling, since one should reflect on the transitory goods and lasting evils of those things in relation to the fleeting world and the abiding Hereafter.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** frames the permission by its intention: the intent is the setting aright of the orphans' property by guarding, maintaining and trading with it, and the mixing of food and the rest is permitted in a manner that does not harm them, since they are your brothers and a brother mixes with his brother. The reference is to the intention and the deed: whoever God knows to intend the orphan's good, with no greed for his wealth, is not blamed if something comes to him without intent; while whoever God knows to intend, by the mixing, the taking of the orphan's wealth, is the one who is constrained and held sinful. And the means take the ruling of their ends. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the detailed fiqh that follows from the licence: the guardian may sell for the orphan on credit when he judges it sound, may spend on the orphan's wedding what is fitting of preparation and perfume, according to his state and the state of the one he marries and the size of his wealth, and likewise on his circumcision — but if he fears being suspected of partiality, he should raise the matter to the ruler, who will order him to moderation; whatever he does with a view to the orphan's interest is permitted, and whatever he does out of favoritism and bad judgment is not. He adds that the outward sense of the verse indicates that the guardian should teach the orphan the affairs of this world and the next, and should hire for him and from him in learning crafts, and that if something is given to the orphan as a gift, the trustee may take possession of it for him, since that is part of setting things aright. And there are two states for what the trustee and the guarantor spend from the orphan's wealth: one in which witnesses can be produced, and there his word is not accepted without proof, and one in which they cannot.

**Rulings and reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** draws from the verse the general permissibility of mixing in food, drink, contracts and the rest, and reads the closing attributes as the verse's own argument: this licence is a kindness from God, a goodness and an expansion upon the believers — for had He willed He would have put them to hardship by withholding the licence, so that they would be constrained, distressed and sinful. God is Mighty — possessed of complete power and the subjugation of everything — yet along with that He is Wise, doing only what His complete wisdom and full care require: His might does not contradict His wisdom, and it is not said of Him that He does whatever He wills whether it agrees with wisdom or opposes it, but that His acts and His rulings follow His wisdom. He creates nothing in play, and He legislates nothing for His servants stripped of wisdom: He commands only what holds an unmixed or preponderant benefit, and forbids only what holds unmixed or preponderant harm. **[Maʿārif]** puts the same point in the context of the series of answers to the Companions' questions: the question here was about the maintenance of orphans; the warning about consuming their property had made the guardians separate their meals so scrupulously that the leftovers spoiled — a loss to the orphans themselves — and so the guidance came that the purpose is not to compromise the children's welfare, since their welfare is better served by a joint expense system, and there is nothing to fear, for they are brothers in faith and brothers share; the permission, however, is hemmed by the warning that God watches the guardians' performance, and that He could have set up a harder code had He willed. It is the Sūrah's pattern: a scruple answered by a licence, and a licence guarded by a warning.


## 2:221

*"And do not marry idolatrous women until they believe; a believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even though she pleases you. And do not marry believing women to idolaters until they believe; a believing slave is better than an idolater, even though he pleases you. Those invite to the Fire, but God invites to the Garden and forgiveness, by His leave, and He makes clear His signs to people, that they may remember."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** reads the verse as a rebuttal of a notion: do not marry idolatresses until they believe — and a believing slave girl is better than an idolatress who may be free, this being aimed at the idea that marrying a slave girl was shameful and that an idolatress free woman was preferable, though you may admire her for beauty or wealth. The exclusion of the women of the People of the Scripture, he notes, comes from 5:5, "and the chaste women among those who were given the Scripture." The verse continues to the other direction: do not marry off believing women to idolaters until they believe, for a believing slave is better than an idolater, though you may admire him for his wealth and good looks. And then the reason: those, the people of idolatry, call to the Fire, because they invite to deeds that merit it; while God calls, through the voices of His prophets, to the Garden and to pardon — that is, to the deeds that merit them — by His leave, and He makes His signs clear to people that they may remember and be admonished. **[Saʿdī]** states the principle the reasoning yields: the believer, even if she reaches the utmost in plainness, is better than the idolatress even if she reaches the utmost in beauty — and the prohibition of marrying a Muslim to a disbeliever rests on the fact that such people call to the Fire in their words, deeds and states, so that close association with them is a risk, and the risk is not one of this world's dangers but of eternal wretchedness. From the verse's reasoning he draws a wider inference: if marriage is forbidden even though it carries many benefits, then mere mixing with an idolater or an innovator is forbidden a fortiori — especially mixing in which the idolater or his like is raised above the Muslim, as in service and the like. And he notes that the address "do not marry" yields a ruling on the *walī*: the guardian's role in marriage is recognized, since the command governs the contract.

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** records the occasion: Muqātil said the verse came down about Abū Marthad al-Ghanawī — also given as Marthad b. Abī Marthad, whose name was Kannāz b. Ḥuṣayn al-Ghanawī — whom the Messenger of God ﷺ sent secretly to Mecca to bring out a man of his companions; he had a woman in Mecca whom he loved in the days of *jāhiliyyah*, called ʿAnāq, and she came to him and he said to her, "Islam has forbidden what was in the days of ignorance." She said, "Then marry me." He said, "Until I ask the Messenger of God ﷺ." He came to the Prophet ﷺ and sought his permission, and he forbade him to marry her, because he was a Muslim and she an idolatress. **[Study Quran]** notes that Islamic law allows marriage with women of the People of the Book but not with idolaters, on the strength of 5:5; some commentators hold that 5:5 partially abrogated the ruling of this verse so as to allow marriage between Muslim men and women from among the People of the Book, but the question only arises if the People of the Book are classed among the idolaters, and many maintain the prohibition was never directed at them; in either case the final legal ruling allows marriage with Jews and Christians, though some jurists have included Zoroastrians and, in India, Hindus; a minority held the reverse — that this verse abrogates 5:5, so that no marriage with a non-Muslim is allowed. "And marry none to the idolaters," it adds, is most often understood as a command not to give any Muslim woman in marriage to a non-Muslim man. **[Maʿārif]** lays out the same alternatives as a matter of interpretation: if *mushrik* is taken to mean non-Muslims as a whole, it is necessary to except the women of the People of the Book expressly, because 5:5 says, "and the good women from among those given the Book before you"; but if the word is taken to mean specifically those non-Muslims who are not of the People of the Book, the verse needs no exception, since it covers only those who believe in no prophet and no scripture. He then answers why the People of the Book were excepted at all, given the reason the verse gives: their difference with Islam is relatively lesser and lighter. Islamic belief is threefold — the Oneness of God, the Hereafter, and prophethood — and on the Hereafter the Jews and Christians of the original faith agree with the Muslims according to their own Scripture, and it is disbelief even in the original faith to attribute partners to God, whatever happened later among the Christians in their love for Jesus; the difference that remains is that they do not believe in Muḥammad ﷺ as Messenger, which in Islam is cardinal, but the difference is still lighter than that of the peoples who have no prophet and no book at all.

**Rulings.** **[Ṭabarī]** frames the whole question of the verse as the exegetes did: whether it was sent down meaning every idolatrous woman, or only some, and whether anything was abrogated from its ruling after it became binding. Some said it came down forbidding the marriage of every idolatrous woman to every Muslim, of whatever kind of idolatry — an idol-worshipper, a Jew, a Christian, a Magian or any other class — and that the prohibition of marrying the women of the Book was then abrogated by the words of 5:5, "and the chaste women from among the believers and the chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you." **[Qurṭubī]** sets out the positions with their partisans: one party holds that God forbade the idolatresses in al-Baqarah and then abrogated the women of the People of the Book from that generality, making them lawful in al-Māʾidah — reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and held by Mālik b. Anas, Sufyān al-Thawrī and al-Awzāʿī; Qatādah and Saʿīd b. Jubayr hold that the verse's wording is general for every disbelieving woman but the intent is specific to the Book-women, with al-Māʾidah making the specificity clear, so that the generality never included them — one of al-Shāfiʿī's two views. Against both stands the report of Nāfiʿ that ʿAbdullāh b. ʿUmar, asked about a man marrying a Christian or a Jewish woman, said, "God has forbidden the idolatrous women to the believers, and I do not know of any idolatry greater than that a woman should say her lord is Jesus, or a servant of God's servants" — a position al-Naḥḥās places outside the consensus of those by whom the proof is established, since a body of the Companions and Successors permitted it: among the Companions ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥah, Ibn ʿAbbās, Jābir and Ḥudhayfah, and among the Successors Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk — with the jurists of the cities on that position.

**Reflection.** The verse's closing words give the prohibition its horizon: two invitations stand opposed — the people of idolatry calling to the Fire by their deeds, God calling to the Garden and forgiveness by His leave. **[Saʿdī]**'s inference is that marriage is the closest of associations, and the closest of associations is measured by the direction in which it pulls; the verse does not disparage beauty or wealth, which it explicitly concedes may please, but sets them against a scale that weighs the Hereafter. And the phrase "God invites" keeps the door open: the prohibition is "until they believe," and the call to the Garden remains extended to the idolater who turns.


## 2:222

*"They ask you about menstruation. Say: it is a hurt, so keep away from women during the menses, and do not approach them until they are pure; and when they have purified themselves, come to them as God has commanded you. Truly God loves those who turn in repentance and loves those who purify themselves."*

**Meaning and occasion.** **[Qurṭubī]** names the questioners: al-Suddī said it was Thābit b. al-Daḥdāḥ; others said Usayd b. Ḥuḍayr and ʿAbbād b. Bishr, and this is the majority's view. The reason for the question, according to Qatādah and others, was that the Arabs in Madīnah and its surroundings had adopted the practice of the Children of Israel in avoiding a menstruating woman's food and her company — so this verse came down. Mujāhid's report gives the other half of the problem: they would avoid women during menstruation and come to them in their anuses during the period — so the verse came down. **[Jalālayn]** reads the answer: it is an ailment — filth, or the place from which it issues; so part from women in the monthly period, in this time or the part affected, and do not approach them for intercourse until they are pure, that is, until they have cleansed themselves after its cessation; and when they have cleansed themselves, come to them in intercourse as God has commanded you — by avoiding the female organ during menstruation and not resorting to any other part. **[Saʿdī]** reads the command as the prohibition of approaching the place of blood while it flows, and the condition for the return of the permission as two things: the cessation of the blood and the washing. When the blood ceases the first condition is gone and the second remains — hence "and when they have purified themselves," that is, when they have performed the major ablution — "then come to them as God has commanded you," meaning in the front, not in the back, since that is the place of cultivation. This, he notes, is the proof that the major ablution is obligatory for the menstruating woman, and that the cessation of blood is a condition of its validity.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the report of Anas, recorded by Aḥmad and Muslim: the Jews used to avoid their menstruating women — they would not eat with them or have them in the house — so the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ asked about the matter, and God revealed, "They ask you about menstruation. Say: it is a hurt, so keep away from women during the menses." And the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Do everything except intercourse." When the Jews were told of the Prophet's statement they said, "What is the matter with this man? He will not hear of any of our practices without opposing it." Then Usayd b. Ḥuḍayr and ʿAbbād b. Bishr came and said, "Messenger of God, the Jews say such and such — should we have intercourse with our women, meaning during the menstruation?" and the face of the Messenger of God ﷺ changed color until the Companions thought he was angry with them, and they left. Soon after, some milk was brought to the Messenger of God ﷺ as a gift, and he sent some of it to them to drink, and they knew then that he was not angry with them; Muslim also reports this. Ibn Kathīr collects the āthār of permission for everything else. Abū Dāwūd reports from ʿIkrimah, from one of the Prophet's wives, that when the Prophet ﷺ wished to fondle one of his wives during her menses he would cover her sexual organ with something. Ṭabarī reports that Masrūq came to ʿĀʾishah, greeted her and was greeted in return, and said, "I wish to ask you about a matter, but I am shy." She said, "I am your mother and you are my son." He said, "What may a man enjoy of his wife when she is menstruating?" She said, "Everything except her sexual organ" — the view also of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and ʿIkrimah. ʿĀʾishah said, "The Messenger of God ﷺ used to ask me to wash his hair while I was menstruating; he would lay in my lap and recite the Qurʾān while I was menstruating." And in the Ṣaḥīḥ: "While menstruating I used to eat from a piece of meat and give it to the Prophet ﷺ, who would eat from the place I had eaten from; I used to drink from a vessel and give it to the Prophet ﷺ, who would put his mouth where I had put my mouth." Maymūnah bint al-Ḥārith said, "Whenever the Prophet ﷺ wished to fondle any of his wives during their menses he would ask her to wear an *izār*," a lower garment.

**Rulings.** **[Study Quran]** sets the verse in its legal frame: it is understood to prohibit vaginal intercourse during menstruation without prohibiting other contact. It notes that before Islam menstruating women would not sleep in the same bed or eat from the same plate as others, Arab customs that may have been influenced by Jewish prescriptions in Leviticus or Zoroastrian rules in the Vendidad, which mandated a high level of separation and the ritual purification of objects the woman had touched — and that some take the *adhā* as the discomfort menstruation causes the woman, while many understand it as the uncleanness specifically of the menstrual blood, and others gloss it simply as the blood without attaching the notion of uncleanness to it. On "until they are purified," some interpret it as the cessation of the flow; most schools of law understand the verse to mean that the woman should perform the major ablution, the *ghusl*, before intercourse, while under certain circumstances the Ḥanafī school allows intercourse after the cessation of blood but before the major ablution. **[Saʿdī]** gives the divine reasoning that closes the verse: since this prohibition is a kindness from God to His servants and a safeguarding from harm, He said, "Truly God loves those who turn in repentance" — from their sins, continually — "and loves those who purify themselves," those who keep themselves clean of offenses. And this includes both physical purification from impurities and ritual states and moral purification from vices, base traits and low deeds: because God loves the one described by it, purification in general is legislated, and it is for this reason that purification is a condition of the validity of the prayer and the circumambulation and the permissibility of touching the Qurʾān.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the philology: *al-maḥīḍ* is a name for the menses itself, on the pattern of *al-maʿīsh* in Ruʾbah's line, "To you I complain of the hardship of living and the passing of years that plucked my feathers"; and the root of the word is in flowing and pouring forth — one says the torrent *ḥāḍa* and *fāḍa*, and a tree *ḥāḍat* when its moisture flows; from the same root comes the *ḥawḍ*, the pool of water, because the water flows into it; the Arabs interchange the *wāw* and the *yāʾ* because they belong to one class. Ibn ʿArafah said *al-maḥīḍ* and *al-ḥayḍ* are the gathering of the blood in that place, and by that the pool is named because water gathers in it; a woman is said to menstruate, and she is described by a series of names; but when blood flows outside the known days and from other than the vein of menstruation, she is said to have *istiḥāḍah*, an irregular flow. The two readings *yaṭhurna* and *yattaṭharna* — the latter with the assimilated *tāʾ* — are both read.


## 2:223

*"Your women are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth as you will. And send forth for your own selves; and reverence God, and know that you shall meet Him; and give glad tidings to the believers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the image its sense: your women are the place where your children are sown — come to the place where you sow as and where you will. They are called a *ḥarth* because they are among the causes of the sown field, though *ḥarth* properly is the tilth itself; Ibn ʿAbbās said the *ḥarth* is the place where the child grows, and al-Suddī said it is the field in which one ploughs.
