He notes that "coming to" here is a euphemism for intercourse. **[Jalālayn]** renders it: your women are a tillage for you — the place where you sow the seeds of your children — so come to your tillage, that is, the specified place, the front, in whatever way you wish: standing, sitting, lying down, from the front or from behind. **[Saʿdī]** puts the permission and the boundary together: "as you will," facing or turned away, but it may only be in the front, because that is the place of cultivation, the place from which the child comes — and in this is proof of the prohibition of intercourse in the back, since God did not make the woman lawful to approach except in the place from which the tilth grows; and the reports from the Prophet ﷺ on its prohibition, and cursing the one who does it, are numerous.

**Context and ḥadīth.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the report of Jābir b. ʿAbd Allāh, transmitted by the imāms and in Muslim's wording: the Jews used to say that when a man came to his wife from behind — in her front — the child would be born cross-eyed; and the verse came down, "Your women are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth as you will." In al-Zuhrī's version there is the addition: if he wishes, with her bent over; if he wishes, without; but that is in one aperture only. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the same from al-Bukhārī, Muslim and Abū Dāwūd, adding the Prophet's ﷺ answer to the men of the Anṣār who came to him and asked: "Come to her in any way, so long as it is in the front." Aḥmad records from ʿAbdullāh b. Sābit that he went to Ḥafṣah bint ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Abī Bakr and said, "I wish to ask you about something, but I am shy," and she said, "Do not be shy, my nephew" — and on his asking about coming to women from behind, she said, "Umm Salamah told me that the Helpers used to refrain from it; the Jews claimed that the child born of it would be cross-eyed, and the Emigrants, who had married Helpers, wanted to do as their people did, and the Helpers refused" — until the matter was raised to the Prophet ﷺ, and this verse came down. **[Ṭabarī]** collects the āthār of the early interpreters: Ibn ʿAbbās, in one report, "he comes to her however he wishes, so long as he does not come to her in her back or during menstruation"; in another, "come to her as you wish, from the front or from behind, so long as you do not come to her in the back or in menstruation"; in a third, "the *ḥarth* means the *farj*; come to it as you wish, facing it or from behind, in any way you intend — provided you do not pass beyond the *farj* to something else, which is the sense of 'come to them as God has commanded you'." ʿIkrimah said, "He comes to her however he wishes, provided he does not do the deed of the people of Lot"; Mujāhid said, "He comes to her however he wishes, but fear the back and the menstruation." And Ibn Kaʿb's report gives the postures: lying down, standing, turned on her side, facing or turned away, however you wish, so long as it is in the front. **[Study Quran]** notes that some see the verse as permission for any kind of vaginal intercourse, the symbolism of tilth referring to procreation, and that the jurists' attention here goes to what part of the body and from what direction — they are generally emphatic that the verse does not speak of "when" or "how" or at whose behest intercourse takes place.

**Rulings.** On "and send forth for your own selves," **[Jalālayn]** says it means offering up good deeds — such as saying "In the name of God" when one begins — while **[Saʿdī]** reads it as drawing near to God by doing good, and specifically that a man should approach his wife and have intercourse as an act of seeking nearness and expecting reward, and in hope of obtaining offspring through whom God benefits others. From the same phrase **[Maʿārif]** draws the verse's answer to a notion of marriage as mere appetite: the woman is compared to soil and the husband to a cultivator to indicate that intercourse is not permitted for the satisfaction of lust alone, but to be a valid source of children — and by that expression the Qurʾān gives a subtle indication of the prohibition of the practice that can never be productive, for there is no cultivation in it. **[Saʿdī]** then reads the close: "and reverence God" — in all your states be steadfast in God-fearing, helped in that by your knowledge; "and know that you shall meet Him," and He will repay you for your deeds, good and otherwise; "and give glad tidings to the believers" — the good news is left general, indicating that it covers both this world and the Hereafter, every good and every aversion of harm that is tied to faith, and in it is God's love for the believers and His pleasure in what gladdens them, and the recommendation to encourage and awaken their desire by what God has prepared for them of reward in this world and the next.

**Reflection.** The verse answers a scruple about posture with a permission bounded by the purpose of the act itself: the woman is named by what she is for in the created order — a place of sowing — and the permission to vary the manner returns to that. **[Ṭabarī]**'s three reports from Ibn ʿAbbās carry the whole rule in one sentence, and they are the same rule expressed three ways: come as you wish, but do not pass beyond the *farj*, and do not do the deed of the people of Lot. Then the verse raises its head from the bedchamber to the meeting with God, and joins the two with an imperative: send something ahead for yourselves. It is the Sūrah's characteristic movement — a question about the body answered by a ruling, and the ruling closed by the Hereafter.


## 2:224

*"And make not God a hindrance, through your oaths, to doing good, and reverencing Him, and making peace among people. And God is Hearing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the context of the prohibition: when God had commanded spending, the company of orphans and good treatment of women, He said — do not hold back from any of the noble acts on the pretext that you have sworn not to do such-and-such. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Nakhaʿī, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ and others give this sense. Saʿīd b. Jubayr's formulation is concrete: it is the man who swears that he will not do good, will not maintain ties, will not reconcile between people; when he is told to do good he says, "I have sworn." A second view is that the verse means: do not swear by God falsely when you intend good, piety and reconciliation — so the sense needs no elided negative. A third is: do not multiply oaths by God, since He is most to be held in awe by hearts; and it is for this that God said, "and guard your oaths" (5:89), and censured the one who abounds in oaths, "and obey not every contemptible swearer" (68:10). The Arabs, he notes, used to praise fewness of oaths. **[Jalālayn]** reads it as: do not make God, by swearing in His name, a cause of impediment in your oaths — that is, do not set up such impediments by swearing in His name frequently so as not to be pious and God-fearing; in such instances oaths are hateful and result in perjury requiring the expiation of doing the opposite of the oath — such things as righteous deeds and the rest of the acts of obedience — and of setting things right between people. So do not be prevented from the righteous deeds because you swore against them; rather do them and make the expiation. This understanding, he says, is justified by the reason for the verse's revelation, namely their refraining from such deeds; and God is All-Hearing of what you say, Knower of your circumstances.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** begins from the purpose of oaths: the point of an oath and a vow is to magnify the one sworn by and to confirm the matter sworn to; and God had commanded the guarding of oaths, the requirement of which would be to keep them in every case. But God excepted from that the case where keeping faith with the oath involves leaving what is more beloved to Him — and so He forbade His servants to make their oaths an *ʿurḍah*, a barrier and a screen, preventing them from doing good, fearing evil and setting things right between people. The rule that follows is precise: whoever swears to leave an obligation, breaking the oath is obligatory and continuing in it is forbidden; whoever swears to leave a recommended act, breaking the oath is recommended; whoever swears to do something forbidden, breaking it is obligatory; to do something disliked, breaking it is recommended; and as for a permissible matter, the oath should be kept. From this verse, he notes, one derives the well-known principle that when keeping the oath entails a greater harm, the oath is broken and expiated. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth: "By God, for one of you to persist in his oath concerning his family is more sinful in God's sight than to give the expiation God has made obligatory upon him" — that is, continuity in a sinful vow is more grievous than breaking it by expiation; and he cites the parallel verse of 24:22, in which God forbids those of grace and wealth to swear off giving to kinsmen, the poor and the emigrants in God's way, then says, "and let them pardon and overlook. Do you not love that God should forgive you?" **[Study Quran]** notes the related verses on oaths, 5:89 — "God will not take you to task for that which is frivolous in your oaths, but He will take you to task for the oaths you have pledged in earnest" — and 68:10, "and obey not any vile oath-monger": all convey the message against excessive oaths and emphasize the seriousness of taking one; even in pre-Islamic Arabia it was considered a vice to be immoderate in oath-taking. It gives the targets of the present verse: oaths against righteous behavior, such as swearing never to speak to relatives, to give charity, to make peace between two people, to reverence God, or in general to perform some good deed. **[Maʿārif]** states the offense in a sentence: by swearing that they will not do certain virtuous deeds or make a compromise between two parties such people are using the name of God as a barrier against good deeds, which is a severe violation of the sanctity of that name and must be avoided in every case.

**Reflection.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the closing clause its edge: God is Hearing of what the swearer says when he swears, "By God, I will not do good, nor fear Him, nor reconcile between people" — and Knowing of what you intend and seek in that oath, whether you mean good by it or other than good, since He is the knower of hidden things and what breasts conceal. He calls the verse a threat. The verse's target is not the oath as such — the Sūrah will legislate expiation in the next verse and elsewhere — but the oath used as a shield: the name of God invoked not to bind a man to his word but to release him from his duty. The two attributes at the close are the fitting seal: a God who hears the formula and knows the motive is not a God who can be made an excuse.


## 2:225

*"God will not take you to task for carelessness in your oaths, but He will take you to task for what your hearts have earned. And God is Forgiving, Forbearing."*

**Meaning.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the philology: *laghw* is the verbal noun of *laghā yalghū* and *yalghā*, and *laghiya yalghā laghan*, when a man says what is not needed in speech, or what holds no good, or what exempts its speaker from sin; and in the ḥadīth, "When you say to your companion, 'Be quiet,' while the imam is giving the sermon on Friday, you have committed *laghw*" — Abū Hurayrah's dialect giving it as *laghīta*. He cites the poets: al-ʿAjjāj's line on pilgrim bands "restrained from *laghw* and from obscene word," and al-Farazdaq's, "I am not to be taken to account for idle speech you utter, so long as you do not intend the binding oaths." **[Ṭabarī]** records the first and best-attested interpretation: God will not take you to task for what your tongues outrun you in, swearing hastily and quickly, so as to oblige you to expiation, when you did not intend the oath — as when a man says, "I did this, by God," or "I will do it, by God," or "I will not do it, by God," the tongue carrying the oath along with the speech. From Ibn ʿAbbās: it is "yes, by God," and "no, by God." From al-Qāsim, from ʿĀʾishah: "no, by God," and "yes, by God." **[Jalālayn]** gives the rule as the verse states it: no sin and no expiation required for the slip that runs from the tongue; but the accounting is for what the hearts have earned — their intention when a man commits perjury in his oath; and God is Forgiving of slips and Forbearing, since He delays the punishment of the one who deserves it.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** sets out the three categories the jurists draw from this verse and the next: the *laghw* oath, which carries no expiation because it is not a sinful act; the *ghamūs*, the deliberate oath uttered knowing it to be false, which is an act of sin — the ḥanafī school holding that it too carries no expiation — and the *munʿaqidah*, the oath one deliberately binds oneself by, to do or not do a thing, in which acting contrary to the oath requires the expiation. The verse before, he notes, treats the two categories that carry no expiation. **[Study Quran]** gives the practical senses: some interpret the verse as referring to the habit of repeating "by God" for emphasis in ordinary speech, common among the Arabs and still common today; others say it may refer to a situation in which a person believes something to be true, swears to it, and then finds out the belief was incorrect, in which case no expiation is required. It also notes that the verse is taken by some to exclude oaths taken in anger. **[Qurṭubī]** accordingly collects the views on which oaths are *laghw*: Ibn ʿAbbās's — the man's word in the flow of his speech and haste; others' — the oath about a past matter in which the swearer thought himself truthful; and the extension of these to oaths spoken in anger. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the same from the early interpreters: Ibn ʿAbbās said the sense of the previous verse is, "Do not vow to refrain from doing good works; if you make such a vow, break it, pay the expiation and do the good work" — and that is also the saying of Masrūq, al-Shaʿbī, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ, ʿIkrimah, Makḥūl, al-Zuhrī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and others.

**Belief and reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the theological point on which the verse rests: God does not hold you to account for the idle oaths that run on your tongues, spoken without intention and without the earning of the heart, merely because the tongue has carried them — as when a man says in the course of his speech, "no, by God," "yes, by God," or swears about a past matter, thinking himself truthful in it. The accounting falls upon what the heart intended; and in this is proof that intentions are taken into consideration in speech as they are in acts. And God is Forgiving — to those who repent to Him — Forbearing toward those who disobey Him, in that He does not hasten the punishment upon them but forbears with them, covers them, and pardons, with full power over them and with them standing before Him. **[Maʿārif]**'s category of the *ghamūs* oath, an act of sin that carries no worldly expiation, shows why the verse closes with the two names that answer it: the deliberate perjury the world's courts cannot reach is answered by the forgiveness of the world's Lord, and the delay of the Forbearing is the space of repentance between His knowledge of the heart and His recompense.


## 2:226

*"Those who forswear their wives — a waiting of four months. And if they return, then God is Forgiving, Merciful."*

**Meaning and language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the forms: *yūlūna* means they swear; the infinitive is *īlāʾ*, *aliyyah*, *alwah* and *ilwah*; Ubayy and Ibn ʿAbbās read "those who swear," and "those who swear" is plainly the explanation of "those who forswear." He cites the poets on the oath and its keeping — "I swore I would never cease driving a poem that would be a proverb for me and it after me," and "sparing of oaths, watchful of his right hand, and if an oath has once passed from him, he fulfills it." **[Ṭabarī]** gives the same equation from Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab — *yūlūna*, that is, they swear — with the poetry on *aliyyah* and *alwah*, and he goes on to collect the āthār on when an oath counts as *īlāʾ* at all. From Umm ʿAṭiyyah's household comes the report of Jubayr: he swore that he would not approach his wife until she weaned a child; when the child was weaned and the four months had passed, the people of the gathering told him, "This is *īlāʾ*" — and he went to ʿAlī to ask his ruling, and ʿAlī said, "If you did that in anger, your wife is not lawful for you; otherwise she is your wife." He says the same distinction: an oath not sworn in anger and without intent to harm does not make the swearer a *mūlī* — if he has sworn not for the purpose of harming her and not in anger, he is not one forswearing his wife. **[Jalālayn]** gives the plain sense: for those who forswear their women by swearing that they will not have intercourse with them, a waiting of four months; if they revert from the oath and resume relations, God is Forgiving of the harm they caused their women by swearing, Merciful to them.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** lays out the cases as a scale: if the oath is for less than four months, it is like all other oaths — if he breaks it he expiates and there is nothing against him, and if he completes it there is nothing upon him and his wife has no claim against him, because God has given him ownership of four months; but if the oath is forever or for a period longer than four months, then the term of four months is fixed for him from the moment of his oath if his wife demands it, because the right is hers. When the four months are complete, he is commanded to the *fīʾah* — returning, that is, resuming intercourse. If he does so, there is nothing upon him but the expiation of the oath; if he refuses, he is compelled to divorce; if he still refuses, the judge pronounces the divorce against him. But the *fīʾah* and the return to his wife is more beloved to God, and it is for this that He said, "And if they return" — if they go back to what they swore to leave, namely intercourse — "then God is Forgiving," forgiving them the oath they made because of their return, "Merciful," in that He made their oaths expiable and not binding upon them without release, and merciful to them too in that they returned to their wives and inclined to them and showed them mercy. **[Maʿārif]** sets out the four situations of an oath not to have intercourse: no time-limit fixed, a limit of four months, a limit more than four months, and a limit less than four months; the first three are termed *īlāʾ* in the Sharīʿah, and their injunction is that if the swearer breaks the oath within four months and resumes intercourse, he owes the expiation and the marriage remains intact; but if the four months pass without his breaking it, an irrevocable divorce takes effect on his wife, so that taking her back without a new marriage is no longer valid — though if they mutually consent to a new marriage that is valid. **[Study Quran]** gives the practice the verses address: a man staying away from his wife but not divorcing her, leaving her without the benefits of marriage and without the freedom to marry another, which in pre-Islamic times could last years; to forswear means to swear that one will not have sexual relations with one's wife; and the period of four months sets an upper limit on abstention within marriage — it is understood to draw the line beyond which the abstention is taken as an intent to cause harm to the wife. It notes the difference over "if they return": it means resuming intercourse; the return is still valid if one intends to return but is hindered, since the intent to harm has gone, while for some it simply means that one should bear witness that he has returned. Many understand "God is Forgiving, Merciful" here to indicate that no expiation is necessary if they return, though others hold that some form of expiation, such as feeding the poor, is necessary, since returning to one's wife would constitute going back on the oath. And some restrict these stipulations to the oath made in anger with intent to harm: when a man swears for another reason — protecting the well-being of a nursing child, for example — the ruling of the verse does not apply, which is the position reported from Ibn Kathīr, Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī; others take the forswearing as any oath that keeps a man from intercourse with his wife, or even any oath whose intent is to cause harm.

**Reflection.** The verse limits a practice that had turned marriage into a punishment: the pre-Islamic *īlāʾ* could hold a woman suspended for a year or more, neither a wife in fact nor free to marry. **[Qurṭubī]** reports Ibn ʿAbbās's statement that the *īlāʾ* of the days of ignorance was a year or two years and more, and this verse cut it to four months. The close — "if they return, God is Forgiving, Merciful" — puts the preference where **[Saʿdī]** puts it: the return is more beloved to God than the completing of the oath, and the mercy named is not only the erasure of the harm but the provision of an exit, since the oath was made expiable and not welded shut. The next verse gives the other branch: if they resolve upon divorce, God is Hearing, Knowing.


## 2:227

*"But if they resolve upon divorce — then truly God is Hearing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** reads the resolve as the decision carried through: if they resolve upon divorce by not repealing it, then let them go through with it — God is Hearing of what they say, Knowing of their resolve — meaning that after the waiting period mentioned they have only two courses, to return or to divorce. **[Saʿdī]** fills in the movement: if they refuse the *fīʾah*, that refusal is itself proof of their aversion to their wives and of their not wanting them as spouses, and that cannot be but a resolve upon divorce; so if the divorce, which is their right, is carried out directly by them, well and good, and otherwise the judge compels them to it or carries it out for them. And "God is Hearing, Knowing" carries in it a threat and a warning to the one who swears this oath intending harm and contention.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** draws two rulings from the verse and its neighbour. First, *īlāʾ* is specific to the wife, since the verse says "their wives": the oath of abstention that carries this legal consequence is an oath concerning a man's wife, not concerning anyone else. Second, intercourse is obligatory once in every four months: because after the four months a man is compelled either to intercourse or to divorce, and that compulsion cannot be for anything but the leaving of an obligation. **[Maʿārif]** gives the fourth case that completes the scale: when the oath is fixed at less than four months, breaking it requires the expiation and completing it, even then, leaves the marriage valid — so that the time-limit of the shorter oath carries no threat to the marriage itself, and only the open-ended oath and the oath beyond four months fall under the ruling of *īlāʾ*. **[Study Quran]**, reading 226 and 227 together, notes that the four months are understood to draw the line beyond which the abstention is taken as an intent to cause harm to the wife — and that the commentators are accordingly divided over whether the ruling attaches to the oath sworn in anger with intent to harm, or to any oath that keeps a man from his wife, or even to any oath whose intent is harm; the position reported from the earlier authorities, including Ibn Kathīr, Qurṭubī, al-Rāzī and al-Ṭabarī, restricts it to the oath of harm.

**Reflection.** The two verses together end a man's ability to use an oath as a means of indefinite coercion: the waiting is bounded, the return is preferred and made easy by expiation, and the alternative is a divorce granted with the knowledge that God hears the words and knows the resolve. The Sūrah's method here is characteristic — it takes a pre-Islamic instrument of harm, measures it, and either turns it toward reconciliation or ends it, closing on the two attributes that make the court of conscience the real court: God is Hearing, Knowing.


## 2:228

*"Divorced women shall wait by themselves for three courses, and it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs, if they believe in God and the Last Day. And their husbands have better right to restore them during that time, if they desire to set things right. And they have rights the like of those they owe, in an honorable way; and men have a degree over them. And God is Mighty, Wise."*

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** places the verse after the discussion of *īlāʾ*: since God had mentioned the oath of abstention and that divorce may occur through it, He then made clear the woman's ruling after the divorce. He reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, in Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī, the pre-Islamic background: a man who divorced his wife remained most entitled to her even after pronouncing three divorces, and this was abrogated by "divorce is twice" (2:229). He notes that "the divorced women" is a general expression whose intent is specific to those whose marriages have been consummated; the woman divorced before consummation is excluded by the verse of al-Aḥzāb, "you have no waiting period to reckon against them" (33:49). **[Study Quran]** explains the legal frame: in this *ṭalāq*, the husband declares the divorce and the wife observes a period of waiting — the *ʿiddah* — of three courses, during which the couple do not have sexual relations, before the divorce becomes final; these are three menstrual periods, with disagreement over whether the courses are marked by the onset of the flow, its cessation, or the ritual washing that follows.

**The three courses.** **[Ṭabarī]** records the exegetical disagreement over the word: some said the *qurūʾ* are the menstruations — from Mujāhid, "menses," and al-Rabīʿ, "three menstruations," and Qatādah, and others; and **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the roster of those who held this: Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Abū al-Dardāʾ, ʿUbādah b. al-Ṣāmit, Anas b. Mālik, Ibn Masʿūd, Muʿādh, Ubayy b. Kaʿb, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī and Ibn ʿAbbās, and among the Successors Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab, al-Aswad, Ibrāhīm, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, Muḥammad b. Sīrīn, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Shaʿbī, al-Rabīʿ, Muqātil b. Ḥayyān, al-Suddī, Makḥūl, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī. The report that anchors the position: ʿAlqamah said, "We were with ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb when a woman came and said, 'My husband divorced me one or two periods ago; then he came back to me while I had prepared my water for bathing, took off my clothes and closed my door.'" ʿUmar asked ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, "What do you think?" and he said, "I think she is still his wife, so long as she is not allowed to resume praying" — that is, until the third period ends before he takes her back — and ʿUmar said, "This is my opinion too." And Ibn Kathīr cites the ḥadīth of Fāṭimah bint Abī Ḥubaysh, whom the Messenger of God ﷺ told, "Leave off prayer during your *aqrāʾ*" — your menstruations. **[Jalālayn]** notes the two positions in the word itself: *qurūʾ* is the plural of *qarʾ*, from purity or from menstruation, these being two different opinions, and the courses begin from the moment of divorce. **[Saʿdī]** reports the same disagreement and states his own conclusion that the correct view is that the *qarʾ* is the menstruation. He also notes the exclusions that leave the general rule: pregnant women, whose waiting is the delivery (65:4); women not consummated, who have no waiting at all; and slave women, whose waiting is two periods, as the Companions held — with the verse's context indicating that it speaks of the free woman.

**The purpose and the prohibition of concealment.** **[Saʿdī]** derives the wisdom of the waiting from its function: knowledge that the womb is free of pregnancy, since when the three courses have come and gone it is known that no child is in the womb, so that lineages are not mixed — and it is for this that God required them to inform concerning "what God has created in their wombs," and made it unlawful for them to conceal it, whether pregnancy or menstruation, because the concealment leads to many corruptions. Concealing a pregnancy may cause the child to be attached to one who is not his father — whether out of desire for the man or haste to have the waiting end — and if it is attached to other than its father there follows the cutting of kinship, the corruption of inheritance, the exclusion of the child's own relatives, and even the possibility that a person may marry those who are unlawful to him; the evil of that is known only to the Lord of the servants, and if there were nothing in it but her staying with a man whose marriage to her is void, and her persistence in a great enormity, that would be enough evil. As for concealing the menstruation: if she hastens and reports it falsely, she cuts off the husband's right and makes herself available to another, with the evils that follow; and if she lies that there is no menstruation, to prolong the waiting and take maintenance from him, the maintenance is not owed to her and is unlawful gain from two directions — she does not deserve it, and she has attributed to the religious law a ruling while lying; and perhaps he takes her back after the waiting has ended, and that is *sifāḥ*, since she is a stranger to him. So the verse says, "and it is not lawful for them to conceal what God has created in their wombs, if they believe in God and the Last Day" — the very fact of concealment being proof of a failure of faith in God and the Last Day. And from this, **[Saʿdī]** notes, comes a further proof: the woman's report about herself is accepted concerning what none but she can know — pregnancy, menstruation and the like.

**The right of return, and the mutual rights.** **[Saʿdī]** reads "and their husbands have better right to restore them during that time, if they desire to set things right" as the revocable divorce's own logic: while she is waiting, the husband may take her back if he wants reconciliation, affection and love. And the verse's implication is that if they do not want reconciliation they have no better right to take them back — it is not lawful for them to do so with the intention of harming her and prolonging her waiting; there are two views on whether such a return is legally effective despite its being forbidden, the majority holding that he possesses the right while being sinful, and the correct view being that without the intention of setting things right he does not possess it, as the apparent sense of the verse says. The waiting itself, he adds, holds another wisdom: the husband may regret the separation, and this period is given him to reflect and reconsider — which shows God's love of affection between spouses and His dislike of separation, as the Prophet ﷺ said, "The most hated of lawful things to God is divorce." All of this applies to the revocable divorce; in the irrevocable divorce, the husband has no better right to her return, and if they wish to return to one another there must be a new contract with its full conditions. Then the verse's general rule: "and they have rights the like of those they owe, in an honorable way" — women have against their husbands rights and obligations like those the husbands have against them, and the reference of rights between the spouses is to the *maʿrūf*, the established custom of the place and the time, which varies with times, places, circumstances, persons and habits; and in this is proof that maintenance, clothing, companionship, housing, and intercourse all return to the customary — the requirement of the absolute contract, while a contract with conditions goes by its conditions, unless a condition makes lawful what is unlawful or unlawful what is lawful. **[Maʿārif]** treats the verse as the great charter of the status of woman, which he sets against a history of the world's callousness toward her, and reads the closing clause as the balance of that charter: "men have a degree over them" — a step above, in the sense of guardianship, since man has been made responsible for the rights of woman parallel to her rights over him, and since of the two, the ordering of the household and the charge of the children require a guardianship that secures peace and order.

**The degree.** **[Saʿdī]** explains the *darajah*: a rank, headship and a greater right, as in "men are the maintainers of women, by what God has preferred some of them over others and by what they spend of their wealth" (4:34); the office of prophethood, of judgeship and of authority, greater and lesser, is specific to men; and a man has twice a woman's share in many matters, such as inheritance. **[Jalālayn]** gives the reason the men are above in rights: the husband's payment of the dowry and his being the breadwinner; God is Mighty in His kingdom, Wise in what He has ordained for His creatures. **[Study Quran]** notes the pairing of the two halves of the clause: the obligations owed by the women the like of those they owe, in an honorable way.


## 2:229

*"Divorce is twice; then honorable retention, or release with kindness. And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them — unless the two fear that they will not uphold God's limits. So if you fear that the two will not uphold God's limits, there is no blame on them both in what she gives as ransom. These are God's limits, so transgress them not; and whoever transgresses God's limits — those are the wrongdoers."*

**Context.** **[Saʿdī]** and **[Qurṭubī]** describe the practice the verse ended: in *jāhiliyyah* and for a period of early Islam, there was no limit to divorce — a man would divorce his wife, and when her waiting was near its end he would take her back, then divorce her again, and go on doing that forever, so that she suffered harm known only to God. Qurṭubī gives a concrete report: a man said to his wife in the Prophet's time, "I will neither shelter you nor let you go free." She said, "How?" He said, "I will divorce you, and when your waiting is nearly up I will take you back." The woman complained to ʿĀʾishah, who mentioned it to the Prophet ﷺ, and God sent down this verse as a statement of the number of divorces in which a man may take his wife back without a new dowry or a new guardian. **[Ṭabarī]** records the same setting from the reports: the people of *jāhiliyyah*, and the people of Islam before this verse came down, had no terminus to their divorce by which the woman became definitely separated from her husband if he was taking her back during her waiting; God set a limit, so that when the divorce reached it the wife became forbidden to him short of a new husband, and she became the owner of herself.

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** reads it: divorce that may be revoked is twice; then honorable retention — you are obliged to take them back without harming them — or setting them free kindly. It is not lawful for you, husbands, to take anything of the dowry you gave them if you divorce them — unless the two spouses fear that they will not maintain God's limits, that is, the rights God established for them; the readings vary (*yakhāfā* dual and *yukhāfā* passive, second person *takhāfā*). If you fear that the two will not maintain God's limits, neither of them is at fault if she ransoms herself with some of her property so that he divorces her — no blame on the man if he takes, nor on the woman if she offers. These prescriptions are God's limits; do not transgress them; and whoever transgresses God's limits, those are the wrongdoers. **[Saʿdī]** draws out the logic of "twice": the limit of two revocable divorces gives the husband who does not intend harm room to take his wife back and reconsider his view in that period; beyond that, there is no place for the revocable divorce, since whoever exceeds the two is either transgressing a prohibited thing or has no desire to keep his wife and intends only harm. So God commanded the husband either to retain his wife "with kindness" — good companionship of the kind men of his like give their wives, and this is the preferable course — or to release her "with kindness," and among the acts of kindness is that he take nothing of her property on parting from her, since that would be injustice and taking wealth without anything in exchange.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports the occasion of the verse's ransom clause: it was revealed about Thābit b. Qays b. Shammās and his wife Ḥabībah bint ʿAbdullāh b. Ubayy b. Salūl. In Mālik's *Muwaṭṭa*: Ḥabībah bint Sahl al-Anṣāriyyah was married to Thābit b. Qays, and the Messenger of God ﷺ came out for the dawn prayer and found her at his door in the dark; he said, "Who is this?" and she said, "I am Ḥabībah bint Sahl, Messenger of God." He said, "What is the matter?" and she said, "Thābit b. Qays" — meaning, she could no longer be with her husband. When Thābit came, the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "This is Ḥabībah bint Sahl; she has said what God permitted her to say." And she said, "Messenger of God, I still have everything he gave me," and the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Take it from her" — so he took it from her, and she remained in her family's house. Al-Bukhārī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās: the wife of Thābit b. Qays b. Shammās came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "Messenger of God, I do not criticize his religion or his morals, but I hate to commit unbelief in Islam" — that is, to fail in his rights. The Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Will you give him back his garden?" She said yes, and he said, "Take back the garden and divorce her once." Al-Nasāʾī also transmits it. And the warning for the other case: the Prophet's ﷺ saying, reported from Thawbān — "Whichever woman asks her husband for a divorce without a valid reason, the scent of Paradise is forbidden for her." **[Qurṭubī]** gives the ḥadīth of Muʿādh: the Messenger of God ﷺ said to him, "Muʿādh, God has not created anything on the face of the earth more beloved to Him than emancipation, nor created anything on the face of the earth more hated to Him than divorce." The jurists draw from this the preference for reconciliation and the gravity of a divorce sought without cause, as against the verse's own allowance for the woman who hates to remain in a marriage in which she cannot keep God's limits.

**Rulings.** **[Study Quran]** lays out the structure: a couple can reconcile after a declarative divorce only twice; after the third declaration the divorce is final, the third being referred to either by "release her virtuously" or, in the next verse, "should he then divorce her." And the other main type, the *khulʿ* divorce, in which the wife initiates the divorce and can give a ransom to obtain it: her property becomes material to the *khulʿ* procedure, while a man may divorce without any transfer of wealth — the inverse of the marriage procedure, in which the wife collects a bridewealth from the husband and bears no financial responsibility within the marriage; put another way, a man negotiates his way into marriage through the bridewealth, and a woman may negotiate her way out of it through the ransom. **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the waiting period specific to *khulʿ*: al-Tirmidhī reports that al-Rubayyiʿ bint Muʿawwidh b. ʿAfrāʾ obtained a *khulʿ* in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered her to wait one menstruation period as her *ʿiddah*. **[Maʿārif]** frames the whole section with the status of marriage in the Sharīʿah: it is not merely a mutual transaction like buying and selling, but a *sunnah* and an act of worship by the consensus of the community — and hence has conditions and restrictions that ordinary contracts do not have, among them the limits set out in this verse and the verses around it.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** reads the closing sentence — "whoever transgresses God's limits, those are the wrongdoers" — as a definition of the greatest injustice: what shame is greater than for a man to storm the lawful and pass from it into the forbidden, so that what God made lawful is not enough for him? He divides *ẓulm* into three kinds: the servant's sin as between him and God; the greater *ẓulm*, which is idolatry; and *ẓulm* as between the servant and people. Idolatry God does not forgive except through repentance; the rights of the servants God leaves nothing of unrequited; and what lies between the servant and his Lord, short of idolatry, is left to the divine will and wisdom. In its place, the verse explains the whole apparatus of repeated divorce as a limit set against a man who would keep a woman suspended: two revocable returns to reconsider, then either a retention that respects her or a release that does her no further wrong.


## 2:230

*"And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries a husband other than him. And if he divorces her, there is no blame on the two of them to return to one another, if they think they will uphold God's limits. And these are God's limits, which He makes clear to a people who know."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the sense with Qatādah's summary: God made divorce three; when a man has divorced once he is most entitled to her so long as the waiting period has not elapsed — and the waiting is three menstruations — and if the waiting ends before he has taken her back, she is separated from him by the one divorce and becomes the owner of herself, and he becomes a suitor among suitors. **[Jalālayn]** reads the verse as the third: if the husband divorces her after the two utterances, she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband who has intercourse with her — as the two Shaykhs report — and if the second husband divorces her, neither of them is at fault, the woman and her first husband, in returning to each other in wedlock after the completion of her waiting, if they think they will maintain God's limits; and these are God's limits which He makes clear to a people who have knowledge. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the definition of the consummation that makes the marriage real: Aḥmad and al-Nasāʾī report from ʿĀʾishah that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "*Al-ʿusaylah* is sexual intercourse" — the diminutive used of the honey-taste, that is, the marriage must be an actual marriage, with desire, not a formality.

**Rulings and the curse on the trick.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** states the principle: the reason for the woman who has been divorced three times to marry another man must be that the man desires her and intends an extended married life with her, for these are the legal aims of marriage. If the reason behind the second marriage is to make the woman eligible for her former husband, then this is the *taḥlīl* that the ḥadīths curse and condemn; and if that intention is stipulated in the contract, the contract is invalid according to the majority of the scholars. He reports from Aḥmad, on the authority of ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd: the Messenger of God ﷺ cursed the one who does *taḥlīl*, the one in whose favour it is done, those who consume usury and those who feed it — transmitted by al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī, who declared it *ḥasan*, and acted upon by the people of knowledge among the Companions, including ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and Ibn ʿUmar, and by the jurists of the Successors. And from al-Ḥākim's *Mustadrak*, on the authority of Nāfiʿ: a man came to Ibn ʿUmar and asked him about a man who had divorced his wife three times, and whose brother then married her to make her lawful for him without the brother knowing it — was she permitted to the first? He said, "No, not unless it is a marriage involving desire; we used to consider that an act of adultery in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ." The ruling, then, is not a loophole but a wall: the verse closes the door that the two divorces had left ajar, and the curse falls on those who try to reopen it by a staged marriage.

**The logic of the limit.** **[Study Quran]** explains what the prohibition accomplishes: if a man were free to remarry his wife after three divorce declarations, he would be free to conduct another three and repeat the process indefinitely, keeping the wife from the full enjoyment of marriage through successive waiting periods while denying her the freedom to marry another. Forbidding a man from remarrying a woman after making her wait three sets of three courses — one set after each declaration — limits the harm he can inflict and discourages him from declaring divorce, since the prospect of remarrying a woman who is married to someone else is in most cases unlikely; and according to most jurists the intervening marriage needs to have been consummated. **[Maʿārif]** traces the sequence to its close: when the husband goes on to pronounce the third divorce, something the Sharīʿah does not like, the marriage stands wholly annulled, and he has exhausted his choice of revoking the divorce and taking his wife back; and since he transgressed the limits by the unnecessary third divorce, his penalty is that the two cannot remarry each other even by mutual agreement; the condition of their remarriage is that the woman, after completing her waiting period, should enter into marriage with another man, fulfil its obligations and live with him; and thereafter, if that husband divorces her or dies, she may remarry the first after completing her waiting. **[Qurṭubī]** records a legal argument the Ḥanafī scholars of Khurāsān drew from this verse: that the *khulʿ* divorce counts as a divorce, since God legislated the explicit divorce after the ransom — the *fāʾ* of "and if he divorces her" being the particle of sequence, so that its nearest antecedent is the ransom of the woman, not "divorce is twice."

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** draws a counsel out of the close: since the one who enters upon a matter without the capacity to uphold its limits is blameworthy, a person who wants to take up any affair — especially the offices of authority, small and great — should look into himself: if he sees in himself the strength for it and trusts it, let him go forward; otherwise let him hold back. And on the closing words, "which He makes clear to a people who know": God attached the clarification of His limits to the people of knowledge because they are the ones who benefit from them and who benefit others, and in this is a rank for the people of knowledge that is not hidden — that God made the explanation of His limits their special charge, and that they are its intended audience — and in it is that God loves from His servants the knowledge of the limits of what He sent down to His Messenger and the understanding of them. The verse that legislated the finality of divorce ends, then, not with the penalty alone but with an invitation: these limits are made plain to those who know, and knowledge of them is itself the way back inside them.


## 2:231

*"And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then retain them honorably or release them honorably; and do not retain them to harm them so that you transgress. And whoever does that has wronged his own soul. And do not take God's signs in mockery. And remember God's blessing upon you, and what He sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom, admonishing you thereby. And reverence God, and know that God is Knower of all things."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads "and they reach their term" as reaching the time appointed for them — the end of the three courses if she is a woman of courses, or of the months if she is a woman of months; "then retain them" means take them back if you wish to take them back in the divorce that admits return, whether the first or the second, as in "divorce is twice, then honorable retention or release with kindness." He explains "honorably": taking them back as God permitted, with the witnessing of the return before the waiting ends, and thereafter with the companionship and treatment God commanded. "Or release them honorably": let them complete their waiting and fulfill what remains of their term, giving them their full rights — dowry, parting gift, maintenance and the rest that you owe them. And "do not retain them to harm them so that you transgress": do not take them back during the waiting in order to harm them, to lengthen their waiting, or to take from them part of what you gave them by making them seek a ransom — through your retention and your taking back with harm and transgression. **[Qurṭubī]** supplies the grammatical precision: "they reach" (*balaghna*) here means they approach — by the consensus of the scholars, since after the actual completion of the term a man has no choice of retaining; whereas in the verse that follows it means the actual completion, being literal there and figurative here. He adds the ruling a group of the scholars drew from "retain them honorably": among the honorable retention is that a husband who cannot find what to spend on his wife should divorce her, and if he does not, he has left the bounds of the honorable, and the judge divorces against him because of the harm that comes to her from remaining with him.

**Ḥadīth & āthār: the practice of harm.** **[Ṭabarī]** collects the reports. Masrūq said: "He divorces her, and when she is about to finish he takes her back, then he divorces her and leaves her until her waiting is about to end, and he takes her back — not intending to keep her: that is the one who harms her and takes God's signs in mockery." Al-Ḥasan said: "A man would divorce the woman, then take her back, then divorce her, then take her back, harming her — and God forbade that." Mujāhid said: "God forbade harm: that a man divorce his wife and then take her back on the last day remaining of her term, so as to have her complete nine months, in order to harm her by it." And Ibn ʿAbbās said: "A man would divorce his wife and take her back before the end of her waiting, then divorce her — doing that to harm her and to hold her back" — and God sent down this verse. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Masrūq, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabīʿ and Muqātil b. Ḥayyān: a man would divorce his wife, and when her waiting neared its end he would take her back in order to harm her and to prevent her from marrying someone else, then divorce her again, and so her waiting was prolonged for her; and God prohibited the practice and threatened those who engage in it with the words "whoever does that has wronged his own soul" — meaning, by defying God's commands. He also gives the positive side: one who takes his wife back should do so in a better way, with witnesses to the return, and live with her in kindness; or he should release her after the waiting ends, letting her depart from his house without disputing, fighting or foul words.

**The mockery and the remembrance.** **[Study Quran]** explains "do not take God's signs in mockery" with the reports behind it: to declare divorce and then say, "I was only playing," or to take a similar attitude with any matter of marriage and divorce — a theme the Qurʾān touches elsewhere, at 5:57–58, 31:6 and 45:9; and it notes that the Book and the Wisdom are mentioned together also in 2:129, 3:48, 4:113, 5:110, 45:16 and 62:2. **[Saʿdī]** reads the two-handed call of the verse: since God had clarified His limits so plainly, and since the object was to know them and act upon them and stop at them rather than pass beyond them — for He did not send them down in play but in truth, sincerity and seriousness — He forbade taking them as a jest, that is, playing with them, storming them and failing to fulfil their obligations, as in using harm in the retention or in the parting, or multiplying divorces, or gathering the three at once; whereas God in His mercy made them one after another, gently with the servant and seeking his interest. Then "remember God's blessing upon you" — with the tongue in praise, with the heart in acknowledgment, with the limbs by using it in God's obedience — "and what He sent down to you of the Book and the Wisdom": the Book and the Wisdom, that is, the Sunnah, by which He clarified to you the paths of good and made you long for them, and the paths of evil and warned you against them, and made Himself known to you and His dealings with His friends and His enemies, and taught you what you did not know. He notes that some take the Wisdom as the inner meanings and purposes of the law: the Book contains the rulings, and the Wisdom discloses the divine wisdom in His commands and prohibitions — and both senses are correct. "Admonishing you thereby" inclines him to the second, since admonition comes through explaining the rulings with wisdom and by encouragement or warning: the rulings remove ignorance, wisdom with desire produces longing, and wisdom with warning produces awe. And "reverence God" in all your affairs, "and know that God is Knower of all things" — for this He laid out these rulings with the utmost care and precision, running with the interests of every time and place.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** draws the verse's three rules. First, when revocably divorced women near the completion of their waiting, the husband has two choices: revoke the divorce and let her remain his wife, or let the marriage end and release her. With both choices the Qurʾān places the condition of *maʿrūf*: the retention must be in accordance with what is well recognized, and the parting likewise in accordance with the Sharīʿah and not under the heat of the moment or passing anger — the Qurʾān giving some of the rules and the Prophet ﷺ the rest. Second, the basic rule of giving divorce: if a man finds no other option but divorce, the true method in the Sharīʿah and the Sunnah is a single revocable divorce in clear, unambiguous words, so that the option of taking the wife back remains open; words that cause sudden severance should not be spoken, and reaching three divorces, after which even a fresh marriage between the couple becomes unlawful, must be avoided. And this is indicated by the unqualified "when you divorce women": the injunction of this verse covers the one or two revocable divorces, not the three irrevocable ones — and by mentioning no qualification, the Qurʾān suggests that the true divorce is none other than the revocable divorce the Sharīʿah approves, the other forms not being free of repugnance.


## 2:232

*"And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands, when they have consented to one another honorably. With this are admonished those among you who believe in God and the Last Day. That is purer for you and cleaner. And God knows, and you do not know."*

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the occasion: Maʿqil b. Yasār's sister was married to Abū al-Baddāḥ, who divorced her and left her until her waiting ended; then he regretted it and proposed to her, and she was willing, but her brother refused to marry her to him and said, "My face is forbidden to your face if you marry him." And the verse came down. Muqātil's report adds the sequel: the Messenger of God ﷺ called Maʿqil and said, "If you are a believer, do not prevent your sister from Abū al-Baddāḥ" — and he said, "I believe in God," and married her to him. Al-Bukhārī reports from al-Ḥasan that the sister of Maʿqil b. Yasār was divorced by her husband until her waiting ended, and when he proposed to her Maʿqil refused, and so the verse came down. **[Ṭabarī]** gives the report before naming the man: the verse came down about a man whose sister was married to his cousin, who divorced her and did not take her back until her waiting ended, and then asked for her hand — and he refused to marry her to him and prevented her, though she was eager for him; and then he records the exegetes' disagreement about the man's identity, some naming Maʿqil b. Yasār al-Muzanī, with the report from Maʿqil himself through al-Ḥasan and Qatādah. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of the situation: the verse came down about the man who divorces his wife once or twice and her waiting ends, then wants to take her back and she wants that too, yet her family prevents her from remarrying him — so God forbade her family from preventing her; Masrūq, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Zuhrī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk say the same, and these statements conform to the verse's apparent meaning.

**Meaning and rulings.** **[Jalālayn]** reads it as an address to the guardians: when you divorce women and they complete their waiting, do not debar them from marrying their husbands — the former husbands — when the spouses and the women have agreed together honorably, in accordance with the Law. And he explains why the close says "that is purer for you": because of the suspicion that may be aroused concerning the couple on account of their prior intimacy. **[Saʿdī]** states the ruling and its inner reason: this is an address to the guardians of the woman divorced fewer than three times, when she has left the waiting and her husband wants to marry her and she agrees — it is not permissible for her guardian, father or other, to hold her back, that is, to prevent her from marrying him out of rancor against him over the first divorce, or anger. And God's word, "with this are admonished those among you who believe in God and the Last Day," means that faith in God and the Last Day is what restrains a man from such prevention; then "that is purer for you and cleaner" — purer and cleaner than the guardian's own opinion that not marrying her is the right view. And, **[Study Quran]** notes, the verse allows a couple to remarry even after they have gone through a complete legal divorce — though not in the case of the third consecutive divorce declaration, which the earlier verses had closed.

**The guardian's office.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** draws from the verse the ruling on the guardian's role in marriage: the verse indicates that a woman is not permitted to give herself in marriage; rather she requires a *walī* — a guardian such as her father, brother or adult son — to give her away, as al-Ṭabarī and al-Tirmidhī stated when they discussed this verse. He cites the ḥadīth: "The woman does not give another woman in marriage, and the woman does not give herself in marriage; for the adulteress is the one who gives herself away." And another: "There is no marriage except with a guardian of sound judgment and two just witnesses." **[Maʿārif]** frames the whole matter socially: this verse stops an injustice done to divorced women. In some cases the first husband opposes his divorced wife's remarriage to another and treats it as a violation of his honor; in some families the guardians prevent her from marrying a second time — sometimes out of greed, hoping to marry her off only when there is financial gain for them; and sometimes the divorced woman agrees to remarry her former husband, but the guardians and relatives have developed hostility toward him after the divorce and oppose the remarriage even when the two agree. Stopping free women, without any valid reason admitted by Islamic law, from marrying by their own choice, is a grave injustice whether it comes from the former husband or from the guardians; and this injustice is what the verse prevents. Its formula is exact: the prohibition falls on the preventing, not on the marriage; the right it protects is the woman's, the consent it requires is mutual, and the boundary it sets is the *maʿrūf* — the lawful contract, on honorable terms.

**Reflection.** The verse closes the Sūrah's divorce legislation with the sharpest of its corrections. Three times the man has been addressed — on *īlāʾ*, on repeated divorce, on retention to harm — and here the address turns to the guardian who would make an old grievance into a lifelong sentence. The pairing of "when they have consented to one another honorably" with "God knows, and you do not know" leaves the decision with the two who must live it, and the admonition is pitched to faith rather than to law: the one who believes in God and the Last Day is the one who will not hold her back.


## 2:233

*"And mothers shall nurse their children two full years — for the one who desires to complete the nursing. And upon the father falls their provision and clothing, honorably. No soul is tasked beyond its capacity. Let no mother be harmed on account of her child, nor a father on account of his child; and upon the heir the like of that. And if the two desire weaning, by mutual consent and consultation, then there is no blame on them. And if you wish to have your children nursed by another, there is no blame on you, provided you deliver what you have promised, honorably. And reverence God, and know that God sees what you do."*

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** explains the placement: after mentioning marriage and divorce, God mentioned the child, since the spouses may separate with a child between them — and so the verse concerns the divorced women who have children from their husbands, as al-Suddī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others said. The mothers are more entitled to nursing their children than strangers, because they are more tender and compassionate, and the snatching away of a small child is a harm to him and to her; and this indicates that even after weaning the mother is more entitled to custody, because of the abundance of her tenderness and care — though she is more entitled when she has not remarried. **[Ṭabarī]** is precise on the legal character of the command: the mothers are more entitled to nurse their children than others, but this is not an obligation imposed upon them by God when the child's father is alive and well-off, because God said in Sūrat al-Ṭalāq, "and if you find yourselves in difficulty, let another woman nurse for him" (65:6) — showing that the nursing is the mother's right and not, in that case, her duty. **[Maʿārif]** sets the practical frame: the verses before and after deal with divorce, and in between come the injunctions of nursing, because disputes over the feeding and upbringing of children commonly follow a divorce; since such disputes lead to violence, the verse offers a moderate system that both parties can carry out, covering nursing and weaning whether they occur during the marriage or after it, in a way that stops mutual bickering and injustice.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** begins with the form of the address: the statement carries the force of a command, being delivered in the form of settled information — "mothers shall nurse their children two years." And since the year may mean the full year or most of it, He said "two full years" — for whoever desires to complete the nursing. When the infant has completed two years, its nursing is complete, and milk thereafter is like other foods; and so nursing after the two years is not taken into account and does not establish the marriage prohibition, as **[Ibn Kathīr]** states: the nursing that establishes *taḥrīm* is that which occurs before the two years end, and al-Tirmidhī's chapter gives the same. Then: "and upon the father falls their provision and clothing, honorably" — the child's father owes the nursing mothers their maintenance and clothing, whether she is still in his household or divorced; and this, **[Saʿdī]** notes, shows that when she is still his wife she is owed no separate nursing wage beyond maintenance and clothing, while when divorced the maintenance and clothing are the wage of nursing; each is according to his state. Hence "no soul is tasked beyond its capacity": the poor man is not tasked with the provision of the wealthy, nor is one who has nothing tasked with spending until he finds.

**The two harms.** **[Saʿdī]** reads "let no mother be harmed on account of her child, nor a father on account of his child" as a bilateral protection: it is not lawful for the mother to be harmed because of the child — whether by being prevented from nursing him, or by being denied the maintenance, clothing or wage owed to her — nor for the father to be harmed because of the child, whether by her refusing to nurse him out of spite or by her demanding more than is due, and other kinds of harm. And he draws a fine point from the wording: the verse says the father is "the one to whom the child is born," indicating that the child belongs to the father, being given to him and being of his earning; that is why even if the child has property, the father may take from it with or without the child's consent — unlike the mother. Then "and upon the heir the like of that": the heir of the child, when the father is absent, and the child has no property, bears the like of what the father owed of provision and clothing for the nursing woman — which shows the obligation of supporting poor relatives upon the relative who inherits from them and is well-off. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same reading: upon the father's heir is incumbent the like of what was incumbent on the father — and God knows best.

**Weaning and wet-nursing.** **[Saʿdī]** continues: "and if the two desire weaning" — the two parents — that is, the weaning of the child before the two years, "by mutual consent and consultation" between them as to whether it is in the child's interest; if it is in his interest and they both agree, then there is no blame on them for weaning before the two years — and the verse's implication indicates that if only one of them agrees without the other, or if it is not in the child's interest, then weaning is not permitted. Then "and if you wish to have your children nursed by another, there is no blame on you, provided you deliver what you have promised, honorably" — that is, to the wet-nurses, their wages — "and reverence God, and know that God sees what you do," and will repay you for it with good and evil. **[Jalālayn]** reads the permission with the same limit: if you desire to seek nursing from other than the mothers for your children, there is no blame, provided you hand over what you intend to give in wages, honorably — in kindness and good nature. **[Study Quran]** frames the whole passage in its context: the verse addresses the status of women who bear children from husbands who have divorced them, since feeding and clothing one's wife is an obligation of marriage in all cases, and two full years is the maximum period during which the father must provide for the mother nursing his child.


## 2:234

*"And those among you who are taken in death and leave wives behind — they shall wait by themselves four months and ten nights. And when they have fulfilled their term, there is no blame upon you in what they do concerning themselves honorably. And God is Aware of what you do."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** notes the ellipsis at the verse's head: the predicate of "those among you who are taken in death" is dropped, since the object is not to report about the dead but to report the obligation of the waiting upon the widows; the report is turned from those whose mention opened the verse to their wives and the waiting due from them, because the meaning was known and understood — as when one says, "Some of your cloak is torn," and the sense is supplied. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the placement's logic: when God mentioned the waiting of divorce, and the mention of nursing was connected to it, He mentioned the waiting of death too, so that no one should suppose that the waiting of death is like the waiting of divorce. The men are those who die among you, who leave wives; the wives are the subject of the waiting. **[Jalālayn]** gives the rule: those of you who die leaving wives behind — the wives wait by themselves after their death, refraining from marriage, four months and ten nights, and this applies to women who are not pregnant; for the pregnant woman, the waiting is until she gives birth, as stated in Sūrat al-Ṭalāq (65:4); the slave-girl waits half of this period, two months and five days, according to the Sunnah; and when they have fulfilled their term, you are not at fault, O guardians, in what they may do with themselves in the way of adorning themselves and offering themselves to suitors honorably, in accordance with the Law.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ruling for the pregnant widow from the verse of al-Ṭalāq, "and those who are pregnant — their term is that they lay down their burden," and from the ḥadīth of Subayʿah al-Aslamiyyah in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, through several chains: her husband Saʿd b. Khawlah died while she was pregnant, and she gave birth only a few nights after his death; when she finished her post-natal bleeding she beautified herself for those who might seek her in marriage. Then Abū al-Sanābil b. Baʿkak came to her and said, "Why do I see you beautified — do you wish to marry? By God, you will not marry until four months and ten nights have passed." Subayʿah said, "When he said that to me, I gathered my garments when night fell and went to the Messenger of God ﷺ and asked him about the matter. He said that my waiting had finished when I gave birth, and he allowed me to marry if I wished." He also gives the wisdom of the legislated waiting from Saʿīd b. al-Musayyab and Abū al-ʿĀliyah: the womb might contain a fetus, and when the woman waits this period it becomes evident whether she is pregnant — with the support of Ibn Masʿūd's ḥadīth in the two Ṣaḥīḥs on the stages of the creation of the child in its mother's womb: forty days as a drop, then a clot, then a lump, and then the angel is sent. **[Study Quran]** notes the contrast with the days of ignorance: it is related that widows were often required to wait a year, wearing their worst clothes, neither grooming nor bathing, and marking the end of their mourning by leaving the house — the end being marked by flinging a piece of animal dung and rubbing the front of their bodies with an animal, acts of unclear significance.

**Rulings.** **[Study Quran]** notes the two readings of "wait by themselves": some jurists take it to mean that the widow cloisters herself in her home, on the basis of certain aḥādīth pointing to widows keeping to the home and not putting on perfume or ornaments, while other prominent early jurists, such as al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, hold that the text simply refers to refraining from marriage. **[Maʿārif]** sets out the practical injunctions: for the woman whose husband dies, it is not correct to wear perfume, make-up, kohl or hair oil, or to beautify herself unnecessarily, or to apply henna, or to dress gaudily; nor is it correct to speak of a second marriage in clear and unambiguous words, as the next verse makes plain; nor to stay overnight in homes other than her own. The wording "keep themselves waiting" indicates these avoidances; and the same applies to the woman who has received an irrevocable divorce, in which return is not possible — though it is not right for her to leave the house even during the daytime unless there is extreme compulsion. He adds a rule many are unaware of: if the husband dies on the night of the new moon, these months are completed according to the lunar calendar, whether the months are twenty-nine or thirty days; and if he died after the night of the new moon, the reckoning is worked out accordingly. **[Saʿdī]** gives the purpose in a sentence: the waiting is obligatory, and its wisdom is that pregnancy should become apparent within the four months and the child move at the beginning of the fifth — and this general rule is specified by the verse concerning pregnant women, and there is consensus of the scholars on it.

**Reflection.** "And when they have fulfilled their term, there is no blame upon you in what they do concerning themselves honorably": **[Saʿdī]** draws from the address to the guardians a proof of their function — that the guardian watches over the woman and prevents her from what is not lawful and obliges her to what is due, and that he is addressed by this and obliged by it. The guardianship, in other words, is not a lock but a trust: the same men who are responsible for her waiting are told that once its term is fulfilled they must not stand in her way. And the close, "God is Aware of what you do," covers what the term's legal form could not — the intentions of the family, the subtleties of pressure and permission — with the knowledge of the One who sees the outward and the inward of every act.


## 2:235

*"And there is no blame upon you in intimating a proposal of marriage to women, or in concealing it within yourselves. God knows that you will remember them; but do not make a secret appointment with them — unless you speak an honorable word. And do not resolve upon the marriage tie until the term prescribed has reached its end. And know that God knows what is within your souls, so beware of Him; and know that God is Forgiving, Clement."*

**Meaning and language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the word: *junāḥ* means sin, and this is the sounder view in the religious law; it is also said to mean the difficult and burdensome matter, and this is the sounder in the language — al-Shammākh's line speaks of a rider remembering "what there is with him of *junāḥ*." The address, he says, is to all people, but the ruling concerns the man who intends in himself to marry a woman in waiting: there is no guilt in the intimation of a proposal during the waiting of widowhood. And *taʿrīḍ*, intimation, is the opposite of *taṣrīḥ*, explicit speech: it is conveying the meaning by something that may bear it and may bear other than it — from the *ʿurḍ* of a thing, its side, as though the speaker circles around it rather than landing on it. **[Jalālayn]** gives the examples by which the intimation is conveyed: a man saying, "How beautiful you are!" — or, "Who could find one like you?" — or, "How many a man must desire you!"; God knowing that you will mention them in proposing impatiently, and so permitting such offers; but do not make arrangements of marriage with them secretly — unless you speak the honorable words that the Law acknowledges, that is, such proposals as are permitted to you; and do not resolve upon the consummation of marriage until the term prescribed has reached its end and been completed. **[Ṭabarī]** records the same with the āthār: the intimation permitted in the waiting of widowhood is, as Mujāhid reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, that one says, "I want to marry," and "I love a woman whose affair is thus and thus," intimating to her with the speech that is honorable.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the distinction and its reason. The verse's ruling concerns the woman in waiting after her husband's death, or the one irrevocably separated in his lifetime: for the man who is not her husband, explicit speech to her about betrothal is forbidden — which is the sense of "do not make a secret appointment with them" — while intimation carries no blame, because the two differ in kind. Explicit speech admits no interpretation other than marriage, and so it is forbidden out of fear that she should hasten, and lie about her waiting being over, in desire for the marriage; in this there is a proof of the prohibition of the means to what is forbidden, and the fulfilment of the first husband's right that no pledge be given to another during her waiting. Intimation, which admits marriage and other meanings, is permitted: for example, that one says to her, "I wish to marry," or "I would like you to consult me when your waiting ends," and the like — permitted because it is not of the rank of explicit speech, while the soul has a strong impulse toward it; and likewise the man's concealing in his heart the intention to marry her when the waiting ends. Hence "or in concealing it within yourselves: God knows that you will remember them" — and all this detail concerns the preliminaries of the contract; as for the marriage contract itself, it is not lawful "until the term prescribed has reached its end," that is, until the waiting is complete. And on the close: "know that God knows what is within your souls" — so intend the good and do not intend the evil, in fear of His punishment and hope of His reward; "and know that God is Forgiving" — of those from whom sins have come and who then repent and return to their Lord; "Clement" — in that He does not hasten the disobedient to punishment, though He is fully able over them.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the reports: al-Thawrī, Shuʿbah and Jarīr report from Ibn ʿAbbās that the intimation means saying, "I want to marry and I am looking for a woman of such-and-such qualities," talking of her in general, in a way that is better; and in another narration from him, "I wish that God would bestow a wife upon me" — but he should not make a direct proposal. Al-Bukhārī reports from Ibn ʿAbbās: the man could say, "I wish to marry," "I desire a wife," "I wish I could find a good wife." Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs, ʿIkrimah, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Zuhrī, Yazīd b. Quṣayṭ, Muqātil b. Ḥayyān, al-Qāsim b. Muḥammad and many others among the Salaf and the imams held that it is permitted to mention marriage indirectly to the woman whose husband has died. **[Study Quran]** states the same line clearly: intimating a proposal means that one may express a desire for marriage while stopping short of proposing and making an agreement; a man may say, "I hope to marry a righteous woman," or "I do not wish to marry any other woman," or "I desire to marry" — but he may not say, "Promise me you will marry me and no other." Contracting a marriage during the waiting period is forbidden. "Save that you speak in an honorable way" means that his dealing with her should not go beyond the limits of the intimation mentioned at the verse's head, and "do not pledge your troth with them secretly" can mean either that they should not agree to marry or that they should not consummate a marriage.

**Reflection.** The verse keeps two goods in view at once — the widow's dignity and freedom, and the seriousness of the marriage tie — and marks the middle line with unusual care. **[Saʿdī]**'s observation about the means is the key: because a long waiting with a strong impulse invites both parties to invent ways around the limit, the verse forbids the explicit proposal not because the desire is unlawful but because the pressure it creates is; and it permits the intimation because the desire itself is honest and should not be driven underground. The close locates the enforcement: "God knows what is within your souls, so beware of Him" — the rule of the outward word is backed by the knowledge of the inward intention, and the final pairing of Forgiveness with Clemency leaves the door of repentance open to the man who resolves before the term is out.


## 2:236

*"There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them, nor appointed for them a dowry. But provide for them — the one of ample means according to his means, and the one of straitened means according to his means — a provision in kindness; an obligation upon the doers of good."*
