**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** gives the reading and the rule: you would not be at fault if you divorce women while you have not touched them — the verb read *tamassūhunna* or *tumāssūhunna*, meaning sexual intercourse — nor appointed any obligation, a dowry, for them; so divorce them; yet make provision of comfort for them honorably, in accordance with the Law — giving them what they can enjoy, the one of ample means among you according to his means, and the needy man of restricted income according to his means — an obligation upon the virtuous, the obedient. **[Qurṭubī]** explains why the verse was needed at all: when the Messenger of God ﷺ forbade marrying for the sake of taste and the satisfaction of appetite, and commanded marrying for the seeking of chastity, the desire of God's reward and the intention of lasting companionship, it fell into the believers' minds that one who divorces before consummation had committed a part of that disliked thing — and so the verse came down, lifting the blame in that case, when the basis of the marriage was the good intention. And a group read "there is no blame" in the sense that there is no claim to the full dowry: half of what was fixed is owed for the one whose dowry was fixed, and the *mutʿah*, the parting provision, for the one for whom nothing was fixed. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the meaning of "touched" from Ibn ʿAbbās, Ṭāwūs, Ibrāhīm and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī: sexual intercourse; so the husband is permitted to divorce his wife before consummating the marriage or giving the dowry, if it had been deferred.

**The parting gift.** **[Ṭabarī]** establishes the word: "or appoint for them" means to make obligatory for them, and "a dowry" is the obligatory bridal payment — Ibn ʿAbbās said, "the dowry"; and the root of *farḍ* is the obligatory, as the poet's line says, "my coming to you was an obligation, as stoning was the obligation of fornication." **[Saʿdī]** gives the reasoning behind the gift: there is no blame or sin upon you, husbands, in divorcing women before consummation and before the fixing of the dowry — even though in that there is a breaking of her — because that break is repaired by the *mutʿah*; and since they caused her anticipation, her longing and the attachment of her heart, and then did not give her what she hoped for, they owe the *mutʿah* in return — a right and an obligation upon the doers of good, who must not stint her of it. He closes with an exclamation on the ruling: how excellent this divine ordinance, and how indicative of the wisdom of its Lawgiver and His mercy — and who is better than God in judgment for a people who are certain? **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the Prophetic instance: al-Bukhārī reports in his *Ṣaḥīḥ* from Sahl b. Saʿd and Abū Usayd that the Messenger of God ﷺ married Umaymah bint Sharāḥīl, and when she was brought to him he extended his hand to her, but she did not like that; so the Prophet ﷺ ordered Abū Usayd to provide provisions for her along with a gift of two garments — the parting gift in practice, from the Prophet's own household.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** sets out the four situations that the two verses (236 and 237) dispose of, according to whether the dowry was fixed and whether consummation took place. Where the dowry was not fixed and consummation has not taken place: no dowry is due, but the husband must give something of his own to the woman, the least being a set of clothes; the Qurʾān fixes no amount for this gift, though it indicates that the affluent should give according to their means, and the poor according to theirs. Where the dowry was fixed but consummation has not taken place: half the dower is due, as the next verse states. Where the dowry was fixed and consummation has taken place: the fixed dower must be paid in full — an injunction appearing elsewhere in the Qurʾān. And where the dowry was not fixed but the divorce came after consummation: the full *mahr al-mithl*, a dower such as is customarily given in the woman's immediate family, is owed — also taken up in another verse. **[Study Quran]** notes the parallel verse 33:49 on divorce before the consummation of a marriage, and that "not having touched them" refers to consummation; the case addressed is that of a couple who have contracted the marriage but have not consummated it or agreed upon the bridewealth — and, as with the bridewealth itself, a wealthy man would give a different amount from a poorer man in these circumstances; some say that if the couple cannot agree on an amount, it should be half the bridal payment of those with similar means, as the next verse indicates.

**Reflection.** The verse is a study in what a contract without consummation still leaves behind. **[Qurṭubī]**'s report of the believers' scruple is the key to its placement: they feared that a divorce before consummation was a slight to the woman and a degradation of the marriage's purpose, and the answer is not to forbid the divorce but to require the gift — the wound is acknowledged, and the remedy is a payment measured by the giver's means. **[Saʿdī]**'s phrase captures the legal imagination at work: since they caused her attachment and then withheld what she hoped for, the *mutʿah* stands in the place of what was hoped. And the closing words fix the obligation's rank: "an obligation upon the doers of good" — not a favor to be given grudgingly, but a debt of *iḥsān* owed by those who claim to do good.


## 2:237

*"And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already appointed a dowry for them — then half of what you appointed, unless they remit it, or the one in whose hand is the marriage tie remits. And that you remit is nearer to reverence. And forget not bounteousness among you. Truly God sees what you do."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the clarification of the one before it: this ruling explains "there is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not touched them, nor appointed for them a dowry" — that is, you may divorce them, and where you had already appointed a dowry, they have against you half of what you appointed them, half of what you gave as bridal payment. **[Jalālayn]** gives the structure: if you divorce them before touching them while you have already appointed an obligation for them, then half of what you appointed must be given them, and the other half returns to you — unless the women make remission and forgo it, or the one in whose hand is the knot of marriage makes remission, leaving her the entire amount. And he notes the report from Ibn ʿAbbās that the holder of the knot may be the legal guardian where the female is a minor. Then "that you remit is nearer to piety" — the remitting being the subject, its nearness to *taqwā* the predicate — and "forget not kindness between you," that is, be bountiful toward one another; surely God sees what you do and will requite you accordingly.

**Rulings.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** states the settled rule: this verse is not a continuation of the *mutʿah* gift mentioned in the verse before it; it requires the husband to relinquish half of the appointed dowry when he divorces before consummation; and giving half the bridal money in this case is the agreed practice of the scholars. "Unless they remit it" means the wife forfeits the dowry and relieves the husband of further financial responsibility; he cites the report of al-Suddī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās on the phrase. **[Saʿdī]** gives the alternative: when the women are divorced before consummation and after the fixing of the dowry, they have half of the appointed dowry and the husbands the other half — this is the obligation, so long as no remission or pardon enters, whether the woman forgoes her half to her husband, when her remission is valid, or "the one in whose hand is the knot of marriage" forgoes. And he settles the identity: he is the husband according to the sound view, since it is he in whose hand is the loosening of the knot; and the guardian may not remit what has become due to the woman, since he neither owns it nor acts as her agent. Some said it is the father, and the wording of the verse perhaps indicates that. **[Study Quran]** sets out the same two readings: the holder of the marriage tie is the husband, in which case he forgoes the half of the bridal payment he could legitimately expect to get back — and "holding the marriage tie" refers to the husband's prerogative of divorce, since it is he who exercises the power to divorce; the party nearer to reverence would then be the one who forgoes his half and lets the other side take the entirety, realizing the virtue of bounteousness. Others interpret the holder as the legal agent whose permission is usually necessary for a woman to marry, in which case the wife would, with the guardian's approval, forgo the half she was entitled to keep — with the difficulty, it notes, that this position has.

**The preference for remission.** **[Qurṭubī]** records the earlier discussion of whether this verse excludes the woman whose dowry was fixed from the parting gift, since "and provide for them" would cover her: Mālik and others say it excludes her, since the half-dowry rule takes her case; Ibn al-Musayyab said this verse abrogated the verse of al-Aḥzāb, which had included a parting gift for every woman not consummated with; Qatādah said it abrogated the verse before it. Qurṭubī himself demurs: the conditions of abrogation are not present, and reconciliation of the texts is possible — Ibn al-Qāsim in the *Mudawwanah* held that the gift pertains to every divorced woman, by "and for the divorced women a provision in kindness," and to the unconsummated by the verse of al-Aḥzāb. **[Saʿdī]** then draws the moral the verse is built to urge: since God encouraged remission and made the one who remits nearer to His reverence, because remission is a kindness that expands the breast, and because a person should not neglect himself of kindness and good treatment, nor forget the bounty that is the higher of the two degrees of dealing between people. For people's dealings with one another are of two degrees: either justice and fairness, which is obligatory — taking what is due and giving what is due — or bounty and kindness, which is giving what is not obligatory, and tolerating rights, and swallowing what is in the soul. A person should not forget this degree, even at some times, especially toward one with whom he has dealings or association; for God repays the doers of good with bounty and generosity — and hence "truly God sees what you do."

**Reflection.** The verse disposes of a contract that never became a marriage: a knot tied and untied before consummation, with a dowry named and now to be divided. Its legal answer is arithmetic — half goes back — but its moral answer is not, and the two clauses that follow the rule move the parties from the arithmetic to the higher degree. **[Saʿdī]**'s distinction between justice and bounty explains why: the law can compel only the half; the verse invites the whole, and names the One who sees what is done, so that the unforced generosity between two people who were briefly married is not lost. It is the same movement the Sūrah made in the case of the parting gift: where the law sets a floor, the verse commends a ceiling.


## 2:238

*"Be watchful over the prayers and the middle prayer, and stand before God in devout obedience."*

**Meaning and language.** **[Qurṭubī]** opens with the address and the word: "be watchful" is an address to the whole community, a command to keep up the prayers at their times with all their conditions, and *muḥāfaẓah* is persevering in a thing and staying with it. *Al-wusṭā* is the feminine of *awsaṭ*, and the *wasaṭ* of a thing is its best and most just — as in "and thus We made you a middle community" — and an Arab praising the Prophet ﷺ said, "O most middling of all people in their glories, and most generous of people in mother and father." He notes that the middle prayer is singled out for mention after being included in the general term, as a mark of honor, as in "when We took from the prophets their covenant, and from you, and from Noah." **[Jalālayn]** gives the command and the dispute: maintain the five prayers by performing them at their appointed times, and the middle prayer — either the afternoon or the morning or the midday or another, for there are many opinions on the matter; God singled it out for mention because of its merit. And "stand in prayer submissive to God": some say it means obedience, on the strength of the Prophet's saying — reported by Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal and others — that wherever the expression *qunūt* appears in the Qurʾān it denotes obedience; and it is also said to mean in silence, on the basis of Zayd b. Arqam's ḥadīth: we used to speak to one another at times during prayer, but when this was revealed we were commanded to be silent and were forbidden to talk, as reported by the two Shaykhs, al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

**The middle prayer.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth case for al-ʿAṣr in detail: al-Bukhārī and Muslim report from Ibn Masʿūd that he asked the Prophet ﷺ which deed is dearest to God, and he said, "Prayer at its fixed time"; he asked, "Then which?" and he said, "Jihād in the path of God"; he asked, "Then which?" and he said, "Dutifulness to parents" — and ʿAbdullāh added, "The Prophet ﷺ told me these words, and had I asked more, he would have told me more." As for the middle prayer, it is the ʿAṣr prayer according to the majority of the scholars among the Companions, as al-Tirmidhī and al-Baghawī stated; al-Qāḍī al-Māwardī added that the majority of the Successors also held this view, and al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-Barr that it is the opinion of the majority of the scholars of the *athar*. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said it is the majority's interpretation; and Abū Muḥammad ʿAbd al-Muʾmin b. Khalaf al-Dumyāṭī, in his book on the middle prayer, stated that it is the ʿAṣr prayer, and listed as holding this the interpretation of ʿUmar, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Ayyūb, ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAmr, Samurah b. Jundub, Abū Hurayrah, Abū Saʿīd, Ḥafṣah, Umm Ḥabībah, Umm Salamah, Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿĀʾishah — and of ʿUbaydah, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Razīn, Zirr b. Ḥubaysh, Saʿīd b. Jubayr, Ibn Sīrīn, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Kalbī, Muqātil, ʿUbayd b. Abī Maryam and others. Then the proof: Aḥmad reports from ʿAlī that the Messenger of God ﷺ said during the battle of the Confederates, "They busied us from the middle prayer, the ʿAṣr prayer — may God fill their hearts and houses with fire," and he performed the ʿAṣr between Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ; Muslim and al-Nasāʾī recorded it. Aḥmad also reports from Samurah b. Jundub that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "The middle prayer is the ʿAṣr prayer," and al-Tirmidhī graded it *ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ*. And from the emphasis on it: whoever misses the ʿAṣr prayer is as one who has lost his family and his property; and the Prophet's instruction to perform the prayer early on a cloudy day, "for whoever leaves the ʿAṣr prayer, his deeds are annulled."

**[Study Quran]** frames the uncertainty: the prayers are the five canonical prayers, but there is no general consensus on the meaning of the middlemost prayer; it is identified variously as one or another of the five, though some maintain that its identity is unknown; others consider it the congregational Friday prayer, or the ʿĪd prayer, or even the five prayers together. And on "devout obedience," which also connotes silence, obedience and humility among other virtues, it refers to its own discussion at 4:34c. **[Maʿārif]** records the majority's reasoning: on the authority of some aḥādīth a very large number of the scholars have said the middle prayer is the ʿAṣr, because before it there are two daytime prayers — Fajr and Ẓuhr — and after these come two evening prayers, Maghrib and ʿIshāʾ; special emphasis is placed on it because it falls at a time when most people are busy at their work. Incidentally, the Qurʾānic word *qānitīn*, obedient or submitting, rendered "stand before God in total devotion," has been explained in ḥadīth as denoting *sukūt*, motionless silence; and it was through this very verse that talking in prayer was forbidden — earlier, talking had been permissible.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** gives the purpose: God commands the guarding of the prayers in general and the middle prayer in particular, and the guarding of them is their performance at their time, with their conditions, pillars, humility and all their obligatory and recommended parts; and by the guarding of the prayers one guards all the other acts of worship, and it yields the prohibition of indecency and wrong, especially when one completes it as commanded. The verse thus sits at the hinge of the Sūrah's domestic legislation — after the waiting periods, the nursing, the proposals and the dowry — and gathers the community back to the pillar that outlasts all of it. Its single imperative, placed at the center of household law, answers the question of what holds the household together when the contracts have been dissolved: the same prayer that keeps a person standing before God keeps him just in his dealings with a woman in waiting or a wife divorced before consummation; and the call to *qunūt* — obedience, silence, stillness — sets a standard of attention against which all the haggling over half-dowries and parting gifts is measured.


## 2:239

*"And if you fear, then on foot or riding. But when you are secure, remember God as He taught you what you did not know."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse in the flow of the one before it: "and stand before God in your prayer, obedient to Him" — then, if you fear an enemy, dreading for yourselves when you meet them, that you cannot pray standing on your feet on the ground, then pray *rijāl* — walking on your feet while in war and fighting and striving against your enemy — "or riding," upon the backs of your mounts; for that will suffice you in place of standing, in devout obedience. And he notes the grammar: *rijāl* is set in the accusative by a verb omitted, since the meaning is "then pray on foot." **[Qurṭubī]** gives the lexicography at length: *rijāl* is the plural of *rājil* or of *rajul*, from their saying *rajila* — a man walks when he lacks a mount — and it has many plural forms, *rijāl, rajlā, rujjāl, rajjālah, rujālā, rujlān, rijl* and *rijalah*, *arjilah, arājil, arājīl*. His second point: since God commanded standing before Him in prayer in a state of *qunūt*, which is dignity, tranquility and silence — and commanded it in the perfect form — the concession follows for the one who cannot attain it. **[Jalālayn]** reads the fear broadly: if you are in fear of an enemy, or a torrent, or a predatory animal, then praying while walking or mounted, in whatever way you can, facing the qiblah or otherwise, making the gestures of bowing and prostration. But when you are secure from fear, then remember God by performing the prayer as He taught you what you knew not before — He taught you its obligations and its proper ways; the *kāf* of *ka-mā* having the meaning of *mithl*, "like," and the *mā* relating to the action.

**The fear prayer.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the practice: after commanding His servants to perform the prayer perfectly and emphasizing it, God mentioned the situation in which a person may not be able to perform it perfectly, in battle and combat. Mālik reports from Nāfiʿ that Ibn ʿUmar used to describe the fear prayer when asked about it, and would then add, "If there is intense fear, pray on foot, riding, facing the qiblah or otherwise." Nāfiʿ said, "I think he related that to the Prophet ﷺ." **[Study Quran]** adds the detail: one can be fearful in battle or under persecution; in cases of fear one can pray while riding or walking, whether facing the qiblah or not; and rather than bow and prostrate, one may nod and lightly move the head corresponding to the motions of the prayer; according to some, one may shorten the prayer down to one cycle rather than two, three or four. It refers to the detailed discussion of prayer in conditions of fighting and fear in 4:101–102. **[Maʿārif]** states the juristic result: this verse allowed a special way of offering the prayers in the state of fear, the state of war. In such a state one can offer the prayer while standing, on condition that one can stand in one place without moving, and can make the gesture of prostration in a lower position than the gesture of bowing — but prayer cannot be performed while walking; if it is not possible to pray otherwise, one performs it as best one can.

**Remembering God as He taught.** **[Saʿdī]** opens the concession widely: "if you fear" deletes the object of the fear so as to include fear of the enemy, of a predatory beast, and of missing what a person would be harmed by missing — so pray "on foot," walking on your legs, "or riding," on horses, camels and all mounts; and in this state the facing of the qiblah is not required. This is the description of the prayer of one excused by fear; but when security comes, one prays the prayer in full — which is part of "remember God when you are secure" — and included in it too is abundance of God's remembrance in gratitude for the blessing of security and the blessing of being taught what brings the servant's happiness. And in this noble verse there is a virtue of knowledge: the one whom God has taught what he did not know should multiply God's remembrance; and it hints further that abundance of His remembrance is a cause of being taught other knowledge, since gratitude is joined to increase. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s ḥadīth material ties the earlier command to the same point: "and stand before God with obedience," meaning with humility and lowliness before Him, indicates that speaking during prayer is not allowed, since speech contradicts the nature of the prayer. This is why the Prophet ﷺ did not answer Ibn Masʿūd when he greeted him while he was praying, and said afterward, "Prayer has its own occupation." Muslim reports that the Prophet ﷺ said to Muʿāwiyah b. al-Ḥakam al-Sulamī when he spoke during the prayer, "This prayer is not fit for anything of people's speech; it is only glorification, magnification and the remembrance of God." And Aḥmad reports that Zayd b. Arqam said, "One used to address his companion about various affairs during the prayer; then when this verse was revealed — 'and stand before God with obedience' — we were ordered to refrain from speaking." The Group, except Ibn Mājah, reported it.

**Reflection.** The verse is the Sūrah's law of necessity. Having set the prayer as the fixed center — five times, at their times, with the middle one doubly guarded — it makes room at the very center for the man on the ground in fear, and gives him the prayer in the only form he can manage: standing or mounted, facing or not, with nods in place of bowing. **[Saʿdī]**'s expansion of the deleted object of fear is the key to the spirit of the ruling: the concession is not only for the battlefield but for every fear that would keep a person from prayer. And the second half returns the worshipper to the norm — "remember God as He taught you what you did not know" — where the gratitude for the teaching is itself the substance of the remembrance, and the remembrance becomes the cause of more knowledge still.


## 2:240

*"And those among you who are taken in death and leave wives behind — a bequest for their wives: a provision for a year, without eviction. But if they leave, there is no blame upon you in what they do concerning themselves honorably. And God is Mighty, Wise."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the ellipsis as in the earlier verse: the report is turned from those whose mention opens the verse to the wives and what is due to them — the men who die leaving wives behind them, wives joined to them by marriage and not by ownership; and the sense of the verse is the bequest owed for them: a provision and enjoyment for a year, without turning them out of the dwelling. **[Jalālayn]** puts it as a command to the dying or their family: let them make a bequest for their wives as an obligation, giving them provision for a year — of property and clothing — without expelling them from their habitations; but if the women go out of their own accord, you are not at fault, O guardians of the dead man, in what they do with themselves honorably, such as adorning themselves or leaving off mourning and the like; God is Mighty in His kingdom, Wise in His acts. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the reading: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, al-Kisāʾī and ʿĀṣim in Abū Bakr's transmission read *waṣiyyatun* in the nominative — a subject whose predicate is "for their wives," with the sense "a bequest is owed to them" — while Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah and Ibn ʿĀmir read the accusative, carried by an implied verb.

**The dispute over abrogation.** This is the verse the Sūrah's commentators discuss most at length, and the seven sources split over it. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the majority account: a group of exegetes — Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn Zayd and al-Rabīʿ — held that the widow of a deceased husband used to sit in his house for a year, maintained from his estate as long as she did not leave it; if she left, the heirs bore no blame for cutting off her maintenance; then the year was abrogated by the four months and ten, and the maintenance was abrogated by the quarter and the eighth in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ. He records al-Bukhārī's report from Ibn al-Zubayr: I said to ʿUthmān, "This verse in al-Baqarah — 'and those who die leaving wives... without eviction' — the other verse has abrogated it, so why do you not leave it out?" He said, "O son of my brother, I will not change anything of it from its place." **[Ibn Kathīr]** explains what Ibn al-Zubayr was asking: if its ruling has been abrogated by 2:234, why is it still in the Qurʾān, where it might suggest the ruling still stands? ʿUthmān answered that this is a matter of the revelation, which placed these verses in this order — so he left the verse where he found it. **[Maʿārif]** gives the same historical sequence: in the Age of Ignorance the waiting of a widow was one year; in Islam it became four months and ten days; but because the injunction of inheritance had not yet been revealed, and people's rights still revolved around the will of the deceased, the woman was given the additional right to live in her late husband's house for a full year if she wished, with maintenance from his estate, and husbands were instructed to make wills to that effect. Since the right was hers, the heirs could not evict her; but she could leave at her discretion and leave her due to the inheritors, once the waiting of four months and ten days was complete — after which she could leave and marry again. This is what the verse means, and it was abrogated when the verse of inheritance came and she received her ordained share. **[Saʿdī]** dissents explicitly: the opinion commonly reported among many exegetes — that 2:234 abrogated this verse, and that the woman was first commanded to wait a full year and then it was reduced to four months and ten — has no proof, and its defenders answer the awkward fact that the abrogating verse stands earlier in the Book only by saying that precedence was in placement and not in revelation, which is no proof at all. Whoever reflects on the two verses sees that the other view is the correct one: 2:234 makes the four months and ten a binding obligation upon the woman, while this verse is a bequest to the family of the deceased — that they keep their dead man's wife among them for a full year, to console her heart and honor their dead. Hence "a bequest for their wives": a bequest from God to the deceased man's people that they should care for his wife, provide for her and not turn her out; if she wishes she stays under the bequest, and if she prefers to leave, no harm — "if they leave, there is no blame upon you in what they do with themselves," that is, in adorning and dressing, provided it is in the *maʿrūf* that does not take her beyond the limits of religion and decency. **[Study Quran]** records both positions and its own resolution: some believe the verse's ruling was abrogated by the waiting period of four months and ten days in 2:234, but others see no contradiction, understanding the verse to affirm the widow's option to receive up to one year of maintenance while living in her late husband's house — if she remarries before that, there is no blame upon the husband's heirs for stopping their support; others again say it was abrogated by the inheritance shares of 4:12 — but if it is seen as a right to reside and receive sustenance for a year with the option of leaving earlier, there is no necessary contradiction and no need for abrogation.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports al-Bukhārī's narration from Mujāhid, whose report he calls sound and established: the waiting used to be observed obligatorily with the husband's family; then God revealed the verse of the bequest, and He made the completion of the year — seven months and twenty nights — a bequest for her: if she wished she stayed under her bequest, and if she wished she left, which is His saying "without eviction; but if they leave, there is no blame upon you." Ibn Jurayj likewise narrated from Mujāhid what the people hold, so consensus formed and disagreement ceased. Yet Qurṭubī himself judges the first view more apparent, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying, "It is only four months and ten; one of you in the Age of Ignorance used to throw a piece of dung at the head of the year" — this being his report of the widows' condition before the Law came; then Islam commanded them to keep to the houses a year, and then that was abrogated by four months and ten. He adds, on the authority of Abū ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-Barr, that the scholars of the Muslims are in consensus on this, with no disagreement, and that the report from Mujāhid going beyond four months and ten is anomalous, abandoned and unsupported — no scholar of the Companions, the Successors or those after them held it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** carries the same materials with Ibn ʿAbbās's two statements: that the widow used to reside with provision for a year in her deceased husband's house, and that this was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, so that she inherits a fourth or an eighth; and, through ʿAṭāʾ, that the verse abrogated the requirement that the widow spend her waiting in her husband's family's home, so that she spends it wherever she wishes — and then the inheritance verse came and abrogated the residence altogether. The verse's close, **[Saʿdī]** notes, seals it with the two names that indicate perfect might and perfect wisdom: these are ordinances issuing from His might and showing His wisdom in placing them where they belong.

**Reflection.** The verse is a hinge in the Sūrah's treatment of the widow: a bequest of a year's shelter and maintenance, given at a time when inheritance shares had not yet been fixed and the dying man's will was the widow's only provision, then read by most of the community as superseded when the waiting was reduced and the shares were assigned. The dissenting reading of **[Saʿdī]** and the tradition behind **[Ṭabarī]**'s Mujāhid keeps the verse legible as a rule of equity rather than a dead letter: the widow's year was never a second waiting but a shelter offered without compulsion, and the two exits the verse names — the heirs may not turn her out, and she may leave when she chooses — are the two freedoms the verse protects on both sides. In either reading, the ethical center is the same: a household grieving its dead man is told to console his widow, and the widow is told she may go honorably when she is ready. The Sūrah's closing names, al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm, mark the legislating as both authoritative and wise.


## 2:241

*"And for the divorced women a provision in kindness — an obligation upon the reverent."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the sense: for the women divorced by their husbands there is a *matāʿ* — meaning what she enjoys, of clothing, garments, maintenance, a servant, and the like. **[Jalālayn]** reads: there shall be provision for divorced women, which they are given honorably, as is feasible — an obligation upon those who fear God; and he notes why the rule is repeated here when it was already given in 2:236: to include the woman who has been touched sexually, since the earlier verse addressed a different case. **[Study Quran]** makes the same point: the message resembles 2:236, but that verse concerned a marriage not yet consummated, whereas this verse has a general import and places an obligation upon all men to make some manner of provision for the women they divorce. **[Saʿdī]** connects it forward and backward: having explained the provision of the woman separated by death, God mentions here that every divorced woman has against her husband the right that he provide for her and give her what suits his state and hers — and that it is a right upheld by the reverent.

**Whom the verse covers.** **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the disagreement. Some said it means the previously married who have been consummated with, since the obligations owed to the untouched are laid down in the verses of *mutʿah* elsewhere. Others — and this is the reading he reports with its chains — held that the verse proves every divorced woman has a *mutʿah*, and that God revealed it because it adds to the other verses of *mutʿah*: those state the ruling of the untouched woman when divorced, while this states the ruling of all divorced women together. Saʿīd b. Jubayr said, "Every divorced woman has a provision in kindness, an obligation upon the reverent." Al-Zuhrī, asked about the slave-woman whom her husband divorces while she is pregnant, said she observes her waiting in her house, and she has the provision until she gives birth. ʿAṭāʾ was asked whether the slave-woman married to a free man has a *mutʿah*, and said no; and whether a free woman married to a slave has it, and said no — while ʿAmr b. Dīnār said yes, citing this verse. A third group said the verse was revealed in response to an objection: when God had sent down "provide for them — the one of ample means according to his means and the one of straitened means according to his means" concerning the untouched woman, some asked what provision was owed to the others.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** carries the debate further. Abū Thawr said the verse is *muḥkamah*, not abrogated, and the provision belongs to every divorced woman — al-Zuhrī said the same, even for the slave-woman divorced by her husband — and Saʿīd b. Jubayr likewise; and it is one of the two views of al-Shāfiʿī, held on the strength of this verse. Mālik's position: every divorced woman has the provision — whether the divorce was the second or the first, whether the marriage was consummated or not, whether a dowry was named or not — except the woman divorced before consummation whose dowry had been named, for whom the half suffices; if no dowry had been named for her she has the provision, less than the *mahr al-mithl* or more, for the *mutʿah* has no fixed limit — as Ibn al-Qāsim reported from him. Ibn al-Qāsim said in his commentary on the *Mudawwanah*: God made the *mutʿah* for every divorced woman by this verse, then made the exception in the other verse, for the one whose dowry was fixed. **[Saʿdī]** resolves the kinds: where no dowry was named and the divorce came before consummation, it is obligatory according to the man's means or lack of them, as already stated; where a dowry was named, her provision is half of what was named; and where the marriage was consummated, the provision is recommended in the view of the majority of scholars, while some scholars held it obligatory, inferring from "a right upon the reverent" — since the root meaning of "right" is what is owed, especially as God attached it to the reverent and *taqwā* itself is obligatory. **[Maʿārif]** lays out the same scheme from the angle of what *matāʿ* is taken to mean. The earlier verses had restricted it to two kinds of divorce before consummation — a set of clothes where no dowry was fixed, and half the dower where it was. What remains is the divorce after consummation: there, provision for the woman whose dower was fixed means the full dower, and for the woman whose dower was not fixed, the *mahr al-mithl*, the equivalent customarily given in her family. If the word *matāʿ* is taken in the sense of the dower, its payment is obligatory on these details; if it means a particular benefit — a gift or a set of clothes — then it is obligatory only for the types already identified, and desirable in the remaining cases; and if it means maintenance, it is obligatory until the expiry of the waiting period in the case of a divorce after which the waiting is observed, revocable or irrevocable alike. The verse, by its universally applicable wording, covers all the situations.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** closes the passage's account with its purpose, turning from the ruling to the Giver of the ruling: when God had explained these mighty ordinances between spouses, He praised His own ordinances, His clarifying them to His servants, and their agreement with sound minds — and the aim of His clarifying to His servants is that they should grasp what He has made clear, holding it in memory, understanding it, and acting on it, for that is the completion of understanding. **[Jalālayn]**'s note that the verse was repeated to cover the woman who had been touched sexually makes the sequence coherent: the Sūrah has now spoken of the widow's year, of the woman divorced before consummation with and without a dowry, and of the woman divorced after the marriage was complete — and "a provision in kindness" is the common thread. The obligation is graded by circumstance and the amount left to what is fitting, but the closing phrase sets its rank: "an obligation upon the reverent." What the law may fail to enforce, God-fearingness is expected to supply.


## 2:242

*"Thus does God make clear to you His signs, that haply you may understand."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the "thus" as binding this verse to all that preceded it: as I have made clear to you, O believers, what you owe to your spouses and what they owe to you, and made known to you My rulings and the right due from one of you to the other in these verses — so do I make clear to you the rest of the rulings in My signs that I sent down upon My prophet Muhammad ﷺ in this Book, so that you may understand My limits, O you who believe in Me and My messenger, and grasp what is binding upon you of My obligations, and know thereby what holds the good of your religion and your world, your present and your Hereafter. **[Jalālayn]** puts the same in a sentence: in the same way that He has explained to you what has been mentioned, God makes clear His signs for you, so that you might understand and reflect. **[Study Quran]** notes the phrase's wider life in the Qurʾān: the making clear of God's signs is a recurring refrain — in 2:266, 3:103, 5:89, 24:61 — and the word *kadhālika*, "thus," points to a specific referent, namely that it is on the preceding questions of divorce that God makes His signs clear, while also serving as a reminder that He does so in general.

**The close of the passage.** **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the seal on the whole unit of domestic legislation: when God had explained these mighty rulings between spouses, He praised His rulings, and His explaining of them, and their agreement with sound minds — and the purpose of His explaining them to His servants is that they should understand from Him what He has made clear, understanding it with preservation, comprehension and practice; for that is the completion of understanding it. **[Qurṭubī]**'s discussion of the provision carries into this verse the last dispute of the passage: al-Shāfiʿī held that the woman whose dowry was fixed has no *mutʿah* when divorced before consummation, since she has taken half the dowry without consummation, while the consummated woman divorced has the *mutʿah*, the dowry being in exchange for consummation and the *mutʿah* on account of the exposure brought by the contract; and he made the *mutʿah* obligatory for the woman who ransoms herself out of the marriage and for her counterpart who seeks mutual release. Mālik's companions objected: how should the woman who pays a ransom have a provision, when she is the one giving? — and so, in their view, there is no *mutʿah* for the woman who herself chooses the separation, consummated or not, dowry named or not.

**Reflection.** The verse closes a stretch of the Sūrah that has moved through nursing, waiting periods, proposals, dowries, parting gifts, the fear prayer, the widow's bequest and the divorcee's provision — and it names the whole body of it as God's *āyāt* made clear. The pairing is exact: the rulings are called signs, and the purpose of the clarification is understanding, not memorization. **[Saʿdī]**'s formulation keeps both halves in place — preservation in memory, comprehension of meaning, and practice — so that the household law of the preceding verses is not a code consulted in disputes but a part of the recitation by which the community understands God's intent. It is the same closing cadence the Sūrah will use again after its other great legislative passages, and it turns the reader back to the beginning of the passage with new eyes: the command to guard the prayers, and the commands to guard the rights of women, belong to the same explained book.


## 2:243

*"Hast thou not seen those who went out from their homes, and they were thousands, wary of death? Then God said to them, 'Die' — then He revived them. Truly God is Possessed of bounty toward mankind, but most of mankind do not give thanks."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the question as a matter of the heart's sight, not the eye's: "have you not seen" means "have you not known, O Muhammad?" — for the Prophet ﷺ did not live in the time of those God reports of here, and the sight of the heart is what a man sees and knows. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same sense, with Sībawayh's formulation: the meaning is "be aware of the affair of those who..." — and he notes that Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read the verb with a sukun on the *rāʾ*, the hamzah dropped without carrying its vowel, the original being *a-lam taraʾ*. **[Maʿārif]** explains why the Qurʾān uses "seeing" of a story generations earlier: the address *a-lam tara* employs the sight of the heart, knowledge and insight, and carries the sense of "did you not know" — but the chosen form points out that the incident is so well attested that it is as though it were seen, and is worth seeing; and the particle *ilā*, "toward," reinforces the direction of that insight.

**The story.** **[Qurṭubī]** relates on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, and **[Ibn Kathīr]** reports from him and from ʿAlī b. ʿĀṣim: they were a people of the Children of Israel in a village called Dāwardān — a place some miles from Wāsiṭ in Iraq — where the plague fell; they went out fleeing it and camped in a valley, saying, "We shall come to a land where there is no death," and God caused them to die. Then a prophet passed by them and asked his Lord to revive them that they might worship Him, and He revived them. **[Jalālayn]** gives the sequence compactly: God said to them, "Die," and they died; then He gave them life, after eight days or more, at the supplication of their prophet Ezekiel, and they lived on with the marks of death still on them — so that when they put on garments these turned into shrouds for the dead, a phenomenon that remained with their descendants. **[Ṭabarī]** carries the fuller Israelite accounts: Wahb b. Munabbih's report that affliction and hardship fell on a group of the Children of Israel, who cried out that they wished they had died and been at rest; God then revealed to Ḥizqīl (Ezekiel): do they think I cannot raise them after death? Go to such-and-such a graveyard, where four thousand of them lie — their bones scattered by birds and beasts — and call them; and he called, "O bones, God commands you to gather," and each man's bones came together, then were clothed with flesh and skin, then the souls were commanded back into the bodies, and they stood and uttered one *takbīr*. And ʿAmr b. Dīnār's account in **[Ṭabarī]**: the plague struck their village three times; the third time they all went out except a few, and God put them and their animals to death, then revived them, and they returned to their land and multiplied there until they would ask one another, "Who are you?" *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the version many of the Salaf related: their climate did not suit them and an epidemic broke out; they fled and took refuge in a fertile valley, filling the space between its two sides; God sent two angels, one from the lower side and one from the upper, who screamed once and all the people died as the death of one man; they were later walled up, their bodies rotted, and long afterwards one of the prophets of the Children of Israel — Hizqil — passed by and asked God to bring them back to life by his hand, and God answered, commanding him to call, "O rotted bones, God commands you to come together," then "O bones, be covered with flesh, nerves and skin," then "O souls, return each to the body it used to inhabit" — and they came back to life, looked around, and proclaimed, "All praise is due to You, and there is no deity worthy of worship except You." **[Qatādah]**, in **[Ṭabarī]**, gives the theological reading: God detested them for fleeing death, so He caused them to die as a punishment, then raised them to complete the remainder of their terms — had their terms come, they would not have been raised after their death.

**Their number.** **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the reports: Ibn ʿAbbās said four thousand; ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī, three thousand or more; Ibn ʿAbbās again, through Ibn Jurayj, forty thousand and eight thousand; and his own preferred view is the report that puts their number above ten thousand, since God described them as *ulūf*, and *ulūf* is the plural of multitude, not used of fewer than that. **[Qurṭubī]** lists what the reports give: six hundred thousand, eighty thousand, forty thousand (Ibn ʿAbbās), thirty thousand (Abū Mālik), thirty-seven thousand (al-Suddī), seventy thousand (ʿAṭāʾ b. Abī Rabāḥ), and forty thousand plus eight thousand again from Ibn ʿAbbās. **[Maʿārif]** notes that *ulūf* is the plural of multitude and not used for something less than ten, which tells us their number was not less than ten thousand. **[Ṭabarī]** also records a second reading of the word itself: some said "and they were *ulūf*" means they were *muʾtalifūn* — united, bound to one another — a report he gives from Ibn Zayd's circle before settling the sense on number.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** The passage's practical rulings come from the plague traditions. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth of ʿUmar at Sargh, on the road to Syria, met by the army commanders Abū ʿUbaydah b. al-Jarrāḥ and others; when the news came that plague had broken out in Syria, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. ʿAwf told them that the Messenger of God ﷺ had said: "When you hear that it has broken out in a land, do not go to it; and when it breaks out in a land you are in, do not leave it fleeing from it." ʿUmar thanked God and turned back — a ḥadīth also in the two Ṣaḥīḥs. **[Qurṭubī]** adds the other side of the same teaching: al-Bukhārī reports from ʿĀʾishah that she asked the Messenger of God ﷺ about the plague, and he told her it was a punishment God sends upon whom He wills, which God made a mercy for the believers — so that no servant in whose land it appears, who stays there patiently knowing that nothing will befall him but what God has written for him, but he has the like of the reward of a martyr; which is the meaning of "the plague is martyrdom, and the one struck by it is a martyr": the one who is patient under it and seeks his reward from God, knowing that nothing will strike him but what God has decreed — whereas the one who panics at the plague and hates it and flees has not entered into the sense of the ḥadīth. Abū ʿUmar adds that no bearer of knowledge is known to have fled the plague, apart from ʿAlī b. Zayd b. Judʿān, of whom Ibn al-Madāʾinī reports that he fled to al-Sayālah and would return each Friday. **[Study Quran]** records both readings of the incident: a group among the Children of Israel who fled either a plague or a war, apparently in disobedience, seeking safety, and were nevertheless caused to die, after which a prophet was sent to revive them — and in this connection some commentators mention the Prophet's command not to flee a place where there was plague or to travel to one. Some say the historical people or time is unimportant: the theme is that God has power of life and death over human beings, that they cannot determine their own life and death, and that the Prophet and believers should take a lesson from it, especially since the next verse commands fighting in the way of God. It also notes that some see the verse as a reference to Ezekiel 37:1–14, where Ezekiel is commanded to revive a valley of dry bones — while the Biblical account does not say why the valley was full of bones, and beyond the revival there are no similarities between the two accounts.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the lesson the placement demands: in this story there is a proof that God is powerful over all things, and a tangible sign of the resurrection — the event being well known and transmitted among the Children of Israel, which is why God brought it in the form of settled, established report. And, he adds, it likely concerns those who went out of their homes in fear of enemies and cowardice at meeting them — supported by the fact that God mentions the command to fight right after it, and by His informing us that the Children of Israel were driven from their homes and their children; on either reading it inspires desire for striving and warns against hanging back, for that avails nothing against death: "Say, if you had been in your houses, those decreed to be killed would have come out to their deathbeds" (3:154). **[Ibn Kathīr]** states the same with the verse's own words: the story shows that no caution can avert destiny, and that there is no refuge from God but to God Himself; they left their land fleeing the epidemic and seeking long life, and what they earned was the opposite of what they sought. **[Maʿārif]** frames the whole unit: the two verses here and the one that follows present guidance prompting the sacrifice of life and property in the way of God, and before the injunctions an event of history is taken up which makes clear that death and life are subject to the destiny God has determined — going to battle is not the cause of death, and running from it out of cowardice is not the means of avoiding it. **[Saʿdī]** closes on the verse's own cadence: "God is Possessed of bounty toward mankind" — not least in this: that He brought these men back — "but most of mankind do not give thanks," most people falling short of the duty of gratitude, while His bounty to people continues.


## 2:244

*"And fight in the way of God, and know that God is Hearing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the command in its setting: fight, O believers, in God's way — that is, in His religion, which He has guided you to, not in the obedience of Satan — against the enemies of your religion who bar the way to your Lord; do not shrink from fighting them when you meet them, nor turn cowardly from warring them, as those who went out of their homes fleeing death came to it: their flight did not save them from it when God's command and decree arrived, nor did those who stayed behind suffer the thing they had guarded against, since their terms defended them. So fight in God's way against those I have commanded you to fight of My enemies and the enemies of My religion; whoever of you lives, I give him life, and whoever is killed, his killing was by My decree. Then the close: know, O believers, that your Lord is *Samīʿ* — Hearing what the hypocrites among you say of those killed in My way, "Had they obeyed us and sat in their homes, they would not have been killed" — *ʿAlīm*, Knowing what their breasts conceal of hypocrisy, disbelief and scant gratitude for His favors. **[Jalālayn]** gives the purpose in a phrase: so fight in God's way in order to elevate His religion; and know that God is Hearing of your sayings, Knowing of your affairs, and He will requite you accordingly.

**Whom the address reaches.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes the disagreement: this is an address to the community of Muhammad ﷺ with fighting in the way of God according to the majority — and it is that by which one intends that the word of God be uppermost. The ways of God, he says, are many, and the command is general in every way; Mālik said the ways of God are many and there is no way but that one fights for it or in it, and the greatest of them is the religion of Islam, on which there is no disagreement. And it was also said that the address is to those revived of the Children of Israel — reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk — the *wāw* of "and fight" joining this command to the command implied in the preceding story. **[Study Quran]** records both: some think the fighting was commanded to those who were revived in the previous verse, while others hold that because the grammar indicates a direct address and not a historical narration, the verse should be read as a general moral injunction to the believers to struggle for the truth — which can be a spiritual as well as a physical struggle. If the latter is correct, the mention of fighting indicates that it was revealed after armed struggle was permitted for Muslims.

**The fixed term.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** draws the verse's doctrinal edge: it indicates that just as caution does not alter destiny, abandoning fighting neither brings the appointed term closer nor delays it; destiny and the appointed provisions are fixed and shall never be changed, by addition or deletion. God said, "Say: avert death from your own selves, if you speak the truth" (3:168), and, "Wherever you may be, death will overtake you, even if you are in towers built up strong and high" (4:78). **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse together with the one that follows, since God joined the command to strive with wealth and body: fighting is commanded with both, because the striving does not stand except on the two; and He urged sincerity in it — that the servant fight so that God's word be uppermost — for God is *Samīʿ* of words however hidden, and *ʿAlīm* of what the hearts contain of sound intentions and their opposite. And, he adds, when the one striving in God's way knows that God is Hearing and Knowing, the burden becomes light for him: he knows that his trial is under God's eye, and that God will surely aid him with His help and His kindness. **[Maʿārif]** frames the whole passage: these verses present guidance prompting the sacrifice of life and property in the way of God, and they take the lesson of the plague story as their premise — that running from a battle is not the means of avoiding death, and entering it is not the cause of it, since death comes at its appointed time, neither earlier nor later.

**Reflection.** The verse converts a history lesson into a command. The story of those who fled in thousands, died, and were revived taught that flight cannot outrun the decree; the imperative that follows draws the consequence — not a counsel of recklessness, but a release from the illusion that safety is a place. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s three parallel verses press the point: those at home in their houses are overtaken, and those in strong towers are overtaken, since the term is written and no caution writes it again. And the two names at the close fix the inner measure of the command: the fighter is told that God hears what his enemies say of him and the hypocrites after him, and knows what he intends in his own heart when he goes out — so that the struggle's worth is settled where no observer can see it, in the intention weighed by the One who hears and knows.


## 2:245

*"Who is he that will lend God a goodly loan, that He may multiply it for him many times over? And God withholds and outstretches, and unto Him shall you be returned."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the naming: who is this who spends in the way of God — helping one whose mount is foundered, or strengthening a man in need who wants to strive in God's way, or giving to one in straits? That is the goodly loan a servant lends his Lord. And God called it a loan because *qarḍ* in the speech of the Arabs is a man's giving his property to another as his possession, for him to repay the like when he asks for it; since the one who gives to the needy in God's way gives what he gives seeking the abundant reward promised on the Day of Resurrection, God named it a loan. He made it "goodly" because the giver gives it at God's prompting and urging, seeking His count, from a sound heart and a generous soul. And the verse, he notes, is the counterpart of "the parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is as the parable of a grain that brings forth seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains" (2:261), and it is the same sense Ibn Zayd gave: this is in God's way; "that He may multiply it for him many times over" — the one becomes seven hundred. **[Jalālayn]** reads "goodly" as spending for the sake of God, out of purity of heart, and "He will multiply it" — the verb read *yudāʿif* or *yudaʿʿif* — up to ten or seven hundred times or more; and God straitens sustenance for whom He wills, to try him, and enlarges it for whom He wills, to test him; and to Him you shall be returned in the Hereafter through the resurrection, where He will requite you for your deeds.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** ties the verse to the fighting preceding it: since God had commanded struggle and the making of war for the truth — for there is nothing in the Law but that fighting may be undertaken for it and in its defense, and the greatest of its subjects is the religion of Islam, as Mālik said — He then stirred up the desire to spend in that cause; and so the one who fights in God's way enters into this address, for he is lending his Lord, in hope of reward, as ʿUthmān did in the army of hardship. He relates that Abū al-Daḥdāḥ heard the verse and said, "O Messenger of God — is it that God wants a loan from us?" and he said, "Yes, Abū al-Daḥdāḥ"; he said, "Show me your hand," and when the Prophet ﷺ gave it, he said, "I have lent God a walled garden with six hundred palms." He then walked to the garden where Umm al-Daḥdāḥ was with his children and called to her, "Umm al-Daḥdāḥ!" — she said, "At your service" — "Come out; I have lent my Lord a garden with six hundred palms." And in Zayd b. Aslam's report: Abū al-Daḥdāḥ said, "May my father and mother be your ransom, O Messenger of God — does God ask us for a loan when He is free of all need of it?" He said, "Yes; He wishes to bring you into the Garden by it." He said, "If I lend my Lord a loan, will He guarantee me and my children the Garden with me?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Give me your hand" — and the Messenger of God ﷺ gave him his hand — "I have two gardens, one below and one above; by God I own nothing besides them; I make them a loan to God." The Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Make one of them for God and keep the other a living for you and your family." So he said, "I call you to witness that I have made the better of them for God — a walled garden of six hundred palms." He said, "Then God will repay you the Garden by it." **[Ṭabarī]** gives the same report through Zayd b. Aslam and adds the Prophet's ﷺ word: "How many a laden date-cluster there is for Ibn al-Daḥdāḥ in the Garden!" **[Maʿārif]** carries it in the same shape, with the ending that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Countless trees laden with dates and spacious palaces eagerly await Abū al-Daḥdāḥ." It also gives the ḥadīth on lending: "No Muslim lends another Muslim a loan but it is counted for him as charity twice" (Ibn Mājah, as cited by Maẓharī), and the report that a date given in God's way is increased by God until it outgrows the mountain of Uḥud.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports Ibn al-ʿArabī's observation that people divided in three groups on hearing this verse. The first, the contemptible, said, "Muhammad's Lord is poor and in need of us, while we are rich" — a folly not hidden from anyone of understanding, and God answered them in another verse: "God has surely heard the saying of those who said, 'God is poor and we are rich'" (3:181). The second, hearing it, preferred niggardliness and miserliness and the love of wealth, so they spent nothing in God's way, freed no captive and helped no one, out of idleness from obedience and inclination to this present house. The third, hearing it, hastened to comply, and the promptest of them gave his property, as Abū al-Daḥdāḥ and others did. And on the word: al-Zajjāj said *qarḍ* in the language is the good trial and the evil trial — as Umayyah's line has it, "every man shall be repaid his loan, good or evil" — so that the verse's "loan" is what a man sends ahead of himself, whether good or ill. **[Maʿārif]** draws the legal point that belongs to the dealings it names: in repaying a loan, paying a little more than one took is a favorable practice only where the increase has not been made a precondition; if increase is stipulated, it is forbidden and is *ribā*. **[Saʿdī]** supplies the definition of the goodly loan: it is what gathers the qualities of goodness — sound intention, generosity of soul in the spending, its being placed where it belongs, and the spender's not following it with reminders of generosity, harm, or anything that nullifies or diminishes it.

**Reflection.** **[Study Quran]** notes that some take the verse as continuing the previous one, in which case the goodly loan is a metaphor for the effort and risk of fighting in the way of God; others hold it begins a new subject and refers to giving one's wealth in charity or for religious causes, while others deny any contradiction between the two — and it points to the parallel instances at 5:12, 64:17, 73:20 and 57:11, where the commentators observe that serving God and doing good is always, as it were, a good bargain, against the "unprofitable" transactions by which one sells God's signs for a paltry price. On "God withholds and outstretches," it observes that these are two important concepts of Islamic spirituality: withholding is related to the state of contraction (*qabḍ*), and outstretching to expansion (*basṭ*), and read spiritually the verse describes a threefold process — inner purification, the acquisition of virtues, and finally realization and illumination, "and unto Him shall you be returned"; some Sufis describe contraction and expansion as two states that follow each other in the heart like night follows day, and they are related to the twin states of fear and hope, which must be kept in balance for a soul to progress. **[Saʿdī]** reads the same clause as consolation: since the greatest obstacle to spending is the fear of poverty, God informed of His withholding and outstretching — that provision is in His hand, and that the one who spends for His sake will have it replaced, so that the spender's act lands in the divine hand with a weight that cannot be expressed.


## 2:246

*"Hast thou not seen the assembly of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs, 'Raise up for us a king, that we may fight in the way of God'? He said, 'Might it be that, were fighting prescribed for you, you would not fight?' They said, 'And what is wrong with us that we should not fight in the way of God, seeing that we have been driven from our homes and our children?' Yet when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned back — except a few of them. And God knows the wrongdoers well."*

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** explains the placement: this is another story from the Children of Israel, told to stir the desire for fighting. *Al-malāʾ* are the notables of a people, as though they were filled with honor — al-Zajjāj said they are so called because others are filled with what they need from them; and the word in this verse means the people, since the sense requires it, being a collective noun like *qawm* and *raht*. The request came "after Moses," that is, after his death, to a prophet of theirs — and it is said he was Shamuwayl b. Bālī, the Samuel of the Israelite histories. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives Mujāhid's identification: the prophet is Shamwīl. He reports from Wahb b. Munabbih that the Children of Israel remained on the straight path for a time after Moses, then innovated in the religion until some worshipped idols; prophets were always sent among them commanding good and forbidding evil and ruling by the Torah, but when the evil grew, God caused their enemies to overwhelm them: many were killed, a great number taken captive, and large areas of their land seized. Earlier, whoever fought them lost, because they had the Torah and the *tābūt*, which they inherited generation after generation from Moses, who spoke with God directly — until a king took the *tābūt* from them in a battle, and with it the Torah, so that only a few who had memorized it remained. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* **[Ṭabarī]** relates the same stream of Israelite history at length, including the account of the *tābūt* carried before them in battle, so that no enemy met them without their advancing it among them. **[Maʿārif]** gives the historical setting in brief: these people had abandoned God's injunctions, and when the infidel Amalekites were made to rule over them, they began to think of correcting the situation; the prophet named here is Samuel. **[Study Quran]** notes that the request to raise up a king can be compared with the Israelites' words to Samuel in 1 Samuel 8:19–20: "But we are determined to have a king over us, so that we also may be like other nations, and that our king may govern us and go out before us and fight our battles."

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** follows the exchange: when they said to a prophet of theirs, "Send us a king to unite us, to whom we may refer our affairs, that we may fight with him in God's way," the prophet said, "Might it be that, if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?" — the interrogative being intended to confirm the expectation that follows, namely that they will not. They said, "Why should we not fight in the way of God, when we have been expelled from our homes and our children?" — the children having been taken captive or killed by Goliath and his men; the meaning being, "There is nothing to prevent us fighting, provided what we asked for is forthcoming." Then God says: yet when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned their backs in cowardice, except a few of them — those who crossed the river with Saul, as will come. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammar and the readings of the prophet's question: *ʿasaytum* may be read with a fatḥah or a kasrah on the *sīn*, two dialects, Nāfiʿ reading the kasrah and the rest the fatḥah, which is the better known; Abū Ḥātim said the kasrah has no ground, though al-Ḥasan and Ṭalḥah read it — and the sense of the sentence is, "Are you near to turning away and fleeing?" So the prophet's question was not doubt about God's promise but a knowledge of his people's resolve, and their answer came back with a full vow: "And what is wrong with us that we should not fight?" — **[Ibn Kathīr]** renders it: after our land has been confiscated and our children taken from us?

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** opens the story, which he reads through the end of the Sūrah's account of Saul and Goliath, with its purpose: God relates this story to the community so that they may take heed and desire the striving and not recoil from it — for the patient have the praiseworthy outcomes in this world and the next, while those who hang back lose. The narrative's judgment is exact and quiet: the people asked for a king so that they could fulfil their vow to fight, and when the fighting was prescribed, their vow collapsed except in a few. **[Saʿdī]**'s reading of the prophet's question shows where the story's lesson lies: their prophet feared that their request was words with no deed behind it, and events proved him right — a nation's confidence in its own resolve is not the same as its steadiness when the cost arrives. And the close, "God knows the wrongdoers," keeps the judgment measured: God knows precisely who held back and why, and the wrong of breaking so solemn a vow is left with Him to weigh.


## 2:247

*"And their prophet said to them, 'God has raised up for you Saul as king.' They said, 'How should he have kingship over us, when we have more right to kingship than he, and he has not been given ample wealth?' He said, 'God has chosen him over you, and increased him amply in knowledge and body. God gives His kingship to whom He wills; and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing.'"*

**Context.** **[Ṭabarī]** supplies the setting from the Israelite histories: their prophet Shamuwayl told the assembly that God had granted what they asked and raised up Saul as their king, and their objection followed — Saul was of the tribe of Benjamin, and the tribe of Benjamin had neither kingship nor prophecy in it, while they, being of the tribe of Judah, held themselves more entitled; and he had not been given ample wealth, since he was a water-carrier, and it is said a tanner. He relates the account of how the kingship came to him: the prophet was told to watch the horn of oil in his house; when a man entered and the oil in the horn murmured, that man was to be king of the Children of Israel — anoint his head with it and make him king over them. Saul, a tanner working leather, of the tribe of Benjamin, went out seeking a stray animal with his servant; they passed by the prophet's house, the servant suggested asking him about the beast and seeking his prayer, and as they sat speaking of the animal the oil in the horn murmured; the prophet rose, took it, said, "Bring your head near," anointed him, and said, "You are the king of the Children of Israel whom God commanded me to make king over them." **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same report from Wahb b. Munabbih and adds the detail of Saul's trades: a water-carrier, it is said a tanner, it is said a muleteer, and he was learned — which is why God raised him, as the verse will say; and he was of the tribe of Benjamin, while prophecy was in the house of Levi and kingship in the tribe of Judah, which is why they objected. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that Saul was then a soldier, and not of the house of kings among them, which was exclusively in the offspring of Judah; some say he used to bring water to the people, others that his profession was dyeing skins. The Jews, he says, disputed with their prophet when they were supposed to obey him and to speak good words to him. **[Study Quran]** points to the parallel in the Book of Samuel: Saul's low social status, which is the source of the Israelites' disdain, is mentioned by Saul himself when Samuel first speaks to him — "I am only a Benjaminite, from the least of the tribes of Israel, and my family is the humblest of all the families" (1 Samuel 9:21) — and in 1 Samuel 10:27 the Israelites express the disdain: "But some worthless fellows said, 'How can this man save us?' They despised him and brought him no present." It adds the wider analogy: their aversion to Saul's election is similar to the aversion of the Quraysh and the Jews to Muhammad at his election as a prophet — his lack of wealth and status among the Quraysh, and his non-Jewish lineage among the Jews; and the commentators understand the account to mean that Saul was from neither a kingly nor a priestly line but from the tribe of Benjamin.

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** follows the exchange closely: their prophet said to them, "God has raised up Saul for you as king" — and their objection was that they had better right to kingship, since he was not of the tribe of monarchs or of prophets; he was a tanner or a shepherd; and he had not been given amplitude of wealth by which to establish a kingdom. The prophet answered: "God has chosen him over you, and increased him amply in knowledge and body" — at that time he was the most knowledgeable and the most handsome of the Children of Israel, and the most perfect in character. God gives kingship to whom He wills, in the way He does, and there is no objection to be raised; and God is Embracing in His bounty, Knowing of those who deserve it. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the prophet's answer as the correction of the objection's premise: I did not choose Saul as your king of my own accord — God commanded it in answer to your request; and God chose him while knowing better about him, and increased him in knowledge and stature, so that he is more knowledgeable and honorable than you, stronger and more patient in combat, with more knowledge of warfare. In short, the king should have sufficient knowledge, be fair of appearance, and have a strong soul and body. **[Ṭabarī]**'s report adds the detail that after the anointing the prophet also gave Saul the news of what had come to him, so that he knew by what sign the kingship had reached him.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** reads the exchange as the answer to a claim of entitlement: the people asked for a king to end their dispute by his appointment and to secure full obedience, and their prophet feared their request was mere words with no deed; they answered with a firm resolve, and the prophet named Saul to lead them in the matter — for it needs a leader who is skilled in command. Then they found the appointment strange, since there were among them men of better house and more wealth; and their prophet answered that God had chosen him over them by what God gave him — strength of knowledge of governance and strength of body, which are the instruments of courage, aid and good management — and that kingship is not a matter of abundance of wealth, nor of the king's coming from a house in which rule and lordship have been, for God gives His kingship to whom He wills. **[Study Quran]**'s comparison with the Prophet Muhammad's reception closes the circle: the same argument by which the Children of Israel measured Saul — lineage and wealth — is the argument by which the Quraysh and the Jews measured God's final messenger, and the Sūrah's answer in both cases is one: sovereignty, like prophethood, is God's to give. The verse's close holds the two names that settle the dispute before it is raised — *Wāsiʿ* in bounty, *ʿAlīm* of who deserves it — so that the community's quarrel over the appointee is placed under the appointment of the One who knows.


## 2:248

*"And their prophet said to them, 'The sign of his kingship is that the ark shall come to you, wherein is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the house of Moses and the house of Aaron left behind, borne by the angels. Truly in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** draws the significance of the sign from the flow of the passage: the fact that God reports this word of the prophet proves that the Israelite assembly did not accept Saul's appointment when their prophet announced it to them and told them of the excellence God had given him; rather they asked him for a proof of the truth of what he said — so the sense is that they said, "What is the sign of that, if you are truthful?" and their prophet answered, "The sign of his kingship is that the ark shall come to you." **[Jalālayn]** fills out the contents: a chest containing the images of the prophets, which God sent down to Adam and which was handed down among the Israelites until the Amalekites seized it from them in battle; they used to begin their fighting invoking it before their enemy and marching behind it, and they found peacefulness in its presence — so that in it there was a spirit of tranquility from their Lord, and a remnant of what the people of Moses and the people of Aaron left: Moses' pair of sandals and his staff, Aaron's turban, a measure of the manna that used to come down on them, and the pieces of the broken tablets. The angels bore it while they looked on, until they set it down before Saul; then they acknowledged his kingship, hastened to enlist in the struggle, and he chose seventy thousand of their young men. **[Study Quran]** notes that the commentators relate that the ark was returned, after being lost or taken in battle, as a sign of Saul's right to lead — though in the case of this passage much or all of the information in the commentaries seems to be based on Biblical or Talmudic material; in the Biblical account the ark was returned from its capture by the Philistines after they were afflicted with plagues, but it resided in a private dwelling for many years at Kiriath-jearim, and biblical commentators point out that during this time the Israelites were in religious decline; the fate of the ark in Saul's days is not described in the Bible except as neglect. It observes that the ark here reenters the life of the Israelites as a sign for Samuel's truthful prophecy concerning Saul, without details or chronology.

**What the ark contained.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the ark's history as reported: God sent it down to Adam, and it remained with him until it reached Jacob, and it was among the Children of Israel, by which they overcame whoever fought them, until they disobeyed and were overcome — the Amalekites, Goliath and his men in al-Suddī's account, stripped it from them. Qurṭubī pauses over the lesson: this is the clearest proof that disobedience is the cause of abandonment. Al-Naḥḥās adds that the sign of the ark, it is related, was that a moaning was heard within it; when they heard it they set out for war, and when it was absent from them they did not fight. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the meanings of *sakīnah*: peace or grace and reassurance; Qatādah said it means grace, al-Rabīʿ said mercy, and this is the meaning given by Ibn ʿAbbās as al-ʿAwfī narrated it. On the remnant: Ibn ʿAbbās, through Ibn Jarīr, said it means Moses' staff and the remnants of the tablets — the same as the interpretation of Qatādah, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ b. Anas and ʿIkrimah, who added the Torah; al-Thawrī, asked about it, said some held it contained a pot of manna and the remnants of the tablets, others that it contained Moses' staff and his two sandals. And Ibn Jurayj reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that the angels came down carrying the ark between the sky and the earth until they placed it before Saul. **[Study Quran]** notes that if the *sakīnah* is understood as something whose presence causes tranquility, it might refer to prophecies from the books of Moses and Aaron telling of the victories Saul would lead them to; and it lists the interpretations of the remnant — the staff of Moses, the fragments of the stone tablets, the manna, and the clothing of Moses and Aaron including Moses' sandals. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The Israelite ark narratives here, as the Study Quran and Maʿārif both note, rest largely on material from Jewish sources, and should be handled as such.
