**Reflection.** **[Ṭabarī]** names the purpose this story serves for the Sūrah's first audience: these reports of the Israelite notables — their asking their prophet to raise up a king for them, then their refusal to accept him, their demand for a sign, and their holding back from the fight with him — are a discipline for the Jews of Qurayẓah and al-Naḍīr living among the emigrants of the Prophet ﷺ and their descendants: they will not escape, in belving Muhammad ﷺ in what he commands and forbids while knowing his truthfulness, being like their ancestors and predecessors who belied their prophet Shamuwayl, while knowing his truthfulness, and refused to strive with Saul when God raised him as king over them. And the same reports are a call to the believers in God and His messenger among the companions of Muhammad ﷺ to strive in His way, and a warning lest they be, in holding back from His prophet when he meets the enemy and contends with the people of disbelief, like the Israelite notables in holding back from their king Saul when he marched against God's enemy Goliath — preferring ease and comfort over the heat of struggle and fighting in God's way. The sign of the ark, in other words, is not only a wonder from a lost past; in the Sūrah's telling it is a mirror held up to the community, showing what it looks like when a people who demand proofs receive them and still hang back.

**[Jalālayn]**'s detail that the sight of the ark lifted the people to enlist by the tens of thousands is the counterweight the Sūrah keeps in view: the same sign that convicts the hesitant also supplies the courage the following verses will test at the river.


## 2:249

*"And when Saul set out with the hosts, he said, 'God will try you with a river. So whoever drinks of it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me — except one who scoops a handful with his hand.' But they drank of it, except a few of them. Then when he crossed it, he and those who believed with him, they said, 'We have no power today against Goliath and his hosts.' Those who deemed that they would meet God said, 'How many a small company has overcome a large company, by God's leave! And God is with the patient.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** notes the ellipsis at the verse's head: the report of what happened is left out, because the mention of the sign suffices to indicate it — the sense being that the ark came to them with tranquility and a remnant, so they believed their prophet and acknowledged that God had raised Saul as king over them, and submitted to him; the proof being that "when Saul set out with the hosts" follows, and he would not have set out with them except after their acceptance and submission of the kingship to him. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the word: *faṣala* means he went out with them, from *faṣaltu al-shayʾa fa-nfaṣala* — I cut it, so it was cut off. Wahb b. Munabbih relates that when Saul set out, they said to him that the waters would not carry them, so ask God to run a river for us; and Saul said, "God will try you with a river." Al-Suddī puts the army at eighty thousand; and Wahb adds that none held back from him but one with an excuse of smallness, age or illness. *Ibtilāʾ* is testing; *nahar* and *nahr* are two dialects, the word derived from breadth, as is *nahār*, the day; Qatādah says the river with which God tried them lay between the Jordan and Palestine; and the test's meaning is that it is a trial of them — whoever's obedience appears in leaving the water, it is known that he is obedient in what lies beyond it, and whoever's appetite overcomes him in the water is known by that.

**Whom the test separated.** **[Jalālayn]** gives the scene: when Saul went out with the hosts from the Holy House — Jerusalem — the heat was intense, so they asked him for water, and he said, "God will try you with a river": whoever drinks of it is not of my followers, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except for one who scoops a handful with his hand, satisfying himself with it and taking no more — he too is of my followers. But they drank of it when they reached it and saw it abundant, except a few of them who confined themselves to a scoop; it is reported that a single scoop sufficed each man and his horse, and that they numbered over three hundred. And when Saul crossed it with those who believed — those who kept to the one scoop — those who had drunk their fill said, "We have no power today against Goliath and his troops," being cowardly, and did not cross; while those who were certain they would meet God at the resurrection said, "How many a small company has overcome a numerous one by God's leave; and God is with the patient," providing them with help and assistance. **[Saʿdī]** reads the test's purpose from Saul's own knowledge of his army: he had seen in them weakness of resolve and will that needed the patient to be distinguished from the one who hangs back; so "whoever drinks of it is not of me" — he does not follow me — because that is a proof of scant patience and abundant panic; and "whoever does not taste it is of me," because of his truthfulness and patience; and those who scooped a handful were excused in that. When they reached the river, needing water, they all drank except a few, who held back; and when he crossed with those who believed, the ones who had held back — or those who crossed — said, "We have no power today against Goliath and his hosts," whether that was an excuse offered by those who flinched or a kind of self-deprecation in those who crossed; but the people of full faith encouraged them to steadfastness and advance: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's leave; and God is with the patient," by His help, support and victory — so they stood firm and endured the fight against Goliath and his troops.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the army's number from al-Suddī — eighty thousand — and the river from Ibn ʿAbbās and others as the one flowing between Jordan and Palestine; "whoever drinks of it is not of me" means he shall not accompany me today; and from Ibn Jurayj, Ibn ʿAbbās explained that whoever took some of the water in the hollow of his hand quenched his thirst, while those who drank freely from it were not quenched. And he reports from Ibn Jarīr that al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib said: we used to say that the companions of Muhammad ﷺ who were with him at Badr were more than three hundred and ten, just as many as the soldiers who crossed the river with Saul. **[Qurṭubī]** draws the legal-theological line: "he is not of me" means he is not of my companions in this war, and does not put him outside faith; al-Suddī said they were eighty thousand, and inevitably among them were the believer and the hypocrite, the earnest and the lazy — as the ḥadīth has it, "whoever deceives us is not of us," meaning not of our companions and not on our path and guidance. He adds that some held that ʿAbdullāh b. Ḥudhāfah al-Sahmī, the companion of the Messenger of God ﷺ, ordered his men to light a fire and enter it only as a test of their obedience, carrying his jesting to the harshness of the command he laid on them. **[Maʿārif]** explains the wisdom of the test: such occasions create great excitement, but not many stay firm in the hour of trial, and when such a time comes the weakness of such people becomes contagious and makes others panic — so God willed that they be pruned out; and the test was fitting, because steadfastness is necessary in fighting, so that patience when water is available without asking, in a state of intense thirst, is a proof of steadfastness, and dashing for water is a proof of its absence. It adds a report from *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, on the authority of Ibn Abī Ḥātim from Ibn ʿAbbās, that those who drank too much water became mysteriously more incapacitated. And it draws out the three kinds in the story: the weak in faith who failed to make the grade in their hour of trial; the perfect who fully succeeded in their trial but felt concerned at how few they were; and the most perfect, who did not bother even about that.

**Reflection.** **[Study Quran]** observes the typological parallels: some have drawn a parallel with Gideon's crossing of the Jordan in Judges 7:4–7, though the similarities are typological and not historical — in the Gideon account the test was known to Gideon alone, the army was not aware they were being divided into two categories, and the purpose was to reduce the army to three hundred men, to show that God's will could be carried out with a small number; and there is also the crossing of the Jordan by the Israelites under Joshua. That the incident echoes Gideon's crossing, whose purpose was to show that God could defeat many with few, is reinforced by the statement of those who believed that they would meet their Lord: "How many a small company have overcome a large company by God's leave!" Those who deemed they would meet their Lord, it notes, were either certain of the Hereafter or prepared to die. The verse's architecture is now fully visible in the Sūrah's argument: the story that began with a people demanding a sign of God's chosen king moves to a river where the sign demanded is not a wonder but a discipline — a handful of water standing in for the whole of what a believer will be asked to give up, and the little band that passes the test becoming the pattern for the little band at Badr.


## 2:250

*"And when they went out to face Goliath and his hosts, they said, 'Our Lord, pour out upon us patience, make firm our feet, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the word: when Saul and his hosts came out to face Goliath and his hosts; and *barazū* means they came into the *barāz* of the earth, which is what is open and level of it — which is why a man who goes out to relieve himself is said to *tabarraz*, because people in the days of ignorance relieved themselves in the flat open ground. **[Jalālayn]** gives the scene in a sentence: when they went forth against Goliath and his troops, facing them in military ranks, they said, "Our Lord, pour out upon us patience, and make firm our feet by strengthening our hearts for this struggle, and grant us victory over the disbelieving folk."

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** supplies what the verse does not: Goliath was the commander of the Amalekites and their king, whose shade — that is, whose stature — was a mile; it is said that the Berbers are of his descendants; and he was, as reported, in command of three hundred thousand horsemen, while ʿIkrimah says ninety thousand. And when the believers saw the multitude of their enemy, they humbled themselves before their Lord — this being like His saying, "And how many a prophet has fought, with whom were many devoted men, and they did not lose heart for what befell them in the way of God, nor weaken nor give in" (3:146). In the report quoted of this moment in **[Ibn Kathīr]**, the promise made by Saul was kept in a notable way: whoever killed Goliath, he had promised, would marry his daughter and share his kingship and authority — and he kept his promise; the kingship then passed to the Prophet David. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The details of Goliath's height and descent belong to the Israelite reports the exegetes transmit, and are noted as such.

**The army's prayer.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the three petitions as the exact distribution of the soldier's need: "Our Lord, pour out upon us patience" means send down patience upon us from You; "and make firm our feet" — against the enemy, and keep us from running away and from feebleness; "and grant us victory over the disbelieving people." **[Study Quran]** combines the two armies' speeches to show the contrast the Sūrah is drawing: those who drank their fill said, "We have no power today against Goliath and his hosts," while those who were certain they would meet God answered them with the confidence of faith — "How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's leave; and God is with the patient" — and this verse shows the little band at prayer as the two armies face one another: no complaint about their own small number is lifted to God, only the request that patience be poured over them, their footing steadied, and the victory granted.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** treats the prayer as the seal on the episode of the river: the people of full faith encouraged the rest to steadfastness and advance, and then they stood, asked for the three things that make a stand possible — patience poured out on the heart, feet made firm beneath it, and the outcome from God's hand — and the Sūrah's own judgment on their plea comes in the next verse: the prayer was answered, the enemy was routed by God's leave, and the victory came not from numbers but from the leave by which the small company had overcome the large. **[Maʿārif]**'s reading of the river gives the moment its meaning within the story: the test had pruned away the ones whose fear would infect the rest, and there remained — in its division — the perfect who had succeeded but were concerned at how few they were, and the most perfect who did not trouble even over that; and the prayer of this verse is the voice of the second kind, who knew the size of the enemy and asked God for what they lacked. The Sūrah honors the request without correcting it: the concern is not shameful, provided it is carried to God rather than nursed among the ranks.


## 2:251

*"So they routed them, by God's leave; and David slew Goliath, and God gave him the kingship and the wisdom, and taught him of what He wills. And were it not for God's repelling people, some by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted; but God is Possessed of bounty toward the worlds."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** notes the omission at the verse's head: the report of the answer is left out, the sense being that when they faced Goliath and his hosts and said, "Our Lord, pour out upon us patience, make firm our feet, and grant us victory over the disbelieving people," their Lord answered them — pouring out His patience upon them, making their feet firm, and granting them victory over the disbelieving people — so that they routed them by God's leave; and the words "so they routed them by God's leave" suffice to show that God had answered their prayer. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the word: *hazama* means he broke them, from the same root as a waterskin *mutahazzim*, folded over on itself in dryness, and as the *hazmah* of Gabriel at Zamzam, the hollow he struck with his foot so the water came out. **[Jalālayn]** gives the sequence: they broke them by God's leave, and David — who was among the ranks of Saul's army — slew Goliath; and God gave him the kingship over the Children of Israel and the wisdom, that is prophethood, after the death of Samuel and Saul, and the combination of kingship and prophethood had never come to anyone before him; and He taught him of what He willed, such as the manufacture of coats of mail and the speech of birds.

**The slaying.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the scene from the Israelite reports: Saul the king chose him from among his people for the combat with Goliath; David was a short man, sickly, yellow-skinned, youngest, blue-eyed, while Goliath was of the strongest and most powerful of people, who used to rout armies by himself; he was the head of the Amalekites, and his killing was at David's hand — David son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah b. Jacob b. Isaac b. Abraham. **[Ṭabarī]** relates the fuller account from Wahb b. Munabbih: Goliath called out for a champion, offering that whoever killed him would have his kingship; David was brought to Saul, who agreed with him that if he killed him he would marry his daughter and be given authority over his wealth; Saul dressed him in armour, but David disliked fighting him with arms and said, "If God does not grant me victory over him, arms will not avail"; he went out with his sling and a bag of stones, and Goliath said, "Woe to you — you have come out against me only as one comes out against a dog with a sling and stones! I shall scatter your flesh and feed it to the birds and beasts today"; David said, "Rather you are the enemy of God, worse than a dog"; he took a stone and hurled it with the sling, and it struck him between the eyes and pierced to his brain, so Goliath fell and those with him were routed, and David cut off his head. When they returned, people came claiming to have killed Goliath, each bringing some weapon or part of him; David had hidden the head, and Saul said, "Whoever brings his head is the one who killed him" — and David brought it. **[Qurṭubī]**'s report adds the wonderful detail that David was among the most accurate of people with the sling, and that Goliath's helmet weighed three hundred pounds; and that David, going out to him, put his hand into the stones and — it is related — they came together into one stone, which he placed in the sling, named God, whirled it and hurled it. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The elaborate details of the combat, the armour that fits only the killer of Goliath, and the like belong to the Israelite traditions the exegetes transmit, and are marked as such.

**Kingship and wisdom.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives al-Suddī's explanation of "and God gave him the kingship and the wisdom": God gave him the kingship of Saul and the prophethood of Samuel — the one who had been their prophet; and what He taught him of what He wills includes the making of coats of mail and other crafts. **[Study Quran]** reads the gift in the line of the Biblical narrative: the Quranic account assumes a general knowledge of the story of Saul, David and Goliath — though a young boy, David is appointed to face Goliath as the Israelites' champion and fells the giant with a stone from his sling (compare 1 Samuel 17); he was given wisdom, meaning that as a major prophet in the Islamic tradition he inherited the prophethood of Samuel, and sovereignty, meaning he inherited the kingship of Saul; and for further description of David and his prophethood and reign it points to 38:17–29. **[Qurṭubī]** adds, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, a report of a chain joined to the Milky Way whose head was at David's cell, by which events in the air were known and the diseased were healed, and by touching which his people entered the religion — "and they used to judge by it after David until it was lifted up." *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* This too is from the Israelite reports and is not soundly established. **[Qurṭubī]** also draws from David's single combat a ruling attributed to the jurists: al-Shāfiʿī said there is no harm in single combat, and Ibn al-Mundhir said single combat with the imam's permission is good, while the one who does it without the imam's permission bears no blame, since no report forbids it.

**God's repelling.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads "were it not for God's repelling people, some by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted" as the lesson of the story: were it not that God checks one set of people by another — as He checked the Children of Israel's enemies by Saul and the bravery of David — people would perish; and he sets beside it the parallel of 22:40, where but for that repelling monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques would have been pulled down. Then the close, that God is full of bounty to the worlds, means that by His mercy and favor He fixes some of them by means of others; and God has the wisdom, the supreme authority and the clear proof against His creation in all His actions and statements. **[Study Quran]** records the interpretations of who repels whom: some say it refers to the "Substitutes" (*abdāl*) — human beings who are inwardly members of a spiritual hierarchy through which God dispenses grace and protection to the world; they are forty in number, and when one dies another is put in his place; others say the prayerful and the pious are used to repel those who do not pray and are impious, whose sins would otherwise destroy humanity, or that the obedient repel the evil of the disobedient; and it cites the ḥadīth: "God repels the punishment of the one who does not pray by means of the one who prays, and of the one who does not give alms by means of the one who gives alms, and of the one who does not fast by means of the one who fasts, and of the one who does not make the ḥajj by means of the one who makes the ḥajj, and of the one who does not struggle by means of the one who struggles."

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** seals the story with its fruit: David killed Goliath, and by that the victory and triumph over their enemy came; and God gave David the kingship and the wisdom — prophethood and the sciences of benefit — and granted him wisdom and decisive speech; then God explained the benefit of the struggle: were it not for God's repelling people, some by means of others, the earth would be corrupted by the dominance of the disbelievers, the wicked and the people of evil; but God is Possessed of bounty toward the worlds, in that He was kind to the believers and defended them and their religion by what He legislated and what He decreed. The verse, then, closes the Sūrah's account of Saul, the river, the small company and the giant with a general law: the preservation of the earth is not automatic but is the work of God through the courage and patience of believers, and the deliverance of a people comes through a hand God has chosen — here, the hand of a boy whom no one in the army had counted.


## 2:252

*"These are the signs of God, which We recite to thee in truth; and truly thou art among the messengers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads "these" as all that the passage has narrated: the signs in which God recounted the affair of those who went out of their homes in thousands, wary of death; the affair of the Israelite assembly after Moses who asked their prophet to raise up Saul as king; and the verses that follow to "and God is Possessed of bounty toward the worlds." And "the signs of God" means His proofs, His marks and His evidences — that is, these are the proofs I have told you of, O Muhammad, and made you know: My power to put to death in a single hour those who fled death though they were thousands, and then to bring them back to life; My giving Saul authority over the Children of Israel after he had been a water-carrier or a tanner, not of the house of kingship, and My stripping that from him for his disobedience of My command, and My turning his kingship over to David for his obedience to Me; and My granting victory to the companions of Saul, few in number and weak in strength, over Goliath and his hosts, many in number. **[Ibn Kathīr]** puts the same conclusion: these verses of God that We have narrated to you in truth conform to the exact manner in which these stories occurred, and to the truth that still remains in the Divine Books.

**The word to the Prophet.** **[Jalālayn]** reads the verse as the address to the Prophet ﷺ: these are the verses of God, which We recite to you as narration in truth; and "surely you are one of the messengers" — the emphasis of *innaka* being a rebuttal of the disbelievers' saying, "You are no messenger." **[Qurṭubī]** gives only the grammar: "these" is a subject, "the signs of God" its predicate, or an apposition with the predicate being "which We recite to you in truth." **[Study Quran]** notes that the verse is addressed directly to the Prophet, and that some commentators see the whole stretch from 2:243 to 2:251 as an encouragement for him in his own struggles with his enemies, reminding him that the messengers and prophets of the past underwent similar trials.

**The lessons of the story.** **[Saʿdī]** gathers what the account is for — a series of lessons for the community. Among them: the excellence of striving in God's way, its benefits and fruits, and that it is the only means of preserving religion, homelands, bodies and property; that those who strive, however hard their circumstances, have praiseworthy outcomes, while those who hang back, however much they rest a little, will tire long. Among them: the appointment to leadership of the one who has competence, and that competence comes back to two things — knowledge, which is the knowledge of governance and management, and strength, by which the right is carried out; whoever unites the two is more entitled than any other. Among them: the inference, from Saul's inspection of his troops at the river, of what the scholars said — that the commander of armies should inspect them at their departures and prevent those unfit for fighting, among men, horses and mounts, whether for weakness, weak patience, discouragement or fear of harm from their company; for this sort is pure harm to the people. Among them: that at the moment of conflict the fighters should be strengthened and encouraged, urged to strong faith and complete reliance on God and dependence on Him, and to asking God for steadfastness, help in patience, and victory over the enemies. And among them: that the resolve to fight is not the same as the fight itself — a person may resolve, and when the moment comes his resolve dissolves; which is why the Prophet ﷺ asked God in his supplication for "steadfastness in the matter and resolve upon right guidance," and asked for "contentment after the decree" — for contentment after the arrival of what is hateful to the soul is the true contentment. **[Study Quran]** adds the same moral from the companions of the river: those who deemed they would meet their Lord were either certain of the Hereafter or prepared to die, and the Sūrah leaves the reader with their cry rather than their numbers — "How many a small company has overcome a large company by God's leave."

**Reflection.** The verse seals the passage the way 2:242 sealed the divorce legislation, and with the same move: it names the whole narrative as signs, and turns the reader from the story to the One whose power and knowledge of affairs the story demonstrates. But here the seal is sharper, because the address is to the Prophet himself, and the conclusion drawn is not only about history but about his own standing: a Book that recites these matters "in truth" — matching what the People of the Book still possess of them — is a proof of the revelation, and a messenger who is told of Saul's rise from a tanner's bench, of the few who crossed the river, and of a boy who felled the giant, is being shown the pattern of his own mission before it unfolds: the small band, the long odds, the victory by God's leave, and the patience that alone qualifies for it.


## 2:253

*"Those messengers — some We have favored above others. Among them is he to whom God spoke, and some He raised in ranks. And We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs, and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them — but they differed, some believing and some disbelieving; and had God willed, they would not have fought one another. But God does what He wills."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads "those messengers" as the ones whose stories God has told in this Sūrah — Moses b. ʿImrān, Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Shamuwayl, David, and the rest whose accounts are mentioned — and says: these are My messengers, some of whom I favored above others; I spoke to some of them, and the one I spoke to among them was Moses; and I raised some of them in ranks above others by honor and elevation of station. Mujāhid said: the meaning is that among them is he to whom God spoke and some He raised above others in ranks — God spoke to Moses, and sent Muhammad to all people. **[Jalālayn]** gives the same structure and its details: some messengers We have preferred above others by assigning to one a particular trait not found in another; among them are those to whom God spoke, such as Moses; and some He raised in rank — namely Muhammad ﷺ, on account of his call being to all peoples, his being the Seal of the Prophets, the superiority of his community over all others, his various miracles and many special qualities. And We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear proofs, and confirmed him — strengthened him — with the Holy Spirit, namely Gabriel, who would accompany him wherever he went. And had God willed that the people be guided, those who came after them — that is, their communities — would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them, because of their disagreement and their leading one another astray; but they fell into variance as He willed: some of them believed and adhered firmly to his faith, and some disbelieved, as the Christians did after the Messiah Jesus. And the clause "had God willed, they would not have fought one another" is repeated for emphasis; but God does whatever He desires, giving success to whom He will and abandonment to whom He will.

**The difficulty and its resolution.** **[Qurṭubī]** names the problem at once: this verse shows that the messengers differ in rank, while the ḥadīths are established in which the Prophet ﷺ said, "Do not give preference among the prophets," and "Do not prefer me above the prophets of God" — that is, do not say, "So-and-so is better than so-and-so." Scholars differed over the resolution: some said this prohibition came before it was revealed to him that he was the master of the children of Adam, and before he knew it, and that the Qurʾān then abrogated the prohibition. Ibn Qutaybah said that his saying "I am the master of the children of Adam" meant on the Day of Resurrection, because he is the intercessor on that day, and his is the banner of praise and the Pool; and that "do not prefer me over Moses" was said as an instruction in humility. Then Qurṭubī gives the resolution he prefers: the prohibition of preferring pertains to prophethood itself, which is a single trait in which there is no ranking; the ranking is in the added states, distinctions, honors, graces and differing miracles — so the verses and the ḥadīths are joined without abrogation. He notes that Ibn ʿAbbās pointed to this when he said that God favored Muhammad above the prophets and above the inhabitants of heaven, and when asked how, he answered that God's nearness to the Prophet is such that He needed no intermediary. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth that provoked the question: a Muslim man and a Jew argued, and the Jew said, "No, by Him who gave Moses superiority over all human beings!" — and the Muslim raised his hand and slapped the Jew's face; when the matter was reported to the Messenger of God ﷺ he was angered and said, "Do not give me superiority over Moses: the people will become unconscious on the Day of Resurrection, and I will be the first to be resurrected, and I shall see Moses holding on to a pillar of God's Throne, and I shall not know whether the unconsciousness that struck him at the Trumpet sufficed for him, or whether he rose before me. So do not give me superiority above the prophets." His resolution: the ḥadīth prohibits preferring some prophets above others in cases of dispute and argument, and it indicates that it is not for creation to decide which prophet is better — that is God's decision, and creation is only required to submit to it. **[Maʿārif]**, following Maẓharī, reads the prohibition as forbidding preference by our own opinion without proof: a prophet's higher status means a high station with God, and that knowledge cannot be acquired through conjecture; but where proof from the Qurʾān and the Sunnah establishes the precedence of some over others, believing it is necessary. The sayings "I cannot say that anyone is better than Jonah b. Mattā" and "Do not give me precedence over Moses" relate to the time before he was given the knowledge that he had precedence over all other prophets; this was disclosed to him later through revelation, and he told the Companions of it. As for "among them is he to whom God spoke," Maʿārif notes that the conversation with Moses was without an angel as intermediary but not without a veil, so there is no conflict with 42:51, "It belongs not to any mortal that God should speak to him" — since that verse negates speech without a veil, and this verse speaks of speech without an intermediary.

**Jesus and the Holy Spirit.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads "the clear proofs" as the arguments and evidences of his prophethood: healing the blind and the leper, reviving the dead and the like, together with the Gospel sent down to him, in which God made clear what He imposed on him; and "we strengthened him" means we strengthened and aided him with the Spirit of God, which is Gabriel. **[Ibn Kathīr]** agrees: the clear proofs testify that he was God's servant and messenger to the Children of Israel, and the Holy Spirit is Jibrīl. **[Saʿdī]** notes the same and adds: he was given the proofs showing that he is truly God's messenger and truly His servant, and that all he brought was from God — healing the blind and the leper, reviving the dead by God's leave, and speaking to people in the cradle as an infant; and he was strengthened with the Holy Spirit, meaning the spirit of faith, so that his spirituality surpassed that of others, and by it strength and support came to him. He notes that while the support of this spirit is general to every believer according to his faith — "and He strengthened them with a spirit from Him" — what belongs to Jesus is greater than what belongs to others, which is why God singled him out for mention; and some said the Holy Spirit here is Gabriel, by whose help and backing God supported him, but the first meaning is stronger. **[Study Quran]** frames the whole verse within Islamic belief: the ranking in degrees is understood to pertain to the prophets' missions, not their individual spiritual perfections — thus all prophets are considered equally protected from sin, but they are given varying levels of earthly power (Solomon had a great kingdom, Jesus did not), different kinds of miraculous signs (Moses' staff, Solomon's command of the wind), and so on; and it points to the further discussion in the comment on 2:213 concerning the conflict between communities that have received revelation, with the parallels at 3:19, 42:14, 45:17 and 98:1.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** draws the verse's doctrinal conclusion: God informs us that He differentiated among the messengers in lofty excellences and beautiful distinctions according to what He granted them and what they fulfilled of complete faith, firm certainty, high character, noble courtesy, calling, teaching and general benefit. Among them is he whom He took as a close friend; among them is he to whom He spoke with speech; among them is he whom He raised above creation in ranks; and all of them are beyond the reach of any human being's attainment. When God had told of the messengers' perfection, of what He gave them of favor and distinction, and that their religion is one and their call to good one — the requirement of that was that the nations should gather in believing them and submitting to them, on account of the clear proofs they brought; but most of them turned aside, and disagreement fell among the nations: some believed and some disbelieved, and for that reason fighting broke out, and had God willed He would have gathered them upon guidance and they would not have differed. In this verse, he concludes, is the greatest witness that God disposes of all causes that lead to their effects: if He wills He keeps them, and if He wills He prevents them, all of it following His wisdom alone — for He does what He wills, and His will has no preventer, no opponent and no helper.


## 2:254

*"O you who believe, spend out of what We have provided you, before a day comes in which there is no bargaining, nor friendship, nor intercession. And the disbelievers — they are the wrongdoers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the command as spending in God's way: spend, O believers, out of the wealth We have provided you; give charity from it and pay the rights We have made obligatory upon you. Ibn Jurayj said it means the zakāt and the voluntary giving. Then He warns: store up for yourselves with God in your world before a day comes in which there is no bargaining — for it is a day of recompense, reward and punishment, not a day of action, acquisition, obedience and disobedience, so that you might then buy the dwellings of the people of honor by spending — nor friendship that benefits, such as the friendship of this world, where a man's close friend profited him by helping him against whoever sought to harm him, nor intercession, so that they might be released through it — for none on the Day of Resurrection helps another against God; rather "friends on that day shall be enemies to one another, except the reverent" (43:67). **[Jalālayn]** gives the same: spend out of what We have provided you — what is due of it as alms — before a day comes in which there is no commerce or ransom, nor friendship that can be of benefit, nor intercession except by His permission; and the variant reading has all three nouns in the nominative. And the disbelievers — those who disbelieve in God or in the obligations He has imposed — they are the wrongdoers, for not respecting God's command. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the sense of the three negations: no one will be able to bargain on his own behalf, or ransom himself with any amount even if the earth were filled with gold; nor will his friendship or his kinship to anyone profit him — "so when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship among them that day, nor will they ask of one another" (23:101) — nor will he profit by anyone's intercession.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** records the disagreement over the object of the command: al-Ḥasan said it is the obligatory zakāt; Ibn Jurayj and Saʿīd b. Jubayr said the verse gathers both the obligatory zakāt and the voluntary giving. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said this is sound, but the preceding verses on fighting and God's repelling through the believers in the breasts of the disbelievers make the more probable reading that this directive concerns spending in the way of God, and the verse's ending strengthens it — "and the disbelievers are the wrongdoers," that is, fight them with your lives and your wealth. Qurṭubī adds: on this reading, spending wealth is sometimes obligatory and sometimes recommended, according to whether the striving is individually required or not. And on the readings: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read "no bargaining, nor friendship, nor intercession" in the accusative without tanwīn, after the pattern of 14:31 and 52:23. **[Maʿārif]** frames the whole passage's design: many injunctions of worship and of dealing have been taken up in this Sūrah, especially those a person finds burdensome; and the most difficult of acts is spending one's life and possessions, and when a person falls into sin it is, in most cases, caused by his love of life or his attachment to possessions — so love of these two is the root of sins, and guarding against them is the object of all obedience. That is why, after the injunctions of worship and dealing, fighting in God's way was taken up at 2:244 and spending at 2:245; the first was then emphasized by the story of Saul, and now the second is emphasized by "spend from what We have given you." The time to act is still here: in the Hereafter deeds are not on sale, nor can they be borrowed from a friend, nor can one be released by anyone's intercession unless God Himself forgives.

**Belief.** **[Ṭabarī]** draws a fine point from the placement of the final clause: in "and the disbelievers are the wrongdoers" there is a clear indication that the negation of friendship and intercession is intended for the people of disbelief — which is why He follows it with that clause; so the sense is: We have deprived the disbelievers of help from friends and of intercession from the nearest and dearest, and We have not wronged them in doing so, since it is a requital from Us for their disbelief in God in this world; rather the disbelievers are the wrongdoers — those who put their denial where it does not belong, do what they have no right to do, and say what they have no right to say. **[Saʿdī]** connects the same clause to the contrast of purpose: God created them for His worship, provided for them and kept them sound so that they might use that to obey Him, but they went outside what He created them for, associated partners with God without warrant, and used His favors for disbelief, transgression and disobedience — so they have left no place for justice, and that is why absolute wrong is confined to them. **[Study Quran]** notes that intercession is unavailable to the disbelievers specifically, per many commentators, and points to the treatment of intercession at 2:48 and 2:255; and it gathers the parallels on the Day's severing of human supports: 14:31, 40:18, 43:67 ("Friends on that Day will be enemies to one another"), 44:41 and 70:10.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** opens his comment on the verse with the verse's own persuasion: God urges the believers to spend in all the paths of good — for the deletion of the object of the verb gives generality — and reminds them of His favor: that it is He who provided them and varied His blessings upon them; and that He did not command them to give out all that is in their hands, but brought the word *min*, "from," which indicates a part, and this too calls them to spend. And another call: the news that these spendings are stored with God for a day in which buying and selling will not avail, nor gifts, nor intercessions; every soul will then say, "What I have sent ahead for my life!" and all causes will be cut off except those tied to obedience of God and belief in Him — the day when neither wealth nor children avail, "unless one comes to God with a sound heart" (26:88–89). The verse thus stands where the Sūrah's great argument turns from the law of struggle to the law of wealth, and it states the exchange in the language of the market the hearers knew best: there is a day when commerce ends, so the trade that matters is the one made now.


## 2:255

*"God — there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither slumber seizes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth. Who is there that intercedes with Him except by His leave? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills. His Pedestal embraces the heavens and the earth, and their preservation tires Him not. He is the Sublime, the Tremendous."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the opening as the declaration and the prohibition together: "God, there is no god but He" is the forbidding of worshipping anything other than God — the Living, the Self-Subsisting, whose description God has given in this verse; so worship nothing other than the Living, the Self-Subsisting, whom neither slumber nor sleep seizes, and whose description is what follows. He adds that this verse is God's clarifying to those who believe in Him and His messenger concerning what the differing parties have said about the signs. **[Jalālayn]** distributes the sense sentence by sentence: "God, there is no god" — none worthy of worship in all existence — "but He, the Living, the Everlasting, the Sustainer," the One constantly engaged in the management of His creation; "slumber does not seize Him" — neither *sinah* nor *nawm* — "neither sleep"; to Him belongs all that is in the heavens and the earth as possessions, creatures and servants; "who is there that shall intercede with Him" — that is, none is there that shall — "save by His leave"; "He knows what lies before them," that is, of the affairs of this world, "and what is after them," of the affairs of the Hereafter; "and they encompass nothing of His knowledge" — they know nothing of what He knows — "save such as He wills" to inform them of by way of His messengers; "His Pedestal embraces the heavens and the earth" — it is said that His knowledge encompasses them both, and it is said that the *kursī* itself embraces them on account of its vastness, as in the ḥadīth "the seven heavens compared to the *kursī* are like seven silver coins lying in a metal shield"; "the preserving of them wearies Him not" — does not burden Him; "He is the Sublime" above His creation by His subjugation of them, "the Tremendous."

**[Saʿdī]** unfolds the same clauses as a summary of tawḥīd: the Prophet ﷺ informed us that this verse is the greatest of the Qurʾān's verses because of the meanings of oneness, majesty and the breadth of the Creator's attributes it contains. It announces that He is *Allāh* — the One who has all the meanings of divinity, so that no other deserves divinity or worship, and the divinity and worship of anything besides Him is void; that He is *al-Ḥayy*, who has all the meanings of perfect life — hearing, sight, power, will and the other attributes of the essence; and that *al-Qayyūm* includes all the attributes of action, because He is the Self-Subsisting who stands by Himself, free of all His creatures, and who sustains all existing things, bringing them into being, keeping them in being and supplying them with everything they need to exist and endure. From the perfection of His life and self-subsistence is that neither *sinah*, drowsiness, nor sleep seizes Him — for drowsiness and sleep only come upon a creature subject to weakness, incapacity and dissolution, and do not come upon the One of majesty, greatness and glory. He then informs that He owns all that is in the heavens and the earth; every one of them is a servant of God, owned, none escaping that station — "there is none in the heavens and the earth but comes to the Compassionate as a servant" (19:93). And from the completion of His ownership is that no one intercedes before Him except by His leave: all the personages and intercessors are His owned servants, who do not venture upon intercession until He permits them — "Say, to God belongs intercession altogether; His is the kingdom of the heavens and the earth" (39:44) — and God permits no one to intercede except for whom He approves, and He approves only of His oneness and the following of His messengers; so whoever is not described by that has no share in intercession. Then He informs of His vast, all-encompassing knowledge: He knows what lies before His creatures of the affairs to come, which have no end, and what lies behind them of the past matters, which have no limit; nothing hidden is hidden from Him — "He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal" (40:19). And creatures do not encompass anything of God's knowledge or of what He knows except what He wills — that is, what He has informed them of, of the matters of law and decree, and that is a very small part compared with the knowledge and the known things of the Creator, as the most knowledgeable of creation — the messengers and the angels — said: "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us" (2:32). Then He informs of His majesty and glory: His *kursī* encloses the heavens and the earth, and He has preserved them and all the worlds within them by the causes and systems He has placed in creatures; and even so the preserving of them does not tire Him, because of the perfection of His greatness, His power and the breadth of His wisdom. "He is the Sublime" in His essence above all His creatures, sublime in the greatness of His attributes, the Sublime who has subjugated creatures, to whom existing things are submissive, before whom difficulties are humbled and necks bowed; "the Tremendous," who gathers all the attributes of greatness, majesty, glory and splendor.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** introduces the verse with its virtues: this is Āyat al-Kursī, and tremendous virtues are associated with it, for the authentic ḥadīth describes it as the greatest āyah in the Book of God. Aḥmad recorded from Ubayy b. Kaʿb that the Prophet ﷺ asked him which āyah of the Book of God was greatest, and Ubayy answered, "God and His messenger know better"; when he repeated the question several times, Ubayy said, "Āyat al-Kursī" — and the Prophet ﷺ said, "May your knowledge rejoice you, Abū al-Mundhir! By the One in whose hand is my soul, it has a tongue and two lips with which it praises the King at the leg of the Throne." This was also collected by Muslim, without the words "By the One in Whose hand…". He records, too, the report of Abū Ayyūb and the *ghūl* that used to take dates from his *ṣadaqah* store: when he seized her and she begged to be released, she taught him words by which nothing would harm him — Āyat al-Kursī — and when he told the Prophet ﷺ, he said, "She is a liar, but she told the truth" — a ḥadīth recorded by al-Tirmidhī, who graded it *ḥasan gharīb*; and in Arabic the *ghūl* is the jinn when they appear at night. And al-Bukhārī records the better-known story from Abū Hurayrah: when he was set to guard the *ṣadaqah* of Ramadan and caught the thief three times, the man said at the last, "Let me teach you some words by which God will benefit you: when you go to bed, recite Āyat al-Kursī from beginning to end, and God will appoint a guard for you who will stay with you, and no devil will come near you until morning." He released him, and in the morning the Prophet ﷺ said, "He told you the truth, though he is a liar — that was a devil." **[Maʿārif]** gathers further reports: from Aḥmad, that it is the most meritorious verse; Abū Dharr asked which was the greatest āyah and was told, Āyat al-Kursī; Abū Hurayrah reported that the Prophet ﷺ said there is a verse in Sūrat al-Baqarah which is the *sayyidah*, the chief, of the Qurʾān's verses, and that Satan leaves the house in which it is recited; and in al-Nasāʾī's collection, that if one recites Āyat al-Kursī after every obligatory prayer, nothing prevents him from entering Paradise except death. **[Qurṭubī]** adds, from Muḥammad b. al-Ḥanafiyyah: when Āyat al-Kursī was sent down, every idol in the world fell down, and every king fell and the crowns dropped from their heads, and the devils fled, striking one another, until they came to Iblīs and told him; he ordered them to search for the reason, and they came to Medina and learned that Āyat al-Kursī had been revealed — and it had come down by night, and the Prophet ﷺ called Zayd and he wrote it.

**The Pedestal.** **[Maʿārif]** treats the *kursī* with care: its spatial vastness houses within itself the seven heavens and the earth; God is above and beyond sitting and standing and all spatial location; such verses should not be taken up on the analogy of our own states and affairs, for the reality of His being and attributes is beyond human reason — but there are authentic narrations telling us that the *ʿarsh* and the *kursī* are heavenly bodies many times larger than the heavens and the earth. Ibn Kathīr reports from Abū Dharr that he asked the Prophet ﷺ what the *kursī* was and what it looked like, and he said: "By the One who is master of my life, the seven heavens and the earth compared with the *kursī* are like the small circle of a finger-ring lying on a plain" — and, elsewhere, that the *kursī* compared with the *ʿarsh* is like a ring on a plain. **[Study Quran]** notes that this verse — Āyat al-Kursī, the "Pedestal Verse," sometimes rendered "Throne Verse" — is perhaps the most well-known single verse of the Qurʾān, often recited when setting out on a journey or seeking spiritual or physical protection, and often among the first passages memorized; the Prophet told his Companions to recite it before going to sleep, identified it as the greatest verse of the Qurʾān, and said that it was "a fourth of the Qurʾān," and it is among the most common passages adorning mosques and homes and carried on one's person as a pendant or amulet. It observes that the declaration "God, there is no god but He" appears in this form more often in the Qurʾān than "There is no god but God," and that *al-Ḥayy* is doctrinally one of the most important divine names in Islam, counted among the "mothers of the names" and occupying, in Islamic theology, a place conceptually equivalent to Being — a living being being that which is able to fully actualize all its perfections.

**Reflection.** The verse stands at the center of the Sūrah as the doctrine that holds all its legislation, its stories and its exhortations together: over against the kings and armies, the small companies and great hosts, the guardians and husbands and heirs of the preceding verses, stands the One who owns all who are in the heavens and the earth, whose permission alone gives an intercessor his word, and whose knowledge encloses all that the finite mind can neither reach nor bear. **[Saʿdī]** closes his comment on the note on which the verse is built: an āyah containing these meanings — which are the most sublime of meanings — deserves to be the greatest of the Qurʾān's verses, and whoever recites it thoughtfully, understanding it, deserves that his heart be filled with certainty, knowledge of God and faith, and that he be guarded by that from the evils of Satan. Between the Sūrah's grand narrative of the Children of Israel and its next great verse — the verse of the Throne's next-door neighbor, 2:256, on there being no compulsion in religion — the movement is exact: the community is first shown the sovereign whose kingdom the kings of earth can neither match nor escape, and is then told that His way is not to be imposed by force but to be believed in and defended by those who choose it.


## 2:256

*"There is no compulsion in religion. Sound judgment has become clear from error. So whoever rejects false deities and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold, which will never break. And God is Hearing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reports the occasion: a group of the Anṣār — or a man among them — had children whom they had raised as Jews or Christians, and when God brought Islam they wanted to compel their children into it, and God forbade them that, so that the children should choose to enter Islam of themselves. His chain to Ibn ʿAbbās through Saʿīd b. Jubayr gives the form of the practice: a woman whose children did not survive would vow, if a child lived for her, to have him raised as a Jew; so when Banū Naḍīr were expelled, among them were sons of the Anṣār, and the Anṣār said, "We will not abandon our children" — and God revealed, "There is no compulsion in religion; sound judgment has become clear from error." **[Jalālayn]** reads the verse as: there is no compulsion in entering the religion — sound judgment, that is faith, has become manifest from error, that is disbelief, through clear proofs; and this was revealed concerning the Anṣār of Medina who tried to compel their sons to enter Islam. Then: whoever disbelieves in the false deity — *ṭāghūt*, the word being used in a singular and plural sense — and believes in God has laid hold of the most firm handle, the tight knot that cannot be severed. And God is Hearing of what is said, Knowing of what is done. **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as a statement of the religion's perfection: this is a declaration of the completeness of the Islamic religion — that, because of the perfection of its proofs and the clarity of its signs, and because it is the religion of reason and knowledge, of natural disposition and wisdom, of soundness and reform, of truth and right guidance, it does not need compulsion. Compulsion is only applied to what hearts recoil from and what conflicts with truth, or to what has hidden proofs and signs; whoever this religion reaches and he rejects it, does so out of stubbornness — since sound judgment has become clear from error, no one is left with an excuse or an argument when he rejects it.

**The objection about fighting.** **[Saʿdī]** answers it directly: there is no contradiction between this meaning and the many verses that enjoin striving in God's way, for God commanded fighting so that the religion might be wholly God's, and to repel the aggression of the aggressors against the religion; and the Muslims are agreed that striving continues with the righteous and the wicked alike, and that it is among the continuing obligations — striving with speech and striving with action. Whoever among the exegetes thought this verse contradicted the verses of striving and therefore asserted that it is abrogated, his claim is weak in wording and in meaning, as is plain to anyone who reflects on the verse. **[Maʿārif]** puts the same case: the objection is not valid, since the teaching of striving and fighting in Islam is not to coerce people into accepting faith — had it been so, why would there be the injunctions of *jizyah* providing an umbrella of security for the disbelievers that protects their life, property and honor? It is, rather, to remove disorder and strife, for God dislikes corruption, which is what the disbelievers are after: "and they strive upon the earth spreading corruption, and God does not love the corrupters" (5:64). **[Qurṭubī]** sets out the six positions held on the verse and then settles: it was said to be abrogated, because the Prophet ﷺ did compel the Arabs and fought them; it was said to be addressed to the People of the Book, who may not be compelled to Islam when they pay the *jizyah*; and so on. His own conclusion is that the prohibition of compulsion is not absolute but that the verse governs the means: with the Arab idolaters, whose enmity and violation of pacts made fighting the means, force was used; but the people of other kinds of disbelief, when they offer the *jizyah*, are not compelled to Islam, whether they are Arabs or non-Arabs, Quraysh or others. And Nāḥḥās said: the report of Ibn ʿAbbās on this verse is the most worthy of the views because of the soundness of its chain, for the like of it is not taken by opinion.

**The reports of the occasion.** **[Qurṭubī]** records two more. Al-Suddī: the verse came down about a man of the Anṣār called Abū al-Ḥuṣayn who had two sons; traders came from Syria to Medina carrying oil, and when they wanted to leave, the two sons of al-Ḥuṣayn came to them, were invited to Christianity, became Christians and went with them to Syria; their father came to the Messenger of God ﷺ complaining of their case and wishing that he would send someone to bring them back — and "there is no compulsion in religion" was revealed, and on that day he was not commanded to fight the People of the Book; and he said, "God has put them far away; they are the first to disbelieve." **[Ibn Kathīr]** adds the report that the Anṣār were the occasion of revelation although the verse's indication is general in meaning, and records Abū Dāwūd's note that *al-muqlāt* is the woman whose children do not live; and he carries a report that some said, "We only did what we did thinking their religion was better than ours; but now that God has brought Islam we would compel them" — whereupon the verse came down: whoever wishes may join them and whoever wishes may enter Islam. He also addresses the ḥadīth Imam Aḥmad recorded, in which Anas said that the Messenger of God ﷺ said to a man, "Embrace Islam," and the man said, "I find myself averse," and he said, "Even if you are averse" — reconciling it with the verse's prohibition: the command there concerned a particular man of the idolaters whom the Prophet ﷺ invited at the point of fighting, and the verse's general import stands as the rule for invitation; compulsion is not the way by which faith enters the heart. **[Study Quran]** gathers the parallels: 10:99–100, "And had thy Lord willed, all those on the earth would have believed together. Wouldst thou compel men till they become believers? It is not for a soul to believe save by God's leave"; and 18:29, "It is the truth from your Lord: so whosoever will, let him believe, and whosoever will, let him disbelieve." It reports the occasion accounts — the Muslim parents whose children were among the exiled Banū Naḍīr, the Muslim man whose two sons became Christians and went to Syria, and the Muslims who had been wet-nursed by Jews and whose families forced them to remain Muslim — and notes that according to some sources the verse refers specifically to the People of the Book or to anyone from whom the *jizyah* can be taken; indeed, many argue the import is not absolute, since the Prophet in his campaign against the idolatrous Arabs did not give them the option of remaining idolaters or paying the *jizyah*.

**The firmest handhold.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads the second sentence as the description of the believer: whoever shuns the rivals of God, the idols and all that Satan calls to be worshipped besides God — whoever believes in God's oneness, worships Him alone and testifies that there is no deity worthy of worship except Him — has grasped the most trustworthy handhold that will never break; he has acquired firmness in the religion and proceeds on the correct way. He cites al-Baghawī's report from ʿUmar: "Jibt is magic and *ṭāghūt* is Satan; verily courage and cowardice are two instincts that appear in men — the courageous man fights for one he does not know, and the coward runs away from defending his own mother. A man's honor resides in his religion, and his status is based on his character, even if he is Persian or Nabataean." And ʿUmar's saying that the *ṭāghūt* is Satan is very sound, for this meaning includes every type of evil into which the ignorant people of the age of ignorance fell — worshipping idols, referring judgment to them, and invoking them for victory. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the word's grammar: *ṭāghūt* is from *ṭaghā*, to exceed the limit by going beyond it; its measure is *faʿlūt*, and Sībawayh held it a masculine singular, as if it were a generic noun covering few and many; Abū ʿAlī held it a verbal noun like *rahabūt* and *jabarūt*, used to describe one and many; and al-Jawharī said the *ṭāghūt* is the soothsayer and Satan and every headship in error, and it may be a single one. **[Saʿdī]** closes: then God mentioned the division of people into two — a party who believe in God alone, with no partner, and disbelieve in the *ṭāghūt*, which is everything that contradicts belief in God, of association and other than it: this one has held fast to the firmest handhold, which has no breaking, and he remains on the true religion until it brings him to God and the abode of His honor. And from the verse's implication the second party is taken: whoever does not believe in God but disbelieves in Him and believes in the *ṭāghūt*, his ruin is everlasting and his punishment eternal. And God is Hearing of all voices in their differing languages and varied needs, Hearing the supplication of those who call and the humility of those who entreat; Knowing what the breasts conceal and what is hidden of hidden things, repaying each one according to what He knows of his intentions and his work.

**Reflection.** The verse is set at the exact point where the Sūrah's argument needs it: after the story of kingship and compulsion in Israel, and next to the verse of God's sovereignty over all who are in the heavens and the earth, it states the rule of the new community's mission — the religion is offered with its proofs, and the proof does the work that force cannot. **[Saʿdī]**'s reasoning is the verse's own logic: compulsion is for what hearts recoil from or what has hidden proofs; this religion has neither defect, so it stands on clarity — "sound judgment has become clear from error" — and the choice of the heart follows the light. The exegetes' long discussions of abrogation and of whom the rule covers do not disturb the center: the sword may clear away the aggression that bars the way, but it cannot put faith in a heart, and the verse states that limitation at the heart of the Book's longest chapter. What follows is its natural completion — the two ways set before the hearer, and the handhold that does not break for whoever takes it.


## 2:257

*"God is the Protector of those who believe; He brings them out of the darknesses into the light. And those who disbelieve — their protectors are the false deities, who bring them out of the light into the darknesses. Those are the inhabitants of the Fire; they shall abide therein."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads *walī* as helper and backer: God is the patron of those who believe, taking charge of them by His help and His enabling; He brings them out of the darknesses — meaning the darknesses of disbelief — into the light of faith. And why the darknesses were made the likeness of disbelief: because darkness veils the eyes from perceiving things and confirming them, just as disbelief veils the eyes of the hearts from perceiving the realities of faith and from knowing its soundness and the soundness of its causes. **[Jalālayn]** gives the contrast: God is the Protector and helper of the believers, bringing them forth from the shadows of unbelief into the light of faith; and the disbelievers — their protectors are the false deities, bringing them forth from the light into the shadows. He notes that the repetition of "bringing forth from" here is either a reflection of God's earlier words, "He brings them forth from the shadows," or a reference to those Jews who had believed in the Prophet before he was sent and then rejected him. Those are the inhabitants of the Fire; therein they shall abide. **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammar: *al-walī* is on the pattern *faʿīl* with the sense of the active participle; al-Khaṭṭābī said the *walī* is the helper who aids His believing servants — as God says, "That is because God is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector" (47:11). Qatādah said the darknesses are error and the light is guidance, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabīʿ said the same. And Mujāhid and ʿAbadah b. Abī Lubābah said that "God is the Protector of those who believe" was revealed about a people who believed in Jesus, and when Muhammad ﷺ came they disbelieved in him — and that is their being brought out from light into darkness.

**The two ways.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** draws the lesson of the contrast: God stated that whoever follows what pleases Him, He will guide him to the paths of peace, that is Islam, or Paradise; God delivers His believing servants from the darkness of disbelief, doubt and hesitation to the light of the plain, clear, explained, easy and unequivocal truth; and He stated that Satan is the supporter of the disbelievers, beautifying the paths of ignorance and misguidance that they follow, and so causing them to deviate from the true path into disbelief and wickedness. And from the verse's wording he takes a fine point: God mentioned the light in the singular while mentioning the darknesses in the plural, because the truth is one while disbelief comes in several types, all of them false — as He said, "And verily this is My straight path, so follow it, and follow not other paths, for they will separate you from His path" (6:153). **[Saʿdī]** explains the verse's placement: it is built on the verse before it — the previous verse is the foundation and this is the fruit. God informs that those who believe in Him, and confirm their faith by fulfilling faith's obligations and leaving all that contradicts it, have Him as their patron: He takes charge of them with His special patronage and undertakes their upbringing, bringing them out of the darknesses of ignorance, disbelief, disobedience, heedlessness and turning away, into the light of knowledge, certainty, faith, obedience and complete turning to their Lord; He illumines their hearts with what He casts into them of the light of revelation and faith, makes easy for them the easy way, and keeps them from the hard. And as for those who disbelieve: when they took as patrons other than their true Patron, God left them to what they chose for themselves, abandoned them, and consigned them to the care of patrons who have neither benefit nor harm — so they led them astray, made them wretched, and deprived them of the guidance of beneficial knowledge and righteous action, depriving them of happiness; and the Fire became their dwelling, abiding therein forever. He closes with the prayer the verse's sense invites: "Our God, take charge of us among those whom You take charge of." **[Maʿārif]** puts the whole in one sentence: this verse also tells us that faith is the greatest blessing and disbelief the greatest misfortune, and that there is darkness in friendship with those who disbelieve.

**Reflection.** The verse turns the abstract into a picture the Sūrah will return to again and again: two roads, one out of many darknesses into a single light, the other out of a single light into many darknesses — and each traveler walked by the hand of a patron. **[Ibn Kathīr]**'s observation about the singular light and the plural darknesses is the key to the asymmetry: error multiplies because it has no ground to stand on, while truth, being one, gathers all who hold it into a single way. And **[Saʿdī]**'s phrase for the believers' patronage — that God "undertakes their upbringing" — shows where the two roads part: not in the amount of light granted at the outset, but in whose hand one consents to be led by. The verse stands immediately after the "firmest handhold," and it shows what the handhold is: not a thing the believer grasps, but the Protector who grasps him.


## 2:258

*"Hast thou not seen him who disputed with Abraham about his Lord because God had given him kingship? When Abraham said, 'My Lord is He who gives life and causes death,' he said, 'I give life and cause death.' Abraham said, 'Then God brings the sun from the east — bring it from the west.' So the disbeliever was confounded. And God guides not the wrongdoing people."*

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the setting: this *a-lam tara* is the *alif* of attention, and the speech carries the sense of wonder — marvel at him. Al-Farrāʾ said the phrase means "have you seen him who disputed with Abraham, and have you seen him who passed by a town" — and the disputant was Nimrod b. Kūsh b. Kanʿān b. Sām b. Noah, the king of his time, the owner of the fire and the mosquito. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatādah, al-Rabīʿ, al-Suddī, Ibn Isḥāq, Zayd b. Aslam and others. He relates how his destruction came when he set out to fight God: God opened against him a door of mosquitoes, which covered the eye of the sun and ate his army, leaving only the bones, and one of them entered his skull and ate it until it became like a mouse, so that afterwards the dearest of people to him was the one who struck his brain with a sledgehammer kept ready for it — and he remained in that torment forty days. **[Ibn Kathīr]** names him from Mujāhid as Nimrod son of Canaan son of Kush son of Sām son of Noah, and another genealogy is given; and he records Mujāhid's further word: the kings who ruled the eastern and western parts of the world are four — two believers and two disbelievers: the believing kings Solomon b. David and Dhū al-Qarnayn, and the disbelieving kings Nimrod and Nebuchadnezzar. **[Study Quran]** is careful here: commentators sometimes understand the antagonist to be Nimrod, though this is based on folkloric material — he is not named in any ḥadīth, and his place even in the Bible is ambiguous at best. It notes that grammatically the recipient of the sovereignty could be either Abraham or his antagonist, since Abraham's descendants are described as having been given a mighty sovereignty (4:54), but most commentators believe it refers to the worldly power of the other person; and that a similar dynamic appears in the exchange between Moses and Pharaoh, when Pharaoh said, "I am your lord most high" (79:24).

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the dispute's course: Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death" — that is, my Lord is the One in whose hand is life and death, who gives life to whom He wills and causes whom He wills to die after giving him life. Nimrod said, "I do that; I give life and cause death" — meaning that he would spare whomever he wanted to kill, so that his sparing him was, in the usage of the Arabs, called giving him life, as God said elsewhere of such sparing. **[Jalālayn]** fills in the scene: Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death" — the One who creates life and death in bodies; Nimrod said, "I give life by sparing and cause death by killing" — and he had two men brought before him, killed one and spared the other. When Abraham realized that the man was a fool, he resorted to a more decisive argument: "God brings the sun from the east; so bring it from the west." Then the disbeliever was confounded, perplexed and amazed; and God does not guide the people of evil to the art of argument. **[Saʿdī]** reads the exchange as the contest between a tyrant's illusion and the manifest truth: God relates the story of His close friend Abraham, when this tyrannical king — Nimrod the Babylonian, the denier and rejecter of the Lord of the worlds — set himself up to resist Abraham and dispute with him about the thing that admits no doubt, no ambiguity and no uncertainty: God's oneness and lordship, than which nothing is clearer. But the tyrant was deluded by his kingship and made tyrannical by it, until matters reached the point that he disputed Abraham; and Abraham, in the debate, said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death" — He alone is the Creator, the Disposer, the Giver of life and the Bringer of death — mentioning the most manifest of that kind, life and death. Then the tyrant said, in bravado, "I give life and cause death," meaning that he would kill whom he wished and spare whom he wished — which is evidently a falsification and a distortion of the point, for the point is that God alone brings life into the non-existent and returns it to the dead, and that He causes servants and animals to die at their appointed terms, whether by means He has linked to them or without means. When Abraham saw that he was making a distortion that might pass with the rabble, he pressed him to confirm his claim if it were as he said: "God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west" — and the disbeliever was confounded, his argument cut off and his confusion dissolved. And **[Saʿdī]** insists that this was not Abraham's transition from one proof to another but the entrapment of Nimrod by the very claim he had made: if he was truthful, let him bring the sun from the west, a thing that admits no falsification, distortion or illusion. All the proofs, transmitted and rational and innate, stand as witnesses to God's oneness, acknowledging His sole disposal of creation and command; and all the messengers agree on this great principle, and none denies it but a stubborn denier like this obstinate tyrant.

**Reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** gives the moral of the encounter: the king referred to is Nimrod, emperor of Babylon, who denied the very existence of God and debated Abraham on the issue; God had given him political power over a large territory, and he should have been grateful to his Lord — but his power inflated him with pride and arrogance, and he began to deny the very existence of Him. In the argument he asked Abraham about God's attributes, and when told that God gives life and brings death, the foolish king did not understand the real nature of giving life and bringing death, and argued that he too could kill by an order and spare a condemned man, and so give life. His argument was absurd, because giving life means giving life to the lifeless, and bringing death is a power that removes life from every living thing without the necessary intervention of an apparent cause. When Abraham felt that his addressee could not understand the real nature of the matter, he moved to another argument — the sun from the east — and the king was baffled and could not answer, though even after the truth became clear to him he persisted. **[Study Quran]** closes the reading: Abraham's triumph exposes the pretense of the ruler who sought to mimic God's power over life and death, and reflects a general Quranic theme that the world of nature is full of the signs of God — for the same Abraham who here summons the east and west would later, in another context, watch the rising sun and be drawn by it toward its Maker (6:78); and God's closing word, that He does not guide the wrongdoing folk, is the verse's own verdict on the debate: a heart that has used what it was given to dispute the Giver is not argued into faith.


## 2:259

*"Or like him who passed by a town fallen upon its roofs. He said, 'How shall God give life to this after its death?' So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. He said, 'How long hast thou tarried?' He said, 'I tarried a day or part of a day.' He said, 'Nay, thou hast tarried a hundred years. Look at thy food and thy drink — they have not spoiled. And look at thy donkey — and that We may make thee a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We set them up, then clothe them with flesh.' And when it was made clear to him, he said, 'I know that God is powerful over all things.'"*

**Context.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the "or" as joining this story to the previous one by meaning, not by wording: "or like him who passed by a town" is attached to "have you not seen him who disputed with Abraham," because the two are alike — the sense being, "Have you seen, O Muhammad, the like of him who disputed with Abraham about his Lord? — or the like of him who passed by a town?" And the Basran grammarians said the *kāf* in "or like him who" is extra, the sense being "have you not seen him who disputed Abraham, or him who passed by a town?" **[Qurṭubī]** reports the disagreement over the man's identity: Sulaymān b. Buraydah, Nājiyah b. Kaʿb, Qatādah, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Rabīʿ, ʿIkrimah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said he is ʿUzayr (Ezra); Wahb b. Munabbih, ʿAbdullāh b. ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr and ʿAbdullāh b. Bakr b. Muḍar said he is Irmiyā (Jeremiah), and that he was a prophet; and Ibn Isḥāq said Irmiyā is al-Khaḍir — a saying Ibn ʿAṭiyyah notes and treats cautiously. **[Ibn Kathīr]** records that ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib said the verse meant ʿUzayr, and that Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported it from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Suddī and Sulaymān b. Buraydah; Mujāhid said it refers to a man of the Children of Israel, and the town was Jerusalem after Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed it and killed its people. **[Study Quran]** surveys the same identifications — Ezra, Ezekiel, even Khiḍr — and notes that others say the verse refers not to a saint or prophet but to a disbeliever who is shown the reality of the resurrection; it explains that "fallen upon its roofs" means the roofs had collapsed onto the walls, the word *khāwiyah* also evoking emptiness. *(Isrāʾīliyyāt)* The identifications rest on reports outside the text, and the verse itself gives none of them.

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** tells the story: he passed by the Holy House — Jerusalem — riding an ass and carrying a basket of figs and a cup of juice, after Nebuchadnezzar had destroyed the city; he said, "How shall God give life to this now that it is dead?" — challenging the power of the Exalted One; so God made him die and remain dead a hundred years, then raised him, to show him how it could be done. God said, "How long have you tarried?" — and he said, "A day, or part of a day," because he had fallen asleep before noon and been made dead and then brought back at sunset, so he thought it was a single day's sleep. He said, "Nay; you have tarried a hundred years.
