Look at your food and your drink — the figs and the cup of juice — it has not spoiled, despite the length of time" (the final *hāʾ* of *yatasannah* being taken as belonging to the root, or as silent, and a variant reading omitting it); "and look at your ass" — and he saw that it had died and all that remained were its withered white bones. "We did this so that you would know, and so that We would make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We set them up" — *nunshiruhā* or *nanshiruhā*, from *nashara* and *anshara*, and a variant reading *nunshizuhā*, meaning how We move it and make it stand — "and then clothe them with flesh." And when he looked, he saw that the bones had been reconstituted and clothed with flesh, and that the spirit had been breathed into it, making it bray. So when it was made clear to him by witnessing it, he said, "I know" — and a variant reading has the imperative "know!" — "that God has power over all things."

**Readings.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the readings of the verse and the report behind them: on the resurrection, the man died in the early part of the day and was raised in the latter part, so that when he saw that the sun was still apparent he thought it was the sun of that very day. He had grapes, figs and juice, and he found them as he had left them — the juice had not spoiled, the figs had not turned bitter, the grapes had not rotted. And on "look at the bones, how We *nunshizuha*" — meaning how We collect them and put them back together — al-Ḥākim recorded in his *Mustadrak*, from Khārijah b. Zayd b. Thābit from his father, that the Messenger of God ﷺ read this āyah as *nunshizuha*, and al-Ḥākim said its chain is sound though the two Shaykhs did not record it; the verse was also read *nunshiruha*, meaning bring them back to life, as Mujāhid said. Al-Suddī said ʿUzayr observed the bones of his donkey scattered all around him to his right and left, and God gathered them.

**Belief and the lesson.** **[Saʿdī]** insists on the reading the verse itself supports: the two are great, tangible proofs in this world, before the Hereafter, of resurrection and requital — one of them God performed at the hand of a man who was doubting the resurrection, as the verse indicates, and the other at the hand of His close friend Abraham. This man passed by a town utterly destroyed, fallen upon its roofs, its people dead and its buildings ruined, and said, in the manner of doubt and finding it far-fetched, "How shall God give life to this after its death?" — meaning, that is far off in this state, and others like it, according to what had arisen in his heart in that moment. So God willed mercy for him and for the people and caused him to die for a hundred years, and with him his donkey; and with him there was food and drink, which God kept in their state all that long stretch of time. When the hundred years had passed, God raised him and said, "How long have you tarried?" and he said, "A day or part of a day," according to what he supposed; and God said, "Nay, you have tarried a hundred years." Then, in the completion of God's mercy to him and to the people, he was shown the sign with his own eyes, so that he would be convinced: look at your food and your drink, unchanged over all those long ages — and that is among the signs of God's power, for food and drink, particularly what the exegetes mention of fruit and juice, do not usually last without changing, and this God preserved for a hundred years; and look at your donkey — it had been torn apart and scattered and had become crumbling bones; and look at the bones, how We raise them one to another and join them after they were scattered and torn, then clothe them with flesh, then restore life to them. And when it became clear to him — a seeing by the eye that admits no doubt — he said, "I know that God is powerful over all things"; he acknowledged God's power over all things and became a sign for the people, who knew of his death and his donkey's death and knew his case, and then witnessed this great sign. And **[Saʿdī]** rejects the common exegetical view that the man was a believer or a prophet — ʿUzayr or another — and that his question meant "how will this town be rebuilt?": neither the wording nor the sense supports it, for the great sign is his own revival after death, the revival of his donkey, and the preservation of his food and drink without rot or change; and his words "when it was made clear to him" are explicit that nothing had become clear to him until he witnessed this state pointing to the perfection of God's power with his own eyes. **[Study Quran]** notes that some think God's making this person a sign means that he was made a prophet — but elsewhere Pharaoh was also made a sign (10:92), and he is the opposite of a prophet; and if the person is understood to be a prophet, his question is not taken as pernicious doubt, but in the same spirit as Abraham's question in the verse that follows: "My Lord, show me how Thou givest life to the dead."

**Reflection.** The verse is built to be seen, not merely argued: a man's doubt is answered not with a syllogism but with a hundred years, a food-basket unspoiled, and a donkey reassembled before his eyes, so that the lesson enters by the senses and the verse can close on the first-person confession, "I know that God is powerful over all things." **[Saʿdī]**'s reading of the man as a doubter rather than a prophet is the reading that keeps the story's edge: the Sūrah is not illustrating how the certain grow more certain, but how a heart that finds resurrection far-fetched is taken by God out of time and shown the thing itself. And the sign is granted to the onlookers as much as to the man: "that We may make thee a sign for the people" — his hundred-year death and return becomes public evidence in his own community, the tangible counterpart to the argument Abraham had won with the sun.


## 2:260

*"And when Abraham said, 'My Lord, show me how Thou givest life to the dead.' He said, 'Dost thou not believe?' He said, 'Yea, but that my heart may be at peace.' He said, 'Take four birds, then draw them to thee; then place a piece of them on every mountain; then call them — they will come to thee in haste. And know that God is Mighty, Wise.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the connection: "and when Abraham said" is joined to the preceding verses because "have you not seen" does not mean seeing with the eyes but seeing with the heart — its sense is "have you not known, so remember"; and since the phrase is a form of seeing, it is followed sometimes by what agrees with its wording and sometimes by what agrees with its meaning. So Abraham said: my Lord, show me with my eyes how You give life to the dead. And God said, "Do you not believe?" — and he said, "Yes, I believe, but that my heart may be at peace": that it may find rest through the direct vision of what faith had told him. **[Jalālayn]** follows the scene to its end: God asked him this though He knew his belief in His power, as a response to his request and so that the listeners would know the purpose of the request; and Abraham said, "Yes, I do believe, but I ask so that my heart may be reassured," at peace through direct vision in addition to the certainty sought through reasoning. Then, "Take four birds and twist them to you" — *sirhunna* or *surhunna*, turn them toward you, cut them up and mix together their flesh and feathers — then set a part of them on every hill around you, then summon them, and they will come to you in haste; and know that God is Mighty, nothing beyond Him, Wise in His actions. Abraham took a peacock, an eagle, a raven and a cock, did with them as has been mentioned, but kept their heads with him; and he called them, and all the parts flew back together, combining until they were whole and returning each to its own head.

**Did Abraham doubt?** **[Qurṭubī]** sets out the question: did Abraham's request come from doubt or not? The majority hold that Abraham never doubted God's giving life to the dead, and that he sought direct vision — for souls long to see what they have been told of; and for this the Prophet ﷺ said, "Report is not like eyewitness," a report narrated by Ibn ʿAbbās and by no one else, as Abū ʿUmar notes. Al-Akhfash said he did not seek the sight of the heart but the sight of the eye. Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, Saʿīd b. Jubayr and al-Rabīʿ said he asked in order to add certainty to his certainty. Then Qurṭubī records the other side: al-Ṭabarī entitled a chapter "those who said he asked it of his Lord because he doubted the power of God," and under it brought Ibn ʿAbbās's word, "There is no verse in the Qurʾān more hopeful to me than this one," and from ʿAṭāʾ b. Abī Rabāḥ that some of what enters hearts entered Abraham's heart — and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah objects to al-Ṭabarī's framing, noting that the reports under it do not support the heading. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth of al-Bukhārī from Abū Hurayrah, in which the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "We are more liable to doubt than Abraham when he said, 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead'; He said, 'Do you not believe?'"— the Prophet's words being an expression of humility before God and of the high rank of Abraham, whose question is not to be taken as doubt in the power of God but as the seeking of the increase of certainty, as the verse itself explains: "Yes, but that my heart may be at peace." And he records the exchange of the two Companions: Ibn ʿAbbās met ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAmr b. al-ʿĀṣ and asked him which āyah of the Qurʾān carried most hope for him; Ibn ʿAmr said, "Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, despair not of the mercy of God" (39:53); and Ibn ʿAbbās said, "But I say it is God's statement, 'And when Abraham said, My Lord, show me how Thou givest life to the dead' — for the Lord did not rebuke him for his request but told him how it was done." **[Saʿdī]** frames this as the second of the two great tangible proofs of resurrection: Abraham asked God to show him how He gives life to the dead, and God said, "Or do you not believe?" — to remove any doubt from His close friend; and Abraham said, "Yes, I have believed that You are powerful over all things and that You give life to the dead and requite the servants, but I want my heart to be at peace and to reach the station of the eye's certainty." So God answered his prayer as an honor to him and a mercy to the servants. **[Study Quran]** gathers the several contexts the commentators give for the request — a scene on a coast where sea, land and air creatures devoured one another, and he wondered how the pieces could be gathered; the exchange with his antagonist in 2:258; the sacrifice of his son; a desire for confirmation of his prophetic station — and records the spiritual reading: many interpret it as the revival of dead hearts through the Spirit. On "Dost thou not believe?" it reads a kind of implicit affirmation — "You believe, so why are you asking?" — and on "that my heart may be at peace" it notes the parallel of 89:27 and 13:28, and the commentators' resolution: there are degrees of spiritual knowledge, and Abraham speaks of going from one depth to another, not of doubt about God or His power; since believers acknowledge no end to the glories of God, his question can be seen as a desire to witness ever more of God's self-disclosure.

**The manner of the sign.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the procedure as the reports describe it: Abraham took the birds, kept them and made them tame, then slaughtered them, plucked the feathers, tore them to pieces and mixed the pieces; he placed parts of the mixed pieces on four or seven hills; and Ibn ʿAbbās said he kept their heads in his hand. Then God commanded him to call them, and he did, and he witnessed the feathers, blood and flesh fly to one another and the parts fly each to its body, until every bird came back to life and came walking at a fast pace toward him — each bird coming to take its own head from his hand, and if he offered a bird another head it refused it, until each was given its own. **[Maʿārif]** explains the details' purpose: Abraham was to keep the birds as pets until they were so domesticated that they came at his call and he knew them well enough that no stranger bird could take their place; then he was to kill them, mince everything — bones and feathers included — divide it into portions, place one portion on each of several hills, and call them. And the Qurʾān's word that they will come *saʿyan*, running, tells us they will not come flying: had they come through the air, the doubt would remain that they went out of sight and were replaced on the way; coming on the ground, they are fully in sight. In Tafsir *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*, on the authority of Ibn al-Mundhir from al-Ḥasan, it is narrated that when Abraham called, in no time bone joined bone, feather joined feather, flesh joined flesh, everything took its original form, the birds came alive and came running to him — and God said, "O Abraham, this is how, on the Day of Resurrection, I shall assemble in no time all parts and bodies, and breathe life into them." **[Study Quran]** records the alternative interpretation reflected in its translation: that no killing of the birds is mentioned in the verse — rather Abraham first made each bird be drawn to him, then placed them alive, each on a mountain, and then called them, representing the reunification of souls and bodies with the ease of a man calling to a bird that comes in haste; and it notes that many different lists of birds are given in the commentaries.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** draws out why the sign had to be so emphatic: God chose four birds rather than one, and had them torn apart and scattered, and placed on the tops of mountains, so that the sign would be manifest and public, seen from near and far; and He had them placed far from Abraham so that no one could suppose he was working some trick; and He had him call them so that they came hurrying — making this the greatest proof of the perfection of God's might and wisdom. And in it is a reminder that the resurrection displays to the servants the perfection of God's might, His wisdom and greatness, the breadth of His authority, and the completeness of His justice and grace. **[Maʿārif]** puts the human situation the verse answers: the rising after death is the disbelievers' greatest difficulty — they think man becomes dust, scattered by wind and water, reappearing in trees and fields, its particles spread to the far sides of the world, and to gather those scattered parcels and infuse life into them seems hard to the short-sighted, who measures everyone by the scale of his own power and does not deliberate on the non-analogous power above him — although, were he to look into his own being, he would see that even today his existence is a collection of parts and particles gathered from all over the world. The verse's last words set the seal on the whole: "And know that God is Mighty, Wise" — the power that cannot be resisted, working in the wisdom that puts every act in its place. And the two hopes the Companions compared belong together in the Sūrah's design: the verse that shows how God answers the request of His friend without rebuke is itself, as Ibn ʿAbbās said, among the most hopeful in the Book — for it teaches that the desire to see more of God's signs is not unbelief but the heart's peace being sought at a deeper level.


## 2:261

*"The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is as the likeness of a grain that brings forth seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains. And God multiplies for whom He wills; and God is All-Encompassing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens by tying the verse back: this āyah returns to "who is he that will lend God a goodly loan, that He may multiply it for him many times over? And God withholds and outstretches, and unto Him you shall be returned" (2:245) — the verses between being the stories of the Children of Israel with Saul and Goliath, the report of him who disputed Abraham, the affair of him who passed by the ruined town, and the story of Abraham's question to his Lord; so the Sūrah now resumes the call to spend, and the parable answers the promise of multiplication. **[Jalālayn]** gives the figure and its arithmetic: the likeness of the quality of the spending of those who spend their wealth in the way of God — that is, in obedience to Him — is as the likeness of a grain of corn that sprouts seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains; likewise what they spend will be multiplied seven hundred times; and God multiplies even more than this for whom He wills; God is Embracing in His bounty, Knowing of those who deserve such multiplication. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that the parable is more impressive to the heart than the mere mention of the number seven hundred, and that the verse indicates that God "grows" the good deeds for their doers just as He grows the plant for whoever sows it in fertile land; Saʿīd b. Jubayr commented that "in the way of God" means spending in God's obedience, and Makhūl that it means spending on striving, on the stalls of horses, weapons and so forth.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the Prophetic instances of the multiplication: Aḥmad recorded from Abū Masʿūd that a man once gave away a camel with its bridle on in the cause of God, and the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "On the Day of Resurrection you will have seven hundred camels with their bridles" — recorded also by Muslim and al-Nasāʾī, Muslim's narration reading, "You will earn seven hundred camels as reward for it on the Day of Resurrection." **[Study Quran]** adds the ḥadīth that God makes the good deed of the son of Adam tenfold, or seven hundredfold, "except the fast, for God says, 'The fast is for Me, and I reward it'" — and the concrete imagery of the reports: when a man came to the Prophet and said, "This camel I give in the way of God," he replied, "On the Day of Judgment you shall have seven hundred camels." **[Qurṭubī]** records a report from Ibn ʿUmar, in al-Bustī's *Ṣaḥīḥ Musnad*: when this verse was revealed the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "My Lord, increase my community" — and "Who is he that will lend God a goodly loan, that He may multiply it for him many times over?" was revealed; and he said again, "My Lord, increase my community" — and "Only the patient shall be paid their reward without measure" (39:10) was revealed. He also notes the ellipsis in the verse's wording: the construction is "the likeness of the *spending* of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is as the likeness of a grain."

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** unfolds the verse's scope and its measure. This is a great urging from God to His servants to spend their wealth in His way, which is the path that leads to Him; included in it is spending on the advancement of beneficial knowledge, on preparation for striving in His way, on equipping and outfitting those who strive, and on all the charitable projects beneficial to the Muslims — and after that, spending on the needy, the poor and the destitute; and the two may come together, so that the spending both meets a need and aids obedience and good, and such spendings are multiplied with this multiplication of seven hundred and more than that. Hence "God multiplies for whom He wills" — according to what is established in the heart of the spender of faith and complete sincerity, and according to the fruits of his spending and its benefit; for some paths of good produce from the spending in them chained benefits and varied interests, so the recompense matches the deed. And this is why the Sūrah goes on, in the next verse, to the further reward of those whose spending issues from a sincere heart and fulfills its conditions and is free of what nullifies it.

**Reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** sets the verse in the Sūrah's architecture: with it begins the section of the Sūrah on wealth, and the sections that follow — from 2:262 to 2:283 — present special instructions and points of guidance concerning financial transactions, in two parts: it teaches how to spend what is beyond one's needs to help the poor and the needy, which is *ṣadaqah* and *khayrāt*, and it declares the taking and giving of *ribā* unlawful, with directions on how to guard against it. If these were followed in full, the ideal economic order the world worries over would be solved; instead the world has been reduced by the confrontation of its systems to a hotbed of aggression. The verses make a three-unit statement: the merit of spending in God's way; the conditions that make charity acceptable and merit-worthy with God; and the attitudes that destroy charity, so that the good goes and the sin stays. The parable is the opening of that argument, and it makes the point by an image every farmer in the audience knew: a single grain, buried in the dark, brought out by God as seven ears of a hundred grains — the spender is not losing his wealth when he gives it; he is planting it in the ground where God makes it grow.


## 2:262

*"Those who spend their wealth in the way of God and then follow not what they spent with reminders of generosity nor with injury — their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** identifies the givers meant: those who give their wealth to those striving in God's way, aiding them against the enemies of God — providing for them, for their mounts and for the rest of their needs. Then they do not follow the spending they made on them with *mann* — that is, by showing them that they have done them a favor through their act and their gift, whether by tongue or by deed — nor with *adhā*, which is complaining about them on account of what one gave them and strengthening them with.

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** records the occasion reported for the verse: it was said to have been revealed concerning ʿUthmān b. ʿAffān, and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Samurah said, "ʿUthmān came with a thousand dīnārs for the expedition of hardship and poured them into the lap of the Messenger of God ﷺ; I saw him putting his hand into them, turning them over, and saying, 'Nothing will harm Ibn ʿAffān after what he has done today. O God, do not forget this day for ʿUthmān.'" And Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said, "I saw the Prophet ﷺ raising his hands, praying for ʿUthmān, saying, 'O Lord of ʿUthmān, I am pleased with ʿUthmān, so be pleased with him' — and he kept praying until dawn rose; then 'Those who spend their wealth in the way of God, and then follow not what they spent with reminders of generosity nor with injury' was revealed."

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes the sequence: since the previous verse mentioned spending in God's way in general terms, this verse makes clear that the ruling and the reward belong only to the one who does not follow his spending with *mann* or *adhā*. And under the same heading he records the condition of sincerity: only what is given for God, with the bulk of one's purpose seeking what is with God, is accepted; what is given as a mere habit, to repay an obligation, or for some other attached motive, does not seek God's face — and this is the meaning of the gift of ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb to the bedouin who came to him with his verses and would not leave until he was given, until ʿUmar wept so that his beard was soaked and said, "Boy, give him my shirt." **[Saʿdī]** gives the same condition in his own words: the next reward is for those who spend their wealth in God's way with a spending that issues sincerely, fulfills its conditions and is free of what nullifies it — who do not follow the one they spent on with *mann*, counting his favors and harming him by word or deed — and for such people their reward is with their Lord, according to what He knows of them and according to their spending and its benefit, and by His grace, which their charities neither reach nor attain; and "no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve" removes the hateful from them both past and future — grief and fear — so that they have obtained what is loved and are rid of what is hated.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that God praises those who spend from their money in His cause and then refrain from reminding the recipients of it, whether the hints take the form of words or of actions, and that "nor with injury" indicates they do not cause harm to those to whom they gave, for this harm only annuls the charity. He appends the ḥadīth of Muslim from Abū Dharr, in which the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Three persons God shall neither speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at, nor purify, and they shall have a painful torment: the one who reminds people of what he gives, the one who lets his garment hang below the ankles, and the one who markets his goods by a false oath" — and it is for this that God said in the following verses, "O you who believe, do not render in vain your charities by reminders of generosity or injury" (2:264).

**Reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** sets the verse's two negative conditions at the head of the section: after the parable of the grain showed the reward's abundance, this verse states the conditions that make charity go in vain — do not publicize your favor after spending, and do not consider the receiver disgraced or do anything to cause him insult or pain. The Sūrah's sequence is itself the teaching: the promise comes first and wide, and then the qualifications, so that the reader understands the multiplication of 2:261 to be attached not merely to the transfer of money but to its manner. A charity that limps after the giver with a reminder and a sting has not been planted in the ground of God's way but in the field of one's own reputation; and the verse's closing formula — no fear, no grief — is the reward of one who has really let the money go, and so has nothing left over which to reproach anybody.


## 2:263

*"An honorable word and forgiveness are better than a charity followed by injury. And God is Self-Sufficient, Clement."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains: "an honorable word" is beautiful speech and a man's supplication for his Muslim brother; "and forgiveness" is his covering for him what he knows of his need and his bad state; these are better with God than a charity given to him that is followed by injury — that is, that he complains of him on account of it and harms him because of it. **[Jalālayn]** gives the same reading in the setting of a beggar: honorable words, kind talk and a generous reply to the beggar, and forgiveness toward him for his persistence, are better than a voluntary almsgiving followed by injury, through reproach and deriding him for his begging; and God is Independent of the voluntary almsgiving of His servants, Forbearing in His delaying the punishment of the one who reproaches and injures.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the grammarians' account of the sentence: "an honorable word" is a subject whose predicate is omitted, the sense being "an honorable word is preferable and better," as al-Naḥḥās and al-Mahdawī said; or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject, "that which you are commanded is an honorable word." And the honorable word itself is supplication, friendliness and giving hope of what is with God — better than a charity that is charity in its outward appearance while in its inward reality it is nothing, since mentioning an honorable word carries reward while that charity carries none.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** brings the Prophetic saying under this verse: "A good word is charity, and among the honorable is that you meet your brother with a cheerful face" — recorded by Muslim. So one should receive the asker with cheerfulness and welcome, and meet him with an open face and closeness, so that one is thanked if he gives and excused if he withholds; and one of the sages said, "Meet the one in need with cheerfulness, for if you lack the thanking of the giver, you will not lack the excuse of the withholder." **[Study Quran]** summarizes the commentators: exulting in one's generosity or reminding the needy of their neediness destroys the virtue in charitable giving; it is better to offer an honorable word to the poor who ask for help, and forgiveness for any harm they may cause — either because their manner is rough or because they may cause embarrassment; one should be kind and gentle with the poor, and if their asking causes one trouble or discomfort, one should forgive them for it.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** arranges the whole passage into four ranks of doing good. The highest rank is the spending that issues from a sound intention and is not followed by *mann* or *adhā*. Below it comes the honorable word — spoken kindness in all its forms, which brings joy to a Muslim, and apologizing to the asker when one has nothing to give, and other such honorable speech. The third is doing good by pardoning and forgiving one who has wronged you in word or deed. And these two are better than the fourth, which is the charity that the giver follows with injury to the recipient — for he has muddied his good deed, and has done both good and evil; and pure good, even if it is of lesser rank, is better than good mixed with evil, even if that is of higher rank. In this is a great warning against harming the one to whom one gave charity, as people of meanness, folly and ignorance do. And "God" — exalted is He — "is Self-Sufficient" of their charities and of all His servants; "Clement" — with the perfection of His self-sufficiency and the breadth of His gifts He forbears with the disobedient and does not hasten them to punishment, but grants them well-being, provides for them and pours out His good upon them while they are defying Him with sins.

**Reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** explains why the comparison can even be made: it is a thousand times better to offer some reasonable and appropriate word to the person who asks, if the giver is unable to give, and if the asker angers the giver by impolite behavior it is better to forgive him than to give a charity followed by pain — for God is Himself *Ghanī* and *Ḥalīm*, need-free and forbearing, needing nothing from anyone. One who spends does so for his own good; and an intelligent person should keep this in mind while spending in the way of God, that he is not favoring anybody but spending for his own good; and should he sense ingratitude from people he has treated well, he should clothe himself in the divine attribute of forbearance, show obedience, and forgive and forget. The verse thus ranks the kinds of giving by what they leave behind in the heart: money that is given and then regretted leaves a sting; a kind word and the covering of a poor man's need leave nothing behind but peace. And the two names with which the verse closes — the Rich, the Clement — are the corrective to the frame of mind in which any giver imagines himself a patron: the one who needs nothing sets the standard of giving forgivingly.


## 2:264

*"O you who believe, do not annul your charities with reminders of generosity and injury, like him who spends his wealth to be seen of men and believes not in God and the Last Day. His likeness is the likeness of a smooth rock with dust upon it: a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything of what they earned. And God guides not the disbelieving people."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains: "O you who believe" — those who have affirmed God and His Messenger — "do not annul your charities," that is, do not annul the rewards of your charities with *mann* and *adhā*, just as the disbelief of him who spends his wealth "to be seen of men" annulled his spending: he shows people that outwardly he intends God and so they praise him for it, while he does not intend God by it and does not seek reward from Him — he spends only so that people will praise him, saying he is generous and noble and a righteous man, while they do not know what is hidden in his intention. **[Jalālayn]** reads the comparison as it stands: do not annul the rewards of your voluntary charities with reproach and injury, in the manner of the annulment of the spending of one who spends to show off to men and believes not in God and the Last Day — that is the hypocrite; his likeness is that of a smooth rock on which there is soil, and a torrent of intense rain smites it and leaves it barren and smooth, with nothing on it. "They have no power over anything they earned" — that is, they find no reward for it in the Hereafter, just as one finds nothing of the dust that was on the surface of the smooth rock after the rain.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** states the doctrine carefully: God expressed non-acceptance and deprivation of reward by "annulment," and what is meant is the charity that one follows with *mann* and *adhā* — not others; and the creedal principle is that evil deeds do not annul good deeds in general, so *mann* and *adhā* in one charity does not annul another charity. The majority of scholars say of this verse that the charity which God knows its giver will follow with *mann* or *adhā* is not accepted; and it was said that God has placed a mark on it for the angel, so that he does not write it — and this is a fine saying. He notes the Arabs' idioms: what is given with a reminder is a "black hand," what is given without being asked is a "white hand," and what is given on request is a "green hand"; and one of the eloquent said, "Whoever reminds of his favor loses its thanks, and whoever admires his own deed loses its reward." And he distinguishes voluntary charity from obligatory: if the reward of a voluntary charity is voided, one is safe from the threat and is as one who did not do it; but if the reward of an obligation is voided, the threat attaches to him, since he is as one who did not do it.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** explains that the boasting person pretends to give charity for God's sake while in reality seeking people's praise and the reputation of being kind or generous, or other gains of this life, never thinking of God or His pleasure and reward — and that al-Ḍaḥḥāk commented that the example fits the one who follows his charity with reminders or harm. He gives the imagery: *ṣafwān* is from *ṣafwānah*, the smooth rocks; *wābil* is heavy rain; and the heavy rain leaves the rock completely barren of dust — such is God's action with the work of those who show off, whose deeds are bound to vanish. **[Ṭabarī]** records the saying of ʿAmr b. Ḥurayth as an illustration of the same law in another field: a man goes to war and neither steals, nor fornicates, nor embezzles, and yet does not return with his due — and when he was asked why, he said that the man sets out, and when some affliction from God that has been decreed for him strikes him, he curses and damns his leader and the hour he went out, and says he will never go on an expedition with him again; that counts against him and not for him — like spending in God's way followed by *mann* and *adhā*, of which God has struck the parable in the Qurʾān.

**The parable.** **[Saʿdī]** sets this verse inside the three parables of the passage: God strikes here three similitudes — for the one who spends seeking His face without following his spending with *mann* or *adhā*; for the one who does follow it with *mann* and *adhā*; and for the show-off. The third is the one who does deeds for people's eyes with no faith in God and no reckoning of His reward: his heart is likened to the *ṣafwān* — the smooth, bare stone on which there is dust, so that a beholder thinks that if rain falls on it, it will sprout as good soil sprouts; but when a heavy rain strikes it, it takes away the dust and leaves the rock bare. That is exactly the heart of the show-off, in which there is no faith, but which is hard, neither softening nor humbling: so his deeds and his spending have no root to be founded on and no goal to reach; what he does is void for want of the condition. The one before him in the parable — the believer who invalidated his charity with *mann* — is voided after the condition existed, because of an impediment that arose; and the first is accepted and multiplied, because its condition of faith, sincerity, firmness, and the absence of corrupting impediments were all present. These three parables apply to all who act, so let the servant weigh himself and others by these just scales and fitting similitudes.

**Reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** notes that the verse adds a further condition governing the acceptance of charity: spend only to seek God's good pleasure and with the intention of reward in the Hereafter; spending for public exposure, name and fame, is wasting what you spend — and if a Muslim who does believe in the Hereafter spends merely for name and fame and under hypocritical motivation, he too will get no reward for it. In the words "and believes not in God" there is a hint that hypocrisy and name-seeking are not the sort of thing a person who believes in God and the Last Day would ever do, since hypocrisy is a sign that something is wrong with his faith. And the closing words, "God guides not the disbelieving people," mean that Qurʾānic guidance is universal — common to all human beings — but the disbelievers do not take notice of it and go further and make fun of it, and so God lets them be deprived of the very enabling to accept guidance. The Sūrah's farming imagery makes the whole matter visible: the same rain falls on the rock and on the garden, and the difference is not in the rain but in the ground; so the difference between charity that survives and charity that is washed away is not in the amount but in the heart on which it falls.


## 2:265

*"And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking God's good pleasure and out of a confirmation in their own souls is as the likeness of a garden upon a hill: a heavy rain strikes it and it yields its fruit twofold; and if no heavy rain strikes it, then a drizzle. And God sees whatsoever you do."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the first phrase: those who spend their wealth in charity, carry provisions on it in God's way, and strengthen with it the needy among the raiders and those striving in God's way and in other acts of obedience — seeking His good pleasure. And "a confirmation in their own souls" has two reported senses. Some said it means certainty and assent from themselves: al-Shaʿbī said "assent and certainty," and again "an assent from themselves, firmness and support"; Qatādah said "a certainty from themselves — *tathbīt* is certainty"; and Abū Ṣāliḥ said "a certainty from their own selves." And others said it means that they used to be deliberate and careful about where they placed their charities: Mujāhid said, "They would make sure where they placed their wealth" — asked again what that *tathbīt* was, he said the same. **[Jalālayn]** gives the parable: the likeness of the spending of those who spend seeking God's good pleasure and to confirm themselves — that is, to realize the reward of it, in contrast to the hypocrites, who do not hope for it because they do not believe in it — is as the likeness of a garden upon a hill, a high ground (read *rabwah* or *rubwah*); a torrent smites it and it yields its produce twofold, twice the fruit of another garden; and if no torrent smites it, then dew — a light drizzle that falls on it and suffices it because of its elevation. In other words it grows and bears fruit regardless of how much rain falls; and likewise are the expenditures of those mentioned: they will increase with God regardless of how much they were. **[Ibn Kathīr]** reads "confirmation in their own souls" as certainty that God will reward them for these righteous acts with the best rewards, and compares the ḥadīth agreed upon by al-Bukhārī and Muslim, "Whoever fasts Ramadan out of faith and expectation" — believing that God commanded the fast while awaiting His reward for it. On the garden he follows the majority: a *rabwah* is a height above the ground, and Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Ḍaḥḥāk added that it also has flowing rivers.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** does the grammar: "seeking" is an object denoting cause, and "and a confirmation in their own souls" is joined to it; Makkī said in *al-Mushkil* that both are causal objects, and Ibn ʿAṭiyyah rejected this, since the spending is not undertaken *for the sake of* confirmation, and the correct reading is that "seeking" is an infinitive in the accusative in the position of a state, accusative though it is, in parallel with the infinitive "confirmation." **[Study Quran]**, whose verse-block 264–65 is read together, explains the symbolism of the rain: when a downpour strikes the earth on a smooth stone it can only wash it away, meaning it produces no real benefit; when it lands on a fertile garden the surplus of water causes the garden to double its yield, symbolizing the fruit of charity with the right intention; and if a downpour strikes it not, then a soft rain is taken to mean that even if the amount of rain is not great, the garden will at least thrive normally and bear its fruit. It notes that some commentators mention that certain kinds of oases flourish and have rich earth collect on them when they are slightly elevated, and that this is what is meant by a garden upon a hill — and that on a hill of this sort there are no streams.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** draws the passage's conclusion: those who spend in the way of God solely and sincerely, to seek nothing but His pleasure, and thus fortify their selves with steadfastness, are in the situation of a fruit farm on a mound which heavy rains strike so that it brings forth double its usual yield; and should the rain not be heavy, a light drizzle becomes sufficient for it. Here the merit of spending in the way of God — with sincerity of intention and obedience to the conditions set — is made clear through the similitude: spending with good intention and sincerity, even if it be little, becomes enough and helps one receive the gains of the Hereafter. **[Saʿdī]**'s reading of the first of the three parables fits here: when the spending is accepted and multiplied because it issues from faith and complete sincerity — "seeking God's good pleasure and a confirmation in their own souls," meaning they spend while firm in generosity and truthfulness — its likeness is a garden on high ground, which is visible to the winds and the sun and whose water is abundant; and if the abundant rain does not strike it, then a drizzle suffices it, given the goodness of its soil and the completeness of the causes of its growth and fruitfulness; therefore it gives its fruit twofold — and this garden, with this description, is the highest thing people seek, so this deed is of the highest stations.

**Reflection.** The verse answers the previous one point for point, and the geometry of the two images is the argument: the rock and the hill receive the same rain, and the difference lies entirely in what the rain finds. The Sūrah's attention falls on the interior — the intention ("seeking God's good pleasure") and the settled state of the soul ("a confirmation in their own souls") — and the two reported senses of that phrase, certainty of reward and care about where one's charity is placed, are not rivals but companions: the one who trusts what God has promised also takes pains over where he puts his wealth. The closing words, "God sees whatsoever you do," gather the passage: the eye that matters is not the eye of men, which the show-off courts, but the eye that sees the rock and the hill alike, and the rain, and the soil beneath both.


## 2:266

*"Would any one of you wish to have a garden of date palms and vines, with rivers running beneath it, partaking therein of every kind of fruit, while old age befalls him and he has weak progeny — and a whirlwind with fire strikes it, so that it is consumed? Thus does God make clear to you the signs, that haply you may reflect."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** unfolds the picture: would any of you wish to have a garden of date-palms and vines with rivers flowing beneath it, in which there is for him all manner of fruit, and then old age strikes him and makes him too weak to profit from it, and he has seed — but they are weak young children who cannot manage it — and then a whirlwind, *iʿṣār*, violent winds with fire, smites it and it is consumed? He loses what he is most in need of, and now he and his children are incapacitated, confused, without any resources. This is a similitude of how the expenditure of the one who spends for show, or the one who reproaches after having spent, vanishes, and how it is of no avail when he will be most in need of it in the Hereafter; the interrogative "would any wish" is intended as a denial. And according to Ibn ʿAbbās, this is the person who performs deeds of obedience, but when Satan comes to him he begins to work disobedience until all his good deeds have been consumed.

**Context.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the report from al-Bukhārī that Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr said: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb asked the Companions of the Messenger of God, "According to your opinion, about whom was this āyah revealed?" They said, "God knows best" — and ʿUmar became angry and said, "Say: we know, or we do not know." Ibn ʿAbbās said, "O Leader of the Faithful, I have an opinion about it." ʿUmar said, "O my nephew, say your opinion and do not belittle yourself." Ibn ʿAbbās said, "It is an example set for a deed." ʿUmar said, "What type of deed?" He said, "For a wealthy man who works in God's pleasure, and then God sends Satan to him, and he works in disobedience, until he annuls his good works." **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes that this report suffices as an explanation, for it explains the example by a person who does good first and then follows it with evil — so he annulled his earlier good works with his latter evil when he desperately needed the former kind and there were none. **[Qurṭubī]** records the line of interpretation: al-Ṭabarī related from al-Suddī that this āyah is another parable for the spending of showing off, and Ṭabarī preferred this view; and it is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that this is a parable God struck for those who show off with deeds, nullifying them on the Day of Resurrection at the time of their greatest need for them, like a man who had a garden and small children who could not help him: he grew old, and a whirlwind — a storm-wind with fire in it — struck the garden and burned it, and he lost it when he needed it most.

**The parable's design.** **[Maʿārif]** explains the qualifications built into the similitude — that the man is old, that he has children, and that the children are young and weak. These have a purpose. If a person is young, he can look forward to having a new farm when his old one burns; if he has no children and no hope to reactivate his burnt farm, his worry is less, since a single man can get by in adversity one way or another; and if his children are grown and able, he is less shaken, since they can carry him through. So the three riding restrictions were introduced to describe the intensity of need: a person who spent his capital and labor and set up a fruit farm that became ready and began yielding fruit, and then old age came with its days of weakness, and he has young, weak children — under these circumstances, should the farm he groomed burn out, his shock would be severe and the pain limitless. And similarly, one who has given his charity with hypocrisy is as if he set up a farm, and then came death, after which his condition is equal to that of the old man who cannot earn his living and cannot set up the farm again, because human deeds cease at death, and he needs his previous earnings kept safe for the time of old age. Thus spending in charity against the conditions given is like hoping to invest profusely in the Hereafter, when with God that investment comes to naught.

**Reflection.** **[Study Quran]** records both readings: for some this verse is a parable of those who follow up their charitable giving with preening and injury, as in 2:264 — meaning that at the end of their life they will have nothing of value to leave behind and nothing will bear fruit for them in the Hereafter: their charity is like the fruits of the garden, and their insults and boasting are like the fiery whirlwind that devours it, and they have no progeny who could protect or support them; and according to another interpretation attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, the verse refers to those who do good works but afterward turn to evil works, thereby wiping away the value of earlier past actions. **[Saʿdī]**, whose three parables are mapped in the preceding verses, places this one as the second: the one who spent for God and then followed his spending with *mann* and *adhā*, or did a deed and then brought against it what nullifies it — his likeness is that of the owner of this garden, except that a whirlwind with fire in it is set loose upon it and it burns, while he is weak and has been struck by old age and has weak offspring. This is among the most terrible of states, which is why the parable opens with the interrogative that fixes its horror in the hearers' minds; for its destruction all at once, after the maturity of its trees and the ripening of its fruits, is a great calamity, and then this disaster befalling a man who is old and weakened from work and has weak children who give him no help and whose maintenance falls on him is another disaster. So the subject of this parable — the one who worked for God and then invalidated his work by what contradicts it — resembles the owner of the garden at the moment of his most intense need for it. And **[Ṭabarī]** closes the passage: just as your Lord has made clear to you the matter of spending in His way, how it is to be done, and what you may and may not do in it, so He makes clear to you the other signs, defining their rulings, their lawful and their unlawful, and making plain their proofs — a favor from Him to you — "that haply you may reflect": that you may think with your minds, ponder, take heed of God's proofs, and act accordingly.


## 2:267

*"O you who believe, spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have brought forth for you from the earth, and do not aim at the bad, spending of it, when you would not take it yourselves unless you shut your eyes to it. And know that God is Self-Sufficient, Praised."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the command: "spend" means purify and give in charity, as Ibn ʿAbbās said — "give in charity" — of the good things you have earned by your dealings, whether by trade or by craft, of gold and silver; and "the good things" means the fine ones: purify your wealth that you have earned lawfully, and give in your purification gold and silver of the good rather than the bad. Mujāhid said "of the good things you have earned" means from trade, and al-Suddī said from gold and silver. And "of what We have brought forth for you from the earth" means also spend and give charity and purification from dates, grapes, wheat, barley and whatever of the earth's produce requires charity; ʿUbaydah said he asked ʿAlī about this phrase and he said it means grain and fruit and everything on which there is a purification, and Mujāhid said it means the date-palm and its fruit. **[Jalālayn]** gives the contrast briefly: spend of the good things you have earned of property, and of the good things We have produced for you from the earth, and do not "seek" — that is, do not intend — the corrupt, the vile of it to spend as alms; "for you would never take it yourselves if you were given it as something due to you, without closing your eyes to it, being careless and mindless — so how do you expect to give what is due to God from this? And know that God is Independent of your expenditure."

**Context.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the occasion reported for the verse: it was revealed about the Anṣār — when the season for harvesting the date-trees began, they would collect branches of ripe dates from their gardens and hang them on a rope erected between two pillars in the mosque of the Messenger of God, and the poor emigrant Companions would eat from those dates; but some of them would also add lesser dates between the ripe branches, thinking they were allowed to do so. So God revealed this verse about those who did this: "and do not aim at that which is bad to spend from it." **[Study Quran]** reports the same scene, and notes that the verse is echoed in 3:92, "You will never attain piety till you spend from that which you love," and that the good things can mean either what one considers wholesome and desirable, what one would not reject, or what is lawful and not forbidden — so that one should not seek unlawful or distasteful means to give in charity.

**Language and explanation.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** records the comment of Ibn ʿAbbās, by ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥah, on "you would not take it yourselves unless you shut your eyes to it": if you had a right on someone who would pay you less than what was due, you would not agree until you required more of him to make up the difference — and this is why God said, "unless you shut your eyes to it," meaning, "How do you agree for Me what you do not agree for yourselves, while I have a right to the best and most precious of your possessions?" Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Jarīr recorded this, and Ibn Jarīr added that this is the meaning of God's statement, "By no means shall you attain piety unless you spend of that which you love." And he records Ibn ʿAbbās's summary of the command: God commanded them to spend from the purest, finest and best types of their money and prohibited spending from evil and dishonest money, because God is pure and good and only accepts what is pure and good. **[Ṭabarī]** adds that al-Ḥasan said of the *ṭayyibāt* that they are the lawful: whatever God has made lawful, and the *khabīth* whatever He has made unlawful.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** records the disagreement over which spending is meant: ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib, ʿAbīdah al-Salmānī and Ibn Sīrīn said it is the obligatory purification — God forbidding people to give the bad in it in place of the good; and the apparent sense of the words of al-Barāʾ b. ʿĀzib, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah is that the verse concerns the voluntary charity, urging them not to volunteer anything but the best they choose; and the verse embraces both, though the one who pays the obligatory purification is bound more tightly, since the command carries obligation. And he lays out the three doors of "what We have brought forth for you from the earth": plants, minerals and buried treasure. As for plants, al-Dāraquṭnī recorded from ʿĀʾishah that the standing practice from the Messenger of God ﷺ was "there is no charity in what is less than five *wasq*," a *wasq* being sixty *ṣāʿ*s — three hundred *ṣāʿ*s of wheat, barley, dates and raisins; and there is no charity on vegetables that the earth brings forth. On the authority of Ibn Khuwayz Mindād he adds a ruling taken from this verse: on account of it the father may eat from his son's earnings, since the Prophet ﷺ said, "Your children are among the good things of what you earn, so eat from the wealth of your children with relish."

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Study Quran]** gives the Prophetic material gathered under this command: the ḥadīth that "God distributes your provisions among you just as He distributes your virtues among you; God gives of the world to those whom He loves and does not love, but gives religion only to those whom He loves — and whoever God has given religion, God loves him. By Him in whose hand is my soul, no servant submits until his heart and his tongue submit, and no believer believes until his bodily parts are safe from his misfortunes" — asked what the misfortunes were, the Prophet said, "His lies and his wrongdoing; no servant receives blessing by earning wealth that is unlawful." **[Saʿdī]** draws the verse's general law: it includes the purification of the two kinds of currency and of all goods prepared for buying and selling, and of what comes out of the earth in grain and fruit; and both the obligatory and the voluntary are included in its generality; and the command is to intend the good and not to intend the bad — the inferior and low, which they set aside for God, when if a poor man owing them a right offered them that same inferior thing, they would not be satisfied with it nor accept it except in a spirit of grudging and overlooking. So what is obligatory is to give the middle sort of these things, and perfection is to give the highest, and what is forbidden is to give the bad — for that does not suffice for the obligation, and carries no full reward in the voluntary. **[Maʿārif]** notes that on the basis of the occasion some read *ṭayyib* as "good" because people used to bring bad things and the verse was revealed on that account, while others read it as "lawful," since something is perfectly good only when it is lawful too; and he points out that the verse addresses one who *has* good yet elects to give the bad — as "what you have earned" and "We have brought forth" indicate that good things are available with the giver, while "do not aim at the bad" proves the deliberate choice of the bad; the one who possesses nothing good is exempted from the prohibition, and his giving, even if it be bad, is accepted.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** closes on the two divine names: "And know that God is Self-Sufficient, Praised" — He is self-sufficient of all creatures, self-sufficient of the spending of the spenders and the obedience of the obedient; He commanded and urged them only for their own benefit and out of pure grace and generosity toward them; and with the perfection of His self-sufficiency and the breadth of His gifts, He is Praised in the laws He legislates for His servants that lead them to the abode of peace, praised in His acts, which never depart from grace, justice and wisdom, and praised in His attributes, all of which are beauties and perfections whose inner reality servants cannot reach or describe. The verse's argument turns the giver's own standards against him: he would not accept the bad for himself without closing his eyes to it, yet he sets it aside for God — and the closing names remind him where the whole transaction actually stands: the self-sufficient God needs nothing from him, and the act of giving is for the giver's sake, not the Giver's.


## 2:268

*"Satan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency; and God promises you forgiveness from Him, and bounty. And God is All-Encompassing, Knowing."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as the counterweight to the command to spend: Satan promises you — O people — that you will become poor because of the charity you give and the obligatory purification you discharge from your wealth, and he commands you to acts of disobedience to God and to the abandonment of His obedience; while God promises you, O believers, that He will cover your indecencies by pardoning you from punishing them, and forgive your sins through the charity you give, and promises you *faḍl* — that He will replace for you what you spent, favoring you from His gifts and pouring out His provision upon you. **[Jalālayn]** puts the pair of promises side by side: Satan promises you poverty by making you fear loss when you give in voluntary charity, so that you withhold it, and he enjoins you to indecency — that is, niggardliness and the blocking of almsgiving; but God promises you, in return for your spending, His pardon for your sins and His bounty as provision from Him; and God is Embracing in His bounty. **[Qurṭubī]** notes the connection: the verse joins what precedes, for Satan has an entry into hindering a person from spending in God's way; and he commands indecency, which is sin — and spending in it. And he records the linguistic point that the word for poverty is also read *al-fuqr* with the *fāʾ* vowelled differently, as al-Jawharī noted that *al-fuqr* is a dialect variant of *al-faqr*, like *al-ḍuʿf* and *al-ḍaʿf*. He also notes that in Arabic speech, "promise" when left unqualified means the good, and when qualified by what is promised it may carry either good or evil, like "glad tidings."

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** records from Ibn Abī Ḥātim, from ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Satan has an effect (*lummah*) on the son of Adam, and the angel has an effect. As for Satan's effect, it is a threat of evil and a denial of the truth; as for the angel's effect, it is a promise of good and an affirmation of the truth. Whoever finds the latter, let him know that it is from God, and let him praise God; and whoever finds the other, let him seek refuge from Satan." **[Study Quran]** gives the same ḥadīth and adds al-Rāzī's argument on how the two promises work on the soul: ideally people should give from the best they have, but what begins as a desire to part only with the dregs can lead to a fear of giving any charity at all; this miserliness then infects the rest of the soul, which struggles to keep all that it desires while relinquishing nothing of value; and one's passivity to Satan's promptings then leads to the active commission of other sins, until one gradually ceases doing any good and commits every manner of evil — which is why "commands you to indecency" follows "threatens you with poverty." **[Ṭabarī]** records from Ibn ʿAbbās the neat division of the verse: two things are from God and two from Satan — Satan's "you will be poor, so do not spend your wealth; keep it, for you will need it," alongside his command to indecency; against that, God's promise of forgiveness and of bounty. **[Maʿārif]** turns the verse into practical counsel: when a person is obsessed with the idea that spending in charity will cause him poverty, when he cannot summon the courage to spend even after hearing God's warning, and his mind turns from the divine promise to reliance on Satan's promise, he should be sure that the apprehension is being generated by Satan. He should not say that he has never seen Satan and cannot be taking orders from him; and conversely, when he finds himself thinking that his sins will be forgiven by spending and his wealth will be blessed with increase, he should be sure that this thought has come from God, and be grateful for it.

**Reflection.** **[Saʿdī]** sets the two promises as two callers: having urged them to the beneficial spending, God then forbade them the harmful withholding, and showed them that they stand between two summoners — the caller of the Most Merciful, who calls them to good and promises them good and grace and reward, immediate and deferred, and replacement for what they spend; and the caller of Satan, who urges them to withhold and frightens them that they will become poor if they spend. Whoever answers the caller of the Most Merciful and spends from what God has provided him, let him rejoice in the forgiveness of sins and the attainment of everything sought; and whoever answers the caller of Satan — and Satan only calls his party to be companions of the Blaze — let the servant choose which of the two matters suits him better. And God sealed the verse with "All-Encompassing, Knowing": encompassing in His attributes, abundant in His gifts, knowing who deserves the multiplication among those who act, and knowing who is worthy, so that He grants him success in doing good and leaving the reprehensible. The psychology in **[Study Quran]**'s report of al-Rāzī explains why the verse is placed exactly here, between the command to spend the good and the promise that follows: the enemy does not begin by attacking the deed, but by attacking the giver's picture of his own future — and the cure is to hold the two pictures side by side, the poverty Satan paints and the forgiveness and bounty God promises, and to see which of the two has ever proved true.


## 2:269

*"He grants wisdom to whom He wills; and whosoever is granted wisdom has been granted much good. Yet none remember save the possessors of intellect."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with a general gloss: God grants *iṣābah* — hitting the mark — in speech and action to whom He wills of His servants; and whoever is granted that has been granted much good. Then he sets out the interpretations reported for *al-ḥikmah* in this place: some said it is the Qurʾān and understanding of it — from Ibn ʿAbbās, by ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥah, "knowledge of the Qurʾān: its abrogating and abrogated, its clear and its unclear, its earlier and its later, its lawful and its unlawful, and its parables," and al-Ḥasan said "understanding in the Qurʾān"; Qatādah and Mujāhid said wisdom is understanding of the Qurʾān. Others said it is correctness in speech and action — Mujāhid said "correctness," and again, "He grants His correctness to whom He wills," and again, "the Book; He grants its correctness to whom He wills." And others said it is knowledge of the religion: Ibn Zayd said "reason in religion," and again "wisdom is the intellect"; and Mālik b. Anas, asked what wisdom is, said "knowledge of God's religion and understanding of it and following it," and Ibn al-Qāsim reported from him that wisdom is reflection on God's command and following it, and that it is obedience to God and understanding in religion and acting on it.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** assembles the same field of definitions: al-Suddī said it is prophethood; Ibn ʿAbbās said knowledge of the Qurʾān — its understanding, its abrogating and abrogated, its clear and unclear, its rare words, its earlier and later; Qatādah and Mujāhid said understanding in the Qurʾān; Mujāhid also said correctness in speech and action; Ibn Zayd said it is reason in religion; Mālik gave knowledge of God's religion, understanding of it and following it; al-Rabīʿ b. Anas said it is the fear of God. **[Study Quran]** gives the range and its ordering: wisdom here is interpreted as knowledge of the meaning of the Qurʾān, including the abrogating and the abrogated, the symbolic and the determined (see 3:7), the order of revelation, and the licit and the forbidden — or as the fear of God, in accordance with the saying, "Fear of God is the beginning of wisdom"; and in this context it is sometimes glossed as intelligence (*ʿaql*) or comprehension (*fahm*). Certain theologians see in the verse an allusion to the power of rational demonstration; some interpret the wisdom to mean prophethood, but others dispute this. And it observes that the spirit or the intellect takes its nourishment from wisdom, unlike the desires of the ego, which are satisfied by the indecencies mentioned in the previous verse — and that wisdom as knowledge or understanding differs from right action, though in a sense wisdom is the combination of understanding and the right action based upon it. **[Maʿārif]** reports that in Tafsir *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* all the positions taken by commentators at this point were assembled, and they come to nearly thirty, though at the end it was said that all these positions are close together and there is no contradiction among them, the difference being only one of interpretation. The word *ḥikmah* is the verbal noun of *iḥkām*, which means to complete what is said or done with all its properties and requisites — and this is why in 2:251, where God says He gave David the kingdom and the wisdom, *al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ* explained that the real meaning of *ḥikmah* is to place everything where it belongs, which can only be accomplished ideally through prophethood, and therefore *ḥikmah* there has been interpreted as prophethood. And al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī said in *Mufradāt al-Qurʾān* that when the word *ḥikmah* is used for God it denotes comprehensive knowledge and solid creative excellence of all things, and when attributed to other than the Divine it means the rightly guided knowledge.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** records the Prophetic saying on this bounty, from Aḥmad on the authority of Ibn Masʿūd, that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "There is no envy except in two instances: a person whom God has endowed with wealth and who spends it righteously, and a person whom God has given wisdom, and he judges by it and teaches it to others." **[Study Quran]** gives the ḥadīth in the same sense: "Let there be envy in only two things: a man to whom God has given wealth and who exhausts it in the way of truth, and a man to whom God has given wisdom and who judges by it and teaches it."

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** explains why the verse follows where it does: having mentioned the states of those who spend their wealth, and that God gave them and favored them with the wealth by which they attain the spendings in the paths of good and reach the lofty stations, God now mentions what is better than that — that He gives wisdom to whom He wills of His servants and to those of His creation for whom He intends good. And wisdom is the beneficial sciences, the sound knowledges, the well-directed minds, the sober intellects, and correctness of judgment in speech and action. This is the best of gifts and the most glorious of endowments — hence "and whosoever is granted wisdom has been granted much good" — because he has come out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of guidance, and out of the foolish deviation of speech and action into hitting the mark and soundness; because he has perfected himself with this great good and prepared himself to benefit creation in the greatest way for their religion and their world; and because all affairs are set right only by wisdom, which is putting things in their places, giving matters their proper ranks, advancing where advancing is due and holding back where holding back is due. And he closes: but none remembers this great matter and knows the measure of this immense gift except the possessors of intellect — the people of complete minds and full understanding, who know what benefits and so do it, and know what harms and so leave it.

**Reflection.** The two things Saʿdī places side by side — spending one's wealth and giving one's wisdom — are the two forms the same generosity takes, one with the hand and one with the mind; and the verse elevates the second above the first, since what one spends comes back in reward but what one teaches multiplies in others. The definitions gathered by the commentaries are many but converge: every account of *ḥikmah* comes back to a knowledge that has settled into correct action — knowing the Qurʾān in order to live it, fearing God in order to obey Him, reason that puts things where they belong. And the closing words set the gift's receivers apart: wisdom is offered, but only those with sound hearts will notice what they have been offered — the Sūrah's repeated theme, that the verse's blessing and the reader's perception are two different things, and the second is what makes the first count.


## 2:270

*"And whatever sum you spend, or vow you vow — truly God knows it. And the wrongdoers shall have no helpers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** interprets: whatever expenditure you expend — that is, whatever charity you give — or whatever vow you vow, "vow" meaning what a person makes binding on himself as a free offering in God's obedience and as a means of nearness to Him, whether a charity or a good work — God knows it, that is, all of it lies within God's knowledge, nothing of it escapes Him nor is anything of it, little or much, hidden from Him; rather He counts it against you, O people, so that He may requite all of you for all of it. So whoever's expenditure, charity and vow were seeking God's good pleasure and a confirmation from himself, God will requite him with the multiplication He promised; and whoever's expenditure and charity were for show before people, and his vows for Satan, God will requite him with the punishment and painful torment He threatened. **[Jalālayn]** keeps it brief: whatever expenditure you expend, whether as alms or as a voluntary charity, and whatever vow you make and fulfill, God surely knows it and will requite you for it; and for the evildoers who prevent almsgiving and vows, or expend other than in the way they should, in disobedience to God, there are no helpers. **[Study Quran]** notes that "God knows it" means that He keeps an account of it, and knows what the intention behind the act was, whether great or small — and that the wrongdoers here are understood to be those who give out of hypocrisy.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** notes the structure of the sentence: it is a condition and its answer, and vows were much practiced in the ways of the Arabs, so God mentioned the two kinds — what a person does freely, and what he does after binding himself to it. And the verse carries both promise and threat: whoever's intention was pure is rewarded, and whoever spent in show, or for some other motive that earns him *mann* and *adhā* and the like, is a wrongdoer — his deed goes to nothing and he finds no helper in it. "God knows it" means He counts it, as Mujāhid said. And he notes the grammar: the pronoun is singular although two things were mentioned; al-Naḥḥās said the construction is, "Whatever expenditure you spend, God knows it; or whatever vow you vow, God knows it," and then the text was abbreviated; or the sense is "whatever you spend, God knows it," the pronoun returning to "what," as Sībawayh cited in the poetry. **[Maʿārif]** adds the scope of the two terms: "whatever spending you do" covers all spendings — those in which all related conditions are observed and those in which all or some are not: it may not be in the way of God but in the ways of sin; or the giving may be mixed with hypocrisy; or followed by making a show of the favor before the receiver; or the wealth may not be lawful and good. Similarly, all votive offerings come under the general purview of the vow: it includes the vow of monetary worship, which is why the vow has been introduced along with spending, and may also include the vow of physical worship; it may be absolute or dependent on something else, fulfilled or not. The purpose of saying all this is that God knows all these things and will duly recompense for them — made known so that people are persuaded to observe the limits and conditions and warned against not observing them. And "the wrongdoers" in the text refers to the unjust and the transgressors who do not observe the necessary conditions; to them the clear warning was given.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** draws out what the statement of God's knowledge implies: God informs that whatever the spenders spend, the charitable give, or the vow-makers vow, God knows it; and the import of that informing is requital — God does not let the weight of an atom go to waste with Him, and He knows the intentions, good or bad, from which the acts issued; and the wrongdoers who withhold what God has made obligatory on them, or plunge into what He has forbidden, have no helpers besides Him to aid them and shield them, and the punishments must fall upon them. Then, in the two verses together, he records the further report: charity, if the giver makes it known, is good, but if he conceals it and delivers it to the poor, that is better — for concealing it is yet another kindness to the poor, and it indicates the strength of sincerity; and one of the seven whom God shades in His shade is the one who gives in charity and conceals it so that his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent.

**Reflection.** The verse is the passage's quiet hinge: the Sūrah has been instructing the giver about the manner of his giving — no reminders, no injury, no show, no bad goods — and now it removes the last excuse a giver might contrive, by saying that God knows the act whatever its size and however it is concealed, and knows the intention behind it. And the closing clause answers the giver's fear in another way: the wrongdoers — including the one who gives in show, drawing attention to himself as though he were the source of benefit — will find no helpers when they need them, while the one who gave for God has, in that very act, attached himself to the Helper who needs no reminding of what was given. **[Saʿdī]**'s observation that concealing charity is better "when it is given to the poor" sets the limit of the rule: the aim is the secrecy of the giver, not the suppression of good example — where a public act serves imitation and stirs others to give, the public outweighs the private. In every case, the act is known where it counts; the question the verse leaves with the reader is only whether the giver has forgotten that.


## 2:271

*"If you disclose your charities, that is well; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you. And He will acquit you of some of your evil deeds. And God is Aware of whatsoever you do."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** parses the two clauses: if you make your charities public and give them to those to whom you give, then excellent is the thing; and if you conceal them, not making them public, and give them to the poor in secret, then your concealing them is better for you than making them public — and this concerns voluntary charity, as Qatādah said: "Each is accepted when the intention is truthful, and the secret charity is better." And he relates that it was mentioned to them that charity extinguishes sin as water extinguishes fire. **[Jalālayn]** supplies the qualification: if you proclaim your voluntary almsgivings, that is a fine thing; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is even better for you than making them manifest or giving to the rich. As for the obligatory almsgiving, it is better to make it manifest, so that it serves as an example and so that one is not falsely accused of not giving; and giving it to the poor is obligatory in any case; and "it will absolve you of some of your evil deeds" — read *yukaffir* or *nukaffir*, apocopated as a supplement to the previous clause or with full inflection as the beginning of a new sentence; God is aware of what you do, knowing its inner and outer aspects.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports that the majority of exegetes held this verse to concern voluntary charity, since concealment in it is better than disclosure — and so in the rest of the acts of worship, concealment is better in what is voluntary, because it removes show from them; but not so the obligatory acts. Al-Ḥasan said: making the obligatory purification public is better, and concealing the voluntary is better, because concealment is more indicative that God alone is intended by it. And Ibn ʿAbbās said: God made the secret charity in the voluntary greater than its public form, said to be by seventy-fold, and made the public form of the obligatory charity better than its secret, said to be by twenty-five-fold — and so it is with all obligations and voluntary acts in all things.
