Qurṭubī comments that the like of this cannot be said by way of opinion, but is a matter of transmission; and in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Muslim there is the Prophet's saying, "The best prayer of a person is in his house, except the prescribed one" — since the obligations are not concealed and the voluntary are. **[Maʿārif]** takes the general principle: the verse obviously covers all types of charity, obligatory or supererogatory, and it is preferable to perform them as secretly as possible — secrecy in a charitable act has religious merit, because it is far from the possibility of showing off and more graceful for the receiver, who may feel shy about receiving charity in public; and it is beneficial from a worldly point of view too, because it does not disclose the amount of wealth one owns. But the preferability of secrecy is a matter of principle: there may be situations where it becomes more preferable to do an act of charity openly for external reasons, such as removing an accusation of not paying the obligatory charity, or persuading others to follow the example — and such exceptional cases do not negate the basic principle.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the text from the two *Ṣaḥīḥ*s, from Abū Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "God will give shade to seven on a Day when there is no shade but His: a just ruler; a youth brought up in the worship of God; two persons who love each other only for God's sake, who meet and part in God's cause; a man whose heart is attached to the mosque, so that when he leaves it he remains so until he returns to it; a man who remembers God in private and whose eyes flow with tears; a man whom a woman of rank and beauty invites, and he says, 'I fear God, Lord of the worlds'; and a man who gives a charity and conceals it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." **[Study Quran]** gathers the surrounding tradition: many reports speak to the virtue of giving secretly, often including a variation of the saying, "Let the left hand know not what the right hand is doing"; in an opinion attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, when it comes to obligatory acts such as the institutional alms, performing them openly is twenty-five times better, while voluntary or supererogatory giving is seventy times better when done privately. Open charity, it is reasoned, provides a good example for others, shows the poor that there is recourse among their neighbors, and creates an open bond between people in a community; secret charity is a test of sincerity, since one gives but garners no prestige for one's generosity.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** records the same doctrine in his own words: God informed that the charity which the giver makes known is good, and that if he conceals it and delivers it to the poor, that is better — because concealing it is another kindness to the poor, and because it indicates the strength of sincerity; and one of the seven whom God shades in His shade is he who gives in charity and conceals it so that his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent. And he draws a fine point from the verse's wording: the preferability of concealment applies where the charity is given to the poor; but where the money is spent on a public project of good, the verse contains nothing to indicate a virtue in concealment — rather, the principles of the law here point to weighing the benefit, for sometimes disclosure is better for producing imitation and following, and for stirring souls to good works. Then he reads the expiation: in this verse the charities combine two things — the obtaining of good, which is the abundance of good deeds and reward, and the repelling of evil, both worldly and otherworldly, by the expiation of sins; and God is aware of what you do, so He recompenses each one according to his deed, by His wisdom. **[Maʿārif]** adds the same qualification to the expiation: it does not mean that the expiation of evil deeds is confined to charity made in secret; in fact, charity made in public carries the same benefit — but the mention of expiation comes in context so that even if someone feels a secret charity to be useless in this world, he should not be depressed, because God will forgive his sins, and that is a great gain for him.

**Reflection.** The verse gives the giver two acceptable modes and one preference, and the qualifications scattered through the commentaries keep the preference from hardening into a law: concealment guards sincerity and the poor man's dignity, but disclosure can be required to disprove an accusation or to draw others into giving, so the rule bends to the interest the act serves. And the promise of expiation shows what is really happening in the transaction: the money leaves the hand, and something heavier leaves the record; the charity is not lost to the giver but spent on him, cancelling sin as water puts out fire. The Sūrah has moved through warning and threat, and it now ends the passage on the note that the secret gift, which no one can see and no one will praise, is nonetheless seen and noted where it matters — "God is aware of whatsoever you do."


## 2:272

*"Not upon thee is their guidance, but God guides whom He wills. And whatever good you spend, it is for yourselves — and you spend not save seeking the Face of God. And whatever good you spend shall be repaid to you in full, and you shall not be wronged."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the occasion and the sense: not upon you, O Muhammad, is the guidance of the idolaters to Islam, so that you should withhold voluntary charity from them, nor should you give them from it so that they may enter Islam out of need for it — but God is the One who guides whom He wills of His creation to Islam and grants them success in it; so do not withhold charity from them. He records therefore the reports: from Shuʿbah, that the Prophet ﷺ would not give charity to the idolaters, and then "and you spend not save seeking the Face of God" was revealed, and he gave charity to them; and from Ibn ʿAbbās, by Saʿīd b. Jubayr, that they would not give even a small share to their relatives among the idolaters, and then "not upon you is their guidance, but God guides whom He wills" was revealed. **[Jalālayn]** gives the setting of the Prophetic instruction: when the Prophet was prohibited from giving voluntary alms to idolaters as an incentive for them to embrace Islam, this was revealed — you are not responsible for guiding them, only for conveying the message; but God guides with His guidance whom He wills. And whatever good property you expend is for yourselves, since the reward is for you — for you expend desiring only God's Face — and whatever good you expend, its requital shall be repaid to you in full, and you shall not be wronged, not suffering any diminishment of it.

**Context and rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** states that this speech is connected to the mention of charities, as if to make clear in it the permissibility of giving charity to the idolaters. Saʿīd b. Jubayr related as a *mursal* report from the Prophet ﷺ that the Muslims used to give charity to the poor of the protected peoples, and when the Muslim poor grew numerous the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Do not give charity except to the people of your religion" — and then this verse was revealed, permitting charity to those who are not of the religion of Islam. Al-Naqqāsh related that the Prophet ﷺ was brought charities and a Jew came and said, "Give me," and the Prophet ﷺ said, "You have no share in the charity of the Muslims" — and the Jew went off not far when "Not upon thee is their guidance" was revealed, and the Messenger of God called him and gave him. **[Maʿārif]** draws the ruling precisely: the verse clarifies that a charity given to a non-Muslim also carries a reward in the life to come; and since the basic purpose of a Muslim in giving charity is to get that reward, he should not confine himself to Muslims and avoid the poor non-Muslims in the hope that this will persuade them toward Islam — for a Muslim is not charged with bringing non-Muslims to the right path, and should seek his own benefit, which can also be achieved through giving charity to a non-Muslim. The charity referred to here is the voluntary charity, which may be given to a protected non-Muslim citizen; the obligatory purification is not meant, since it is not permissible to give it to anyone except a Muslim; and no kind of charity may be given to the hostile non-Muslim of a non-Muslim state, while all other types of charities may be given to protected non-Muslims.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Study Quran]** gathers the occasions and the parallel texts: some relate that the Prophet used to give charity to all, but when the impoverished among the Muslim community grew large he restricted charity to Muslims only, at which time this verse was revealed; in another version, a Companion had grandparents who were idolaters and who asked her for charity, and she did not wish to give it to them until she asked the Prophet, at which time the verse was revealed; in yet another, some Companions had relatives among the Jewish tribe of Qurayẓah and would not give them charity unless they became Muslim. It notes that the verse uncouples charity from religious identity, and that a similar message is found in 60:8, "God does not forbid you, with regard to those who did not fight you on account of religion and did not expel you from your homes, from treating them righteously and being just toward them"; and that the Prophet's not being responsible for whether people accept guidance is also related in 28:56, "Surely thou dost not guide whomsoever thou lovest, but God guides whomsoever He wills." And it records the long ḥadīth of the man who gave charity at night and learned the next day that he had given it to an adulterer, then gave again and learned it had gone to a thief, then gave again and learned it had gone to a rich man — and each time the charity was accepted, and it was said to him that perhaps it would keep the adulterer from his vice, inspire the rich man to give, and keep the thief from stealing; and the verse's promise that what is spent "shall be paid to you in full" refers to the reward one receives in the Hereafter for one's good works.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** reads the opening as the Prophetic charge: upon you, O Messenger, is only the conveyance, the urging of people to good and the restraining of them from evil; as for guidance, it is in God's hand. And then the verse informs about the true believers that they do not spend except to seek their Lord's good pleasure and to reckon His reward, because their faith calls them to that — which is a commendation of the believers; and it carries a reminder to them of sincerity; and God repeated His knowledge of their spendings to inform them that the weight of an atom is not lost with Him, and that if it be a good deed He will multiply it and give from Himself a great reward. **[Study Quran]** notes the Qurʾānic refrain behind this: God does not need humanity's good works — "Whosoever works righteousness, it is for his own soul" (41:46) — and the phrase "seeking the Face of God" recurs where the Qurʾān describes those who desire His Face (30:38–39; 76:9).

**Reflection.** The verse quietly redirects the giver's attention away from the effect of his gift on the recipient and back to the giver's own transaction with his Lord: he is not asked to produce a conversion, only to spend for the Face of God — and the reward of that is his own, whether the recipient deserves it or not. The reports gathered by the commentaries show how practical the question was for the first community — relatives among the idolaters, a Jew at the door of the charity distribution, the poor Muslims multiplying while the protected peoples' poor remained — and the verse's answer is not a rule about categories of recipients but a statement about the boundaries of the giver's responsibility: guidance belongs to God, the spending belongs to the giver, and nothing spent for His Face is lost or diminished. The plain sense that a good act's worth lies in the Face it seeks, not in the person it lands on, is the same principle that ran through the passage on the rock and the garden.


## 2:273

*"[Charity is] for the poor who are constrained in the way of God, who cannot travel in the earth; the ignorant one supposes them rich because of their restraint; thou shalt know them by their mark — they do not beg of people importunately. And whatever good you spend, God surely knows it."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the construction first: "for the poor" is a clarification from God of the way and destination of the spending, and the sense is, "Whatever good you spend, you spend it for yourselves — for the poor who are constrained in the way of God." The *lām* of "the poor" returns to the place of the *lām* in "for yourselves," as though He said: whatever charity you give of your wealth is for the poor who are constrained in God's way. And since the speech was interrupted by "it is for yourselves," with the *fāʾ* of the answer inserted, its repetition was dropped at "for the poor," because the sense was already understood — as al-Suddī explained the sequence, the "not upon thee is their guidance" meaning the idolaters. **[Jalālayn]** identifies the poor meant: the predicate of an omitted subject, the charities — those who have confined themselves in preparation for the struggle; and he notes this was revealed concerning the People of the Veranda, some four hundred of the emigrants set apart from the other Muslims for the study of the Qurʾān and to take part in raids; they are unable to journey in the land to engage in commerce and earn their living, since they are fully engaged in the struggle; the ignorant man supposes them, on account of the way they behave, to be rich because of their abstinence — their refraining from asking; but you shall know them by their mark, the signs of their humility and exertion; they do not beg of men and make urgent demands.

**Context.** **[Qurṭubī]** reports that al-Suddī, Mujāhid and others said the poor meant are the poor of the emigrants from Quraysh and others, and that the verse then takes in everyone who enters under the description of the poor for the rest of time; and that the poor of the emigrants were singled out for mention only because there were no others, and they were the People of the Veranda, around four hundred men — who used to come to the Messenger of God ﷺ poor, with no family and no wealth, so a veranda was built for them in the mosque of the Messenger of God ﷺ and they were called the People of the Veranda. Abū Dharr said: I was one of the People of the Veranda, and when evening came we would present ourselves at the door of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and he would assign each man to leave with one of the Companions, and whoever remained among the People of the Veranda would remain with him. **[Study Quran]** explains the vocabulary: the verb "constrained" connotes something that hinders one on a journey or prevents one from setting out; the People of the Veranda were a group of poor and homeless Muslims who stayed in a roofed area connected to the mosque in Madinah and were known for their piety, devotion and asceticism; they were not able to travel the earth either because they were too poor to do so or because they were vulnerable to enemies outside Madinah.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** draws two rulings from the verse. The word "the poor" covers all who cannot engage in other work because of their religious preoccupation; and from "the ignorant one supposes them rich because of their restraint," it follows that a poor man — one who does not own the threshold amount of wealth — who wears expensive dress is not to be taken as need-free because of that; rather he is to be regarded as poor, and paying the obligatory purification to such a person is correct. And from "thou shalt know them by their mark" it follows that it is correct to give rulings based on circumstantial evidence: for instance, if a dead body is found wearing the waist-cord which is a symbol of some religions, and is uncircumcised, it will not be buried in the graveyard of the Muslims. On "they do not beg of people importunately," he notes that on the surface the verse gives the sense that they do not solicit importunately but does not negate soliciting without importunity, as some commentators read it; but in accordance with the consensus of the commentators it means that they simply do not ask at all, since they refrain from asking with complete restraint. **[Study Quran]** adds that, based on certain *aḥādīth*, any who possess a certain amount of wealth — forty dirhams was sometimes mentioned — would be categorized as "importunate" were they to beg; and it gives the ḥadīth: "The indigent person is not the one who wanders about you, whom you feed morsel by morsel; the indigent person is one who restrains himself and does not ask people importunately."

**Stories & occasions.** **[Saʿdī]** states the counsel the verse carries: you should seek out, with your charities, the poor who have confined themselves to God's way and His obedience, who have no desire for earning or no capacity for it, and who restrain themselves — so that the ignorant man, seeing them, thinks them rich. They do not ask people importunately: they do not ask at all, and if they are compelled to ask they do not importune. This class of the poor is the best in whom wealth may be placed, to relieve their need, aid them toward their aim and the path of good, and thank them for the patience and the looking toward the Creator rather than the creation that they have shown. **[Study Quran]** notes that several other verses mention people being known by their mark, including 48:29; 47:30; 55:41; that some interpret the mark as the pallor of hunger or other physical traits signaling their exertions and difficulties; and that many interpret it as the manifestation of the soul in one's physical body, especially the face — with the ḥadīth, "Fear the insight of the believer, for he sees by the light of God." It adds that this spiritual physiognomy is the ability to perceive qualities of the soul through the form of the body, especially the face: so the mark of the truly poor is the manifestation of their humility and self-effacement, perceptible in their bodies while not being of the body.

**Reflection.** The verse paints a poverty that hides itself, and it asks the giver to do the opposite of what the crowd does: not to trust the surface, which reads a modest dignity as sufficiency, but to look for the mark — the humility and the signs of exertion that the eye trained on God can catch. **[Qurṭubī]**'s report of the People of the Veranda gives the picture its human scale: hundreds of men with no wealth and no family, sitting at the Prophet's door each evening while he distributed them as guests among the households of Madinah — the Sūrah's instruction to spend was addressed to a community in which this class was visible and known, and the verse's closing line, "whatever good you spend, God surely knows it," removes the last excuse of the giver who cannot find the deserving among the self-effacing: the One who sees the mark sees the need, and knows exactly where the gift lands.


## 2:274

*"Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly — their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]**'s section on this verse sets out the reward: those who spend their wealth in God's obedience at every time, by night and by day, concealing some of it and making some of it public — their reward is stored with their Lord; and no fear shall come upon them regarding what they face in the Hereafter, nor shall they grieve over what they left behind in this world. He records among the reports the account of a man of Ghāfiq: Abū al-Dardāʾ would look at the horses tethered among the non-Arabian and mixed breeds and say, "The people of these — that is, the horses — are among those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly: they have their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve."

**Context and occasion.** **[Qurṭubī]** records that Ibn ʿAbbās, Abū Dharr, Abū Umāmah, Abū al-Dardāʾ, ʿAbdullāh b. Bishr al-Ghāfiqī and al-Awzāʿī held that the verse was revealed concerning the fodder of horses tethered in the way of God; and he cites Ibn Saʿd in the *Ṭabaqāt*: ʿUrayb reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about the saying, "Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly…" and he said, "They are the people of horses," and by the same chain the Prophet ﷺ said, "The one who spends on horses is like one who stretches out his hand in charity and does not withhold it — and their fodder and their dung are with God on the Day of Resurrection." **[Study Quran]** records the other reading of the verse's reference: beyond its general import, some commentators interpret it as referring to specific people — for example, ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭālib and Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, who are reported to have given a certain sum in the fashion described in the verse, giving one quarter of it by night, one by day, one secretly and one openly. **[Maʿārif]** gives the report from Ibn ʿAsākir in *Rūḥ al-Maʿānī*: Abū Bakr spent forty thousand dīnārs in the way of God, making it ten thousand during the day, ten thousand during the night, ten thousand openly and ten thousand secretly — and some commentators said that this very event concerning Abū Bakr was the background of the revelation of the verse, while other views are also given regarding its occasion.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** draws out the verse's implications: it presents the great reward and excellence of those accustomed to spending in God's way — those who, under all conditions and circumstances, by day and by night, secretly and openly, keep spending in His way in all sorts of ways. By implication it is also stated that there is no time fixed for charities: there is no restriction of night or day; and spending in God's way, secretly and openly, is an act of reward both ways — the condition being that it be done with sincerity and not to earn name and fame. And the excellence of spending secretly is limited to a situation where there is no pressing need to spend openly; where such a need exists, spending openly is certainly better.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** reads the verse as the passage's crowning promise: those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, have their reward with their Lord — God will shade them with His shade on a day when there is no shade but His, and will grant them good things and ward off from them sorrows, fears and hates; and "their reward is with their Lord" means each one of them according to his state, and the specification that it is *with their Lord* indicates the nobility of this state and that it occurs in the greatest place — as in the authentic ḥadīth: "A servant gives in charity a single date from good earnings, and the Compeller receives it with His hand and nurtures it for one of you as one of you nurtures his colt, until it becomes like a great mountain." **[Ibn Kathīr]**, in the same passage, emphasizes the assurance the verse gives the giver: when one spends in charity for God's sake, his reward is with God, and he will not be asked whether the charity unintentionally reached righteous or evil, deserving or undeserving persons — he will be rewarded for his good intention; and God's closing words in the previous verse, "And whatever you spend in good, surely God knows it well," indicate that no charity escapes Him and that He will reward it fully and perfectly on the Day of Resurrection, when it is most desperately needed.

**Reflection.** The verse closes the great charity section of the Sūrah, and it closes it by gathering every category that has been distinguished: the night giver and the day giver, the one who conceals and the one who discloses, the one who funds the horses of the frontier and the one who funds the poor of the Veranda — all of it in one sentence, with one reward. The commentaries' occasions — the cavalry of Madinah, Abū Bakr's forty thousand dīnārs distributed in four ways, ʿAlī's four dirhams — are attempts to attach the verse to a scene, but its language is deliberately broad, and the point of the section is precisely that breadth: the Sūrah spent its last stretch teaching the giver how to give (not with reminders, not for show, not with the dregs of his wealth), and now it removes every condition of time, manner, and visible recipient, leaving only the one condition that God sees — and the reward that is with Him. **[Saʿdī]**'s ḥadīth of the single date, taken in the hand of the Compeller and nurtured like a colt until it becomes a mountain, is the image that seals the passage: what the giver thinks he is losing is exactly what is being grown.


## 2:275

*"Those who devour usury shall not rise except as one rises whom Satan has struck down by his touch. That is because they say, 'Trade is but like usury' — though God has permitted trade and forbidden usury. So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists shall have what is past, and his affair is with God. And whoever returns — those are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** begins with the root: "those who devour usury" means those who practice *irbāʾ*, and *irbāʾ* is the increase upon a thing — one says "so-and-so made an increase upon so-and-so" when he added to him, and the increase is the *ribā*; and a thing "grows" when it increases upon what it was and becomes great, which is why a hillock is called a *rābiyah*, from its increase in height and its rising above the level ground around it, and why one says of a man that he is "in the *rabāwah* of his people," meaning in their loftiness and nobility. So the root of *ribā* is height and increase. Then he takes up the verse's image: they shall not stand — that is, on the Day of Resurrection — except as one stands whom Satan has struck down by the *mass*, meaning madness. And he records the reports: Mujāhid said it concerns the Day of Resurrection, in recompense for devouring usury in this world; Ibn ʿAbbās said they will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with a madness from Satan, and he said they will be raised insane, choking; al-Ḍaḥḥāk said whoever dies while devouring usury will be raised on the Day of Resurrection disoriented, like one whom Satan strikes down by his touch; al-Suddī said it means madness; and Ibn Zayd said this is their likeness on the Day of Resurrection — they will not stand among the people except as one who is choked stands, as if he were choked, as if he were mad. **[Jalālayn]** defines the sin and the argument: those who devour usury — that is, those who seize by way of usury, which is an excess levied in transactions of money or foodstuffs, either on their value or on credit — shall not rise from their graves except as one whom Satan has made prostrate, demented from his touch. And that befalls them because of the fact that they say, "Trade is like usury" in permissibility — a reversed simile used for intensity, the expected order being "usury is like trade" — and God responds to them: God has permitted trade and forbidden usury. Whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists: he shall have his past gains, those made before the prohibition, which cannot be reclaimed from him, and his affair regarding pardon is committed to God; but whoever reverts, treating it as lawful like trade — those are the inhabitants of the Fire, abiding therein.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** opens his long treatment by noting that these verses contain the laws of usury, the permissibility of contracts of sale, and the warning to whoever makes usury lawful and persists in it, and that this comprises thirty-eight questions; and he gives the linguistic key: "devour" means take — the taking being expressed by eating because taking is intended for eating; and *ribā* in the language is increase absolutely: a thing "grows" when it increases, as in the ḥadīth, "By God, no morsel did we take but something grew beneath it," concerning the food over which the Prophet ﷺ prayed for blessing. Then he notes that the law has restricted this absolute sense to some of its instances, applying it at times to unlawful gain, as in God's word about the Jews, "and their taking of usury though they were forbidden it" — not meaning the legal *ribā* in every case. **[Study Quran]** sets out the technical division the term carries in Qurʾān and Ḥadīth: *ribā* means "increase," "gain" or "growth," and it refers to two main types of transactions — growth through deferment (*ribā al-nasīʾah*) and growth through surplus (*ribā al-faḍl*) — and it warns that "usury" is not a strictly synonymous rendering, since not all interest is *ribā* and not all *ribā* is interest. It quotes Mālik in *al-Muwaṭṭāʾ* on the pre-Islamic practice: "Ribā in the pre-Islamic times was that a man would be owed a debt by another for a set term; when the term was due he would say, 'Will you pay it off or give me ribā?' If the man paid, he took it; if not, he increased his debt and lengthened the term for him" — the deferment often leading to a doubling of the principal in a year and then redoubling. Many believe the general prohibitions of the Qurʾān refer to this practice.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the foundational ḥadīth, from the imāms, in the wording of Muslim, from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt — like for like, hand to hand; and whoever adds or asks for more has practiced usury, the taker and the giver in it being alike." And in the ḥadīth of ʿUbādah b. al-Ṣāmit: "When these kinds differ, sell as you wish, provided it is hand to hand" — and Abū Dāwūd recorded from him the fuller wording about gold for gold, coined or uncoined, and wheat for wheat by measure. **[Study Quran]** explains the second type: the ḥadīth "Gold for gold, silver for silver, wheat for wheat, barley for barley, dates for dates, and salt for salt; like for like, hand to hand, in equal amounts; and any increase is ribā" — the surplus being the disparity in amounts between the two objects traded; and it gives the report that Bilāl came to the Prophet with some high-quality dates, and when asked about their source explained that he had traded two volumes of lower-quality dates for one volume of higher quality, and the Prophet said, "This is precisely the forbidden ribā! Do not do this; instead sell the first type of dates and use the proceeds to buy the other." And "hand to hand" was understood to prevent trading, for example, an ounce of gold now for an ounce of gold in the future, since the time factor creates an inequality — the present ounce being worth more because the ability to use it in the meantime is lost. Jurists disagreed over which legal attribute of the six commodities made the rule apply — being measurable, fungible, storable, usable as food, or some combination — and extended the rules by that reasoning. **[Ibn Kathīr]** notes how difficult the subject is: ʿUmar b. al-Khaṭṭāb said, "I wished that the Messenger of God ﷺ had made three matters clearer for us, so that we could refer to his decision: the grandfather, the *kalālah*, and some types of usury" — meaning the transactions where it is not clear whether usury is involved; and he states the principle the law applies to such cases: for anything unlawful, the means that lead to it are also unlawful, since whatever results in the unlawful is unlawful. And he records the ḥadīth agreed upon by the two *Ṣaḥīḥ*s, from al-Nuʿmān b. Bashīr: "The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters; whoever guards against the doubtful protects his religion and his honor, and whoever falls into the doubtful falls into the unlawful, like the shepherd grazing around a sanctuary, soon to graze within it."

**Rulings and reflection.** **[Maʿārif]** sets the passage in its place: from these verses begins the description of the unlawfulness of usury and the injunctions relating to it — an issue important from many angles: on one hand the severe warnings of Qurʾān and Sunnah, and on the other its having become an integral part of the world economy, so that the desired liberation from it seems infested with difficulties. He notes that six verses state the prohibition and set out the related injunctions, and that the first sentence of the first verse points to the sad end of those involved in usury and the disheveled nature of their rising on the Day of Resurrection: the dealer in usury, when he rises from his grave, will rise like the madman driven crazy by some Satan or jinn. The verse's claim, "Trade is but like usury," is the argument of a mind that has reduced the two to their surface resemblance — the transfer of wealth for gain — and the divine answer does not argue the resemblance but dissolves it: God has permitted trade and forbidden usury, and the difference between the two lies not in the form of the transaction but in the justice and risk it embodies, which the Lawgiver has weighed and settled. And the verse's mercy is as striking as its threat: the one who desists after the admonition keeps what is past, and "his affair is with God" — the door is left open for pardon — while the one who returns to it after knowledge has no recourse but the Fire. The doubled punishment, madness of body answering the madness of a soul that traded justice for increase, is the image the Sūrah sets at the head of the passage: the usurer, who in this world walks with the confidence of the clever, will rise stumbling like one possessed — the outward likeness of what his dealings did to the order God placed among His creatures.


## 2:276

*"God effaces usury and causes charities to grow. And God loves not any sinning ingrate."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains: "God effaces usury" means God diminishes usury and takes it away — Ibn ʿAbbās said, "He diminishes it" — and this matches the report from ʿAbdullāh b. Masʿūd, from the Prophet ﷺ: "Usury, though it be abundant, ends in scarcity." And "He causes the charities to grow" means He multiplies their reward, nurturing and growing them for their owner. **[Jalālayn]** states the same pair in one line: God effaces usury, diminishing it and eliminating any blessing in it, but He augments voluntary almsgivings, increasing them and making them grow and multiplying their reward; and God does not love any guilty profligate — the devourer of usury. **[Qurṭubī]** records the Prophetic image of the growth: in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Muslim, "The charity of one of you falls into the hand of God, who nurtures it for him as one of you nurtures his colt or the young of his camel, until it comes on the Day of Resurrection — and the morsel is like Mount Uḥud." And he notes the readings recorded by Ibn al-Zubayr, *yumaḥḥiqu* and *yurabbī*, with the doubled intensive forms, also reported from the Prophet ﷺ. **[Study Quran]** points out that here "causes to grow" is the very verbal form of *ribā*: the God who blights the increase that the usurer claims for himself is the God who generates increase in what the charitable give away.

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** explains how the effacing works: God states that He destroys usury, either by removing this money from those who eat it, or by depriving them of the blessing so that the benefit of their money goes — and because of their usury God will torment them in this life and punish them for it on the Day of Resurrection. He sets beside it the Qurʾānic principle: "Say: Not equal are the evil things and the good things, even though the abundance of evil things may please you" (5:100); and the verse that the wicked are heaped and cast into Hell (8:37); and the word of God, "And whatever you give in gift, desiring increase through the wealth of people, it increases not with God" (30:39) — which shows that the gain sought through people's wealth is precisely the gain that God does not bless. **[Saʿdī]** puts the contrast at the center of the verse: God informed that He effaces the gains of the usurers and causes the charities of those who spend to grow — the opposite of what springs to the minds of many people, that spending decreases wealth and usury increases it. For the source of provision and the obtaining of its fruits is from God, and what is with God is attained only by obeying Him and complying with His command; so the one who defies God by usury is punished with the opposite of his aim — and this is witnessed by experience, and who is more truthful in speech than God? And "God loves not any sinning ingrate": one who has disbelieved God's blessing, denied his Lord's favor and sinned by persisting in his disobedience; and the implied sense of the verse is that God loves the one who is grateful for the favors he has and repentant from the sins and offenses he has committed. **[Qurṭubī]** notes that describing the *kaffār* as *athīm* is intensification, in that the two words differ — and it was said the second word removes the ambiguity of the first, since *kaffār* might apply to the farmer who covers the seed in the earth.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Maʿārif]** gathers the Prophetic warnings that surround this verse: "Abstain from the seven destructive things" — they asked, "O Messenger of God, what are they?" and he said, "To ascribe partners to God, to practice sorcery, to kill unjustly the soul God made inviolable, to consume usury, to consume the property of the orphan, to turn back on the day of battle, and to slander the chaste believing women who are unaware" (al-Bukhārī and Muslim and others). And the dream report from al-Bukhārī: two men came to the Prophet and brought him to a sacred land, and they came upon a river of blood with a man standing in it, and on the bank a man with stones before him; each time the man in the river wanted to come out, the man on the bank threw a stone into his mouth and drove him back — and when asked who he was, he was told, "The consumer of usury." And: "A dirham that a man receives as usury is, in the sight of God, more serious than thirty-three acts of fornication or adultery in Islam" (al-Ṭabarānī). And from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet forbade buying fruit before it is edible and said, "When adultery and usury appear among the people of a town, they have made God's punishment lawful against themselves" (al-Ḥākim). And from Aḥmad: "No people make usury rampant among them but they are seized with famine; and no people make bribery rampant among them but they are seized with terror." And in the report of the night journey: at the seventh heaven the Prophet came upon people whose bellies were like houses, filled with snakes visible from outside them, and Jibrīl said, "These are the consumers of usury."

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** argues that the effacement is confirmed by observation: there are many statements of the experienced and the knowledgeable saying that wealth collected through usury may increase faster and higher, but generally does not survive long enough to run through a man's children and successors — some calamity comes and effaces it all; and Maʿmar said they had heard from their elders that forty years hardly pass over the usury-consumer before a major loss overtakes his wealth. And even if the wealth does not outwardly go to ruin, its benefits, utilities and blessings certainly go — for gold and silver are not desirable or useful in themselves: they cannot remove hunger or thirst, cannot beat the heat or serve as a quilt in winter, cannot be used as clothes or utensils; the only purpose for which a wise person procures them is that they are means to procure what makes man's life pleasant and lets him live in comfort and self-respect, and with the natural wish that his children and relatives enjoy the same. Comparing the two activities then: the wealth of the usury-consumer, no doubt, appears to be increasing — but that increase is akin to the swelling of the human body.

**Reflection.** The verse gives the Sūrah's teaching on wealth its final shape: two ways of making wealth grow are set side by side, the one that takes increase and the one that gives it away, and the divine verdict reverses the human arithmetic — what the usurer piles up is effaced, and what the charitable part with is grown, "nurtured as a man nurtures his colt." The commentaries' practical reports — Maʿmar's forty years, the swelling that mimics health — are attempts to describe in experience what the verse states as law: money that grows by injustice carries no blessing, and money that leaves the hand for God comes back as a mountain. And the closing words name the root of the sin: the usurer is a *kaffār*, an ingrate — for the wealth he trades on was a gift he never thanked anyone for, and the increase he demanded from the needy was a claim on what was never his to guarantee.


## 2:277

*"Truly those who believe and perform righteous deeds and establish the prayer and give the alms — their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall come upon them, nor shall they grieve."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as God's declaration about the believers — those who affirm God and His Messenger and what came to them from their Lord, including the prohibition of usury and its consumption and the rest of the laws of His religion; who perform the righteous deeds God commanded and urged; who establish the prescribed prayer within its limits and discharge it with its practices; and who give the purification made obligatory on their wealth — and this after having previously consumed usury, before the admonition concerning it came from their Lord. For them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall come upon them of what they face in the Hereafter, nor shall they grieve for what they left behind in the world. **[Jalālayn]** gives the same in brief: those who believe and perform righteous deeds and establish the prayer and pay the alms — their wage awaits them with their Lord, and no fear shall befall them, neither shall they grieve.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** explains why prayer and the alms are named again although "righteous deeds" already includes them: it is out of honor for them and to point to their rank, since they are the head of all deeds — the prayer being the head of the acts of the body and the alms the head of the acts of wealth.

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** explains the placement of this verse among the verses on usury: it comes here to show that the greatest cause of avoiding what God has forbidden of usurious earnings is the completion of faith and its obligations — especially establishing the prayer and giving the alms; for the prayer forbids indecency and wrong, and the alms is kindness to creation, and both are the very opposite of dealing in usury, which is injustice to people and harm done to them. **[Ibn Kathīr]** draws the same contrast from the other side: the previous verse's declaration that God does not love any sinning ingrate indicates that God does not love the one who has a disbelieving heart, a sinner in tongue and deed — and there is a connection between the beginning of the passage on usury and its ending, since those who consume usury are not satisfied with the lawful and good resources God has provided them; instead they try to acquire people's money unlawfully by evil methods, which shows their lack of appreciation for God's bounty. Then God praised those who believe in His lordship, obey His commands, thank Him and appreciate Him — those who are kind to His creation, establish the prayer and give the charity due on their wealth — and He informed them of the honor He has prepared for them and that they will be safe from what the others will face. And he records the ḥadīth of the two *Ṣaḥīḥ*s: "Whoever gives in charity what equals a date from honest resources — and God only accepts what is good and pure — God accepts it with His right hand and raises it for its giver as one of you raises his young animal, until it becomes as big as a mountain."

**Rulings.** **[Study Quran]** notes that the alms mentioned here, as in many other places, are obligatory and an integral dimension of Muslim devotional and social life; as a form of institutional charity they are contrasted with their moral opposite, *ribā* — and it reports the Prophet's saying, "The ultimate result for anyone who engages in usury, even if it brings growth, is loss." **[Maʿārif]** notes the Sūrah's general style in the placement: since the verse before this mentioned the punishment of Hell and the disgrace the consumers of usury will face, the merit in the Hereafter of the believing and practicing Muslims — those steadfast in the prayer and the alms — was mentioned alongside, in accordance with the noble Qurʾān's customary pairing.

**Reflection.** The verse is a hinge in the ribā passage, and its function is to show the two roads by their ends: the usurer who takes increase from people's need, and the believer who gives increase to them in the alms and stands before God in prayer. The comparison is exact — the alms is the institutional act of giving, and usury the institutional act of taking by contract, and the Sūrah puts them side by side as the two possible orientations of a life toward others. And its closing formula is the same one given to the spenders earlier in the section: no fear, no grief. The reward with their Lord, and the freedom from the two fears, is where the passage comes to rest: the property of the verse is precisely the security the usurer imagines his interest will buy him, and which the Qurʾān locates instead in the two practices that have no interest and no return in this world but for God.


## 2:278

*"O you who believe, fear God and abandon what remains of usury, if you are believers."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as a call to those who have affirmed God and His Messenger: fear God for yourselves — fear Him by obeying Him in what He has commanded and desisting from what He has forbidden — and leave, that is, give up, the claim to what remains of usury; that is, abandon the demand for whatever remains to you of the increase over the principal sums that were yours before you charged usury on them; "if you are believers" — if you are verifying your faith of word and your assent of tongue by your deeds. **[Jalālayn]** keeps the sense tight: fear God and give up the outstanding usury, if you are believers true to your faith, since it is expected of the believer that he adhere to God's command; and he notes it was revealed when some of the Companions, after the prohibition, wanted to recover the usury owed to them.

**Context and occasion.** **[Ṭabarī]** relates that the verse was revealed about a people who became Muslims while amounts of usury were owed to them by others — they had already collected part of it and part remained; so God pardoned them what they had collected before the revelation of this verse and forbade them to collect what remained. The report: Banū ʿAmr b. ʿUmayr of Thaqīf were demanding their usury, and Banū al-Mughīrah refused to give it in Islam, and the matter was raised to ʿAttāb b. Asīd, who wrote to the Messenger of God ﷺ; and then "O you who believe, fear God and abandon what remains of usury, if you are believers; and if you do not, then take notice of war from God and His Messenger, and if you repent you shall have your principal, and you shall not be wronged" was revealed; and the Messenger of God ﷺ wrote it to ʿAttāb and said, "If they agree, fine; otherwise declare war on them." And ʿIkrimah said: they used to take usury from Banū al-Mughīrah — Masʿūd, ʿAbd Yālīl, Ḥabīb and Rabīʿah, the sons of ʿAmr b. ʿUmayr — and these were the ones who had the usury claims against Banū al-Mughīrah. **[Maʿārif]** tells the story in the same shape: usury was rampant all over Arabia before it was prohibited by revelation; when the verses brought its prohibition, the Muslims, following their Qurʾān-oriented habit, abandoned all their usury dealings — but some people had claims of unpaid usury amounts against others. Two tribes, Banū Thaqīf and Banū Makhzūm, had mutual usury dealings, and people of Thaqīf had claims of unpaid usury against Banū Makhzūm; when Banū Makhzūm became Muslims they considered it impermissible to pay back the usury, while Thaqīf pressed the claim; and since the Makhzūm had their peace agreement, they told the Thaqīf that they had entered Islam and had no intention of spending their Islamic earnings on usury — and the dispute rose in Makkah, after the conquest. **[Ibn Kathīr]** records that Zayd b. Aslam, Ibn Jurayj, Muqātil b. Ḥayyān and al-Suddī said the verse was revealed about Banū ʿAmr b. ʿUmayr of Thaqīf and Banū al-Mughīrah, that when they heard this verse "give up what remains of usury" they all abandoned it — and that the verse serves as a stern threat to those who continue to deal in usury after God revealed this warning.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** extracts the operative sense: after the revelation prohibiting usury, the giving and taking of the amount of usury that remained due against anyone was also prohibited; the earlier-collected usury was pardoned, but the amounts still outstanding could not be claimed. And **[Study Quran]** notes that the debtor remained liable for the original loan, but the verse canceled any additional fees or interest accrued to that loan as a result of deferring it past its original term — so that creditors would not forfeit their wealth and debtors would not be responsible for the increases.

**Reflection.** The verse closes a door that a recently believing community might have kept ajar: the practice was woven through the tribes' relations, and the converts could reasonably have thought that usury contracted before Islam, and still outstanding, might be collected as a matter of what was already owed. The answer leaves no such seam: what was taken before is pardoned, and what remains is to be abandoned — "if you are believers," meaning that this is what the profession of faith, taken seriously, requires of a man's dealings with his own kin and his own pocket. The Sūrah has been teaching that faith is verified by how one handles wealth, and here it puts the test at the sharpest point yet: the believer is asked not merely to give but to forgo, and to hand back a claim that the old world had counted his due.


## 2:279

*"And if you do not, then take notice of war from God and His Messenger. But if you repent, you shall have the principal of your wealth, neither wronging nor wronged."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains "if you do not" — if you do not abandon what remains of usury — then "take notice of war from God and His Messenger." And he sets out the two readings: the majority of the people of Madinah read it with a shortened *alif* and an open *dhāl*, meaning "be on knowledge and notice" — know it and be certain of it, and be on notice from God about it; while others, the majority of the people of Kūfah, read it with an extended *alif* and a kasrah on the *dhāl*, meaning "give notice to others: inform them and tell them that you are at war." Ṭabarī prefers the first reading — know that and be certain of it — and explains why by the case of the one sent against: when a person remains on idolatry that cannot be tolerated, or reverts after Islam, the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to sever and fight, whether the idolaters gave notice of war or not. **[Jalālayn]** reads it simply: if you do not desist, then be informed of war from God and His Messenger against you; and if you repent, you shall have your principal sums — you shall not wrong by taking usury, nor be wronged by having your principal diminished. **[Study Quran]** notes that the second half can also be translated "If you repent, you shall have the principal of your wealth, neither wronging nor being wronged," and records the report from Ibn ʿAbbās: "On the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the one who partook of usury, 'Take up your sword for war!'" — and it notes that some say this means they have made themselves enemies of God and the Messenger, and that usury can be a cause for taking up arms against violators on the part of legitimate authority, forcing them to give up their gains or fighting them if they refuse.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives Ibn ʿAbbās's two sayings: that "take notice of war" means "be sure of a war from God and His Messenger," and that on the Day of Resurrection those who eat usury will be told, "Take up arms for war"; and by ʿAlī b. Abī Ṭalḥah, that whoever kept dealing in usury and did not refrain from it, the Muslim leader should require him to repent, and if he still did not refrain, the leader should cut off his head. And he gives the Prophet's word from the Farewell Pilgrimage, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim from ʿAmr b. al-Aḥwaṣ, in which the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Every usury of the days of ignorance is set aside; your usury is set aside, beginning with the usury of al-ʿAbbās b. ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib; for you is your principal — you shall not wrong and you shall not be wronged." **[Qurṭubī]** gives the same Farewell Pilgrimage text from Abū Dāwūd, on the authority of Sulaymān b. ʿAmr from his father, that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say in the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Every usury of the age of ignorance is set aside; for you is your principal; you shall not wrong and you shall not be wronged." And among the earlier rulings of the passage he records the ḥadīth cursing the parties to the transaction: al-Ṭabarānī and others report the curse upon the consumer of usury, the one who feeds it, its scribe and its witnesses.

**Rulings.** **[Maʿārif]** dwells on the severity: the warning given here is so severe that any other warning of such a kind does not appear anywhere in the Qurʾān in relation to any other sin, no matter how great — except disbelief. And the verse closes with "if you repent, you shall have your principal," which conditions the receipt of the principal on repentance and the resolve to abandon usury in the future: if repentance is not done, receiving the principal is no longer in order. Then he sets out the details of the cases: the person who does not believe that usury can be unlawful, and so does not repent — such a person goes out of the fold of Islam and becomes an apostate, and the ruling on the apostate is that his belongings leave his possession: what he earned while a Muslim goes to his Muslim inheritors, and what he earns after his disbelief is deposited in the public treasury — so if his non-repentance is because he considers usury lawful, he is not entitled to receive even his principal; and if he does not go so far as to consider usury lawful but in practice does not stop dealing in it and stands in confrontation with the Islamic government, he is then a rebel, and his belongings too are confiscated. **[Qurṭubī]** reads the closing words: God returned them, with repentance, to their principals, and said to them, "you shall not wrong" — in taking usury — "and you shall not be wronged" — in having part of your principal withheld so that your wealth is lost; and he notes it may be that "you shall not wrong" refers to the delay of a wealthy debtor, since the delay of the wealthy is wrong, so that the sense is that payment is made along with the dropping of usury — which resembles a settlement (*ṣulḥ*). And he points to the Prophetic precedent: when the Prophet ﷺ indicated to Kaʿb b. Mālik concerning the debt of Ibn Abī Ḥadrad that half of it be dropped, and Kaʿb agreed, the Messenger of God ﷺ said to the other man, "Get up and pay him" — and the scholars took his command to pay as a practice to be followed in settlements.

**Reflection.** The phrase "a war from God and His Messenger" is the harshest expression in the Qurʾān against any economic practice, and the commentaries handle it in two registers: as the interior declaration that the usurer has placed himself in enmity with God — "take up your sword for war," in the report of Ibn ʿAbbās — and as the external authority of the Muslim state to compel the violator, even to the point of arms, per the same report. Both registers underline the same thing: usury is not treated as an ordinary sin to be privately repented of, but as an aggression in the order of society, and the Sūrah answers the aggression with the threat of a counter-aggression. Yet the verse's last words are as gentle as its first: the repentant keeps his principal whole, "neither wronging nor wronged." The balance is exact — no gain from the loan, no loss of the loan — and it defines the Islamic alternative to the usurer's trade: the use of one's wealth by lending it to its owner's need, with no increase claimed, and the reward sought only from God.


## 2:280

*"And if he is in difficulty, then let there be respite until ease; and that you give it as charity is better for you, if you but knew."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the verse as addressed to the creditors at the very gate of the previous command: "and that you give in charity" — that is, that you give your principal sums as charity to this one in difficulty — "is better for you," O people, than that you grant him respite until his ease so that you may collect your principal from him when he is able; "if you but knew" where the merit of the charity lies, and what reward God has made obligatory for the one who drops the debt of his insolvent debtor. And he records the disagreement over the verse's reach: some said its sense is that your giving in charity the principal sums, whether the debtor be rich or poor, is better for you; and Qatādah said of "but if you repent, you shall have the principal of your wealth" that the wealth they were owed was established as their principal when this verse was revealed — as for the profit and the increase, it is not theirs, and they should not take anything of it; and "and that you give in charity is better for you" means giving the principal itself in charity. **[Jalālayn]** gives the command and the option: if the debtor is in difficulty, let him have respite — a postponement — until things are easier (read *maysarah* or *maysurah*, a time of ease); but that you give in charity — the softened form of the verb, the second letter assimilated — to the one in difficulty, by waiving his debt, is better for you, did you but know; if you know that it is better for you, then do it. And he gives the ḥadīth: "Whoever gives respite to one in difficulty or waives his debt, God will place him under His shade on a day when there shall be no shade except God's" — reported by Muslim.

**Context and occasion.** **[Qurṭubī]** opens his treatment with nine questions, and explains the verse's place: when God had judged for the creditors that they receive their principal sums from those who possess wealth, He then judged in the case of the one in difficulty that he be respited until ease. And the occasion: when Thaqīf demanded the wealth they had against Banū al-Mughīrah, the latter complained of difficulty and said they had nothing, and asked for a term until the time of their fruits; and then this verse was revealed: "And if he is in difficulty, then let there be respite." And among the rulings he derives: the verse together with "but if you repent, you shall have the principal of your wealth" shows that the creditor has an established right to demand from the debtor, and that it is permitted to take his wealth without his consent — and it shows that the debtor who holds back from paying the debt when he is able is a wrongdoer, since God says "you shall have the principal of your wealth," making the demand of the principal his right; and since he has the right of demand, it falls on the debtor to pay.

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** states the two obligations the verse lays down: if the one who owes the debt is in difficulty and cannot pay, his creditor must grant him respite to the time of ease; and when he is able, it is obligatory on him — the debtor — to pay in any lawful way; and if the creditor gives him in charity by dropping all or part of the debt, that is better for him. And he notes what makes these ordinances light for a servant to bear — the obligation of the ordinances, the avoidance of usurious dealings, and kindness to the insolvent — namely, the servant's knowledge that he has a day on which he will return to God, who will pay him in full for his deed and will not wrong him the weight of an atom; as God sealed this verse with "And fear a day on which you shall be returned to God; then every soul shall be paid in full what it earned, and they shall not be wronged." **[Maʿārif]** sets the verse against the practice it answers: the general habit of usury-consumers is that once they know their borrower is poor and cannot repay at the appointed time, they add the usury amount to the principal, unleashing a vicious series of usury upon usury and even increasing the rate; but here God, the wisest of lawgivers, gave the law that a genuinely poor borrower who is unable to repay should not be harassed, but should be given respite until he becomes capable — and along with it came the inducement to forgive the loan, which is more beneficial for the lender. And he notes the word used: *ṣadaqah* is used here by the Qurʾān to mean the act of forgiving — the hint being that this forgiveness will become an act of charity in your case and bring forth great merit. And on "if you forgive, that is better for you" he observes how striking the claim is: this action was obviously a total loss in worldly terms, since they were being asked not only to surrender the usury but to lose their own principal, and still the Qurʾān called it "better."

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth of the Resurrection scene: on the Day of Resurrection one of God's servants will be summoned before Him, and He will ask him, "What deeds did you perform for Me in your life?" and he will say, "O Lord, in my life I have not performed a deed for Your sake that equals an atom" — three times; and the third time the servant adds, "O Lord, You granted me wealth and I used to be a merchant; I used to be lenient, giving easy terms to those well-off and giving time to the debtors who faced hard times." And God, Mighty and Majestic, will say, "I am the most worthy of giving easy terms; enter Paradise." Al-Bukhārī, Muslim and Ibn Mājah recorded it from Ḥudhayfah, and Muslim recorded a similar wording from ʿUqbah b. ʿĀmir and Abū Masʿūd al-Badrī. **[Study Quran]** explains the logic of the passage: in the Islamic tradition, loans — as opposed to investments — were ideally charitable in nature, owing to the time factor in giving and taking money, and since other transactions and financial instruments, such as credit sales and leases, were available for non-charitable investment and the raising of funds; hence the invitation here to turn previously usury-laden loans into charity in the case of a debtor in dire financial circumstances.

**Reflection.** The verse completes the reversal the passage has been working: the creditor who in the days of ignorance could double a debt at its maturity is now commanded, when his debtor is poor, to wait — and invited, if he will, to let the debt go altogether and count it as charity. The ḥadīth of the servant in the Resurrection scene shows where such behavior lands: he had no deed the size of an atom to show except that he had been easy with people, and that sufficed to carry him into Paradise. And the word chosen for the act — *ṣadaqah* — reveals the Sūrah's quiet argument: the creditor wanted increase from his money, and the only increase God will accept is the one he gives away; so the loan that cannot be repaid and is forgiven becomes, at the last, the very ribā-free profit the whole passage has been pointing him toward.


## 2:281

*"And fear a day on which you shall be returned to God; then every soul shall be paid in full what it earned, and they shall not be wronged."*

**Meaning.** **[Jalālayn]** gives the plain sense: fear a day on which you shall be brought back to God; then every soul shall be paid in full for what it has earned, and they shall not be wronged, not diminished in the least. **[Maʿārif]** reads it as the section's seal: in the last verse there appear again the subjects of the fear of the Last Day, its accounting, its rewards and its punishment, at which point these verses containing the injunctions of usury end; the verse means: fear a day on which all of you will be assembled before God, when everyone will be fully and equitably recompensed for his deeds, and they will not be wronged. **[Ṭabarī]** notes that the mention of the day comes as the closing motive of the whole passage: after the commands about the principal, the respite, and the charity, God turns them back to the account that will settle every matter that human courts cannot.

**Context.** **[Maʿārif]** records the report of ʿAbdullāh b. ʿAbbās that this verse is the last in the order of its revelation — no other verse was revealed after it — and that thirty-one days later the Holy Prophet ﷺ left this mortal world, while other reports say this happened after only nine days. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the same emphasis on the verse's tone: God advised His servants by reminding them that this life will soon end and all the wealth in it will vanish; and He reminded them that the Hereafter will surely come, when the return to Him will occur, and that He will hold His creation accountable for what they did, rewarding or punishing accordingly; and He warned them against His torment in this closing verse.

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** sets the verse in a wider survey: up to this point the explanations have been restricted to the verses of the Sūrah that concern the injunctions of usury, and he notes — as does **[Maʿārif]** — that dealing with the unlawfulness and prohibition of usury there are in the noble Qurʾān seven verses of this Sūrah, one verse in Sūrat Āl ʿImrān and two verses in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, with yet another verse in Sūrat al-Rūm whose explanation differs, some taking it too in the sense of usury while others hold it has another connotation — so that there are ten verses of the Holy Qurʾān carrying the injunction.

**Reflection.** The verse is the passage's accountant, and its position at the end of the ribā section is the Sūrah's way of saying that the settlement of these transactions will not be left to the parties: every claim and counter-claim about principal and increase, every debt carried by the poor and every delay imposed by the rich, will be brought to a day on which "every soul shall be paid in full what it earned, and they shall not be wronged." The closing formula is exact for this context: the creditor feared that forgiving the debt would wrong him, and the verse replies that no one on that day is wronged — the wealth dropped in this world is repaid in a currency that does not perish. And the report that this was the last verse revealed gives the passage its final shape in the tradition: the community's last word from its Lord, as the commentators record it, was a reminder of the day when the account is closed — delivered, as it were, with the ink still wet on the laws of usury.


## 2:282

*"O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a term appointed, write it down. And let a scribe write it between you with justice, and let not the scribe refuse to write as God has taught him, so let him write, and let him who has incurred the debt dictate; and let him fear God his Lord, and diminish nothing of it. But if he who has incurred the debt is feeble-minded or weak, or unable to dictate, then let his guardian dictate with justice. And call to witness two men from among you; and if there are not two men, then a man and two women such as you approve as witnesses, so that if one of the two errs, the other may remind her. And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called upon. And be not averse to write it down, small or great, with its term; that is more equitable in the sight of God, more upright for testimony, and more likely to keep you from doubt. Unless it be a present trade that you transact among yourselves — then there is no blame upon you if you do not write it. But take witnesses when you buy and sell; and let neither scribe nor witness be harmed. And if you do that, it is surely iniquity in you. And fear God: God teaches you, and God is Knower of all things."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** opens with the scope: "when you contract with one another a debt for an appointed term" — that is, when you sell on credit, or buy on credit, or take up dealings that leave one party owing — the term being a time known and fixed between you. He notes that into this enter the loan (*qarḍ*) and the forward purchase (*salam*), and everything in which a forward sale is permissible with a named term for its sale: it becomes a debt on the seller of what was paid in advance; and it may also take in the sale of what is present and lawfully saleable, at deferred prices. All of this falls under debts deferred to a named term, whenever their terms are known and bounded. **[Jalālayn]** walks the verse clause by clause: when you contract a debt for a stated, known term, write it down as confirmation and security against dispute; let a writer write the contract between you justly, neither increasing nor decreasing the amount or the terms; let no writer refuse to write when requested, since God has taught him to write — just as He gave him the advantage of knowing how, he should not be niggardly with it — so let him write, repeated for emphasis; and let the debtor dictate, for he is the one against whom the acknowledgement is and must be fully aware of the obligation; and let him fear God his Lord when dictating and not diminish anything of the debt. And if the debtor is a squanderer, or weak — not up to dictating through old age or immaturity — or unable to dictate through dumbness or not knowing the language, then let his guardian, the one in charge of his affairs, dictate justly. And summon two witnesses, men, mature, free Muslims; and if two men are not available, then one man and two women, such witnesses as you approve of on account of their probity; the number of women being because of the fact that if one of them errs and forgets the testimony, the other who remembers may remind her — the reminding being the reason for choosing two; and let not the witnesses refuse when they are summoned to bear witness; and be not disdainful or lazy in writing it down, small or great, with its term.

**Context and occasion.** **[Study Quran]** notes that this is the longest single verse in the Qurʾān, and that it is said to have been revealed in connection with agricultural forward sales, but is generally applicable to all agreements, including loans, where payment and delivery do not take place simultaneously. In the forward sale as practiced in Madinah at the time of the Prophet, one could receive payment for agricultural goods to be delivered one, two or three years in the future; and of these transactions the Prophet ﷺ said, "Whosoever contracts a forward sale, let it be for a set amount, a set weight, and a set time." This represents an exception to the general rule that one is prohibited from selling what one does not possess, because the agricultural seller legitimately requires funds to buy seeds and care for the crops before they come in. **[Ṭabarī]** records the same identification through the reports: from Ibn ʿAbbās, "This verse was revealed about the forward sale — in wheat, for a known measure to a known term," and other reports to the same effect; and **[Qurṭubī]** records that Ibn ʿAbbās said the verse was revealed specifically about the forward sale of the people of Madinah, and then took in all deferred dealings by consensus, and that Ibn Khuwayz Mindād said the verse comprises thirty of the rulings. **[Ibn Kathīr]** records from Saʿīd b. al-Musayyib: "I was told that the most recent of the Qurʾān to be [revealed] with the Throne was the verse of debt" — the last to be revealed.

**Language.** **[Qurṭubī]** gives the vocabulary: "with a debt" is emphasis, of the kind of "nor any bird that flies on its wings" and "the angels prostrated, all of them together"; and the reality of *dayn* is an expression for every transaction in which one of the two exchanges is cash and the other is in the obligation, deferred — for *ʿayn*, "cash," with the Arabs is what is present, and *dayn* is what is absent; and he cites the poetry that plays on the two: "He promised us, for our two dirhams, wine and roast meat, ready, not on credit," and "when they kindle fire and stick, that is death in cash, not on credit."

**Rulings.** **[Saʿdī]** gathers the verse's instruction as a whole, noting that it contains the All-Wise's guidance to His servants in their dealings for preserving their rights by the most beneficial means and the reforms than which no clearer or more complete could be devised, comprising many benefits. Among them: the permissibility of dealings with deferred debts, whether the debts of a forward sale or purchases with a deferred price — all of it is permissible, because God informed of it concerning the believers, and what He informs of concerning the believers is among the requirements of faith, and the King, the Judge, has confirmed them in it. Among them: the necessity of naming the term in all debts and in engagements of hire; and if the term is unknown it is not lawful, because it is a risk and a hazard, and so enters under gambling. Among them: the command to write the debts — an obligation when preserving the right is obligatory, as in what a servant holds in guardianship, such as the property of orphans, endowments, agents and trustees; and it approaches obligation when the right is purely the servant's own, becoming stronger or weaker according to the circumstances that require it. In every case writing is among the greatest means by which deferred dealings are preserved, given the abundance of forgetfulness, the occurrence of confusion, and the need to guard against the dishonest who do not fear God. Among them: the command to the scribe to write between the parties with justice, inclining to neither for kinship or the like, nor against either for enmity. Among them: that writing between the parties is among the best of works and an act of kindness to them both, in which their rights are preserved and their obligations discharged — so let the scribe reckon these benefits with God, that he may attain their reward. Among them: the scribe must be one who knows justice and is known for justice; for if he does not know justice he cannot achieve it, and if he is not, in the eyes of the people, just and acceptable, his writing is not considered and the intended purpose, the preservation of rights, is not attained. Among them: the acknowledgement is among the greatest means by which rights are established, since God commanded that the scribe write what the one who owes dictates. Among them: the establishing of guardianship over those incapable — minors, the insane, the squanderer and the like — and that the guardian stands in their place. Among them: that writing is one of God's favors to the servants without which neither their religious nor their worldly affairs stand straight, and that whoever God has taught to write has been favored with a great favor; so part of thanking God for it is that he use his writing to meet the people's needs and not refuse to write — hence, "let not the scribe refuse to write as God has taught him."

**[Maʿārif]** notes the historical point under the command: these are times when writing is the rage and the written word has taken the place of human speech, but consider the days of fourteen hundred years ago, when almost the entire business of the world was conducted verbally and the practice of writing and retaining documents did not exist — it was the Qurʾān that first pointed out its importance. Two principles are stated: that a written document should be prepared when concluding a transaction on a deferred-payment basis, so that it may be availed of in cases of error or refusal; and that the due date must be determined, indefinite deferment not being permissible since it opens the doors of dispute — which is why the jurists stressed that the time limit be free of all ambiguity and specify the exact date and month, so that the time of harvesting, for example, cannot serve as the term, since it varies with the weather. And he notes the rules of witnessing: it is necessary that there be two men, or one man and two women — one man alone, or two women only, not being sufficient witnesses in common dealings; that the witnesses should be trustworthy and just, "from among those you are pleased with"; that refusing to bear witness when required is a sin, since evidence is the way truth is revived and disputes resolved; and that although a hand-to-hand transaction not involving a debt may be left unwritten, two witnesses should be taken as a precaution, in case of later dispute. **[Ṭabarī]** records the disagreement over whether taking witnesses is obligatory in every sale or only recommended: al-Shaʿbī said, "If they wish they may take witnesses, and if they wish they may not"; al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the command to take witnesses applies to what is hand to hand, small or great, while what is on credit is to be written and witnessed; and Ṭabarī himself holds that the testimony on every sale and purchase is a binding right and an obligation, since every command of God is an obligation unless a proof establishes that it is a recommendation and a guidance. **[Maʿārif]** adds the ruling drawn from "let neither scribe nor witness be harmed": the jurists said that the scribe who demands his wages for writing, or the witness who claims his legitimate conveyance allowance, are entitled to it as their right, and that not paying these dues falls under the scope of harming them and is therefore impermissible — the law having made testifying compulsory while also protecting the one who testifies, so that truthful and willing witnesses would remain available.

**The clauses of harm.** **[Ṭabarī]** sets out the readings of "let neither scribe nor witness be harmed": some said it is God's prohibition on the scribe of a document between people who have rights, and on the witness, against harming *the parties* — the scribe writing what was not dictated to him, and the witness testifying to what he was not called to witness. He records from Ṭāwūs: "Let not the scribe be harmed so that he writes what was not dictated to him, nor the witness so that he testifies to what he was not asked to witness"; from al-Ḥasan: "Let not the scribe be harmed" so that he adds something or distorts, "nor a witness" so that he conceals testimony and does not testify except to the truth; and from Qatādah: let a witness fear God in his testimony, diminishing nothing of it and adding nothing false, and let a scribe fear God.
