And the same words carry the second sense, which **[Maʿārif]** brings out: since the scribes and witnesses were commanded not to refuse, they might be given more trouble than necessary, and so the verse forbids harming them — for in protecting one's own rights and benefits one should not disturb the rights of others; "and if you do that, it is surely iniquity in you."

**Reflection.** Āyat al-dayn is the longest verse in the Book, and it is entirely about the ordinary business of a community: debts, terms, scribes, witnesses, guardians, and the writing down of what is small and what is great. Its length is its lesson — the Lawgiver is not too exalted to regulate the loan between two neighbors — and its details are an architecture of justice: the scribe must be just and competent, the debtor acknowledges with his own mouth and fears God while dictating, the guardian speaks for the weak, the witnesses are chosen for probity, and no one may be harmed for serving the truth. The revelation's placement is telling as well: this is the verse the reports call the last sent down, and it comes at the end of the great passage on wealth, after the warnings against usury and the orders to give — as if the Book's final instruction to the community about money were to write it down plainly, name its terms, and keep its records straight, so that the mercy of lending without increase could rest on a foundation of exact documentation. And the verse closes the way the whole section does, with the two names that keep the ledger honest: fear God, God teaches you, and God is Knower of all things — the record that no scribe writes and no witness keeps, but which settles what all the others dispute.


## 2:283

*"And if you are on a journey and find no scribe, then pledges taken in hand. And if one of you entrusts the other, then let him who has been entrusted deliver his trust, and let him fear God his Lord. And conceal not the testimony; and whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful. And God knows whatsoever you do."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** gives the readings and the sense: the readers of the cities all read "and find no scribe" — one who writes for you the document of the debt you have contracted for a named term — while a group of the early readers read it "and find no writing," meaning that you have no way to write the document of the debt, whether because writing materials are lacking or because, even with pen and paper, no scribe is available. Ibn ʿAbbās said: even if they find a scribe but find neither paper nor ink nor pen; Mujāhid read it "and find no ink," and said that it is then that pledges taken in hand apply — and he said the pledge is not [required] except on a journey; and Abū al-ʿĀliyah noted that ink might be found and paper not. Ṭabarī holds that the unalterable reading is "find no scribe." And the sense: if you who are contracting debts are on a journey where you find no scribe and have no way to write the document of the debt that you contracted for a term named between you — which I commanded you to write and witness — then take pledges for your debts by taking possession of them from the debtor, so that they may be security for you for your wealth. Then "if one of you entrusts the other, then let him who has been entrusted deliver his trust": when the creditor trusts the debtor and does not demand a pledge, the debtor must deliver what was entrusted to him; and "let him fear God his Lord" — the debtor; and "conceal not the testimony," whoever holds it, for whoever conceals it "his heart is sinful," and God knows what you do. **[Jalālayn]** gives the same in brief: if you are on a journey and contract a debt and find no writer, then a pledge in hand as security for you; the Sunna clarifies the permissibility of making pledges even in towns where writers may be present, but the stipulation is made in the event of travel because in that case the guarantee is more important; and God's reference to the pledge's being "in hand" is a condition for the validity of the pledge and for its satisfying the pledgee or his representative. And if one of you trusts the other over the debt and does not require a pledge, let him who is trusted deliver his trust; and let him fear God when delivering it; and do not conceal the testimony if you are summoned to give it, for whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful — the heart being mentioned because it is the locus of the testimony, and because if it sins there, other sins follow; and God knows what you do, nothing of which is hidden from Him.

**Rulings.** **[Qurṭubī]** explains the verse's placement: after God urged witnessing and writing for the sake of preserving wealth and obligations, He followed it with the mention of the excuses that prevent writing, and appointed the pledge in their place — and He singled out from the states of excuse the journey, which was the most common of excuses, especially in that time with the abundance of raiding; but every excuse enters by the meaning, for there are times when a scribe is unavailable even in residence, such as at the time of people's abundant business and at night; and also fear for the ruin of the debtor's obligation is an excuse that makes demanding a pledge proper. And he notes the Prophetic practice: the Prophet ﷺ pledged his coat of mail with a Jew who had asked him for a loan of barley. **[Ibn Kathīr]** gives the ḥadīth from the two *Ṣaḥīḥ*s: Anas said that the Messenger of God ﷺ died while his shield was pledged with a Jew in return for thirty *wasq* of barley, which he had bought on credit as provisions for his household — and in another narration, the Jew was among the Jews of Madinah. And he records the ruling that Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī said, with a sound chain: "This verse abrogated what came before it" — that is, what required the recording of the transaction and the presence of witnesses; and al-Shaʿbī said, "If you trust each other, there is no harm if you do not write the loan or have witnesses present." **[Saʿdī]** gathers the benefits of the closing clauses: from the pledge it follows that if the pledger and the pledgee dispute the amount of the debt for which the pledge was given, the word is that of the pledgee, the holder of the right, because God made the pledge a security for it — and had his word not been accepted, that security would be unattainable in the absence of writing and witnesses; and it follows that dealing without a document and without witnesses is permitted, on the strength of "if one of you entrusts the other" — but that in this case there is need of piety and fear of God, otherwise the holder of the right is at risk, and it is for this that God commanded the one who owes the right to fear God and deliver his trust. And he notes the weight of the trust: the one who has been trusted in a transaction has done a great kindness and has been satisfied with the other's religion and honesty, so the obligation to discharge the trust is confirmed from two directions — discharging God's right and complying with His command, and fulfilling the right of the one who trusted him and relied on him. And on the testimony: concealing it is forbidden, and the one who conceals has sinned in his heart, which is the king of the limbs — since concealment is like testifying falsely, and in it rights are lost, dealings corrupted, and sin multiplied against him and against the one who holds the right.

**Reflection.** The verse is the Sūrah's concession to reality, and its ordering of the three safeguards is instructive: the document is the first resort, the pledge the substitute on the journey, and trust the last remainder when neither is at hand. In each case the burden shifts from the machinery of proof to the interior of the person — the debtor is told to fear God when he dictates, the trustee to fear God when he delivers, and the witness not to conceal what he knows — until the passage ends with the gaze that needs no document at all: "God knows whatsoever you do." And the report that the Prophet ﷺ died with his shield pledged to a Jew for barley gives the law its human picture: the one who revealed these verses was himself, at his death, a debtor within the system he had laid down — which is perhaps the strongest of the verse's teachings about the dignity of plain dealing, since no one is exempted, not even the Messenger, from naming the term, writing it down, and leaving behind a record that can be settled.


## 2:284

*"Unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth. And whether you disclose what is in your souls or hide it, God will bring you to account for it; then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. And God is Powerful over all things."*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** explains the opening as the ground of the warning: unto God belongs the dominion of all that is in the heavens and the earth, small and great, and to Him belongs the disposing of all of it; in His hand is its turning and changing, and nothing of it is hidden from Him, because He is its Disposer, its Owner, its Governor. And he explains the warning's first reference: what is meant is the witnesses' concealment of testimony — "do not conceal the testimony, O witnesses, for whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful, and concealment will not be hidden from Me, since I know all things, and in My hand is the turning and owning of every thing in the heavens and the earth; I know the hidden of it and the open. So fear My punishment for concealing testimony." And he records the reports to that effect: from Ibn ʿAbbās, by Miqsam, that the verse means testimony; from ʿIkrimah, "It is the testimony when you conceal it"; from al-Shaʿbī the same; and from Ibn ʿAbbās, "It was revealed about concealing testimony and establishing it." **[Jalālayn]** gives the general reading with its grammar: whether you disclose manifest what is in your hearts or hide it of evil and resolve for it, God shall take you to account for it, informing you of it on the Day of Resurrection; then He will forgive whom He wills and chastise whom He wills — the two verbs read apocopated as answers to the condition, or with full inflection as the beginning of a new clause. **[Saʿdī]** gives the general sense as well: God informs of the universality of His dominion over the people of heaven and earth and of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of what the servants disclose and what they hide in their souls, and that He will bring them to account for it: "then He forgives whom He wills" — the one who turns back to his Lord and repents — "and punishes whom He wills" — the one who persists in disobedience in his inward and his outward.

**The Companions' distress, and the abrogation.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** relates that when this verse was revealed it was hard on the Companions, since out of their strong faith and conviction they feared that such reckoning would diminish their good deeds; and he records from Aḥmad, on the authority of Abū Hurayrah, that when "unto God belongs whatsoever is in the heavens and whatsoever is on the earth; and whether you disclose what is in yourselves or conceal it, God will call you to account for it" was revealed to the Messenger of God ﷺ, it came hard upon the Companions; they came to the Prophet ﷺ and sat down, and said, "O Messenger of God, we have been given a verse we cannot bear: we have been commanded prayer, fasting, striving and charity, and we bore that — but this verse was revealed to you and we cannot bear it." The Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Do you want to say as the People of the Two Scriptures before you said, 'We hear and we disobey'? Rather say, 'We hear and we obey; we seek Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the return.'" And when the people accepted this and their tongues recited it, God sent down afterwards, "The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers; each one believes in God, His angels, His books and His messengers — we make no distinction between any of His messengers — and they say: We hear and we obey; we seek Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the return" (2:285). And when they did that, God abrogated the verse and sent down, "God burdens not a soul beyond its scope; for it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has acquired. Our Lord, take us not to task if we forget or err" (2:286). **[Qurṭubī]** sets out the five positions reported on the verse, the first of them being this: that it is abrogated — said by Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, ʿĀʾishah, Abū Hurayrah, al-Shaʿbī, ʿAṭāʾ, Muḥammad b. Sīrīn and a body of the Companions and Successors — and that this obligation remained for about a year until God sent relief with "God burdens not a soul except to its capacity." And he records in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Muslim, from Ibn ʿAbbās: when "whether you disclose what is in yourselves or hide it, God will bring you to account for it" was revealed, something entered their hearts concerning it that had not entered them from anything; so the Prophet ﷺ said, "Say: we hear and we obey and we submit," and God cast faith into their hearts, and then God revealed, "God burdens not a soul except to its capacity; for it is what it has earned and against it is what it has acquired. Our Lord, take us not to task if we forget or err."

**Belief.** **[Saʿdī]** resolves the apparent conflict with the *aḥādīth* of forgiveness for what a servant's soul whispers to him so long as he does not act or speak: those are the passing thoughts the souls converse with, which a servant does not settle on or resolve upon; whereas the verse concerns the settled resolutions and the fixed attributes of the souls — the attributes of good and the attributes of evil; hence "what is in your souls," meaning what has settled and become firm there of resolutions and traits. And he closes the verse on the divine power: God informed that He is powerful over all things, and part of the perfection of His power is the accounting of the creation and the delivery of what they deserve of reward and punishment. **[Maʿārif]** records the same reconciliation and notes that the verse, in its general sense, covers all articles of faith, modes of worship and mutual dealings — as Ibn ʿAbbās said in his well-known commentary — and that it means God will make all His creatures give an account of all their deeds, including deeds actually done and those they determined to do but kept hidden in the heart and never carried out; and he cites the report of Ibn ʿUmar in al-Bukhārī and Muslim: the believer will be drawn near his most exalted Lord, and God will make him recall his sins one by one, and the believer will confess; and God will say, "I concealed your sins in the life of the world and never allowed them to be known to others; today I forgive them" — while the sins of the disbelievers and hypocrites will be announced before everybody. And from Qurṭubī he gives the scene of the Day: hidden things will be laid out in the open, and God will say that His angels wrote only what was visible on the outside, while He knew what the angels did not know and did not write — "now I tell you all about it; I shall forgive anyone I will and punish anyone I will."

**Reflection.** The verse draws the Sūrah's law of dealings down to its foundation: the transactions of the last two verses — the documents, pledges, witnesses, and trusts — rest on the fact that what is hidden in the heart is also seen, and that concealment is itself a deed. The community's reaction is the measure of the verse's weight: the Companions who had borne prayer, fasting, striving and charity found themselves unable to bear the thought that their interior life was being audited, and their distress brought the Sūrah's next words — faith and the burden that fits. Between the two verses stands the Sūrah's teaching on intention: the resolve that a person settles upon and would carry out is his deed before God, and it becomes outward conduct in the world of records and witnesses; and the two ways out of the audit are named here already, forgiveness for the one who turns and punishment for the one who persists — so that the last word of the verse, "God is Powerful over all things," is not only the threat of the account but the promise that the power to settle it lies with the One who forgives whom He wills.


## 2:285

*"The Messenger believes in what was sent down to him from his Lord, and so do the believers. Each one believes in God and His angels and His books and His messengers — we make no distinction between any of His messengers. And they say, 'We hear and we obey. Thy forgiveness, our Lord, and unto Thee is the journey's end.'"*

**Meaning.** **[Ṭabarī]** reads the opening as confirmation: the Messenger — that is, the Messenger of God ﷺ — affirmed and acknowledged what was revealed to him from his Lord: the Book and what it contains of lawful and unlawful, promise and warning, command and prohibition, and the rest of the meanings it gathers. And it was mentioned that when this verse came down upon the Messenger of God ﷺ he said, "And it is fitting that he should believe." "And the believers" is joined to him: each one — the tanwīn of *kullun* standing in place of the annexed noun, "each one of them" — believes in God and His angels and His books and His messengers; "we make no distinction between any of His messengers," as the Jews and Christians did when they believed in some and disbelieved in others; and they say, "We hear what we have been commanded to hear, and we accept and obey; we ask You Your forgiveness, our Lord; to You is the homecoming" — that is, the return at the Resurrection. **[Jalālayn]** notes the occasion of the verse: when the previous verse was revealed, the believers complained of evil whisperings and it grieved them that they should be taken to account according to the principle expressed in it, and so the following was revealed. **[Ṭabarī]** spells out the same sequence: it was said that this verse came down after "whether you disclose what is in yourselves or hide it, God will bring you to account for it," because the believers among the Companions of the Messenger of God found it hard that God should threaten to call them to account for what their souls concealed; so they complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said to them, "Perhaps you would say, 'We hear and disobey,' as the People of the Book before you said" — and then this verse came down.

**Belief.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** unfolds the content of the faith the verse ascribes: each of the believers believes that God is the One and Only and the Sustainer, there is no deity worthy of worship except Him and no Lord except Him; and the believers also believe in all God's prophets and messengers, in the books revealed from heaven to the messengers and prophets, who are indeed the servants of God; and further, they do not differentiate between any of the prophets — believing in some and rejecting others — but rather, to the believers, all God's prophets and messengers are truthful, righteous, and each was guided to the path of righteousness, even when some of them brought what abrogates the law of some others by God's leave; and later the law of Muhammad, the final prophet and messenger from God, abrogated the laws of the prophets before him, so that the Last Hour will commence with the law of Muhammad as the only valid law, while a group of his community will always remain on the path of truth, apparent and dominant. And on "we hear and we obey": we heard Your statement, O our Lord, comprehended it, implemented it, and adhered to its implications. **[Saʿdī]** draws out the Sūrah's symmetry: God commanded at the beginning of this Sūrah that people believe in all its fundamentals — "Say: We believe in God and what was sent down to us" (2:136) — and He informs here at its close that the Messenger, and those with him of the believers, believed in these great fundamentals and in all the messengers and all the books, and did not do the deed of those who believe in some and disbelieve in others, as the case of the deviant among the followers of deviant religions. And he notes the honor in the verse's construction: in joining the believers to the Messenger ﷺ and informing about them all with a single statement there is great honor for the believers; and in it is that the Messenger ﷺ shares with the community in the address of the law and in its complete discharge, and that he surpassed the believers — indeed surpassed all the messengers — in discharging faith and its obligations. And "they said: we hear and we obey" is an all-inclusive commitment from the believers to all that the Prophet ﷺ brought of the Book and the Sunnah, heard with the hearing of acceptance, submission and compliance; and its import is their supplication to God for help in discharging it, and their asking Him to forgive them for what they fall short of in obligations and what they commit of prohibitions.

**Ḥadīth & āthār.** **[Ibn Kathīr]** records the virtues reported for these two verses: al-Bukhārī's report from Abū Masʿūd that the Messenger of God ﷺ said, "Whoever recites the last two verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah at night, they will suffice him" — recorded by the six books with similar wording and by Aḥmad; and Muslim's report from Ibn Masʿūd: when the Messenger of God ﷺ went on the night journey he ascended to the lote-tree of the furthest limit, where what ascends from the earth ends and what descends from above ends, and "when that covered the lote-tree which did cover it" (53:16) — a mat of gold — and the Messenger of God ﷺ was given three things: the five prayers, the last verses of Sūrat al-Baqarah, and forgiveness for whoever of his community does not associate anything with God, so long as he does not commit the major sins. And he gives the report that the Prophet said: "I have been given the two verses that seal Sūrat al-Baqarah from a treasure beneath the Throne; you will not read a letter of them but you will be granted its benefit." **[Maʿārif]** gathers the reports of the verses' merit: as narrated by Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet ﷺ said that God sent forth these two verses from the treasures of Paradise, and that the Most Merciful had written them with His own hand two thousand years before the creation of all things and beings; and one who is able to recite them after the ʿIshāʾ prayer, they will stand for him in place of the night vigil. And he notes: as it appears in al-Ḥākim's *Mustadrak* and in al-Bayhaqī, the Prophet ﷺ said that God concluded Sūrat al-Baqarah with these two verses, given to him from the special treasure that lies under the Throne — therefore make special effort to learn them, and teach your women and children how to recite them; and this is why ʿUmar and ʿAlī said that they thought anybody with sense would never go to sleep without having recited these two verses.

**Reflection.** The verse answers the anxiety of 2:284 not by withdrawing the account but by supplying the community with the words with which to face it: faith enumerated and accepted without reservation, and the submission that says "we hear and we obey" before it understands every consequence. **[Maʿārif]** captures the Prophet's method in that moment: although he knew the intended meaning of the previous verse, in view of the generality of its words he did not elect to say anything on his own, but waited for revelation and instructed the Companions to obey whatever God ordains — easy or difficult. The community's freedom from the anxiety thus lay not in a lighter command but in a fuller surrender, and the verse records the surrender as the believers' own speech: hearing, obedience, a request for forgiveness, and the acknowledgment that the journey ends with God. That is the posture in which the Sūrah's last two verses teach the community to close: not with the confidence of the litigant who knows his rights, but with the words of servants who have accepted everything and ask for pardon for what remains.
